More broadly, the chatbot creates value by supporting more user-centred access to social-security services and by improving the efficiency and reach of public information delivery.

title: Refugees - Assigning asylum seekers
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: This use case was designed to improve how asylum seekers are assigned to Swiss cantons by replacing purely random allocation with a method intended to increase their chances of labour-market integration. Under the traditional system, individuals were distributed without systematically considering where their profile might best fit local conditions, despite the long-term importance of employment for integration outcomes. The use case therefore involved the Swiss State Secretariat for Migration, canton-level placement officials and policy researchers, with the objective of making placement decisions more effective while still respecting operational constraints such as the limited capacity available in each canton. The implementation used an algorithm developed by the Immigration Policy Lab, together with an affiliated researcher from Dartmouth College, to recommend canton assignments based on the expected likelihood of future employment. At a conceptual level, the system matched individual profiles to cantonal conditions, subject to practical constraints, while preserving human oversight because placement officials retained the final decision in each case. The pilot included 2,000 people, with half assigned using the algorithm’s guidance and half allocated randomly, and outcomes were to be tracked over several years by comparing employment rates between the two groups. The expected impact was improved integration prospects, better use of placement capacity and a more evidence-based approach to allocation. More broadly, the use case supports stronger public-value outcomes by linking operational decisions to long-term social and economic integration results.

title: DVSA MOT - Intelligent, data-driven approach to better target Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) resources
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) needed a more effective way to prioritise inspections across a very large MOT testing ecosystem, covering 23,000 garages and 66,000 testers, at a time when examiner capacity was limited and manual targeting could not easily keep pace with the volume and complexity of testing behaviour. The use case focused on helping enforcement and compliance teams identify higher-risk testing patterns more consistently, even in the absence of labelled data, so that scarce inspection resources could be directed where they were most likely to have the greatest regulatory impact. Its objective was to improve oversight of MOT testing standards, support more efficient examiner preparation and strengthen road-safety and environmental outcomes by targeting non-compliant behaviour more accurately. The implementation used clustering techniques to group garages according to testing behaviour and combined the resulting patterns with historical disciplinary records to generate risk scores. These scores were refreshed every three months, creating a balance between stability and timeliness in inspection planning. At a conceptual level, the solution integrated behavioural analysis and historical compliance data into DVSA’s operational decision-making processes. The impact included a 50% reduction in examiner preparation time and more targeted enforcement activity. In business and public-value terms, the approach improved scalability, increased regulatory efficiency and helped uphold MOT standards, contributing to safer and more environmentally compliant vehicles on the road.

title: HART - Assessment risk tool, predictive policing based on person data
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Harm Assessment Risk Tool (HART) was introduced to support police decision-making by providing a structured assessment of an individual’s likelihood of future harm-related offending. In a policing context where officers must often make rapid judgements about custody, diversion and case handling, the challenge was to use available information more consistently when distinguishing between low-, medium- and high-risk individuals. The use case involved Durham Constabulary and operational policing stakeholders, with the objective of improving risk assessment by supplementing professional judgement with a more systematic analysis of relevant personal and offending-history data. It addressed the need for more consistent triage in early-stage criminal justice decisions, particularly in a period when predictive policing applications were beginning to emerge in practice. The implementation used algorithmic classification techniques applied to variables such as past offending history, age, postcode and other background characteristics in order to produce a three-level risk categorisation. At a conceptual level, the system transformed person-level data into a structured risk score that could be incorporated into policing workflows as a decision-support input. The impact was a more standardised approach to assessing risk and a clearer basis for prioritising interventions and case handling. More broadly, the use case marked one of the earliest reported deployments of predictive policing in the UK, demonstrating both the operational potential and the governance sensitivity of data-driven risk assessment in policing.

title: Amelia - Chatbot helping local residents find city services
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Local residents often struggle to identify which city service they need, where to find it and how to begin an interaction with the relevant department, particularly when public-service structures are complex and spread across multiple channels. This creates frustration for citizens and unnecessary pressure on contact centres and service teams handling routine enquiries. Amelia was introduced to address this access problem by helping residents navigate city services more easily and obtain answers more quickly. The stakeholders include local residents, municipal service teams and customer-support functions, with the objective of simplifying access to public services, improving the user experience and reducing the friction involved in finding the right information or pathway. The solution is implemented through a conversational digital assistant that combines natural-language processing, machine-learning techniques and service-knowledge retrieval. At a conceptual level, the system interprets user questions in everyday language, identifies the relevant intent and matches the query to appropriate city-service information or next steps. This allows residents to interact in a more intuitive way than through static web navigation or complex service menus. The expected impact is faster access to city services, improved satisfaction among residents and lower pressure on frontline support channels for routine issues. More broadly, Amelia creates value by supporting more responsive local-government communication, enabling scalable first-line assistance and improving how citizens connect with municipal services.

title: Babylon - Health interactive symptom checker
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Babylon’s interactive symptom checker was developed to help people obtain timely, structured health information when they were trying to understand possible symptoms and decide what to do next. Many users struggle to interpret symptoms accurately on their own, while traditional health-information channels can be fragmented, overly generic or difficult to navigate under stress. The use case therefore focused on improving access to informed, up-to-date medical guidance in a format that could respond dynamically to the user’s answers. The stakeholders included patients and members of the public seeking early health advice, with the objective of making symptom assessment more accessible, more personalised and more useful than a simple static database search. The solution was implemented as an interactive question-and-answer system designed by doctors and scientists and supported by deep-learning methods. At a conceptual level, the tool combined structured symptom questioning with analysis of known symptoms and risk factors to assess the user’s condition and return relevant medical information. Rather than functioning as a searchable repository alone, it adapted the questioning flow based on earlier responses and used this evolving input to refine the guidance provided. The expected impact was quicker access to structured health information, improved user understanding of possible conditions and a more engaging symptom-assessment experience. More broadly, Babylon created value by offering scalable digital triage support, improving convenience for users and demonstrating how interactive health tools could extend access to medical guidance outside traditional clinical settings.

title: TravelBot - Chatbot for travel information
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Transport for London launched TravelBot to address a common customer-service problem in urban transport: passengers often need immediate answers about bus arrivals, service disruptions and route information, yet traditional service channels can be slower, less convenient or harder to access during travel. The use case was designed to improve how customers obtain real-time travel information through familiar digital platforms, while also making it easier to escalate to a human agent when necessary. The stakeholders included TfL customers, customer-service teams and transport-information providers, with the objective of improving convenience, reducing friction in journey planning and making service information more responsive to passenger needs. The solution was implemented as a social-media chatbot on Messenger, using conversational processing to interact with customers and provide travel-related information instantly. At a conceptual level, the system linked user queries to live transport data so that it could report when a bus was due, provide service updates and share Tube maps, while also offering a handover route to customer-service agents for more complex requests. This created a blended model combining automated assistance with human support where needed. The expected impact was faster access to travel information, easier handling of routine customer queries and a more convenient user experience. More broadly, TravelBot created value by modernising transport communication, improving service accessibility and providing a scalable digital channel for real-time passenger support.

title: EHPS - Early help profiling system to identify children and families considered vulnerable
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Hackney Council introduced the Early Help Profiling System to support earlier intervention for children and families considered vulnerable, in a context where public services were under pressure to identify risk sooner and target limited support resources more effectively. The system was intended to help social workers prioritise households that might require attention by drawing on patterns across education, housing and economic records. Each month, practitioners received a shortlist of 20 families assessed as high risk, with the objective of enabling preventive action before harm escalated. The solution was implemented by combining administrative datasets such as school attendance, housing information and financial records to generate risk profiles and ranked recommendations for frontline teams. At a conceptual level, the system used predictive modelling and cross-dataset analysis to flag cases for further human review rather than making decisions automatically. It was reported to be more than 80% accurate and projected to save around €1 million annually, suggesting potential gains in targeting and efficiency. However, the initiative attracted strong criticism over secrecy, commercial control of data and its perceived relationship to austerity-era service pressures. In the end, Hackney Council discontinued the system after it failed to deliver the expected benefits, making it a notable example of the gap that can emerge between technical promise, public trust and operational value.

title: Automatic posting of invoices - Robot to propose the correct posting
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Norwegian Government Agency for Financial Management
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Customers of the Norwegian Government Agency for Financial Management spend significant time deciding how incoming invoices should be posted correctly, and uncertainty in this process can lead to late payment, interest charges and unnecessary administrative cost. The operational challenge is especially acute where invoice volumes are high and staff must interpret coding requirements repeatedly under time pressure. This use case was introduced to improve efficiency and reduce error in financial administration by supporting more accurate posting decisions from the outset. The stakeholders include DFØ, its customer organisations and accounting staff responsible for invoice handling, with the objective of reducing manual effort, lowering the risk of late payments and improving the reliability of invoice processing. The solution is implemented through a tested accounting robot that proposes the correct posting for incoming invoices. At a conceptual level, the model is trained on historical accounting data and then combines those learned patterns with information from the actual invoice to generate a posting prediction. This allows the system to function as decision support within existing accounting workflows, helping staff resolve uncertainty more quickly and consistently. The expected impact is faster invoice handling, fewer posting errors and reduced risk of additional costs from interest and charges. More broadly, the use case creates value by improving operational efficiency in financial management, increasing consistency in accounting processes and supporting more scalable processing of incoming invoices across public-sector organisations.

title: Misty II - Robot for elderly people
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: This use case was designed to explore whether a social robot could improve the daily lives of older people living alone by providing practical support, companionship and routine assistance in the home. The pilot involved twenty older residents already supported by the City Council’s Area for Social Rights and was launched in the context of a broader challenge focused on improving quality of life for senior citizens through technology. The operational problem was social isolation and the difficulty of maintaining regular reminders, wellbeing monitoring and day-to-day support for people who may be vulnerable but still living independently. The objective was therefore to assess whether a domestic assistive solution could reduce loneliness, support adherence to medication and appointments, and contribute to safer and more confident independent living. The implementation used the Misty II social robot as an in-home interaction platform, capable of providing reminders, supporting simple monitoring functions and engaging users in daily routines. At a conceptual level, the solution combined conversational interaction, scheduling support and basic assistive features within a real-world pilot setting so that user acceptance and practical value could be evaluated directly. The expected impact included better user experience, reduced feelings of isolation and improved support for routine health and wellbeing tasks. More broadly, the pilot explored a scalable model for complementing social-care services and extending support for older people living alone.

title: ARC-D - Automatic Road Condition Detection
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: BMVI, Autobahn GmbH of the Federal Government
source_description: ARC-D addresses the lack of automated, up-to-date condition monitoring across the federal motorway network, a gap that makes it harder for road authorities to detect deterioration early and to plan timely maintenance before defects become more severe and more expensive to repair. The use case involves transport infrastructure authorities and maintenance planners who need consistent, network-wide visibility of road quality in order to prioritise interventions and manage public assets more effectively. Its objective is to create a more systematic and scalable basis for assessing the condition of individual motorway sections, replacing a fragmented approach with one that supports earlier action and better long-term maintenance planning. The implementation uses image data previously classified by experts to train a system capable of partially automating the evaluation of road video footage and classifying stretches of road according to their condition. At a conceptual level, the solution combines supervised classification methods with image-based inspection workflows, with the longer-term intention of integrating additional sensor data to broaden and strengthen detection capability. The expected impact is earlier identification of road degradation, more efficient maintenance targeting and reduced risk of cost-intensive long-term damage. In operational terms, the system improves scalability, enhances the timeliness of infrastructure monitoring and supports more reliable, data-informed management of motorway assets.

title: C-19 - Interdepartmental chatbot on the topic of Corona.
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: During the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, German public services experienced a dramatic increase in citizen enquiries, with volumes reported to rise by up to ten times. This created an urgent operational need for a scalable way to answer common questions quickly and consistently without overwhelming public-service staff. The C-19 chatbot was introduced to address this surge by providing citizens with immediate access to information on coronavirus-related issues and directing them to further official sources where appropriate. The stakeholders included public administrations, service teams and the general public, with the objective of reducing pressure on frontline channels while maintaining accessible communication during a fast-moving crisis. The solution was implemented as an interdepartmental chatbot built from existing FAQ content, which was entered as modular dialogue components to generate automated responses. At a conceptual level, the system combined pre-formulated answer blocks with speech-recognition and dialogue-processing components so that citizens could ask questions in natural language and receive standardised replies. The chatbot also pointed users towards further sources of information, and future ambitions reportedly included support for application creation and status clarification. The impact was improved scalability in handling routine pandemic-related enquiries and faster dissemination of official information at a time of high uncertainty. Although no longer in use, the case remains relevant as an example of rapid chatbot deployment for crisis communication under exceptional service pressure.

title: Study certificates - Automatic recognition for applying for child benefit
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Family benefits offices in Germany face a recurring administrative burden because, to maintain eligibility for child benefit, a student’s current certificate of enrolment must be submitted twice a year. The problem is compounded by the lack of a uniform certificate format across German universities, which means that large volumes of heterogeneous documents must be checked manually. This use case was introduced to reduce processing effort, improve consistency and accelerate validation while retaining staff oversight. The stakeholders include applicants, family benefits offices and case-handling staff, with the objective of making the verification of study certificates faster, more reliable and less labour-intensive. The solution is implemented through a workflow in which the applicant uploads the certificate via a web portal, the text is extracted using optical character recognition, and the resulting content is classified automatically. At a conceptual level, the system checks four points: whether the document is a study certificate, whether it relates to the correct child, whether the semester or validity period is correct, and whether the issuing institution is a recognised German university. The result is displayed within the specialist procedure and must be actively accepted by an employee. The training base currently includes 60,000 semi-automatically annotated certificates, anonymised with a dedicated algorithm, and the classification combines Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine, Logistic Regression, natural language processing and named-entity recognition. The impact is improved efficiency, reduced manual workload and more scalable certificate processing.

title: Trade statistics - Classification system that automatically new data points as relevant
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: This use case was developed to improve the production of official trade statistics by automating the initial classification of incoming units, such as craft enterprises, as relevant or not relevant for inclusion in the statistical process. Previously, this task had been performed manually, which consumed significant staff time, was vulnerable to inconsistency and error, and placed pressure on already limited personnel resources. The use case therefore involved statistical case handlers and official statistics teams seeking to maintain processing quality while increasing efficiency in the treatment of new data points. Its objective was to pre-sort cases more effectively so that staff could focus their effort within the same operational time window but on a more intelligently ordered set of records. The implementation used previously identified classification patterns for units, drawing on information from business registers, to train a classification system that could assess the likely relevance of new cases. At a conceptual level, the solution applied supervised learning to historical administrative patterns and fed the resulting predictions into the case-handling workflow as a prioritisation layer. The impact was a more efficient and reliable screening process, reduced manual burden and better use of scarce staffing capacity. In practical terms, the approach improved throughput, supported more consistent statistical production and created a scalable mechanism for handling growing volumes of administrative data.

title: Indoor Robot - Making a 3D model of a new building
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Federal Ministry of Transport and Digital Infrastructure (BMVI)
source_description: This use case was created to improve accessibility and navigation in public buildings by generating more detailed and practical spatial information than conventional building plans typically provide. The problem was especially significant for people who need barrier-free navigation, including blind people and wheelchair users, because standard plans often lack the information required for independent movement through complex indoor environments. The use case therefore involved public-building managers, accessibility stakeholders and end users requiring reliable orientation information, with the objective of producing accurate indoor models that could support inclusive navigation and better user autonomy. The implementation used a robot equipped with a laser scanner and object camera to measure the entire building and capture detailed spatial data. At a conceptual level, the solution transformed individual measurement points into a 3D vector model of the building through automated modelling techniques, creating a digital representation that could then support orientation maps and display on mobile devices. This provided a richer and more usable description of the indoor environment than static architectural drawings alone. The expected impact was improved accessibility, better navigation support and a stronger basis for inclusive public-space design. More broadly, the use case offers a scalable way to capture building information and translate it into practical guidance tools that enhance independence and user experience for people with disabilities.

title: Child benefit - Voice assistant for parents support
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Hamburg Office for IT and Digitalisation
source_description: In the days immediately following childbirth, parents are legally required to complete a range of formal administrative steps, including providing registration information, determining the child’s name and establishing the first official conditions for receiving parental and child benefits. The operational problem is that these procedures often involve repeated document requests from different institutions and limited electronic data exchange, creating unnecessary bureaucracy at a time when families are already under pressure. This use case was designed to simplify that process by allowing parents to initiate the necessary procedures directly at the maternity hospital, thereby reducing duplication and speeding up access to key documents and benefits. The stakeholders include parents, registry services, benefits administrators and hospital staff, with the objective of making the process faster, more accessible and less burdensome. The solution is implemented through a combined application process supported by a voice-assistance system available on stationary hospital terminals, tablets or smartphones. At a conceptual level, the system guides parents verbally through the application steps and supports a more integrated administrative workflow that links registration, birth certification, tax identification, residents’ registry entry and child-benefit notification. As a result, parents receive the child’s birth certificate, tax number, registration confirmation and child-benefit notice more quickly by post, while benefits can be transferred directly to their account. The impact includes reduced bureaucracy, faster processing and a more user-friendly start to family-related administrative services.

title: AI against pornography - Analysis of suspicious material
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Public prosecutors and investigators face the operational challenge of reviewing very large volumes of seized digital material in cases involving the distribution, acquisition or possession of child and youth sexual abuse imagery. Much of this material may be entirely irrelevant to the offence under investigation, yet it must still be assessed carefully to identify evidential content. The use case was therefore designed to support case workers by accelerating the initial sorting of suspicious images so that the most potentially relevant material could be prioritised for detailed review. Its objective was to reduce the burden of manual screening, improve consistency in the handling of digital evidence and support more efficient investigative and prosecutorial workflows while preserving human judgement in the final assessment. The implementation used automated image-recognition techniques to analyse visual material and identify items most likely to depict illegal content involving children or adolescents. At a conceptual level, the system functioned as a triage mechanism, separating likely irrelevant material from images requiring closer investigation and forwarding flagged content to case handlers and, where appropriate, to the public prosecutor for decision. The impact was faster evidence screening, reduced manual effort and improved focus of investigative resources on the most relevant material. In operational terms, the approach enhanced scalability, supported reliability in evidence handling and improved the efficiency of highly sensitive prosecutorial work.

title: Notification procedure - Automatic control of accident occurring at the workplace
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Employer's Liability Insurance Association for Energy, Textiles, Electrical and Media Products (BG ETEM)
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: When an accident at work, or on the journey to or from work, is caused by a third party, the Employer’s Liability Insurance Association must assess whether recourse proceedings against that third party are likely to succeed. Previously, suspected cases were forwarded through a standardised document flow to a central office, where they were manually pre-checked, creating a slow and resource-intensive process across large case volumes. This use case was developed to improve prioritisation and support case handlers with more structured evidence before they decide whether to pursue recourse. The stakeholders include the insurance association, recourse departments and case officers, with the objective of increasing efficiency, improving the quality of triage and strengthening decisions on whether legal recovery is worthwhile. The solution is implemented using a model trained on around one million completed recourse and subrogation proceedings, both successful and unsuccessful. At a conceptual level, the system estimates the plausibility of a potential recourse action, forecasts the likely probability of success and predicts the level of total costs. In parallel, text-mining methods identify critical keywords, such as whether the police were called or whether an assault occurred, to provide additional decision support. These outputs are delivered through a web interface for the recourse department. The impact is faster pre-assessment, better-informed case selection and reduced manual effort, with broader value in improving consistency, focusing resources on higher-potential cases and making recourse management more scalable.

title: Robot-mediated rehabilitation (IIT-FDG)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: This use case addresses the need to extend rehabilitation support beyond conventional clinical sessions by introducing an assistive robot that can complement therapists’ work in hospitals, rehabilitation gyms and patients’ homes. The context is one in which patients recovering from injury or managing long-term functional limitations often require frequent support with exercises, daily activities and safety monitoring, while clinical staff must balance intensive care needs with limited time and resources. The stakeholders include patients, rehabilitation professionals, ward staff and carers, with the objective of improving continuity of support, reinforcing therapy routines and assisting with everyday tasks that help preserve autonomy and safety. The implementation uses the humanoid robot R1, developed as part of the ETAPAS H2020 project, combining advanced mechanics, sensors and intelligent control capabilities to operate as a low-cost assistive-rehabilitation platform. At a conceptual level, the system supports traditional rehabilitation treatments, assists staff in clinical environments and provides in-home functions such as fetching or locating objects, reminding patients about appointments or medication, and detecting falls to support emergency management. The expected impact includes improved continuity of care, better patient experience and stronger support for independent living. More broadly, the solution offers scalability through lower-cost deployment, reduces pressure on clinical staff and strengthens rehabilitation outcomes by extending assistance into everyday environments.

title: Kari - Chatbot for local governments
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Kari was created to help local municipalities manage large volumes of citizen enquiries about public services in a faster and more consistent way. In many councils, residents need clear answers on procedures, rights and local services, yet frontline teams often face repetitive requests that absorb time and slow response delivery. The use case therefore involves municipal administrations and citizens, with the objective of improving access to information, reducing pressure on service staff and strengthening the quality of digital interaction with local government. The solution is implemented through a virtual-agent platform integrated into municipal service channels and supported by a knowledge base containing more than 6,000 intents, covering a very broad range of local-government questions. At a conceptual level, the system uses conversational language-processing and intent-recognition techniques to interpret citizen requests, match them to the relevant service information and return standardised answers that can be maintained centrally and reused across municipalities. Kari is currently available in 80 Norwegian municipalities, covering about 30% of the Norwegian population, and is being introduced in Sweden, Finland and Denmark. The result is improved user experience, faster access to information and greater scalability in handling routine enquiries, while municipalities benefit from more efficient service delivery, better consistency of responses and reduced administrative workload.
supporting_source_urls: ETAPAS workshop of 30/04/2021. Kari is one of the pilots

title: CERTH-MUKA - Public Organizations Multi-factor Misinformation Handling
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: In the municipality of Katerini, the challenge addressed by this use case is the growing need to identify misleading information quickly and to prioritise emerging issues before they create operational, reputational or social harm. Public authorities must respond in an environment where inaccurate online content can spread rapidly, undermine trust and complicate communication with citizens. The use case therefore involves municipal decision-makers, communication teams and public-sector organisations seeking to manage information risks more effectively, with the objective of detecting problematic content early and handling it in a way that is operationally useful and socially responsible. The solution combines misinformation-detection and issue-prioritisation capabilities with the ETAPAS framework, which is used to assess deployment risks and define mitigation actions. At a conceptual level, the implementation analyses content and signals associated with potentially false or harmful narratives, prioritises relevant issues for attention and embeds an ethical and social impact assessment around the operational system. This allows the municipality to evaluate not only technical performance but also governance risks, unintended consequences and required safeguards. The expected impact is improved responsiveness to misinformation, better prioritisation of public communication efforts and stronger institutional trust. In business and public-value terms, the approach enhances reliability, reduces the risk of harmful side effects and supports scalable adoption through structured risk management.

title: Home Quarantine App - Supporting the use of electronic control for home quarantine
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: In early May 2020, a government decree enabled the use of electronic control to support home quarantine, responding to the practical challenge of monitoring compliance during the COVID-19 pandemic without relying solely on manual enforcement. The app was introduced in a context where authorities needed a scalable mechanism to check whether quarantined individuals remained at home, while also attempting to encourage uptake by linking participation to lower fines for breaches of quarantine rules. The stakeholders included quarantined citizens, state authorities and the developer company Asura Technologies, with the objective of strengthening compliance monitoring and supporting pandemic-control measures. The solution was implemented through a mobile application developed by Asura Technologies, a Hungarian company with experience in facial-recognition and GPS-location technologies. At a conceptual level, the system linked identity verification with geolocation checks, while personal data formally remained with the state and the company’s role was described as establishing the connection between the relevant data points rather than accessing the data itself. Although use of the app was voluntary, the incentive structure created practical pressure to adopt it. The impact lay in providing a digital alternative to more labour-intensive monitoring, but the case also raised broader issues around proportionality, governance and the role of private operators in public enforcement technology. The app is no longer in use, but it remains significant as a pandemic-era example of digitally supported quarantine control.

title: Estimation of income of self-employed and SMES who pay taxes by module
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: In Spain, certain self-employed workers and small and medium-sized enterprises may opt to pay taxes under a modular system rather than declaring their exact income. While this simplifies compliance for taxpayers, it creates an analytical challenge for the tax administration because exact income figures are not directly available for this group, yet they are still needed for the calculation of ratios, statistics and broader economic analysis. This use case was designed to estimate the likely income of those taxpayers more accurately so that official statistical and analytical work can be based on more robust information. The stakeholders include the tax administration, statistical and analytical teams, and indirectly the wider policy community that relies on income-based indicators, with the objective of improving the quality of tax-based estimates without changing the underlying tax regime. The solution is implemented through predictive estimation based on a wider comparison population of taxpayers with similar characteristics who do declare exact income, as well as taxpayers who switch between the modular system and direct declaration from one period to the next. At a conceptual level, the system uses these comparable datasets to infer likely income levels for the target population and feeds the resulting estimates into the calculation of income-related indicators. The impact is improved statistical reliability, stronger analytical precision and better consistency in fiscal reporting, creating value through more accurate measurement and more useful evidence for policy and administration.
supporting_source_urls: Survey Use and impact of AI in the public sector. 2021 (https://ai-watch.ec.europa.eu/news/survey-artificial-intelligence-use-public-sector-2021-06-11_en)

title: Véda-KAFIR-ROBOTZSARU (‘Robocop’) - System Operated by the Police for Traffic Safety Automated Processing
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Hungary’s road-safety enforcement authorities needed a faster and more integrated way to process large volumes of traffic violations with minimal delay and consistent evidential handling. Manual processing of speeding and related road-traffic offences can be time-consuming and vulnerable to bottlenecks, particularly when evidence must be matched against vehicle registries and then transferred into case-management systems. This use case therefore aims to streamline enforcement by linking roadside capture, data verification and administrative processing in a single workflow. The stakeholders include the police, responsible enforcement authorities and road users, with the objective of improving traffic-safety enforcement, accelerating case handling and reducing administrative friction in the imposition of fines. The solution is implemented through the Véda intelligent camera network, which feeds data into KAFIR, the Traffic Safety Automated Processing and Information System, and then into the police’s broader Robotzsaru records and case-management platform. At a conceptual level, the cameras capture the vehicle registration number, speed, location coordinates, date and time, after which KAFIR cross-checks this information against the traffic registry, for example to determine whether a vehicle is stolen, and uploads the data into Robotzsaru. The files are then classified and sent to the competent authority without human intervention at that stage, followed by an ex post administrative check. The impact is highly automated enforcement, faster transmission and classification of cases, and more consistent processing of no-fault traffic infringements.

title: Decision on the Maternity Benefit (TÉBA) - The Family Support Scheme of the Hungarian State Treasury
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Hungarian State Treasury introduced the TÉBA system to address a structural administrative problem in family support: benefits such as family and disability allowances were managed across different databases and processes, making it harder to deliver a unified, efficient and citizen-centred service. Fragmented data access can slow decision-making, increase duplication and make it more difficult for public bodies to manage entitlements consistently. This use case was therefore designed to improve the management of maternity-related and other family support benefits by integrating or guaranteeing access to the relevant information sources required for decision-making. The stakeholders include the State Treasury, benefit administrators and citizens applying for family-related support, with the objective of simplifying administration, improving coordination across databases and making benefits management more coherent and efficient. The solution is implemented through a system architecture that connects or provides access to multiple public databases involved in family and disability allowance administration. At a conceptual level, TÉBA functions as an integration layer that enables the Treasury to consolidate the information needed for benefit assessment and payment within a more unified workflow, reducing fragmentation in case handling. Although the source provides limited quantitative detail, the expected impact lies in faster processing, improved consistency and lower administrative overhead. More broadly, the system creates value by modernising benefits administration, supporting better data availability and enabling a more integrated public-service model for family support.

title: Predicting sick leave duration
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Norwegian Labour and Welfare Service needed a more structured way to support case workers dealing with people on sick leave, particularly when deciding which cases require closer follow-up and which may need less attention. Without predictive support, such decisions depend heavily on individual judgement and can make it harder to allocate case-management effort efficiently across large caseloads. The use case therefore focuses on improving prioritisation in sickness-absence management by estimating how long the current period of sick leave is likely to continue. The stakeholders include case workers, people on sick leave and the wider set of actors involved in return-to-work dialogue, with the objective of improving the quality of follow-up decisions and making case management more targeted. The solution is implemented through a random-forest model that predicts the remaining duration of an ongoing sick-leave episode. At a conceptual level, the prediction is integrated into the information available to the case worker when deciding whether to call a dialogue meeting between the relevant parties. To strengthen interpretability, the outputs are explained using Shapley values, allowing case workers to understand which factors contributed most to the prediction. The impact is better-targeted follow-up, improved allocation of staff attention and more consistent support for decision-making. More broadly, the model creates value by enhancing explainability in predictive public services, supporting more efficient welfare administration and helping case workers focus on the cases where intervention may matter most.

title: Intelligent mechanisms for clinical evaluation - Facilitate the reconciliation of citizens
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Vimercate Local Health Authority sought to reconcile two competing pressures in hospital care: offering citizens the best possible treatment while reducing the time clinicians spend on administrative and forecasting tasks that take them away from patients. In departments such as diabetology, nephrology and internal medicine, doctors must assess patients daily in order to estimate likely discharge times, the risk of complications and the possibility of readmission, including urgent readmission, both for those currently in treatment and for those in protected discharge. The objective of this use case was therefore to improve clinical evaluation and operational planning at the same time, enabling the facility to maintain continuity of care while optimising resources and reducing costs. The solution is implemented through machine-learning mechanisms that support doctors by analysing larger volumes of clinical information and generating suggestions more quickly than manual review alone. At a conceptual level, the system processes patient conditions and historical treatment patterns to assist with predictions regarding discharge timing, complication risk and readmission likelihood, integrating these outputs into daily clinical assessment workflows. This does not replace medical judgement but augments it with faster, broader analytical support. The expected impact includes reduced administrative burden on doctors, more timely and informed clinical predictions, better bed and care-capacity planning and improved service continuity. More broadly, the initiative creates value through better operational efficiency, stronger patient management and a more sustainable balance between care quality and hospital resource use.

title: Scout.AI - Analyse the information recorded within the SNS 24 TAE Service
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: SPMS - Shared Services of the Ministry of Health, EPE
source_description: The SNS 24 Triage, Counselling and Referral Service handles a very large volume of calls across Portugal and plays an important role in ensuring equitable access to healthcare advice. In 2018 alone, more than 1 million calls were answered, each lasting on average seven to eight minutes, and nurses relied on one of 59 predefined clinical algorithms to triage callers and decide on the most appropriate referral. The operational challenge is that choosing the right algorithm is critical to both patient safety and service efficiency: the selected pathway must avoid missing urgent situations while also discriminating effectively between cases. The use case therefore involves nurses, the SNS 24 Contact Centre and the Directorate-General of Health, with the objective of improving algorithm selection in real time and strengthening the design of the clinical algorithms themselves. The solution is implemented through decision-support models trained on anonymised SNS 24 contact data from 2017 and 2018, representing around 2 million cases. At a conceptual level, the system uses classification methods to recommend the most appropriate clinical algorithms for a given symptom profile, adjusted for age and sex, and is then integrated into the TAE workflow as real-time support for nurses. The expected impact is safer and more consistent triage, reduced uncertainty in algorithm choice and better-informed optimisation of referral logic, creating value through improved clinical decision support and more effective telephone-based healthcare access.

title: Machine Learning in Editing and Imputation - Automated editing and correcting of data
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: A key operational issue in official statistics is the need to correct missing, implausible or inconsistent observations quickly enough to keep production cycles on schedule without overloading staff. At the Federal Statistical Office of Germany, editing and imputation are essential steps in data processing, yet manual treatment becomes increasingly difficult as digitisation produces larger and more complex datasets. The use case therefore involves statistical production teams and data-quality specialists, with the objective of reducing routine manual work while preserving the quality and timeliness of published results. The implementation uses observed values, plausibility rules and machine-learning techniques to support automated editing and imputation within the statistical workflow. Conceptually, the system analyses historical and current data patterns, applies prediction methods to infer likely corrections or substitute values, and combines these outputs with existing validation logic so that suspect observations can be treated more consistently and at scale. This creates a more adaptive alternative to purely manual intervention and helps incorporate automation into established statistical processes. The impact is expected to include lower administrative effort, quicker processing of large datasets and improved timeliness of statistical outputs. More broadly, the use case increases scalability, strengthens consistency in data treatment and delivers business value by enabling statistical offices to manage growing data volumes more efficiently without proportionate increases in staffing.

title: Machine Learning in Text Classification Projects - Relieving staff from coding tasks
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Across many official statistics processes, large amounts of text information must be coded into predefined categories before the data can be analysed and published. This coding work is repetitive, labour-intensive and increasingly difficult to sustain as digitisation expands the volume of incoming textual material. The use case at the Federal Statistical Office of Germany addresses this bottleneck by supporting teams responsible for statistical coding and production, with the objective of reducing manual effort, improving turnaround times and enabling staff to focus on the most complex cases rather than routine assignments. The solution is implemented through text-classification models trained on previously coded examples and embedded within statistical production workflows. At a conceptual level, the system uses machine-learning techniques to detect patterns in textual responses, assign likely categories and pre-sort or directly code new records against the required classification schemes. Human review can then be concentrated on ambiguous or higher-risk cases, allowing the overall process to operate more efficiently. The expected impact is improved timeliness of statistical results, reduced pressure on coding staff and greater consistency in the handling of textual information. In operational terms, the approach offers stronger scalability, better use of limited personnel capacity and a more sustainable way to manage growing data volumes while maintaining quality in official statistical production.

title: Project ML-SAST - Machine Learning in the Context of Static Application Security Testing
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Federal Office for Information Security launched the ML-SAST project to address a pressing software-security problem: identifying vulnerabilities and coding errors early enough in the development process to reduce remediation effort, shorten delivery times and improve the overall security of software systems. Static Application Security Testing is already used to examine source code without executing it, but conventional approaches can struggle to recognise new or evolving error patterns efficiently. The use case therefore involves the BSI, software-security researchers and development teams, with the objective of strengthening automated code analysis and exploring whether more adaptive methods can make security testing more effective and less burdensome. The solution is implemented as a staged research and development effort focused on applying machine-learning techniques to static security testing. At a conceptual level, the project begins with a feasibility study and literature review to identify the most suitable model families for detecting code patterns associated with vulnerabilities. On the basis of those findings, an open-source prototype is then developed to demonstrate the method in practice. This combines pattern-recognition strengths from machine learning with the static-analysis context of software assurance. The expected impact is more secure software, lower manual workload for developers and shorter development cycles. More broadly, ML-SAST creates value by exploring a scalable route towards earlier and more autonomous vulnerability detection in software engineering.
supporting_source_urls: Survey Use and impact of AI in the public sector. 2021 (https://ai-watch.ec.europa.eu/news/survey-artificial-intelligence-use-public-sector-2021-06-11_en)

title: Project ROMATRIS
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Project ROMATRIS responds to a practical problem in emergency response: transporting essential materials through difficult or obstructed terrain during rescue operations. In scenarios such as collapsed buildings, rail accidents, road incidents or off-road emergencies, responders often need to carry equipment across gravel, slopes or obstacles, which slows interventions and increases physical strain. The use case therefore involves rescue teams and emergency-service organisations, with the objective of improving field logistics, reducing responder burden and supporting faster, safer access to critical equipment in demanding environments. The solution is based on a partially automated mobile assistance robot designed to accompany a person through impassable terrain while carrying materials needed for the operation. At a conceptual level, the robot combines autonomous mobility, terrain adaptation, person-following capabilities, gesture recognition and feedback mechanisms so that it can remain aligned with the user and respond appropriately in dynamic rescue conditions. By integrating transport support with human guidance, the system is intended to fit into operational workflows without replacing the rescuer’s judgement. The expected impact is greater efficiency in material transport, reduced physical effort for responders and improved continuity of operations in hazardous settings. More broadly, the project offers scalable support for emergency logistics, enhances reliability under difficult field conditions and contributes to safer, more effective rescue missions.

title: Bridge sensors to control car and boat traffic
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Province of South Holland introduced this use case to address the operational challenge of keeping both roads and waterways safe, accessible and efficient in an area where bridge openings directly affect two interconnected transport systems. Through the Smart Shipping programme, developed with the Directorate-General for Public Works and Water Management and the Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management, the province aims to improve the use of inland waterways while reducing unnecessary disruption for road users. The central objective is to coordinate bridge operations more intelligently, so that vessels can pass with less waiting time and road traffic remains manageable when bridges open. The implementation relies on a network of sensors installed across 55 provincial bridges to detect whether each bridge is open or closed, combined with induction loops placed in roads to measure traffic volumes. These data streams are used by a mobility application that supports operational decisions on bridge openings by balancing vessel movements with road traffic conditions. By integrating bridge-status data and traffic-flow measurements, the system enables more responsive planning and contributes to smoother multimodal transport management. The expected value lies in reducing waiting times for ships, limiting avoidable congestion for cars and other road users, improving safety around bridge operations, and supporting the wider competitiveness of waterborne transport as a reliable alternative to road-based logistics.

title: Vegetation detection Friesland - Remote sensing and image recognition to interpret satellite images
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Province of Friesland needed a more efficient and timely way to monitor vegetation on the Dutch Wadden Islands, where traditional field-based registration had been carried out only once every six or twelve years by inspectors travelling to the islands. This approach was both labour-intensive and too infrequent to provide the up-to-date environmental insight needed for effective management. The use case therefore focused on improving how authorities assess the current state of vegetation, with the added importance that many plant communities in the area are sensitive to nitrogen, making accurate vegetation monitoring relevant for broader environmental modelling as well. The stakeholders include provincial authorities, environmental inspectors and ecological planners, with the objective of creating a more scalable and current monitoring method while retaining expert oversight for uncertain cases. The solution is implemented through remote sensing and image-recognition techniques applied to satellite imagery. At a conceptual level, the system analyses satellite data to classify vegetation patterns across the islands, while areas that are difficult to interpret automatically are flagged for manual review by inspectors. This creates a hybrid workflow that combines large-scale automated screening with targeted expert validation. The expected impact is more frequent and less labour-intensive vegetation monitoring, better environmental intelligence and stronger support for nitrogen modelling. More broadly, the approach creates value by improving ecological oversight, reducing fieldwork burden and enabling a more responsive approach to landscape management.

title: Automation subsidy requirements - Application for a subsidy are examined by AI algorithm
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Province of South Holland introduced this use case to address a practical barrier to household sustainability: many homeowners wanted to make their homes more energy-efficient but lacked the financial means to do so. To support this group, the province offered subsidies of between EUR 300 and EUR 3,000 to homeowners whose property value was EUR 200,000 or less, provided that they had taken measures to improve the sustainability of their homes. The operational challenge was that reviewing applications manually was slow, costly and difficult to scale, which delayed support and limited administrative efficiency. The stakeholders therefore included homeowners, subsidy administrators and provincial programme managers, with the objective of accelerating application handling, reducing processing costs and ensuring that eligible applicants received support more quickly. The solution is implemented through automated assessment based on cluster data analysis and rule-based eligibility evaluation. At a conceptual level, the system analyses application data to identify likely eligible cases and processes them automatically, while directing uncertain cases to human staff for review so that applications are not rejected solely by the system. The project was delivered using an innovation-oriented methodology involving funnels, scrum and product owners. The impact includes a reduction in processing time from weeks to days, improved administrative scalability and lower handling costs. More broadly, the initiative creates value by speeding up access to sustainability support and making the subsidy scheme more efficient and citizen-friendly.

title: Tracing potential victims of human trafficking and labour exploitation with AI
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Labour exploitation and human trafficking are difficult to detect because warning signs are often hidden within ordinary-looking financial activity, making traditional investigation methods slow and resource-intensive. To address this, the Inspectorate SZW collaborated with ABN AMRO and the University of Amsterdam to identify patterns in banking data that may indicate possible cases of labour exploitation. The use case does not aim to detect perpetrators directly at the initial stage, but to help authorities identify potential victims more effectively and trigger further investigation where justified. The stakeholders include labour inspectors, banks, researchers, the Financial Intelligence Unit and, ultimately, prosecutors and judges, with the objective of strengthening early detection while preserving human control over escalatory decisions. The solution is implemented through pattern-recognition scripts applied to banking data using risk patterns supplied by the Inspectorate. At a conceptual level, the scripts search for relevant transactional connections, after which human reviewers check the output for false positives. If a pattern is validated, it may justify a further FIU investigation into suspicious transactions, which can then support legal escalation and, where authorised, access to address and transaction details for tracing potential victims. Machine-learning refinement and expansion to four other major banks are under consideration. The impact lies in earlier and more targeted identification, improved investigative efficiency and stronger inter-institutional cooperation in combating labour exploitation.

title: Loting illegally buried cadavers with drones - Use of drones to detect illegaly buried cadavers
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVW
source_description: The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority needed a faster and more accurate way to identify sites where animal cadavers may have been buried illegally, since manual inspection over large areas is resource-intensive and can delay enforcement action. Illegal burial may alter surface vegetation and create subtle irregularities that are difficult to spot consistently from the ground. The use case therefore involves inspectors and regulatory authorities seeking to target investigations more effectively, with the objective of obtaining an early and reliable picture of suspicious locations so that field resources can be deployed where they are most needed. The solution uses drones to collect aerial data and analytical models to detect anomalies associated with disturbed vegetation patterns. At a conceptual level, the implementation combines remote sensing, machine-learning-based irregularity detection and inspection triage, allowing broad areas to be screened quickly and suspect zones to be flagged for human follow-up. Rather than replacing inspectors, the system acts as an early-warning layer that narrows the search area and improves the efficiency of site verification. The expected impact is faster localisation of suspicious burial sites, reduced manual search effort and better prioritisation of inspections. In operational terms, the approach improves scalability, strengthens responsiveness and delivers business value through more efficient environmental and public-health enforcement.

title: AI for detecting illegal substances - AI to index seized data carrier
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Netherlands Forensic Institute needed a faster and more effective way to review large volumes of seized digital material in investigations where images of illegal substances might be present. Manual searching through data carriers is time-consuming and can slow investigative progress, especially when detectives must examine extensive collections of low-quality or mixed-content images. The use case was therefore developed to support forensic and investigative teams by accelerating the indexing of seized data and helping them locate potentially relevant material more efficiently. The stakeholders include forensic analysts, detectives and criminal-investigation units, with the objective of reducing review time, improving search precision and increasing the effectiveness of digital evidence analysis. The solution is implemented through a workflow in which seized data carriers are indexed and their contents scanned for images likely to depict illegal substances. At a conceptual level, the development process involved labelling examples of illegal substances, selecting an appropriate model architecture based on pre-trained deep-learning methods and then fine-tuning the model to perform better on low-quality images. This creates a practical classification layer that can highlight potentially relevant material for further expert examination rather than requiring investigators to inspect all data manually. The impact includes faster evidence handling, improved investigative productivity and more efficient use of forensic resources. More broadly, the system creates value by strengthening digital-forensics capability and allowing law-enforcement teams to focus their efforts more effectively on high-priority material.

title: Debt relief - Chatbot to assist people with debts
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Many people experiencing debt problems struggle to find the right form of help quickly, particularly when they do not know which service to contact or feel overwhelmed by the complexity of support pathways. This creates a significant access problem in debt relief, as delays in finding appropriate advice can worsen financial hardship and make later intervention more difficult. The project, developed through a collaboration between IBM and the Municipality of Rotterdam, was designed to make local debt-relief support easier and faster to reach. The stakeholders include debtors, municipal support services and debt-assistance providers, with the objective of lowering access barriers, guiding people to the most suitable support route and improving the overall responsiveness of debt-relief services. The solution is implemented partly through a chatbot that asks a series of key questions in order to determine the most appropriate next step for the person concerned. At a conceptual level, the system uses structured conversational triage and decision logic to assess the user’s situation and route them towards the correct entry path for debt support. This creates a more accessible first contact point than leaving individuals to navigate multiple service options unaided. The impact includes quicker orientation into support pathways, reduced confusion for users and a more efficient front door for debt-relief services. More broadly, the project creates value by improving early access to assistance and helping local authorities organise debt-support journeys more effectively.
