The impact lies in reduced manual effort and better support for mailroom and intake automation, but also in a clearer understanding of the limits of current extraction tools, including the need for human validation where full accuracy cannot be guaranteed.

title: Creation and management of semantic OTL relationships
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Roads and Traffic Agency of the Flemish Government
source_description: The Flemish Roads and Traffic Agency’s semantic OTL project supports its transition towards data-driven infrastructure management. The operational problem is that road infrastructure assets, including roads, cycle paths, tunnels, bridges and related equipment, generate information across design, construction, maintenance and replacement phases, but this information must be standardised to remain usable throughout the asset lifecycle. The project aims to develop a tool for creating and managing semantic relationships in the Object Type Library, allowing asset data to be collected once, structured consistently and exchanged across models, databases and software systems. Its implementation builds on BIM and semantic data-management methods, defining relationships between infrastructure object types so that asset information can be shared uniformly among project partners. The expected impact is improved data quality, more efficient collaboration, reduced duplication and stronger lifecycle management of public infrastructure. By embedding semantic standards into asset management, AWV can strengthen interoperability and make infrastructure information more reliable for planning, maintenance and operational decisions.

title: Remote interpreting services - Communicating in Flemish sign language
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Flemish Agency for Persons with Disabilities
source_description: The remote interpreting services project aims to improve communication between deaf and hearing people in Flanders by making Flemish Sign Language interpretation available more flexibly and consistently. The service problem is that several comparable services currently operate side by side, creating fragmentation and confusion for users, while existing technical and organisational arrangements do not yet ensure access anytime and anywhere. The project seeks to harmonise and scale remote interpreting so that deaf users can contact everyone by telephone, including emergency services, and can also be contacted by others such as colleagues or doctors in their preferred communication mode. Implementation requires innovation in hardware, software, service organisation, privacy protection and interoperability between existing systems. Conceptually, the solution combines video-remote interpreting, user authentication, service-routing, privacy safeguards and platform harmonisation. The expected impact is improved accessibility, lower organisational costs through consolidation, greater use of remote interpreting and stronger inclusion of deaf users in public, professional and personal communication. Its public value lies in treating language accessibility as an essential service rather than a fragmented accommodation.

title: AI platform for agri-food applications from field to fork
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Flanders Research Institute for Agriculture, Fisheries and Food (ILVO)
source_description: Across ILVO’s living labs, food pilot, greenhouses, laboratories and test environments, large volumes of data are generated every day from IoT sensors, machine-mounted cameras, drones, satellites and analytical equipment. The operational challenge is that these data streams are not processed quickly enough, meaning potentially valuable signals for research, testing and operational improvement can be missed. The use case therefore focuses on helping ILVO researchers make better use of the information already being produced, while reducing the barriers that prevent advanced data methods from being used routinely in day-to-day work. Internal stakeholders across research and innovation teams were involved in defining the needs, with the objective of creating a platform that broadens access to data-driven methods and improves the speed and consistency of analysis from field to fork. The solution is being developed as an integrated platform for agri-food data and analytics, designed through a preparatory phase involving user-centred workshops with ILVO stakeholders and supported by consultancy partner Addestino. At a conceptual level, the platform is intended to connect heterogeneous data flows, support data science and model deployment, and provide functionalities that simplify the practical use of advanced analytics in research workflows. The expected impact is faster extraction of useful information, reduced loss of actionable insight and stronger scalability in handling complex agri-food datasets. More broadly, the platform improves research efficiency, supports innovation and creates value by democratising advanced analytical capabilities across ILVO’s operations.

title: ALTRUIS - Alternative Use of Imaging Systems through Artificial Intelligence
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: DigiPolis, IT provider for the City of Antwerp
source_description: ALTRUIS was launched to help Antwerp respond to severe mobility pressures by extracting useful traffic and mobility insights from existing camera footage. The operational context was particularly challenging because Antwerp already experienced heavy congestion, while major infrastructure works placed additional pressure on mobility and quality of life. Digipolis sought to turn street images, which have limited value in raw form, into mobility intelligence for the city, especially in the Smart Zone. The implementation explored alternative use of imaging systems through artificial intelligence, initially focusing on anonymisation of visual material and then on image recognition and algorithms for mobility insights. The procurement later combined these phases into a single assignment and shifted the technological scope towards edge AI, meaning that interpretation would occur closer to the camera instead of relying only on cloud or on-premise GPU processing. The expected impact was better understanding of movement patterns, more responsive mobility management and support for smart-city traffic solutions. The case also highlights the importance of anonymisation, privacy-by-design and careful governance when repurposing urban camera infrastructure.

title: Capsat - Information from satellite images for a better agricultural policy in Flanders and Europe
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Capsat was developed to support the Department of Agriculture and Fisheries in Flanders in monitoring compliance with agricultural policy requirements linked to the European Common Agricultural Policy. Farmers receiving direct support must respect several climate and environmentally oriented obligations, including crop diversification, grassland maintenance and the creation of ecological focus areas. Traditionally, supervision of these measures has relied on field spot checks, which are resource-intensive, limited in coverage and often unable to provide rapid insight across large agricultural areas. The objective of the use case is therefore to improve follow-up, guidance and control by using remote information that can complement or partially replace manual inspection. The implementation uses high-resolution satellite imagery to map relevant agricultural conditions and detect whether policy measures have been applied correctly and on time. Image-analysis techniques can help identify crops, land use, grassland status or ecological features, while also supporting faster objectification of crop damage caused by drought or flooding. This creates a more systematic evidence base for both compliance monitoring and farmer support. The expected impact is greater efficiency in controls, broader territorial coverage, faster detection of anomalies or damage, and more objective decision-making. In policy terms, Capsat strengthens the administration’s capacity to implement agricultural rules while supporting sustainable, liveable and competitive farming in Flanders and potentially at wider European scale.

title: CATE - Continuous Auditing based on Technological Evolution and Data Mining
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: CATE was developed to rethink how the Flemish Audit Authority audits projects subsidised through European Structural Funds and Flemish co-financing. The operational problem is that a significant share of audits must be outsourced, often at high cost and with uneven added value, while the Flemish Audit Authority still needs to spend substantial time on quality control when external auditors lack sufficient expertise in public procurement or state aid. The project aims to redesign the audit process methodologically and technologically so that audits can provide greater assurance, lower costs, shorter turnaround times, higher added value and reduced loss of European resources. The implementation is based on continuous auditing, data mining and technological evolution, with an innovation partnership structured in phases from proof of concept to increasingly mature functionality. Conceptually, the system uses data-driven risk analysis, audit-process automation, analytical models and continuous monitoring of subsidised projects to identify where audit attention is most needed. The expected impact is a more efficient and targeted audit function, stronger detection of irregularities, better use of audit capacity and improved protection of public funds.

title: Smart Personalisation of the cultural offer in Antwerp Testing (SOCRATES)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The City of Antwerp and Digipolis launched SOCRATES to address a growing challenge in cultural participation: citizens are exposed to a broad and fragmented cultural offer, yet it is often difficult to connect individuals with activities and content that genuinely match their interests. The project therefore focuses on whether a more tailored, user-driven cultural experience can increase engagement and improve how residents discover literature, events and other cultural opportunities. The stakeholders include the city, Digipolis, cultural users and the wider digital-services ecosystem around Antwerp’s public platforms, with the objective of testing the feasibility and usefulness of an individual cultural profile that can power more relevant recommendations. The solution is implemented through a Digital Experience Platform built around a personal culture profile and enriched by recommendation logic, described as a “wonder algorithm”, that can suggest suitable cultural content. At a conceptual level, the platform is designed modularly so that it can connect with existing and future architecture, especially Antwerp City Platform as a Service, which already offers reusable backend components. SOCRATES extends this model to application front ends and digital touchpoints, allowing the user’s “digital cultural DNA” to inform personalised suggestions. The expected impact is more relevant cultural discovery, better use of digital channels and stronger engagement with Antwerp’s cultural offer. More broadly, the project creates value by testing a scalable, interoperable model for citizen-centred cultural personalisation.

title: Smart regulation - Using Artificial Intelligence to train computers to interpret regulation
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Smart Regulation responds to the difficulty of navigating fragmented, divergent and incoherent regulatory information. Regulations are essential for citizens, administrations, businesses and software systems, yet relevant provisions are often spread across basic laws, amendments, additions and corrections, making it hard to retrieve the exact rule that applies to a given situation. The Flemish Domestic Governance Agency and Information Flanders aim to create an engine that can process unstructured legal and regulatory sources and provide users with targeted data and insights according to their needs. The implementation uses artificial intelligence to train computer systems to interpret regulation, extract relevant information and make it available for specific target groups, including people, applications and machines. Conceptually, the solution combines natural language processing, legal text mining, semantic structuring, regulatory knowledge extraction and subscription-based access to structured outputs. The expected impact is faster access to applicable rules, reduced information silos, better reuse of regulatory data and stronger support for digital public services that depend on machine-readable legislation. By turning complex legal texts into more structured and queryable information, the project can improve administrative efficiency and regulatory transparency.

title: Turing - Automatically control Flemish road lighting with local and current data
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Turing addresses the challenge of managing motorway lighting in Flanders in a way that balances energy efficiency, climate objectives, road safety and operational workload. The Agency for Roads and Traffic had already adopted a lighting strategy in 2011 in response to the European Union’s objective of reducing energy consumption by 20% by 2020, and the number of illuminated road sections has since fallen by almost half. However, the existing control approach relies mainly on historical traffic intensities and weather forecasts at provincial level, which limits the precision of decisions on whether lighting is necessary for a specific road segment. The Turing use case aims to make lighting control more localised, timely and evidence-based. Its implementation combines rule-based algorithms with machine-learning techniques to integrate internal and external data sources into the current road-lighting control system. Local and real-time information on traffic intensity and weather conditions can be processed to determine more accurately when lighting should be switched on or off. This allows the system to move from broad assumptions towards segment-level operational decisions. The anticipated results include lower energy consumption, stronger contribution to climate targets, maintained or improved road safety, and a significant reduction in manual workload for operators. The use case also demonstrates how existing infrastructure-management systems can be upgraded through data-driven automation.

title: Elsa - AI-assisted spreading decisions
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Elsa addresses the need for more consistent winter-service decisions across Flemish road districts. The Agency for Roads and Traffic is responsible for controlling slippery road conditions on the roads it manages, but spreading decisions depend on local interpretation of real-time measurements, weather forecasts and staff experience. Because expertise varies across districts and road networks do not stop at administrative boundaries, inconsistent spreading policies can affect safety, environmental impact and operational efficiency. Elsa is intended to support district employees in deciding whether, when and how to spread de-icing material. The implementation combines physical rules and machine-learning techniques with data from AWV’s smoothness measurement system, which already integrates real-time measurements from monitoring points and stations with forecasts from the Royal Meteorological Institute. Conceptually, the system assesses road and weather conditions, estimates the risk of slipperiness and recommends the type of spreading material, quantity and timing needed to keep roads ice-free. The expected impact is more uniform decision-making, better road safety, reduced unnecessary salt use, lower environmental burden and stronger support for staff during winter operations.

title: Innovative functionalities and AI for energy saving in the public sector
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Felmish Energy Company (VEB), Agency for Facility Operations (HFB) and Flemish Energy Agency (VEA)
source_description: The Flemish public sector manages a large and diverse portfolio of buildings and infrastructure, yet turning building and energy data into practical action remains a complex task. Within the Terra patrimony and energy database, substantial information already exists on asset characteristics and energy performance, but the challenge lies in using that information actively and systematically to identify savings opportunities, support renewable energy projects and guide long-term property strategy. This use case brings together VEB, Facilities and Services, and VEA, with the objective of improving how public-sector energy data is used to detect inefficiencies faster, plan interventions more effectively and monitor energy-saving measures with greater precision. The solution explores smart data use through advanced analytics, asset analysis and measurement models, while also assessing where algorithmic methods and a Software-as-a-Service model could add value. At a conceptual level, the approach uses the Terra database as the central information layer for identifying energy-saving potential, informing real-estate strategies, supporting the initiation and monitoring of OEPC contracts, and creating synergies with other digital and sustainability initiatives. The expected impact is earlier identification of savings opportunities, better-managed energy programmes and stronger evidence for investment decisions. In business and operational terms, the initiative supports cost reduction, improves the scalability of energy management and increases the long-term value of public assets through more informed and professionally managed interventions.

title: Naamsestraat - Reduce night noise through technology and nudging
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Naamsestraat in Leuven is a busy transit route for people returning home after a night out, and this regularly generates disturbance for residents through late-night noise. The City of Leuven is addressing this as part of a broader strategy on nightlife nuisance in which preventive and enforcement measures are intended to work together. The use case therefore focuses on making the street more liveable while preserving the vitality of the city centre, involving municipal authorities and a range of local partners with the objective of detecting disturbing noise more accurately, understanding when and where it occurs, and intervening at the right moment. The solution is being developed as a living lab combining real-time data capture, objectified recognition of disturbing night noise, nudging techniques and predictive intervention planning. At a conceptual level, the implementation uses automated sound recognition to define and map nuisance, links live detections to behavioural nudges in the street environment, and supports scheduling of interventions through predictive models that identify likely high-disturbance moments. This creates a dynamic feedback loop between monitoring and action rather than relying solely on retrospective complaint handling. The expected impact is reduced nuisance, more targeted deployment of municipal measures and an improved nighttime environment for residents. More broadly, the initiative enhances urban liveability, supports evidence-based public-space management and creates a scalable model for tackling nightlife-related disturbance.

title: Clearance of dumped war ammunition in the North Sea
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Department of Mobility and Public Works (MOW)
source_description: On the North Sea sandbank De Paardenmarkt near Knokke, around 35,000 tonnes of First World War ammunition, including both conventional and chemical munitions, remain buried beneath the seabed. Although the site is currently regarded as stable, long-term risks persist as corrosion progresses and external factors such as ship strikes could trigger severe pollution, threaten marine safety and constrain coastal and port development. The Flemish government’s Maritime Access department launched this use case to test practical methods for addressing the problem safely and cost-effectively, with the objective of evaluating whether a larger-scale clean-up could be undertaken without creating unacceptable risks for people or the marine environment. The solution is being trialled through a combination of precision detection, environmental monitoring, sediment removal, deepening operations and robotic recovery of buried ammunition. At a conceptual level, the approach integrates seabed sensing, risk monitoring, controlled excavation and remote-handling technologies to locate and retrieve hazardous objects while limiting direct human exposure and minimising ecological disturbance. The expected impact is better understanding of feasible remediation methods, reduced uncertainty around operational risk and stronger preparedness for a full-scale clean-up. In strategic terms, the project supports environmental protection, enhances coastal safety and may unlock future value by reducing obstacles to maritime infrastructure and port development.

title: Customer call analysis - Finding patterns in the reasons for customer inquiries
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Social Insurance Board needed a clearer understanding of why citizens were contacting its services and where recurring pain points in service delivery were causing confusion, delays or repeated enquiries. Traditional review methods made it difficult to obtain both a broad statistical overview and a detailed picture of issues emerging across multiple communication channels. This use case therefore focused on helping managers identify patterns in customer concerns more quickly so that services could be improved in a targeted and timely way. The pilot involved an information-line manager and two service managers, with the objective of generating insights that would support managerial decision-making and lead to faster, more convenient public services. The solution was implemented with Feelingstream, which analysed customer contacts across calls, emails and chatbot interactions. During the pilot, calls from May to August 2020 were transcribed in Estonian and Russian, enabling the system to detect themes and recurring reasons for contact across language groups. At a conceptual level, the approach combines transcription, multilingual text analysis and cross-channel pattern detection to turn customer-contact data into actionable service intelligence. The expected impact is faster identification of service problems, better prioritisation of improvements and more informed management decisions. In practice, this enhances efficiency, improves the citizen experience and creates value by linking everyday customer interactions directly to service redesign.

title: Automatic translation of Riigi Teataja Ametlikud Teadaanded
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Department of Public Relations of the Ministry of Justice
source_description: Estonia’s Official Gazette introduced automated translation to make website content available in English, responding to the need for greater accessibility for foreign businesses and other international stakeholders while preserving Estonian as the only legally binding language. The operational challenge was to broaden access to official information without creating unsustainable translation costs or slowing publication processes. The use case therefore involved the publisher of the official notices service, external technology partners and users who require reliable access to administrative information in a language other than Estonian. Its objective was to support an open business environment and improve usability for non-Estonian speakers, while maintaining clear legal certainty about which language version is authoritative. The solution is implemented through a neural machine translation system developed with Tilde Eesti OÜ and Inversion OÜ and funded 80% by the European Commission. At a conceptual level, the system generates English versions of website content, captures corrections and feeds those improvements back into the model so that translation quality can improve over time. Quality is also monitored and adjusted by the publisher to maintain accuracy and fitness for use. The expected impact is lower translation cost, broader access to official information and improved convenience for foreign stakeholders. More broadly, the initiative strengthens transparency, supports international engagement and delivers scalable multilingual access without changing the legal status of official publications.

title: Automatic translation in the Land Register search portal and Commercial Register
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Center of Registers and Information Systems
source_description: Estonia’s Centre of Registers and Information Systems introduced automatic translation in the e-Land Register and related registry environments to address a practical accessibility problem: non-Estonian speakers often found it difficult to understand detailed registry information, even when they needed only to read and interpret on-screen data rather than obtain a legally binding translation. Registry entries can contain highly technical content, such as information on easements and mortgages, and this can create barriers for foreign users engaging with official systems. The use case therefore involves citizens, businesses and other users of the e-Land Register and Commercial Register, with the objective of improving comprehension of registry data and making these digital public services more accessible internationally. The solution is implemented through a real-time machine translation tool launched in the e-Land Register web environment on 29 October 2021. At a conceptual level, the system uses neural-network-based translation methods that draw links across a large language database and improve over time as vocabulary and patterns are refined. The tool was developed in cooperation between Estonia, Latvia and Belgium, with middleware provided by the Latvian partner TILDE SIA. The translated text is explicitly informative and has no legal force, as Estonian remains the official language of the register. The impact includes improved usability for non-Estonian speakers, greater accessibility of registry information and a more inclusive digital-service experience.

title: Bürokratt – a virtual assistant for the Public Administration
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Information System Authority of the Republic of Estonia
source_description: Estonia’s public sector has sought to simplify how people access government services by reducing the need to navigate multiple agencies, channels and digital systems separately. The underlying operational problem is that citizens and businesses often have to move between different websites, interfaces and institutions to complete related tasks, even when they experience them as part of one life event or administrative need. Bürokratt was conceived to address this fragmentation by creating a more unified service experience in which users can obtain information and complete actions through a single conversational entry point. The stakeholders include citizens, public authorities, national information-system operators and, in some cases, private-sector service providers, with the objective of making service access more seamless, reducing friction and improving the efficiency of digital public administration. The solution is implemented as an interoperable network of public-sector virtual assistants, or “kratts”, connected to national information systems and capable of acting together as one channel from the user’s perspective. At a conceptual level, the system combines conversational interfaces, service orchestration and interoperability across public and selected private systems so that multiple tasks can be handled within one communication session and across devices. The expected impact is a more coherent user experience, reduced channel fragmentation and stronger scalability in digital service delivery. More broadly, Bürokratt creates value by supporting a whole-of-government approach to virtual assistance and making public services more accessible, integrated and citizen-centred.

title: Forecasting models Road Administration (Roads conditions and return of investments)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Estonian Road Administration is developing forecasting models to address a key infrastructure-management problem: how to decide where road investments will have the greatest effect in terms of network condition and value for money. Road budgets are finite, and without stronger predictive insight it can be difficult to prioritise maintenance and improvement projects in a way that maximises long-term benefit. The use case therefore involves transport authorities, infrastructure planners and investment decision-makers, with the objective of improving planning quality by anticipating road conditions and directing funding towards the interventions most likely to deliver the best return. The solution is implemented through forecasting models that estimate both the future condition of roads and the likely return on investment associated with different projects. At a conceptual level, the system combines historical road data, condition trends and investment-analysis methods to identify where deterioration is likely to occur and where spending can produce the highest practical benefit. These outputs can then support prioritisation, maintenance scheduling and broader infrastructure strategy. The expected impact is better-targeted investment, improved road-condition management and more efficient use of public resources. More broadly, the initiative creates value by enabling evidence-based infrastructure planning, reducing the risk of poorly targeted spending and strengthening the long-term reliability and sustainability of the road network.

title: Kama - Multilingual multidisciplinary neuroma machine translation
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Ministry of Education and Research, University of Tartu, Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications
source_description: In multilingual public and professional environments, the need to translate accurately across a range of languages and subject areas is essential for communication, cooperation and access to information. The operational problem addressed by Kama is that multilingual translation often requires separate tools, uneven language coverage or manual effort that reduces efficiency and consistency. This use case therefore focuses on providing a broader, more flexible translation capability that can support different domains and users working across several languages. Its objective is to enable reliable translation between multiple language pairs in a single system, making multilingual communication more practical and accessible. The solution is implemented as a multilingual neural machine translation system supporting seven input and output languages: Estonian, Latvian, Lithuanian, English, Russian, German and Finnish. At a conceptual level, the platform uses neural translation models trained to operate across multiple language directions, allowing users to move between different linguistic contexts within one shared architecture rather than relying on isolated bilingual tools. This design supports more efficient maintenance and broader applicability across disciplines and use cases. The expected impact is improved translation availability, greater consistency across languages and reduced dependence on manual translation for routine needs. In operational and business terms, Kama offers scalability, supports multilingual service delivery and creates value by widening access to information and collaboration across language communities.

title: ESTNLTK - Open source tools for Estonian natural language processing
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Estonia’s digital ecosystem depends on high-quality language tools to support public services, research and software development in Estonian, yet language-technology resources for smaller languages often remain fragmented or incomplete. ESTNLTK was created to address this challenge by making existing Estonian language-technology tools easier to access and by developing new ones where gaps remain. The stakeholders include researchers, developers, public institutions and organisations working with Estonian-language data, with the objective of strengthening the technical foundation for processing Estonian texts and enabling wider reuse of language resources across different domains. The solution is implemented as an open-source toolkit, written mainly in Python, for analysing and editing Estonian text. At a conceptual level, the collection acts both as an integration layer for existing language-technology components and as a development framework for new tools, allowing users to perform a range of text-processing tasks within one extensible environment. Because it is open source and funded through the Estonian National Language Technology Programme, it supports both practical deployment and broader ecosystem building. The expected impact is improved availability of language-processing tools, lower barriers for developers and researchers, and better support for Estonian-language applications. More broadly, ESTNLTK creates value by reinforcing digital capability in a smaller language market, enabling innovation and reuse, and providing shared infrastructure that can support public-sector, academic and commercial work on Estonian text.

title: PPA Information Phone call transcription for customers analysis different languages
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Police and Border Guard Board needed a better understanding of why customers were contacting its information lines and how service bottlenecks were affecting the uptake of digital channels. Calls concerning the issuance of documents had already been identified as the largest category of enquiries, yet the organisation needed richer insight into customer difficulties, especially across different languages and over long service cycles in which people may only renew documents every five to ten years. The use case therefore focused on improving service design, encouraging greater use of e-channels and refining the content and presentation of customer information. The stakeholders include the Police and Border Guard Board, customer-service teams and citizens interacting with document-issuance services, with the objective of reducing avoidable calls and making digital services easier to use. The solution is implemented through an analytical application that processes customer contacts in several languages, including Estonian and Russian, and examines call content to identify recurring patterns and friction points. At a conceptual level, the system combines multilingual transcription and contact analysis to extract service insights from phone interactions and translate them into design improvements. The pilot showed that customers often forgot the correct steps because document requests are infrequent, and it identified specific bottlenecks hindering smoother digital use. The impact includes better-targeted service improvement, stronger support for e-channel adoption and more effective customer communication, creating value through more informed service design and reduced pressure on traditional contact channels.

title: Identification of forest tree species, forest clearing and forest height
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Estonia’s remote forest monitoring information system was created to improve how forest resources are recorded, monitored and shared in georeferenced form. The forestry-management problem is that national forest assessment requires up-to-date spatial information on tree species, forest clearings, forest height and other structural characteristics, but traditional methods can be slow, fragmented or dependent on manual inspection. The Environmental Agency and KEMIT developed a system that supports the collection and sharing of operational forest information, using remote sensing as the main data source. The implementation is semi-automatic, combining machine-learning algorithms, visual inspection of remote-sensing data and third-party software tools. Inputs include satellite or other remote-sensing data, forest notifications, soil maps and teaching and validation datasets. The outputs include nationwide map layers for key assessment features, such as raster maps identifying dominant tree species. Conceptually, the system integrates geospatial data processing, classification models, human validation and forest-resource mapping. The expected impact is more consistent national forest monitoring, better evidence for forest management, improved detection of changes such as clearing, and more efficient sharing of forest data among competent bodies.

title: Transcription Kratt 1247 - Transcribing calls to to crisis number 1247
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Estonia’s crisis-information services introduced this use case to make better use of the substantial volume of calls handled through the national 1247 crisis number. Spoken interactions often contain valuable information on citizens’ concerns, recurring service needs and operational bottlenecks, yet audio recordings are difficult to analyse at scale and manual review is time-consuming. The service therefore needed a way to convert calls into a format that could support structured analysis, service improvement and the development of additional digital-support tools. The stakeholders include the emergency and crisis-information service, public-sector innovation teams and future service designers working on Estonia’s “kratt” ecosystem. The technological implementation is based on automated speech transcription, which converts spoken conversations from the 1247 line into machine-readable text. Once transcribed, the material can be searched, analysed and reused to identify frequent topics, recurring questions, information gaps and patterns in public demand during crisis situations. The resulting text can also provide a practical evidence base for training or designing future conversational assistants. The main impact is improved reuse of call-centre knowledge, reduced effort in extracting insight from audio material and stronger support for evidence-based service design. More broadly, the solution transforms routine crisis-service interactions into a scalable knowledge resource for public administration.

title: Alarm Center Assistant for Risk Assessment
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Estonia’s emergency notification process is highly time-critical and operationally complex: rescue operators must assess threats within roughly a minute while taking into account the information needs and resource rules of at least three different agencies. Under such pressure, mistakes in risk assessment or delays in gathering the right details can directly affect response quality. This use case was developed to support operators in one of the most demanding parts of emergency-call handling, with the objective of reducing error, speeding up assessment and improving the consistency of resource deployment. The stakeholders include the emergency centre, rescue operators and the agencies that depend on accurate threat classification, with the wider goal of making emergency call processing more reliable under severe time constraints. The solution is implemented through software that transcribes the incoming call and analyses it in light of previous actions in order to suggest the most likely event type and a typical case profile for the operator. At a conceptual level, the system combines real-time transcription, contextual analysis and historical pattern support to assist rather than replace the human operator during risk assessment. This allows critical information to be surfaced more quickly while keeping the operator in control of the final judgement. The expected impact is faster and more consistent threat assessment, reduced cognitive burden and better coordination of emergency resources, creating value through higher reliability in high-pressure public-safety operations.

title: Transcription Kratt 112 - Transcribing emergency calls dialed to the emergency number 112
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Emergency-call centres handle high volumes of urgent voice data, yet spoken calls are difficult to search, analyse or reuse unless they are converted into text. Estonia introduced this use case to support the handling of 112 emergency calls by beginning the systematic transcription of those conversations. The operational challenge is that emergency communication must be processed instantly for response purposes, but afterwards authorities also need a usable record for review, quality improvement and possible integration into future support systems. The stakeholders include the emergency centre, call operators and related public-safety services, with the objective of making emergency-call content more accessible for analysis and process improvement while supporting a more modern digital workflow around voice data. The solution is implemented through automated transcription of calls to 112. At a conceptual level, the system applies speech-recognition technology to transform emergency conversations into text, allowing spoken interactions to become searchable, analysable and suitable for downstream use in training, quality monitoring or future decision-support development. Even where the immediate use is modest, the transcription layer creates a reusable digital asset from otherwise transient audio. The expected impact is improved access to operational information, better conditions for service analysis and stronger foundations for future emergency-support tools. More broadly, the project creates value by enabling voice-based public-safety interactions to be incorporated into broader data-driven improvement and digital-service development.

title: Appearance - Identification of objects at the Estonian National Archives
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: The Estonian National Archives wanted to make its vast photographic holdings more accessible by allowing users to search not only through metadata, but also through visual similarity in faces. Historical image collections are rich in public value yet often difficult to navigate when names are unknown, records are incomplete or users are trying to identify ancestors or historical figures from a single photograph. This use case therefore involved the National Archives, researchers, family historians and the wider public, with the objective of improving discoverability and opening new ways of engaging with archival photo collections. The solution is implemented through Ilme, a facial-recognition-based search service linked to Fotis, the National Archives’ photo database. At a conceptual level, users upload a photo, faces are detected and compared against more than half a million archive photographs spanning back to the 1840s, representing around three million faces in total, and the most similar matches are returned by email within 24 hours as a PDF. This creates a visual retrieval workflow that complements conventional catalogue search. The expected impact is easier access to archival imagery, improved usability of large photo collections and new opportunities for users to identify individuals across historical materials. More broadly, the system creates value by making cultural heritage more searchable, more personal and more meaningful for both specialist and public audiences.

title: Calculation of forest resources by remote sensing methods
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Estonia’s forest monitoring system relies on annual field measurements from 5,600 plots, which provide the basis for national reporting and forest policy, but translating those point measurements into broader, map-based resource estimates remains a difficult and labour-intensive task. The operational challenge is to extend detailed statistical inventory information across large forest areas in a way that improves spatial coverage and supports both monitoring and stand-level economic decisions. This use case therefore involves forest-monitoring authorities, policy planners and users of national forest-resource data, with the objective of developing a methodology that can turn inventory data into maps of species composition, stand height and trunk volume. The solution is implemented by combining multispectral satellite imagery, airborne laser-scanning data and accurate tree measurements from sample plots. At a conceptual level, the system uses the plot-based measurements as model inputs and links them with remote-sensing variables in order to estimate forest characteristics spatially and produce map-based resource assessments. This moves the inventory system from pure sampling towards a hybrid model that supports both national reporting and more operationally detailed forest analysis. The expected impact is better spatial representation of forest resources, improved support for monitoring and stronger evidence for policy and economic planning. More broadly, the project creates value by increasing the usefulness of Estonia’s forest inventory, supporting smarter forest management and enabling more scalable environmental analysis through remote sensing.

title: Water level monitoring in coastal seas and lakes using satellite altimetry
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Hydrological monitoring traditionally depends on in situ measurements of water levels and flows at national stations, but these observations do not always provide the spatial coverage needed for large lakes and coastal seas. This creates a challenge for flood monitoring and marine forecasting, where broader and more continuous visibility of water conditions can improve both warning and planning. The use case was developed to enhance water-level observation by combining conventional monitoring with remote methods, with the objective of improving hydrological information available to authorities and the public. The stakeholders include hydrological-monitoring services, marine forecasters and users of water-level information, with the broader aim of strengthening operational flood monitoring and sea-level prediction. The solution is implemented through prototypes that combine radar remote-sensing data, satellite altimetry, forecasting models and analytical methods. At a conceptual level, the platform integrates remote water-level observations with existing hydrometric data and modelling workflows so that water conditions can be observed over a wider area than is possible through ground stations alone. This is particularly relevant for improving observation coverage over the Great Lakes and for feeding better data into forecasting systems. The expected impact is improved spatial coverage, more accurate sea-level forecasts and stronger flood-monitoring capability. More broadly, the project creates value by making hydrological services more comprehensive and by supporting a more resilient, data-rich approach to water-level monitoring in coastal and inland waters.

title: Marakratt - Personal learning path infrastructure
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Education systems increasingly need to support learners whose interests, prior knowledge and abilities differ widely, yet standardised content delivery can make it difficult to provide genuinely individual learning pathways. Marakratt was developed to explore how students could be supported more effectively through educational content and activities that are better matched to their personal learning needs. The use case therefore involved students, educators and digital-learning stakeholders, with the objective of testing whether recommendation models and automation could help build more individualised study paths and improve the relevance of educational material. Rather than redesigning the entire education process, the project focused on creating a proof-of-concept infrastructure able to personalise parts of the learner experience. The solution was implemented through machine-learning experimentation aimed at recommending educational materials and automating the personalisation of learning activities. At a conceptual level, the prototype used learner-related information such as interests, knowledge and abilities to generate recommendations and adapt content pathways, creating models that could serve as the basis for more personalised digital learning environments. This allowed the project to test how recommendation systems might support both educational planning and learner engagement. The impact is primarily exploratory, but it includes a clearer technical basis for individual study-path support, improved understanding of how recommendation models can function in education and a prototype framework for future scaling. More broadly, Marakratt creates value by laying the groundwork for more adaptive and learner-centred digital education services.

title: Salme - Speech recognition in courts
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Courts of Estonia and Registers and Information Systems Center
source_description: Estonia’s courts needed a faster and more efficient way to produce hearing transcripts, since manual transcription of court sessions is slow, labour-intensive and places a heavy burden on clerks. According to the Estonian courts, a single criminal case containing about 14 hours of hearings could require an average of 112 working hours to transcribe manually. The use case therefore involved the courts, the Centre of Registers and Information Systems and judicial staff, with the objective of reducing transcription effort, speeding up protocolling and improving the handling of spoken courtroom data in both physical and remote hearings. The solution is implemented through Salme, a speech-recognition tool developed with CGI Estonia and Tilde and integrated into the Court Information System via X-Road. At a conceptual level, Salme supports both real-time and offline transcription, assigns microphones to speakers, returns transcript text with only a short delay and links recordings, transcripts and notes back into court workflows. The system was trained using more than 800 hours of transcribed audio for acoustic models and over 800 million words of textual data for the custom language model, producing reported word-error rates between 8% and 15% and overall precision of about 92%. The impact includes major time savings, faster transcript production and better integration of courtroom recordings into digital judicial processes, creating value through efficiency, accuracy and secure operation on authorised court infrastructure.

title: Statistical characterization of the sea ice extent in the Gulf of Riga (Baltic Sea) using optical remote-sensing imagery
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Monitoring sea-ice conditions in the Gulf of Riga is important for understanding winter dynamics, environmental conditions and maritime risks, yet consistent large-scale observation is difficult to achieve through field methods alone. This use case addressed the need for a more systematic way to characterise ice extent, ice occurrence probability and ice-season length across different winter scenarios in the Baltic Sea. The stakeholders include researchers, environmental analysts and organisations concerned with marine observation, with the objective of generating a reliable statistical picture of sea-ice behaviour over time and across locations. The solution was implemented using optical remote-sensing data from the MODIS instrument at 250 m resolution, covering the period from 2002 to 2011. At a conceptual level, the method relied on bimodal histogram analysis of remote-sensing reflectance data to distinguish ice from water, then used the resulting classifications to calculate sea-ice extent, occurrence probability and season length. The outputs were compared with official ice charts and multi-sensor products, showing strong agreement with reference data, with R² values above 0.83. The study found large year-to-year variation: the ice season ranged from 68 to 146 days and maximum ice extent from 329 to 15,350 km², with higher ice occurrence in waters shallower than 15 m. More broadly, the work creates value by providing a robust analytical basis for regional ice monitoring and winter-scenario classification.

title: Analysis of customer calls at the Estonian Social Insurance Board
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Estonian Social Insurance Board needed a better understanding of why customers were contacting its service channels and what recurring issues were driving calls and online chats. Routine contact analysis can be difficult to perform manually at scale, especially when interactions take place across multiple channels and in more than one language. This pilot was therefore designed to help the organisation detect patterns in customer appeals and use those insights to improve service design and communication. The stakeholders include the Social Insurance Board, service managers, call-centre staff and citizens using social-insurance services, with the objective of identifying the most common concerns more precisely and supporting more informed managerial decisions. The solution was implemented in cooperation with Feelingstream, whose application transcribed customer calls and chats over a three-month period from May to August 2020 in both Estonian and Russian. At a conceptual level, the system converted spoken and written interactions into analysable text and then examined these data to identify themes, recurring problems and patterns in customer needs. This provided a more detailed basis for service insight than high-level contact statistics alone. The impact includes better understanding of why citizens contact the organisation, improved potential to redesign problematic service areas and stronger evidence for decision-making. More broadly, the pilot creates value by turning everyday customer interactions into a usable source of operational intelligence and by supporting more responsive and efficient social-insurance services.

title: Identification of flammable dwellings
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Estonia’s flammable-dwellings project aims to support fire prevention by identifying residential buildings that may present elevated fire risk. The public-safety problem is that fire services need to prioritise prevention activities, inspections and awareness measures, but risk factors may be distributed across building characteristics, location, past incidents, socio-demographic indicators and other administrative records. The Estonian Fire Department is developing an AI-based solution to detect dwellings that are more likely to be flammable or vulnerable to fire-related incidents. The implementation is described as an AI project under development, likely combining risk indicators, building or housing data, historical fire information and classification models to support prioritisation. Conceptually, the system would produce risk signals for fire-safety professionals, helping them decide where preventive outreach or inspection should be directed. The expected impact is better targeting of prevention resources, earlier identification of risky dwellings, fewer fire incidents and improved protection of residents. Because the system may concern private homes and potentially sensitive household data, its value depends on transparent criteria, appropriate legal basis, careful validation and use as a support tool rather than a fully automated enforcement mechanism.

title: Crop detection from Sentinel-1 and -2 time series using deep learning methods
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Estonia needed a more objective and scalable way to identify agricultural crops for official monitoring and statistics, as traditional methods can be labour-intensive and difficult to apply uniformly across the country. The operational challenge was to create a methodology suited specifically to Estonian conditions and capable of supporting both agricultural administration and the production of consistent national statistics. The stakeholders include Estonian universities, agricultural authorities such as PRIA and the wider state administration, with the objective of improving crop identification, strengthening the quality of agricultural statistics and providing a more standardised evidence base for public-sector use. The solution was implemented through a methodology that combines Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 time-series data with contextual variables including soil type, average daily air temperature and precipitation. At a conceptual level, deep-learning techniques were used to model crop classes from these multi-source inputs and distinguish between different agricultural patterns over time. The results showed that several crop categories could be identified with over 90% accuracy, including potatoes, field peas and beans, summer and winter rapeseed, maize, rye, winter wheat and barley, while berry and fruit plantations, as well as carrot and beetroot plantations, could not yet be classified with sufficient reliability. The impact is a more uniform and objective basis for agricultural statistics, better support for monitoring and a scalable method that can be integrated into PRIA and wider state use.

title: Mapping of flooded areas from satellite images
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Authorities responsible for flood response and environmental monitoring need a dependable way to identify inundated areas quickly, yet flood mapping can be difficult because water detection varies depending on weather, vegetation cover and sensor type. This use case focused on finding the most suitable operational methodology for mapping flooded areas under different conditions, with the objective of improving the reliability and timeliness of flood detection from satellite data. The stakeholders include environmental analysts, emergency-management actors and organisations working with Earth-observation data, all of whom benefit from more consistent flood mapping. The solution was implemented through an evaluation of Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery and the development of a prototype processing workflow. At a conceptual level, the work compared the suitability of radar and optical satellite data, identified the necessary preprocessing steps and selected the most appropriate vegetation index for characterising open water. These elements were then combined into an operational prototype capable of processing Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 data for flood-area mapping. By structuring the method in this way, the project moved beyond ad hoc interpretation towards a repeatable analytical workflow. The impact includes a clearer methodological basis for flood detection, improved operational readiness for mapping inundation and better use of satellite resources under varying environmental conditions. More broadly, the prototype creates value by supporting faster, more systematic flood monitoring and by enabling scalable geospatial analysis for hazard assessment and response planning.

title: Kratt for Estonian Internal Security Service - Combining video and GIS to identify people
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Internal security agencies need tools that help them interpret large volumes of surveillance information quickly and accurately, particularly in situations where location, movement and visual identification must be assessed together. The operational challenge is that video streams and spatial data are often handled separately, which can limit the speed and effectiveness of intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance work. This use case was developed to strengthen situational awareness by combining these sources into a more usable operational picture. The stakeholders include Estonian internal security agencies and the analysts or officers responsible for surveillance and reconnaissance, with the objective of improving identification capability, increasing efficiency in analysis and supporting more informed operational decisions. The solution is implemented as an ISR tool that integrates video streams with GIS data. At a conceptual level, the system links visual input from live or recorded footage with geographic information so that people and movements can be analysed in relation to location, routes and surrounding spatial context. This creates a more structured and operationally useful interface than reviewing video and maps separately. Although the public description is brief, the expected impact lies in faster identification, better situational interpretation and improved coordination of surveillance analysis. More broadly, the project creates value by enhancing the operational effectiveness of security services through integrated spatial and visual intelligence support.

title: Automatic border control - Facial Recognition at border controls
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Estonia introduced automated border-control gates to improve the efficiency and security of border crossing at busy entry points such as Tallinn Airport and the Narva road border crossing. Border authorities face the dual challenge of processing travellers quickly while also verifying identity and right of entry with a high level of reliability. Manual control remains essential, but alone it can slow throughput and leave less room for automated support in detecting document misuse. The stakeholders include border guards, travellers and the authorities responsible for border management, with the objective of speeding up crossings, reducing the risk of identity fraud and strengthening the overall reliability of entry checks. The solution is implemented through biometric ABC gates that use facial-recognition-based identification algorithms alongside document verification. At a conceptual level, the system compares the traveller’s biometric data with the information in the travel document and supports the border guard by automating core identity and eligibility checks before human intervention where needed. The reported performance is notable: initial testing showed that a person could pass through the gates in an average of 15 seconds. The impact includes faster border processing, improved operational efficiency and lower risk of crossing with the wrong document. More broadly, the system creates value by combining speed, security and scalability in border-control operations.

title: Chatbot Vesta - Estonian National Library
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: The Estonian National Library receives a large number of daily questions and information requests, many of which concern recurring topics and consume significant staff time despite following recognisable patterns. With around 14,000 question-related emails each year, the library faced a practical need to reduce repetitive manual work while maintaining a responsive service for users. The use case therefore aimed to improve the handling of first-level enquiries by sorting incoming questions more efficiently and automating answers where repetition made that feasible. The stakeholders include library staff, users seeking information and the institution responsible for maintaining access to knowledge services, with the objective of improving efficiency, reducing routine workload and ensuring that common questions can be handled more quickly. The solution was implemented through a prototype chatbot application capable of classifying incoming questions by topic and responding automatically to repetitive first-level enquiries. At a conceptual level, the system analyses question content, identifies topical patterns and either routes or answers the request on the basis of recurring structures already known to the library. This allows staff attention to be concentrated on more complex requests that still require human expertise. The impact includes faster handling of standard enquiries, better sorting of incoming messages and reduced pressure on library staff. More broadly, Vesta creates value by modernising user support in a high-volume cultural institution and by providing a scalable approach to repetitive information requests in library services.

title: Kratt Sälli - Organising museum inventory
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Kratt Sälli was developed by Estonia’s National Heritage Board to support museums in managing preservation and inventory activities more efficiently. Museum collections require regular monitoring, but traditional inventory work can be labour-intensive, repetitive and difficult to prioritise when institutions hold large numbers of objects with different materials, conditions and preservation needs. The operational challenge is therefore not only to record what is in the collection, but also to identify which objects require attention and when, so that staff time can be used where it creates the greatest preservation value. The objective of Sälli is to make inventory processes faster, more convenient and more need-based. The implementation is described as a prototype using a forecasting model to predict the ageing of museum objects. By analysing available information on collection items and their preservation characteristics, the system can help estimate which objects may be more likely to deteriorate and should therefore be prioritised for inspection. This supports a shift from routine, calendar-based inventory towards targeted monitoring driven by risk and need. The expected benefits include savings in staff hours, better allocation of preservation resources, earlier identification of vulnerable objects and improved planning of museum inventory work. In the longer term, the use case can strengthen cultural-heritage management by helping institutions protect collections more systematically and efficiently.

title: Kratt Folly - Recognition of museum objects
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The National Heritage Board sought to improve how digital objects are described within cultural collections, since manual description is time-consuming, can vary in quality and limits how quickly collections can be made accessible to the public. Heritage institutions increasingly manage large volumes of digital material, yet catalogue enrichment often remains labour-intensive and difficult to scale. Kratt Folly was developed to address this challenge by moving closer to automated description of museum and heritage objects. The stakeholders include the National Heritage Board, memory-institution staff and users of cultural collections, with the objective of increasing data quality, using staff time more intelligently and improving public access to described digital objects. The solution is implemented as a prototype recognition system designed to identify and support description of digital collection items. At a conceptual level, the system applies image-recognition and object-description techniques to digital heritage material so that descriptive metadata can be generated or suggested automatically, reducing the need for fully manual catalogue creation. This creates a workflow in which automation supports curatorial work rather than replacing institutional expertise. The expected impact includes richer and more consistent object descriptions, more efficient use of staff capacity and better accessibility of collections for end users. More broadly, Kratt Folly creates value by supporting scalable digital heritage management and by helping cultural institutions make their collections more searchable, understandable and usable.

title: Kratt for analysing customer conversations - Finding the root causes of customer inquiries
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund needed a better understanding of why customers were contacting its service channels, particularly because recurring enquiry patterns were placing pressure on call volumes and indicated friction in digital services and grant-related communication. From April to August 2019, the organisation worked with Feelingstream on a pilot to identify the root causes of customer calls and use those insights to improve the overall service experience. The stakeholders include the Unemployment Insurance Fund, its customer-service teams and the people using its services, with the objective of reducing unnecessary calls, improving e-environments and addressing the issues most frequently driving customer contact. The solution was implemented through Feelingstream’s multilingual contact-analysis application, which transcribed calls and analysed them in order to detect patterns in customer concerns. At a conceptual level, the system used speech transcription and language-analysis techniques to convert conversations into structured insights, enabling the organisation to see not only what people were asking about, but also when and why certain topics became especially prominent. The pilot showed, for example, that enquiries linked to the receipt of grants rose significantly at the beginning of the month. The impact included actionable insight for service redesign, improvements to digital channels and a stronger basis for reducing avoidable demand, creating value through better customer experience and more efficient service management.

title: Text-to-speech synthesis in Estonian
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Estonian-language digital services need speech technologies that sound natural and handle linguistic details accurately, yet earlier synthesis methods often produced output that was less convincing in rhythm, intonation and pronunciation. This use case was developed to improve the quality of synthetic speech in Estonian and support applications that require clearer, more human-like spoken output.
