The stakeholders include language-technology researchers, developers and future users of Estonian speech services, with the objective of producing a more natural-sounding synthesis system that can better handle the specific features of the language. The solution was implemented by the University of Tartu language-technology research group as a neural-network-based speech-synthesis prototype trained on a corpus of Estonian news. At a conceptual level, the model learns speech patterns from recorded data and can currently imitate the voices of six different speakers, allowing it to generate spoken output with more realistic sound and prosody than previous methods. The project reports particular strengths in natural intonation, as well as pronunciation of numbers, symbols and abbreviations. Although the system remains under development and is not yet considered complete, it already marks a qualitative improvement over earlier synthesis approaches. The impact lies in more natural and intelligible Estonian speech generation, stronger technical capability for future voice services and a better basis for accessible digital applications. More broadly, the prototype creates value by advancing language technology for a smaller language community.

title: Effective tax collection - Identifying companies or person in need for inspection
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Estonia’s Tax and Customs Board has explored how advanced analytical methods could improve tax collection by helping inspectors identify companies more likely to be engaged in undeclared wage payments, often referred to as envelope salaries. The operational challenge is that tax authorities must decide where to focus limited inspection resources, and conventional review methods can make it difficult to distinguish higher-risk entities from the wider taxpaying population quickly and consistently. The stakeholders include the Tax and Customs Board, tax inspectors and compliant businesses affected by the overall fairness of the system, with the objective of improving inspection targeting, increasing efficiency in tax enforcement and strengthening the board’s ability to detect hidden payroll practices. The solution is implemented as an analytical model built on information already available in tax returns, such as turnover and related reporting patterns. At a conceptual level, the system uses predictive modelling to estimate the probability that a company is paying envelope salaries and to support the selection of suitable inspection targets. This does not replace tax investigators’ judgement, but creates a structured risk signal that can be integrated into enforcement workflows. The expected impact is more focused inspections, better use of enforcement capacity and stronger support for fairer tax collection. More broadly, the project creates value by enabling more evidence-based compliance work and improving the efficiency of public revenue protection.

title: Auwi SaaS - Real-time AI-run analysis from millions of message
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland
source_description: The Finnish Ministry for Foreign Affairs needed a faster and more scalable way to understand public discussion during the coronavirus crisis, particularly on social media, where large volumes of posts can shape perceptions, reveal concerns and influence the wider information environment. Manual monitoring of such discussions is difficult to sustain at scale and may fail to provide timely insight for communications and policy support. The use case therefore involved ministry teams responsible for analysis and public-information awareness, with the objective of turning high-volume online discussion into actionable intelligence that could support faster interpretation of emerging themes and sentiment. The solution was implemented through the Aiwo Digital platform, a software-as-a-service environment designed to process and analyse millions of messages in real time. At a conceptual level, the platform applies automated language analysis and classification methods to large streams of social-media content, then presents the results through dashboards and structured findings that are intended to support decision-makers directly. In this case, the system was used to analyse coronavirus-related discussions on Twitter and convert dispersed online conversation into clearer analytical outputs. The expected impact includes quicker access to public-discourse insight, reduced manual review effort and more consistent monitoring of high-volume digital communication. More broadly, the use case creates value by improving situational awareness, supporting evidence-based communications and enabling public institutions to interpret online discussion at a scale that would be difficult to manage through conventional methods alone.

title: Predicting Heat Energy Consumption
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Helen introduced this use case in the City of Helsinki to improve the forecasting of district heat demand, a critical operational task for an energy provider serving an urban environment where consumption fluctuates according to weather, seasonality, building behaviour and customer needs. Accurate heat-demand forecasting is essential for balancing supply and demand, planning production capacity, reducing operational inefficiencies and ensuring reliable service delivery to households, businesses and public facilities. The objective of the use case is to support more precise short-term and medium-term planning by reducing the gap between expected and actual heat consumption. The AI solution uses historical energy-consumption data together with local weather forecasts to predict future heat demand more accurately. At a conceptual level, the model identifies patterns between previous demand levels, meteorological conditions and consumption behaviour, then applies these relationships to forecast upcoming energy needs. This information can be integrated into Helen’s operational planning processes to support production scheduling and resource optimisation. The reported impact is significant: the solution has reduced errors between forecast and actual heat demand by one third. This improves reliability, supports more efficient use of energy-production assets, reduces unnecessary operational costs and strengthens Helsinki’s ability to manage urban energy services in a more data-driven and sustainable way.

title: Sewage - Improving Sewage Pipe Network predicting sewer blockages
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Helsinki Region Environmental Services Authority HSY
source_description: Helsinki Region Environmental Services Authority HSY implemented this use case to improve the maintenance of a sewage network extending over more than 3,000 kilometres. Sewer blockages create operational, environmental and service-continuity risks, as they can lead to local disruptions, emergency interventions, overflow incidents and higher maintenance costs. Traditional sewer cleaning often relies on fixed schedules or reactive responses after problems occur, which may not direct resources towards the sections most likely to fail. HSY therefore sought a more targeted approach to preventive maintenance, enabling cleaning teams to focus on drain ranges where the risk of blockage is highest. The AI solution, Smartvatten Neuro, predicts possible blockages by analysing sewage-network data and identifying pipe sections that show characteristics associated with blockage-prone areas. The system produces recommendations on where cleaning should be prioritised, allowing maintenance activity to be planned according to predicted risk rather than general assumptions alone. By combining operational data with predictive modelling, the solution supports earlier intervention and better allocation of maintenance capacity. The experience showed that the system can predict blockages effectively and that up to one third of annual sewer blockages could be avoided. The main benefits are reduced disruption, more efficient field operations, lower avoidable maintenance costs and improved reliability of wastewater services across the Helsinki region.

title: Optimize the processing of reports of adverse health events
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Health authorities receive large numbers of adverse health event reports, and each submission may contain a mixture of structured details, free-text descriptions and signals of varying relevance or urgency. Processing these reports efficiently is difficult because staff must classify cases, identify the medically significant elements and spot unusual patterns, all while maintaining speed and consistency across a high-volume workflow. This use case therefore addresses the operational need to strengthen pharmacovigilance and health-safety monitoring by helping analysts and case handlers prioritise their effort more effectively. The stakeholders include health-agency professionals, safety-monitoring teams and decision-makers responsible for the assessment of reported incidents, with the objective of improving the speed, quality and consistency of report handling while preserving human oversight of the final assessment. The solution is implemented using the full body of adverse-event reports as a data source for automated classification, concept extraction and anomaly detection. At a conceptual level, the system applies natural language processing and classification models to identify relevant business concepts within reports, categorise incoming cases and highlight submissions that deviate from expected patterns and may require closer attention. These outputs can then be integrated into existing review workflows to support prioritisation and triage. The expected impact is faster case handling, more reliable identification of significant signals and reduced manual burden on specialist teams. More broadly, the approach improves scalability, strengthens health surveillance and creates value through more timely and effective monitoring of adverse events.

title: Facilitate access to patient information - Semantic search in patient records
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: In hospitals and care settings, clinicians and nursing staff often lose valuable time searching through lengthy electronic patient records to locate relevant information needed for treatment, coordination or follow-up. Although the information exists within the record, it may be scattered across notes, reports and historical documentation, making it difficult to retrieve quickly in a busy clinical environment. This use case addresses that practical problem by improving how healthcare staff access and visualise patient information, with the aim of reducing time spent on searching and allowing more attention to be devoted to care delivery. The stakeholders include nurses, physicians and other healthcare professionals who rely on the computerised patient record, with the objective of making clinically relevant information easier to find and use at the point of care. The solution is implemented through a semantic-search prototype for electronic patient records. At a conceptual level, the system uses language-processing techniques to interpret the meaning of search queries and match them to relevant content across structured and unstructured patient data, rather than relying only on exact keyword matching. Results are then presented in a way that helps staff navigate the record more efficiently. The expected impact is quicker access to information, reduced administrative friction and improved workflow efficiency for clinical teams. In practical terms, the use case enhances the user experience, supports more reliable information retrieval and creates value by reducing wasted time in healthcare processes.

title: Ionising radiation exposure monitoring information system (SISERI)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Institute for Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety
source_description: Monitoring occupational exposure to ionising radiation is a critical public-health and workplace-safety responsibility, particularly for workers whose roles involve repeated or potentially high-risk exposure. The challenge is not only to collect exposure data, but also to interpret it in a way that supports personalised follow-up and allows unusual patterns or potential anomalies to be detected early. This use case therefore focuses on strengthening the SISERI monitoring system so that exposure oversight becomes more targeted, responsive and effective. The stakeholders include occupational-health professionals, radiation-protection specialists, regulatory bodies and exposed workers, with the objective of improving individual monitoring and supporting earlier identification of cases that may require investigation or intervention. The solution is implemented using data from the ionising radiation exposure monitoring information system itself. At a conceptual level, the system applies analytical models to historical and current exposure records in order to profile normal and abnormal patterns, support personalised monitoring of worker exposure and flag cases that diverge from expected ranges or trajectories. These outputs can then feed into occupational-health and regulatory workflows for review and follow-up. The expected impact is improved detection of anomalies, more tailored exposure monitoring and better use of specialist oversight capacity. More broadly, the approach strengthens safety governance, improves the reliability of monitoring processes and creates value by enabling a more scalable and preventive model of radiation-risk management.

title: Acts - Develop Artificial Intelligence in dematerialised legality control
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Prefectures receive large volumes of administrative acts through the @ctes (Acts) application as part of the legality-control process, and agents must determine which acts are transmissible, which are not, and which elements merit priority review. This creates a substantial operational burden, particularly where routine sorting and first-level screening absorb time that could otherwise be dedicated to the most sensitive or legally significant cases. The use case therefore addresses the need to make dematerialised legality control more efficient and better targeted. The stakeholders include prefecture agents and supervisory authorities responsible for legality review, with the objective of simplifying intake, improving prioritisation and strengthening the consistency of initial case handling. The solution is implemented using data from the @ctes system to automate sorting and highlight information requiring closer inspection. At a conceptual level, the system combines classification techniques with information-extraction models to distinguish transmissible from non-transmissible acts and to identify the legal or administrative features that should be checked as a priority. These results are integrated into the agents’ workflow as decision-support outputs rather than replacing legal judgement. The expected impact is reduced manual workload, faster processing of incoming acts and more focused allocation of expert attention. In operational terms, the approach improves scalability, enhances reliability in triage and creates value by making legality control more efficient without weakening oversight.

title: Improve the online pre-complaint system - Detecting infringements automatically
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: General Directorate of the National Gendarmerie
source_description: Online pre-complaint services help citizens begin reporting offences before direct contact with law-enforcement officers, but these submissions are not always complete or sufficiently precise to be treated immediately as fully qualified complaints. As a result, complainants may need to repeat information and gendarmerie staff must spend additional time clarifying the nature of the infringement and collecting missing details. This use case addresses that inefficiency by improving the quality of online pre-complaints from the start. The stakeholders include complainants, gendarmerie officers and administrative staff, with the objective of transforming initial digital submissions into better-qualified complaints, reducing duplication and accelerating downstream case handling. The solution is implemented through automated infringement detection and question-generation capabilities applied to online pre-complaint data. At a conceptual level, the system analyses the content entered by the user, identifies the likely type of offence and determines which additional questions should be asked to complete the complaint in a structured way. By dynamically enriching the submission, the tool helps convert a preliminary account into a more usable case file before officer review. The expected impact is time savings for both citizens and law-enforcement personnel, better-quality complaint information and smoother intake processing. More broadly, the approach improves service responsiveness, enhances the user experience and creates operational value through more efficient digital complaint management.

title: Identify false customs declarations using text mining
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: General Directorate of Customs and Indirect Duties
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Customs authorities must review product descriptions in administrative documents to ensure that imported goods are declared under the correct nomenclature, particularly where some classifications attract more favourable tax treatment. The difficulty is that misleading or inaccurate descriptions can be used to place goods in a tax-advantaged category improperly, and manual detection of such cases is challenging across high volumes of declarations. This use case therefore focuses on improving the fight against customs-duty fraud by helping inspectors identify potentially false declarations more efficiently. The stakeholders include customs officers, fraud investigators and revenue authorities, with the objective of strengthening detection capability, improving prioritisation of controls and protecting public revenue. The solution is implemented by applying text-mining techniques to product descriptions contained in single administrative documents. At a conceptual level, the system analyses language patterns in the declared goods, compares them with expected nomenclature characteristics and flags cases where the textual description appears inconsistent with the claimed product category. These outputs can then support targeted inspection and further verification by customs staff. The expected impact is more accurate detection of suspicious declarations, reduced manual screening effort and better targeting of enforcement resources. In practical and financial terms, the approach enhances scalability, improves reliability in fraud detection and creates value by supporting more effective customs control and reducing losses linked to incorrect duty classification.

title: Improve the identification of the employing establishment in the population census
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: In population-census processing, accurately identifying a respondent’s employing establishment is essential for producing reliable statistics on commuting and home-to-work patterns. However, declarations provided in census data may be incomplete, ambiguous or inconsistent with the official business register, creating a manual correction burden for agents and introducing inefficiencies into the production chain. This use case addresses that problem by helping staff reconcile census declarations with the SIRENE database of companies and establishments more accurately and efficiently. The stakeholders include census-processing agents, statistical-production teams and data users who depend on robust mobility and labour-market statistics, with the objective of improving data quality and streamlining correction work. The solution is implemented through a recommendation engine built on census declarations and the SIRENE register. At a conceptual level, the system compares the establishment information entered by respondents with relevant entities in the business database and proposes likely matches to support agent review and correction. This creates a decision-support layer that helps standardise identification work while preserving human validation of the final result. The expected impact is greater precision in the home-to-work statistics produced by INSEE and improved efficiency across the data-production process. More broadly, the approach enhances reliability, reduces manual effort and creates value by strengthening the quality and timeliness of official census-based statistics.

title: Develop a tool to help the establishment of craft businesses
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: New Aquitaine Chambers of Trades and Crafts
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Choosing the right location is a decisive factor for the viability of a new craft business, yet artisans often have limited access to clear, evidence-based information on the characteristics of a territory before committing to an installation decision. Local demand, demographic structure and the existing economic fabric can all influence whether a craft activity is likely to thrive, but assessing these elements in a systematic way is difficult for individual entrepreneurs and for the public bodies that advise them. This use case therefore addresses the need to support craftsmen more effectively when selecting where to establish their business. The stakeholders include artisans, local economic-development actors and advisory services, with the objective of improving business-location decisions, reducing the risk of failure and strengthening the fit between craft activity and territorial opportunity. The solution is implemented by combining data on craft businesses with population data in order to estimate the likelihood of success for a given type of activity in a given area. At a conceptual level, the system uses predictive modelling and territorial analysis to relate business characteristics, local market conditions and demographic patterns, then translates these into decision-support outputs for advisers and business founders. The expected impact is better-informed establishment choices, improved quality of support to craftsmen and more efficient local economic guidance. More broadly, the approach can enhance business survival prospects, reduce wasted investment and create value through smarter alignment between entrepreneurship and territorial demand.

title: AI to Identify molecules contaminating the environment and the sources of pollution
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: National Institute for the Industrial Environment and Risks
source_description: Environmental monitoring depends on the ability to identify contaminating substances accurately and to understand whether different samples point to the same pollutant source or to distinct pollution events. In practice, chemical analyses generate complex spectral outputs whose similarities and differences can be difficult to assess consistently at scale, especially when many compounds or trace signatures must be compared across multiple samples. This use case addresses that challenge by improving how analysts detect polluting molecules and interpret the relationships between molecular spectra. The stakeholders include environmental laboratories, pollution-monitoring authorities and investigators responsible for tracing contamination sources, with the objective of strengthening environmental surveillance and making the identification of pollutants more precise and operationally useful. The solution is implemented by applying analytical models to the results of chemical analyses in order to compare spectra and objectify their proximity or divergence. At a conceptual level, the system uses pattern-recognition techniques on molecular signatures to highlight recurring forms, distinguish substances more reliably and support the identification of contaminants present in environmental samples. This can also help investigators infer whether pollution may stem from similar or distinct origins. The expected impact is more accurate detection of polluting molecules, faster interpretation of analytical results and stronger support for source identification. In practical terms, the approach improves the reliability and scalability of environmental analysis and creates value by enabling more targeted pollution control and remediation efforts.

title: AI to identify entities presenting a risk to economic interests
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Directorate-General for Enterprises - Strategic Information and Economic Security Service
source_description: Authorities responsible for reviewing foreign investment requests must assess not only the immediate transaction but also the broader profile of the entities involved, including whether they may present risks to national economic interests. This is a complex task because the relevant signals may be dispersed across investment files and external information sources, making manual assessment time-consuming and potentially uneven across cases. The use case therefore focuses on improving the processing of foreign investment dossiers and reinforcing economic intelligence capabilities. The stakeholders include public officials reviewing investments, economic-security specialists and decision-makers concerned with strategic assets and national interests, with the objective of identifying higher-risk entities earlier and supporting more consistent risk analysis in investment screening. The solution is implemented by combining information from foreign-investment requests in France with external data sources to detect and characterise entities that may warrant closer examination. At a conceptual level, the system uses entity analysis, cross-source matching and risk-scoring techniques to surface patterns, links or attributes associated with potential threats to France’s economic interests. These outputs are then used to support file processing and prioritisation rather than replace expert judgement. The expected impact is faster and more focused treatment of investment files, improved detection of strategic risks and better use of specialist review capacity. More broadly, the approach strengthens economic-security oversight, improves analytical consistency and creates public value through more informed handling of sensitive foreign investments.

title: Group disputes together with AI for a joint decision
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Administrative courts receive large numbers of claims, and many disputes may concern the same issue, legal basis or factual pattern even if they are filed separately. When these related cases are not identified early, judges and court staff may process them individually, increasing workload, delaying resolution and missing opportunities for more coherent treatment of series litigation. This use case addresses that operational inefficiency by helping courts detect disputes that should be grouped together for joint handling or harmonised decision-making. The stakeholders include administrative judges, court clerks and justice-system managers, with the objective of improving the efficiency of administrative justice while preserving consistency across similar cases. The solution is implemented by analysing the body of requests submitted to administrative courts in order to identify recurring themes and detect case series automatically. At a conceptual level, the system uses document comparison, clustering and thematic similarity techniques to reconcile claims dealing with the same matter and highlight groups of disputes that are likely to benefit from coordinated review. These groupings can then support judicial organisation and case-management decisions. The expected impact is faster processing of repetitive litigation, better consistency in decisions and more efficient allocation of judicial resources. In operational terms, the approach improves scalability in court administration, reduces duplicated effort and creates value by supporting a more streamlined and coherent handling of high-volume administrative disputes.

title: AI for detecting mandatory information and unfair terms in contracts, quotes and invoices
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Directorate-General for Competition, Consumer Affairs and Fraud Control
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Consumer-protection authorities must examine contracts, quotations and invoices to verify whether mandatory information is present and whether contractual terms may be unfair, misleading or detrimental to consumers. This work is legally important but highly document-intensive, especially when investigators recover large numbers of business records during controls and must compare them with prior decisions, opinions and recommendations. The use case therefore addresses the need to strengthen consumer-market oversight while reducing the manual burden involved in document review. The stakeholders include DGCCRF investigators, legal analysts and market-regulation teams, with the objective of improving the detection of non-compliance, enhancing consumer protection and supporting fairer competition. The solution is implemented by analysing reports and documents collected during controls together with the decisions, opinions and recommendations of the Unfair Terms Commission. At a conceptual level, the system uses information extraction, clause classification and thematic analysis to detect mandatory information, identify the subject matter of contract clauses and flag terms that may be unfair according to existing regulatory and interpretative sources. These outputs support investigators in targeting the most problematic documents for closer review. The expected impact is quicker identification of unlawful or problematic contractual content, more consistent enforcement activity and better use of investigative capacity. More broadly, the approach improves reliability, increases scalability in market controls and creates value through stronger consumer protection and more effective competitive regulation.

title: AI to identify breaks in antenna's positioning of terrestrial reference points from satellite data
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: National Institute for Geographic and Forest Information
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Permanent GNSS antennas are essential to the quality of terrestrial reference systems, but interruptions or breaks in their position measurements can degrade the reliability of the data used for geodetic calculations and international reference frameworks. Detecting these discontinuities is technically important because unrecognised shifts may distort downstream analyses, yet manual identification can be difficult across large volumes of satellite-derived positioning data. This use case therefore focuses on improving the monitoring of reference-point measurements so that anomalies can be recognised and incorporated into quality control more systematically. The stakeholders include geodesy specialists, reference-system managers and institutions responsible for maintaining positioning infrastructure, with the objective of preserving the accuracy and consistency of the international terrestrial reference system. The solution is implemented by analysing satellite-based measurements from permanent antennas in order to identify breaks in the observed position series automatically. At a conceptual level, the system uses time-series analysis and anomaly-detection techniques to distinguish genuine discontinuities from normal variation and to flag measurement segments requiring adjustment or expert review. These results can then be integrated into geodetic processing workflows so that identified breaks are taken into account appropriately. The expected impact is improved quality of reference-point data, more reliable maintenance of positioning systems and reduced manual effort in monitoring. In broader terms, the approach enhances precision, supports scalability in geodetic operations and creates value by strengthening a foundational layer of spatial and navigation infrastructure.

title: Identify divergences in case law - Detection of divergent interpretations of the law
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Courts and legal institutions depend on a coherent interpretation of the law, yet divergences can arise when decisions on the same theme evolve differently across jurisdictions or judicial levels. Detecting these discrepancies early is difficult when case law volumes are high and legal reasoning is dispersed across multiple databases and courts. This use case addresses that problem by helping identify decisions that deal with comparable legal issues but may reflect differing interpretations. The stakeholders include magistrates, legal researchers and institutions responsible for ensuring consistency in jurisprudence, with the objective of improving visibility over divergent case law and supporting a more appropriate and harmonised interpretation of legal rules. The solution is implemented using case law data from the Court of Cassation’s Jurinet database and the Courts of Appeal’s JuriCA database. At a conceptual level, the system reconciles decisions dealing with the same subject through thematic comparison and legal-similarity analysis, then highlights areas where the reasoning or legal outcome appears to diverge. These outputs can support expert review, doctrinal analysis and judicial oversight rather than replacing legal interpretation itself. The expected impact is earlier identification of inconsistent jurisprudence, better support for legal harmonisation and more efficient navigation of large case law collections. More broadly, the approach improves reliability in legal analysis, strengthens institutional coherence and creates public value by supporting clearer and more consistent application of the law.

title: Automating coastline correction work - Improve coastal mapping
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Hydrographic and Oceanographic Service of the Navy
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Maintaining an accurate national coastline repository is a demanding task because shorelines change over time and raw observation data often require careful correction before they can be used in official mapping. For the Hydrographic and Oceanographic Service of the Navy, this creates a significant operational burden, as agents must review large volumes of coastal measurements to ensure that reference data remain reliable for navigation, planning and environmental management. The use case therefore addresses the need to speed up and standardise coastline correction work while preserving the quality of the French coastal reference base. The stakeholders include hydrographic specialists, cartographic teams and public authorities that depend on precise coastal information, with the objective of improving production efficiency and reducing the manual effort involved in updating shoreline data. The solution is implemented using laser remote-sensing measurements collected through lidar surveys along the coast. At a conceptual level, analytical models are applied to these geospatial point clouds to detect the relevant coastal contours and automate part of the correction work previously carried out by agents. The resulting outputs are then integrated into the production chain for the national coastline repository, where they support validation and refinement. The expected impact is faster updating of coastal maps, greater consistency in correction processes and better use of expert staff time. More broadly, the approach improves scalability, strengthens the reliability of coastal reference data and creates public value through more efficient management of a critical national geospatial asset.

title: Safe Spotter - AI platform to detect and transmit data of an accident
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Safe Spotter was developed for the Municipality of Monserrato as part of a broader effort to create an innovative and sustainable smart-city model focused on citizen protection and territorial management. The use case responds to a critical road-safety challenge: when traffic accidents occur, emergency response depends on the rapid availability of reliable information on what happened, where it happened and which vehicles may be involved. Delays or incomplete information can affect the ability of public authorities and emergency services to intervene effectively. The objective is therefore to strengthen the municipality’s capacity to govern road safety by detecting accidents automatically and transmitting essential data quickly. The AI platform uses an advanced network of cameras and sound sensors installed on intelligent street lights. The sound sensors are designed to recognise noises associated with traffic accidents and activate a directional camera when a relevant event is detected. The system then collects Minimum Safe Data, including images or videos, time, location, vehicle direction and registration number. This information can be transmitted to support situational awareness and response coordination. The expected impact is faster accident detection, improved evidence for emergency intervention, stronger monitoring of road-safety events and better protection of citizens. The use case also demonstrates how urban lighting infrastructure can be repurposed as a platform for smart public-safety services.

title: Voice-bot ACOSS - answering questions from users
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Central Agency of Social Security Bodies (ACOSS):
source_description: The Central Agency of Social Security Bodies developed the ACOSS voice-bot to answer questions from users of the Chèque Emploi Associatif, addressing a common service-delivery challenge in social-administration contexts: large volumes of routine enquiries can slow response times and place heavy demand on human support channels. The objective of the initiative was to provide faster, more accessible answers for users while easing pressure on administrative teams responsible for handling repeated questions. The stakeholders included ACOSS, users of the Chèque Emploi Associatif service and customer-support staff, with the intention of improving responsiveness and simplifying access to information by telephone. The solution was implemented as a conversational voice agent capable of interacting with callers and supplying responses automatically. At a conceptual level, the system used voice-based dialogue handling to recognise incoming questions, match them to relevant service information and deliver spoken answers within the call flow, creating an automated first-line support channel for the service. This allowed routine issues to be handled without immediate staff intervention and offered a more scalable way to provide information to users. While detailed performance figures are not provided in the source material, the expected benefits included faster access to answers, reduced administrative workload and more efficient handling of common queries. The voice-bot is no longer in use, but it remains a relevant example of how social-security institutions experimented with conversational voice technology to modernise user support.

title: Better guide environmental police checks
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Environmental police services must decide where to direct limited inspection resources across large territories and a wide variety of ecological risks, from habitat degradation to unlawful activities affecting protected areas. Without strong targeting, inspections may be dispersed too broadly, reducing their deterrent effect and limiting the capacity of authorities to intervene where environmental harm is most likely or most severe. This use case addresses that challenge by helping the French Biodiversity Agency improve how controls are planned and prioritised. The stakeholders include environmental inspectors, biodiversity-protection teams and public authorities responsible for safeguarding natural ecosystems, with the objective of making inspections more efficient and strengthening the effectiveness of environmental enforcement. The solution is implemented through analytical methods that help identify patterns of risk and guide control activity towards higher-priority locations or situations. At a conceptual level, the system combines available environmental, territorial and operational information to support risk-based targeting of checks, enabling inspectors to focus attention where potential infringements or ecological pressures are more likely to occur. These outputs complement, rather than replace, field expertise and enforcement judgement. The expected impact is better allocation of inspection effort, more targeted interventions and stronger protection for vulnerable ecosystems. In operational terms, the approach improves efficiency, supports scalability in environmental policing and creates value by increasing the effectiveness of public controls without requiring a proportional increase in field resources.

title: ASN: better use of the data contained in follow-up letter of inspections
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The French Nuclear Safety Authority, ASN, developed this use case to improve how inspection knowledge is exploited in the regulation of nuclear installations. Following the Fukushima accident of 11 March 2011, ASN requested operators on 5 May 2011 to undertake complementary safety assessments of their installations, reinforcing the importance of systematic oversight and evidence-based inspection practices. A major operational challenge was the large volume of information contained in around 20,000 inspection follow-up letters. These documents include observations, recommendations and signals that may be relevant for identifying recurring issues or emerging trends, but manual analysis at this scale is demanding and limits the ability of inspectors to detect patterns across time, sites and themes. The objective was to transform unstructured inspection correspondence into structured information that could support inspectors in their work. The AI solution applies text-analysis techniques to inspection follow-up letters in order to detect weak signals, extract relevant information and identify statistical trends. At a conceptual level, the tool processes regulatory documents, organises their content and makes recurring themes more visible to inspection teams. Its value lies in providing a ready-to-use decision-support capability, improving the exploitation of accumulated inspection evidence, reducing time spent on manual document review and strengthening ASN’s ability to identify cross-cutting safety issues across the nuclear sector.

title: Automatically detecting irregularities in occupancy soils
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Departmental Directorate of Territories and the Sea (DDTM) of L'Hérault
source_description: Monitoring land use across a territory is a complex responsibility, particularly when authorities need to identify irregular developments such as illegal construction, unauthorised land occupation or waste dumping over large areas. Manual inspection alone is costly, slow and often unable to provide timely visibility of emerging problems. This use case, developed by the Departmental Directorate of Territories and the Sea of Hérault, addresses that operational challenge by improving the detection of irregularities in land occupation and use. The stakeholders include territorial authorities, environmental and planning officers and inspection teams, with the objective of strengthening oversight, accelerating detection and improving the protection of land and natural environments. The solution is implemented through the analysis of aerial and satellite imagery to identify patterns that may indicate unlawful or abnormal land-use activity. At a conceptual level, image-analysis and classification techniques are applied to large-scale geospatial data in order to detect changes or anomalies associated with illegal constructions, dumping or other irregular uses of land. These findings can then be routed into administrative and inspection workflows for verification and follow-up. The expected impact is quicker identification of suspect sites, reduced reliance on labour-intensive visual review and better prioritisation of field controls. More broadly, the approach improves scalability in territorial monitoring, enhances the reliability of detection and creates public value by supporting more effective environmental and land-use enforcement.

title: Targeting establishment inspection - refine targeting of establishments for inspections
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: General Directorate of Food (DGAL) of the Ministry of Agriculture and Food:
source_description: The General Directorate of Food of the French Ministry of Agriculture and Food developed this use case to improve the targeting of inspections in establishments that sell or deliver food directly to consumers, including restaurants, catering businesses and distributors. Food-safety inspection authorities must allocate limited inspection resources across a large and diverse population of establishments, where risks may vary depending on hygiene practices, customer experience, operational conditions and previous signals. Traditional targeting methods may not fully capture emerging problems or recent consumer concerns, particularly where relevant information appears first in public feedback channels. The objective of the use case is to refine the prioritisation of establishments to be inspected by using additional evidence from online consumer reviews. The AI component analyses reviews published on online platforms to identify signals that may suggest possible food-safety or hygiene concerns. Natural language processing can be used to detect relevant terms, patterns of complaints or sentiment linked to establishments, which can then inform inspection planning alongside existing administrative data and regulatory criteria. The system is intended to support, not replace, professional judgement by inspectors. Its expected impact is a more risk-informed allocation of inspection capacity, earlier identification of establishments requiring attention, better use of publicly available feedback and improved protection of consumers through more targeted food-safety controls.

title: Intelligence Emploi
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Intelligence Emploi was introduced within Pôle emploi as a transformation initiative aimed at accelerating the return to sustainable employment. The use case addresses a central labour-market challenge: employment services must support large numbers of jobseekers with different profiles, skills, barriers and career objectives, while also responding to employer demand and changing labour-market conditions. Public employment counsellors need tools that help them identify relevant opportunities, personalise support and prioritise interventions without reducing the quality of human guidance. The objective is therefore to strengthen Pôle emploi’s capacity to help people move into stable work more quickly and effectively. The AI implementation acts as a lever within employment-service processes, using available labour-market, jobseeker and vacancy-related data to support matching, guidance and decision-making. At a conceptual level, models may analyse profiles, skills, employment histories, job offers and contextual indicators to identify suitable pathways or opportunities for users. These outputs can help advisers provide more tailored support and improve the relevance of recommendations made to jobseekers. The expected impact is faster return to sustainable employment, better targeting of support measures, improved efficiency for counsellors and greater personalisation of public employment services. For the administration, the use case supports a more data-driven service model while preserving the role of employment professionals in guiding complex individual transitions.

title: AI for targeting fraud and valuing requests (CFVR) to improve the efficiency of tax audits
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Ministry of Action and Public Accounts - DGFIP
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Tax administrations must process very large volumes of information from multiple public sources in order to identify cases where individuals or companies may not be complying with their fiscal obligations. The difficulty lies in distinguishing the truly high-risk situations from the mass of ordinary declarations, especially where discrepancies may result from error, omission or deliberate fraud. This use case addresses that challenge by helping the Directorate General of Public Finances target tax audits more effectively and allocate investigative resources where they are most justified. The stakeholders include tax auditors, compliance teams and public-finance authorities, with the objective of improving the efficiency, fairness and consistency of fiscal controls. The solution is implemented within the CFVR system through large-scale processing and cross-checking of data collected by different administrations. At a conceptual level, the system analyses patterns such as abrupt changes in income, inconsistencies between declared situations and other indicators of risk in order to generate prioritised signals for tax-control teams. These signals support audit selection and case valuation while leaving the final judgement to tax professionals. The expected impact is more accurate targeting of audits, reduced time spent on low-yield controls and better recovery of irregular situations. In operational and public-value terms, the approach increases scalability, strengthens the credibility of tax enforcement and creates value through more efficient use of control resources and fairer treatment of compliant taxpayers.

title: Datascience
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Ministry of the Interior carries out a wide range of missions, from security and territorial administration to crisis management and public-policy coordination, all of which generate substantial volumes of data. The operational challenge is to turn that information into structured insight that can support strategic analysis consistently across the ministry rather than in isolated, ad hoc exercises. This use case focuses on expanding the activity of the scientific laboratory, or datalab, created in 2016 so that data-driven methods can be embedded more systematically across the organisation. The stakeholders include ministry analysts, operational departments and senior decision-makers, with the objective of strengthening strategic analysis, improving cross-cutting understanding of complex issues and enabling broader adoption of advanced analytical methods in support of ministerial missions. The solution is implemented by enlarging the datalab’s role, capabilities and analytical reach, creating a shared environment for data exploitation and the emergence of more advanced modelling approaches. At a conceptual level, this involves structuring data-science practices, developing reusable analytical workflows and promoting the use of predictive and exploratory techniques across multiple business areas of the ministry. The expected impact is better-informed decision-making, stronger analytical consistency and greater capacity to address diverse operational questions at scale. More broadly, the initiative improves institutional agility, supports innovation in public administration and creates value by making strategic analysis more systematic, reusable and relevant to the full range of the Ministry of the Interior’s responsibilities.

title: Health data hub - Creation of a big data infrastructure in health
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Ministry of Solidarity and Health - DREES
source_description: Health systems produce vast quantities of information, yet the value of these data is often constrained by fragmentation, inconsistent access and a shortage of shared tools and expertise to make them usable for research and operational decision-making. This use case addresses that structural problem by creating a health data infrastructure capable of supporting analysis at scale and improving how data are mobilised across the healthcare ecosystem. Led by the Department of Research, Studies, Evaluation and Statistics of the Ministry of Solidarity and Health, the initiative involves researchers, policymakers, planners and healthcare stakeholders, with the objective of strengthening clinical research, improving support for resource-allocation decisions and enabling more predictive and effective forms of medicine. The solution is implemented through a big-data infrastructure in health that brings together datasets, analytical tools and specialist capabilities within a common framework. At a conceptual level, the platform is designed to facilitate secure data use, support large-scale analysis and provide the technical and organisational foundation needed for data-driven research and decision support. This creates an environment in which health information can be used more systematically to generate evidence and operational insight. The expected impact is improved efficiency in the health system, stronger support for clinical and policy analysis and better conditions for innovation in care and research. More broadly, the initiative enhances scalability, strengthens the value extracted from health data and creates public benefit through a more informed, coordinated and forward-looking healthcare system.

title: Expert systems in meteorology and climate to better forecasting
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Ministry of Ecological and Inclusive Transition - Météo France
source_description: Weather and climate services must produce forecasts that are not only scientifically robust but also understandable, timely and useful for a wide range of users affected by meteorological risks. For Météo-France, this means continually improving predictive capability while also adapting communication tools and workforce practices to new operational realities. This use case addresses that dual challenge by modernising forecasting methods and supporting the organisation’s staff as their professional roles evolve alongside new technologies. The stakeholders include meteorologists, climate specialists, operational forecasters and end users of weather information, with the objective of improving the prediction of meteorological phenomena and their impacts while making forecast outputs more actionable and easier to communicate. The solution is implemented through expert systems and machine-learning-based approaches that enhance the modelling and interpretation of weather and climate data. At a conceptual level, these methods are used to refine forecasting processes, support impact-oriented analysis and integrate more effective communication tools into operational workflows. At the same time, the project supports staff in adapting to new modes of work and decision support. The expected impact is better forecasting performance, clearer communication of risks and stronger operational efficiency within the forecasting chain. More broadly, the initiative increases institutional resilience, improves the usefulness of meteorological services and creates value by combining technical innovation with organisational transformation.

title: Indexing of Government photos for better identification on photos using facial recognition
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Government’s Information and Press Service of Luxembourg implemented this use case to improve the management of a large media library of political photographs belonging to the Luxembourg State. The operational problem was the manual indexing of extensive photographic collections, a process described as laborious and time-consuming. Without efficient metadata, the value of the media library is reduced, as photographs are harder to retrieve, identify and reuse by public institutions. The objective was to accelerate the identification of politicians appearing in government photographs and to improve the quality and completeness of metadata associated with the collection. The AI project uses facial-recognition technology to identify political figures in images and generate enhanced metadata for the media library. At a conceptual level, the system analyses visual features in photographs, compares them with authorised reference material and supports the tagging of individuals appearing in the images. The resulting metadata makes the collection easier to search and manage, while reducing the manual effort required from staff. The impact has been to facilitate and accelerate metadata production, improve the usability of the State’s photographic resources and enable better exploitation of the media library’s content across government. The use case delivers administrative efficiency, strengthens information management and supports more consistent reuse of public visual records.

title: Extraction of topographical objects - AI to extract topographical objects from aerial images
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Updating national topographic and land-registry databases is labour-intensive, particularly when officials must identify newly built structures, new roads and emerging construction areas from large volumes of aerial imagery. This creates delays in keeping official spatial records current and can limit the quality and timeliness of services that depend on accurate geographic information. The use case therefore addresses the need to modernise how the Land Registry and Topography Administration detects changes in the built environment and maintains its databases. The stakeholders include mapping specialists, cadastral officials and public bodies that rely on up-to-date territorial information, with the objective of reducing manual workload, accelerating updates and improving the overall quality of topographical data. The solution is implemented through automated extraction of topographical objects from aerial images using computer-vision and object-detection techniques. At a conceptual level, the system analyses imagery to identify features such as buildings and roads, distinguishes new elements from the existing mapped environment and feeds these outputs into the database-update process. This creates a more efficient workflow for detecting construction areas and for enriching official geospatial records. The expected impact is faster database maintenance, improved data quality and lower administrative effort for State officials. More broadly, the initiative enhances scalability, supports the creation of new data and services, and strengthens the public value of official geospatial infrastructure through more timely and reliable mapping.

title: CLAVIS project - Automatic recognition of old handwritten documents
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Historical archives contain vast quantities of handwritten material that remain difficult to exploit because older manuscripts are often challenging to read, search and interpret at scale. For the Luxembourg National Archives, this limits the accessibility of important seventeenth- and eighteenth-century sources and constrains the extent to which researchers can use them effectively. The CLAVIS project addresses this documentary bottleneck by improving the legibility and usability of digitised manuscript collections. The stakeholders include archivists, historians, researchers and cultural-heritage institutions, with the objective of making historic documents more accessible, searchable and useful for future generations while also improving archival description processes. The solution is implemented by submitting digitised manuscript images to Transkribus, a platform for automated handwriting recognition, transcription and search in historic documents. At a conceptual level, the system processes scanned archival pages, converts handwritten text into machine-readable transcriptions and enables downstream uses such as content search, structured retrieval and the automated generation of inventories or indexes of people and places. This transforms previously difficult-to-use archival sources into a more navigable digital resource. The expected impact is greatly improved accessibility to historical records, reduced manual transcription effort and stronger support for archival research and discovery. More broadly, the project improves the scalability of document processing, enriches cultural-heritage services and creates value by opening complex manuscript collections to much wider scholarly and public use.

title: 3D scan underground infrastructure - Prevention damage of critical infrastructure
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Arnhem’s 3D scan project focuses on preventing accidental damage to critical underground infrastructure during construction work. The operational issue is that sewer infrastructure is often located below ground in ways that may be difficult for construction teams to visualise accurately from the surface, creating a risk of costly damage, service disruption and safety hazards. The municipality’s approach combines a precise 3D scan of the main sewer with an application that visualises the sewer’s location above ground. The implementation therefore links geospatial surveying, three-dimensional infrastructure modelling and field-based visualisation, allowing users to understand the position of underground assets before or during works. Conceptually, the system turns hidden sewer infrastructure into a digital and spatially interpretable layer that can be consulted by staff or contractors. The expected impact is fewer accidental strikes, better planning of construction activities, reduced repair costs and improved protection of essential municipal infrastructure. By making underground assets more visible and usable in operational settings, the project supports safer, more data-driven public works management.

title: 8TING - Analysis of drivers to keep people in class
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: 8Ting, business office Work & Income of the municipality of Enschede
source_description: 8TING was used in Enschede to apply psychology and web technology to support people participating in municipal work-and-income or training pathways. The operational problem is that people may drop out of programmes when support is not aligned with their personal motivation, behaviour, context or barriers. The system seeks to make clear who needs what type of attention by monitoring and adjusting more than 80 factors related to internal drivers. Its implementation uses profiles, behavioural data and contextual indicators to plan automatic or semi-automatic interventions, such as measurements, encouragement and targeted support activities intended to keep people engaged in class or training. Conceptually, the tool combines behavioural profiling, motivation analysis, web-based interaction, programme planning and adaptive support. The expected impact is better retention in training, more personalised support, earlier identification of disengagement risks and improved effectiveness of municipal activation services. At the same time, because the tool analyses behavioural and psychological drivers, careful safeguards are needed around transparency, consent, proportionality and the avoidance of overly deterministic profiling of participants.

title: Agent system

source_description: ProRail’s agent system is designed to support train traffic controllers when disruptions or delays occur on the Dutch rail network. The operational challenge is that small delays can propagate quickly through interconnected railway services, requiring rapid decisions on routing, prioritisation and recovery measures. Train traffic controllers must assess complex operational conditions under time pressure, balancing passenger disruption, infrastructure capacity and the need to prevent knock-on effects. The agent functions as an autonomous computer programme that operates with defined goals and associated actions, providing advice to controllers on how to respond to delays and reduce further disruption. At a conceptual level, the system can be understood as a decision-support agent that analyses traffic conditions, expected train movements, available infrastructure and possible operational choices, then proposes interventions for human operators to consider. The expected impact is improved punctuality, better use of available rail capacity and more consistent support during disruption management. By assisting controllers rather than replacing them, the system can help preserve human responsibility while improving the speed and quality of operational advice in complex traffic situations.

title: AI for public space notifications - Image recognition to analyse reports

context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Municipalities receive many citizen reports about defects and inconveniences in public space, ranging from loose paving stones and broken streetlights to potentially dangerous situations requiring urgent intervention. Although these reports are valuable, they can vary greatly in clarity and completeness, which means staff must spend time interpreting the issue before deciding how to respond. This use case, explored by the municipality of Dordrecht, addresses that operational friction by seeking to make reporting easier for residents and the follow-up process more efficient for municipal teams. The stakeholders include citizens, municipal service staff and teams responsible for public-space maintenance, with the objective of improving intake quality, speeding up case assessment and supporting quicker resolution of local problems. The solution is implemented through image-recognition techniques applied to photographs submitted with defect reports. At a conceptual level, the system analyses the uploaded image to identify the type of issue reported, extract relevant visual cues and support routing or prioritisation within the municipal workflow. This gives staff a clearer starting point for action and may reduce the need for repeated clarification. The expected impact is faster processing of public-space notifications, reduced administrative effort and a smoother user experience for residents. More broadly, the approach improves service responsiveness, enhances consistency in case handling and creates value by linking citizen reporting more directly to operational action.

title: AI Chatbot Robin - Answer questions about business transfers

source_description: Agricultural entrepreneurs need accessible and consistent guidance when preparing or managing business transfers, as these processes involve administrative, financial and sector-specific questions that can be difficult to navigate through static information pages alone. AI Chatbot Robin addresses this need by providing a virtual agent for the Netherlands Enterprise Agency that answers questions on agricultural business transfers. The service builds on the earlier Pilot Watson and went live in April 2019, moving from an experimental conversational service towards a more operational support channel for users seeking information from the agency. Its purpose is to offer a first point of contact for recurring questions, helping business owners or prospective successors understand relevant procedures and obtain guidance without immediately relying on telephone or email support. The implementation uses chatbot technology to interpret user questions and match them with prepared knowledge on agricultural business-transfer topics. At a conceptual level, the system relies on natural language understanding, a structured knowledge base and conversational flows that guide users towards relevant answers. The main value is improved availability of information, more efficient handling of repetitive enquiries and a more user-friendly digital service for agricultural stakeholders. For the administration, Robin also supports channel shifting and allows staff to focus on more complex or case-specific requests.

source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Police control rooms handle continuous streams of incident data and real-time reports, yet anticipating where risks may emerge remains a difficult task in fast-changing urban environments. The AICrimePrediction feasibility study, carried out by Amsterdam police and Ciphix, addresses the challenge of improving situational awareness and supporting earlier, better-informed deployment decisions in relation to crime and terrorism risks. The stakeholders include control-room staff, police planners and operational decision-makers, with the objective of understanding whether available data can be used to generate sufficiently accurate risk predictions to strengthen prevention and response. Rather than focusing only on historical review, the use case seeks to inform live operational choices by connecting past patterns with current signals. The solution is implemented by combining historical control-room data, including type of incident, time and location, with real-time reporting inputs. At a conceptual level, the system applies predictive modelling to spatio-temporal and incident-pattern data in order to estimate the likelihood of criminal or terrorism-related risk in particular contexts or locations. These predictions are intended to support operational awareness and resource allocation rather than replace police judgement. The expected impact is more targeted monitoring, improved readiness and better use of police capacity in high-risk situations. More broadly, the feasibility study explores whether data-driven forecasting can strengthen public-safety operations through greater precision, timeliness and coordination in risk assessment.

The expected impact is quicker preparation of learning reports, reduced manual processing and stronger consistency in how findings are compiled.
