source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Plant and tree health monitoring is essential for protecting agriculture, biodiversity and wider environmental quality, yet disease detection across large areas can be difficult, time-consuming and dependent on scarce specialist expertise. The NVWA pilot addresses this challenge by exploring a more efficient way to identify signs of disease in plants and trees before problems spread or become more costly to manage. The stakeholders include inspectors, plant-health specialists and authorities responsible for biosecurity and environmental protection, with the objective of improving early detection, strengthening surveillance capacity and supporting more timely interventions. The use case responds to the practical need for broader, more scalable monitoring in contexts where manual inspection alone may not provide sufficient coverage or speed. The solution is implemented through a pilot that applies image-based analysis to detect disease-related patterns in vegetation. At a conceptual level, the system uses machine-learning techniques trained on visual indicators of plant or tree illness in order to distinguish healthy from potentially affected specimens and to support inspection prioritisation. These outputs can then be incorporated into plant-health workflows to guide follow-up checks and decisions. The expected impact is faster identification of potential disease outbreaks, better targeting of inspection resources and reduced reliance on purely manual screening. More broadly, the approach improves scalability, enhances the reliability of plant-health monitoring and creates value through stronger preventive action in environmental and agricultural protection.

title: AI for detecting Asian Hornbill
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Detecting the presence of the Asian hornet is a growing operational priority because this invasive species can threaten biodiversity, disrupt ecosystems and create risks for beekeeping and public safety. The challenge for inspectors is that suspected nests are not always easy to confirm quickly in the field, particularly across wide outdoor areas, and accurate species identification is essential to avoid unnecessary intervention. This use case, led by the NVWA, addresses that problem by improving how potential sightings and nest reports are verified. The stakeholders include inspectors, environmental authorities and members of the public reporting possible nests, with the objective of accelerating detection, improving species recognition and supporting more targeted intervention against the invasive hornet. The solution is implemented through two complementary tools: drone surveys equipped with thermal-imaging cameras for suspected nest areas, and an image-recognition application that helps distinguish between the Asian hornet and the European hornet. At a conceptual level, the system combines aerial thermal sensing with visual classification models to support both field detection and species verification. These capabilities can then be integrated into the NVWA’s inspection workflow to prioritise action and reduce uncertainty. The expected impact is faster confirmation of nest locations, more reliable differentiation between species and better use of inspection resources. More broadly, the approach enhances scalability, supports environmental protection and creates public value through a more responsive and accurate invasive-species control process.

At a conceptual level, the system combines aerial imaging, machine-learning-based pattern detection and inspection workflows so that unusual features can be highlighted and assessed for follow-up. These outputs can then support decisions on where to deploy staff, laboratory analysis or specialist equipment. The expected impact is more efficient use of inspection capacity, improved targeting of controls and stronger food-safety protection through earlier and more reliable anomaly detection. title: AIDA (Artificial Intelligence Disaster Advisor), and Horizon 2020 project
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: During major incidents, control rooms are confronted with a flood of potentially relevant information arriving from social media, public channels and other data sources, yet it is rarely possible for emergency staff to collect, validate and assess all of it in real time. This creates an information paradox: there is abundant data, but not enough operational clarity, which can hinder decision-making, slow coordination and ultimately endanger lives. AIDA was developed to address this challenge by helping emergency services identify and use the most relevant information during a crisis. The stakeholders include control-room operators, emergency responders and coordinating authorities, with the objective of improving situational awareness and enabling faster, more informed action in high-pressure scenarios. The solution is implemented by combining big-data processing, data-science methods and streaming architectures to ingest and filter information from multiple public and non-public sources. At a conceptual level, the system analyses incoming data flows, evaluates relevance and rapidly distributes prioritised information to emergency services so that operational teams can focus on the most important signals. This supports live crisis management rather than retrospective analysis. The expected impact is better-informed emergency handling, faster access to critical intelligence and improved coordination across services. In practical terms, AIDA strengthens responsiveness, increases the usability of complex data in crisis settings and creates public value by supporting actions that can better save and protect human lives.

title: Anti-cheat software for exams
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: University of Rotterdam and other 14 dutch universities
source_description: Higher education institutions conducting remote examinations need to preserve the integrity of assessments while managing the practical limitations of supervising students outside traditional examination rooms. Anti-cheat software for exams refers to the use of Proctorexam by several Dutch higher education institutions, including the University of Rotterdam and other universities, to monitor students during online tests. The operational challenge is to detect possible cheating in a digital setting where invigilators cannot physically observe candidates, but where fairness, equal treatment and the reliability of qualifications remain essential. The software enables remote surveillance through a student’s webcam, microphone and web browser, allowing examination behaviour and the digital environment to be monitored during the assessment. Its technical implementation combines online proctoring functions with automated or semi-automated detection of behaviours that may be classified as suspicious, such as unusual movements, browser activity or environmental signals. The system can flag students for further review, rather than necessarily determining misconduct on its own. The expected benefit for institutions is greater capacity to run remote examinations while maintaining oversight and reducing manual invigilation constraints. However, the use of such systems also raises important concerns around privacy, proportionality, transparency and student trust, meaning that its operational value depends strongly on governance safeguards, review procedures and clear communication with candidates.

source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Rijkswaterstaat needed a more efficient and affordable way to inspect national roads and waterways, since traditional inspection approaches often depend on expensive professional camera equipment and limited collection capacity. Routine infrastructure inspection is essential for maintaining safety and service quality, but manual processes and specialist hardware can restrict coverage and raise costs. The use case therefore focused on expanding inspection capability while lowering the barriers to large-scale visual data collection. The stakeholders include Rijkswaterstaat, inspection teams and infrastructure managers, with the objective of automating a larger share of road and waterway inspection and improving the timeliness and consistency of asset monitoring. The solution is implemented through standard Android smartphones mounted on cars and ships, each running an application that captures an image every second. At a conceptual level, these images are combined with geographic data and used to train a cloud-based neural network that can recognise relevant infrastructure conditions and support automated inspection tasks. By using inexpensive, widely available devices instead of specialist cameras, the system creates a more scalable and flexible inspection model. The expected impact is lower equipment cost, broader inspection coverage and faster collection of infrastructure data. More broadly, the project creates value by modernising public-asset monitoring, improving operational efficiency and demonstrating how low-cost sensing combined with cloud-based analysis can reshape large-scale infrastructure inspection.

title: Combating Online Child Abuse

source_description: Authorities and online-safety stakeholders face the urgent challenge of identifying illegal child sexual abuse imagery on the internet quickly enough to support removal and limit further harm. These capabilities are intended to complement, not replace, human oversight in highly sensitive decision-making. The expected impact is faster detection of illegal material, reduced manual burden on specialist teams and more effective support for online removal. More broadly, the approach improves scalability, strengthens digital safeguarding and creates public value through better protection of children online.

title: Tree Monitor - Detecting illegal logging
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Province of Gelderland, NEO, Wageningen Environmental Research
source_description: Regional authorities responsible for environmental protection need reliable methods to identify tree loss and possible illegal logging across large territories where field inspections alone may be slow, selective or reactive. Tree Monitor gives the Province of Gelderland an additional monitoring tool for detecting potential illegal felling by comparing satellite images from different years. Operational since December 2017, the system helps authorities locate areas where trees appear to have disappeared and visualises these changes on a map. The objective is to improve the detection of irregular tree removal and support more targeted follow-up by enforcement or environmental-management teams. The implementation uses Earth observation data, with satellite imagery analysed across time to identify changes in vegetation cover. At a conceptual level, image-comparison techniques detect differences between historical and more recent satellite data, highlighting locations where tree cover has declined. These outputs can then be reviewed by officials and used to prioritise inspections or further investigation. The initiative involves the Province of Gelderland, NEO and Wageningen Environmental Research, combining public environmental responsibilities with specialist geospatial expertise. The implementation combines machine-learning methods with administrative tax data, inspection histories and feedback loops from previous control results. Models are progressively refined as additional outcomes become available, improving their capacity to identify relevant risk patterns. The potential impact is more efficient allocation of inspection and recovery resources, faster identification of actionable cases and improved use of existing administrative data. At the same time, such systems require careful governance to ensure transparency, legality, non-discrimination and appropriate human oversight in tax decision-making.

The objective was to provide public authorities with a decision-support capability that helps them understand crowd dynamics and take timely measures to improve the use of public space. The emerging technology implementation centres on the Crowd Management Decision-Support System, a software-based platform licensed through City Analytics to government authorities. At conceptual level, the system combines pedestrian-flow data, urban analytics and operational decision-support functions to help authorities assess crowding conditions, anticipate risks and select appropriate interventions. title: CrossWalk in Smart City Rijswijk
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The municipality of Rijswijk tested CrossWalk to address a concrete accessibility and road-safety challenge: standard pedestrian crossing times are often insufficient for older people, people with disabilities or citizens with reduced mobility. This can create unsafe situations at intersections and reduce the autonomy of residents who require more time to cross the road. The pilot involved the Municipality of Rijswijk and Dynniq, with the objective of making pedestrian infrastructure more responsive to the needs of vulnerable road users while avoiding permanent changes to signal timing for all pedestrians. The emerging technology implementation is based on a mobile application connected to traffic signal systems. When a registered user with mobility difficulties approaches or waits at a crossing, the app uses location data to communicate with the traffic control software and signal the user’s presence. The traffic light system can then automatically extend the green phase, allowing additional time for a safe crossing. At conceptual level, the solution integrates mobile positioning, traffic-light control logic and intersection management systems. Its impact lies in improving pedestrian safety, accessibility and user experience for residents who walk more slowly. It also demonstrates how smart-city infrastructure can provide targeted support without redesigning the entire traffic system, making the approach potentially scalable to other intersections and municipalities with similar accessibility objectives.

The problem addressed is not a single faulty dataset, but the broader need to maintain trustworthy records across the systems that underpin local public services. Poor data quality can lead to delays, incorrect processing, duplicated work or reduced confidence in digital administration. The implementation uses Phinion’s Qbot product, which applies machine-learning techniques to discover patterns and deviations within and between registrations. At a conceptual level, the system examines relationships in administrative data, identifies anomalies and highlights inconsistencies that may require correction or further investigation. This enables the municipality to move from ad hoc data-quality checks towards more continuous monitoring. The expected impact is higher-quality registrations, earlier detection of data problems, improved operational reliability and better support for service delivery. By helping staff identify structural issues in the data, the pilot also contributes to more efficient back-office processes and strengthens the foundation for future digital services that depend on accurate municipal information.

title: Algorithm Impact monitor bridge openings
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Province of South Holland must manage the movement of both road traffic and shipping across a region where bridge openings can create delays, congestion and competing demands between transport modes. The smart bridge addresses this challenge by using digital monitoring and predictive analytics to support more informed bridge-operation decisions across an infrastructure portfolio that includes more than 100 bridges. The initiative forms part of South Holland’s wider work on smart shipping and focuses on linking up-to-date road-traffic information with live shipping information, so that the impact of bridge openings can be better understood and anticipated. In the project “impact monitor bridge openings”, the province has taken an important step towards predicting traffic intensities around several key bridges. The technological implementation combines sensor-based data collection, traffic information and algorithmic analysis, including Long Short-Term Memory neural networks designed to forecast traffic conditions up to 21 minutes ahead. These models are suited to time-series prediction because they can learn from sequential patterns in traffic behaviour and bridge-operation data. The reported correlation-efficient accuracy of 60–80% indicates that the approach can provide useful short-term forecasts for operational planning. The main value is improved anticipation of congestion, better coordination between road and waterway mobility, more evidence-based bridge management and a stronger basis for reducing disruption while keeping both transport networks accessible and safe.

The implementation uses video analytics and behaviour-recognition models to process visual information from cameras, identify movement or interaction patterns associated with abnormal events, and generate alerts for security or assistance personnel. Conceptually, the system combines computer vision, behavioural classification, anomaly detection and real-time alerting. The expected impact is faster deployment of staff, reduced harm to the public, more efficient incident response and better management of safety risks in large public areas. title: Firework nuisance detection system - AI to determine if bangs are firework
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Dutch municipalities face recurring public order and safety issues linked to illegal fireworks, particularly during evenings and festive periods, placing strain on enforcement capacity and generating resident complaints. The firework nuisance detection system was introduced to help municipalities such as Amersfoort identify when and where fireworks are being set off, enabling more targeted enforcement. Stakeholders include municipal authorities, enforcement officers, residents and public safety services. The objective is to distinguish fireworks from other loud noises, identify nuisance hotspots and optimise patrol routes and response times without relying solely on citizen reports. The system combines a distributed network of acoustic sensors placed in public space, which capture sound events and triangulate their location when multiple sensors detect the same bang. Signal-processing and classification techniques analyse acoustic signatures to distinguish fireworks from other impulsive sounds such as slamming doors or vehicle backfires. When a sound is classified as fireworks, alerts are automatically sent to municipal enforcers via mobile devices, alongside spatial and temporal data. The pilot has improved situational awareness and allowed more selective deployment of enforcement resources. Qualitatively, municipalities report faster response times, better evidence-based planning and improved transparency around nuisance patterns, while residents benefit from more visible and timely enforcement.

From a technological perspective, the system functions as a search and retrieval tool that can scan public sources, interpret user queries and return potentially relevant material for policy officers to review. source_description: Organisations that generate residual materials often lack efficient mechanisms to identify potential reusers, assess the value of surplus flows and close material loops across sectors. The operational objective is to move residual materials away from disposal or low-value treatment and towards productive reuse by making information about available materials more visible, comparable and actionable. The technology implementation relies on artificial intelligence to read, interpret and structure data on material streams, including information on composition, availability, quality, location and potential applications. Matching algorithms then identify possible links between suppliers and buyers, including combinations that may not be obvious through manual brokerage. The platform’s intelligence lies not only in listing materials, but also in actively bringing together parties whose residual flows and needs may align. The expected impact is faster matching, greater scalability in circular-material exchange, reduced transaction costs and improved resource efficiency. For participating organisations, EME can support waste reduction, lower procurement or disposal costs, and contribute to broader sustainability and circular-economy objectives.

organization: Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA)
source_description: The Graasdierpremie pilot examines whether drones and automated image analysis can improve the counting and monitoring of grazing animals. The operational problem is that animal-distribution and abundance monitoring is traditionally carried out manually on foot or through aerial recording from manned aircraft, both of which can be costly, slow and labour-intensive. For public authorities such as the NVWA, more efficient monitoring can support nature conservation, agricultural control and subsidy-related verification. The implementation uses drone imagery to collect visual data on animals in the field, combined with computer-vision methods that detect, classify and count animals automatically. Conceptually, the system replaces broad manual observation with aerial data capture, image-processing pipelines and automated counting models, while still requiring quality checks and validation by competent staff. The expected impact is faster monitoring of animal populations, reduced inspection costs, improved geographical coverage and more consistent evidence for administrative or conservation decisions. If validated, the approach could make field verification more scalable and less dependent on resource-intensive manual methods. It may also support more timely insights into animal distribution, enabling better planning and more targeted follow-up inspections.

title: Hansken - Recognizing images of narcotics in digital seizure
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Criminal investigations increasingly involve very large volumes of seized digital material, making it difficult for forensic experts and investigators to manually review every phone, computer, hard drive or storage device in time-sensitive cases. Hansken - Recognizing images of narcotics in digital seizure responds to this challenge by helping the Netherlands Forensic Institute and investigative authorities identify relevant visual or textual evidence more quickly within large datasets. The operational aim is to accelerate the discovery of incriminating or case-relevant material while reducing the burden of exhaustive manual review. The technological implementation uses a self-learning algorithm integrated into the Hansken digital-forensics environment. The system can be trained to recognise specific categories of images, such as weapons or drugs, and to detect text elements appearing in images, including licence plates or account numbers on stolen bank cards. At a conceptual level, image-recognition and pattern-detection techniques classify visual content and highlight items that may deserve closer examination by experts. The tool supports forensic prioritisation rather than replacing evidentiary assessment, which remains subject to professional and legal review. Its impact is faster search across seized data, better use of investigative capacity, improved ability to find hidden or dispersed evidence and stronger support for serious-crime investigations where digital material is extensive and operational timelines are demanding.

title: HKV Eye - Line in Water
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: HKVEYE supports the inspection and monitoring of dikes, water defences and water systems by adding data-driven visual analysis to water-management practice. The operational challenge is that water authorities and infrastructure managers face expanding management areas while staffing capacity for inspection can be limited. Manual inspection of dikes, structures and water systems can be time-consuming, and early recognition of deterioration is essential for flood safety and maintenance planning. HKV Lijn in Water developed HKVEYE to provide additional “eyes” on water infrastructure, using visual data to examine the condition of dikes and related assets in more detail. The implementation applies data-science techniques to interpret images and other visual data, supporting questions such as monitoring vegetation quality, assessing revetment condition, detecting sand-carrying boils and conducting difference analyses over time. Conceptually, the system combines visual monitoring, data interpretation, anomaly detection and inspection-support workflows. The expected impact is more precise, efficient and evidence-based inspection, helping managers focus attention on areas that require intervention. By extracting useful information from increasingly available visual data, HKVEYE can improve maintenance prioritisation, support flood-risk management and strengthen the reliability of water-safety monitoring.

title: Identifying people at risk of falling into large debts
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Municipal debt-prevention services increasingly try to intervene before financial problems become unmanageable, because late intervention can lead to enforcement costs, housing insecurity, health impacts and long-term dependence on social support. The Amsterdam use case concerns the use of predictive or data-driven methods to identify residents who may be at risk of accumulating large debts, so that support can be offered earlier. The operational problem is that signs of debt distress may be distributed across different municipal or service-provider datasets, while front-line staff may only become aware of the situation once arrears have already escalated. At a conceptual level, the system would combine available administrative signals, risk indicators and historical patterns to prioritise cases for preventive outreach. The intended value is not to automate sanctions, but to surface possible vulnerability so that human professionals can offer assistance, advice or referral to debt-support services. The expected impact is earlier identification of residents in financial difficulty, better targeting of municipal support, reduced long-term debt escalation and more efficient use of social-service capacity. However, such systems require careful safeguards because financial-risk profiling can reproduce biases in historical data, affect vulnerable households and create opacity around why a person is flagged.

title: Infobox criminal and unexplained assets (iCOV)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Public Prosecutor's Office, the National Police, the Tax Authorities, Customs, the FIOD and the Financial Intelligence Unit, the Social Affairs and Employment Inspectorate (Investigation Directorate), the Intelligence and Investigation Service of the Environment and Transport Inspectorate (ILT-IOD), the Intelligence and Investigation Service of the Dutch Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA-IOD), the Media Commissioner
source_description: Financial crime investigations often require analysts to understand relationships between people, companies, assets, income, transactions and public records that are dispersed across different authorities. The Infobox Crimineel en Onverklaarbaar Vermogen, known as iCOV, provides Dutch public partners with data-driven reports that support the detection and disruption of money laundering, tax evasion, fraud and unexplained wealth. The operational problem is that individual agencies may each hold partial information, while criminal financial structures often exploit fragmentation between enforcement, tax, customs, labour and supervisory bodies. The implementation is a formal cooperation between public organisations, including the Public Prosecutor’s Office, National Police, Tax Authorities, Customs, FIOD, Financial Intelligence Unit and several inspection and investigative services. At a conceptual level, iCOV combines authorised data access, risk indicators, analytical models and reporting formats to generate insight into assets, income relationships, companies and suspicious patterns. The system is not a fully autonomous enforcement mechanism; its outputs support investigation, prosecution and asset recovery by giving professionals a richer picture of potential criminal or unexplained wealth. The expected impact is faster financial investigation, improved targeting of asset-confiscation work, stronger inter-agency cooperation and more effective action against organised financial crime. Current public information describes iCOV as an active cooperation that helps partners through data-driven reports, including practical examples of use by investigation and prosecution services.

title: Inspection bridges with drones
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Ministry of Instrastructures and market parties
source_description: The bridge-inspection drone pilot explores how unmanned aerial vehicles can reduce reliance on manual inspection capacity for bridges and viaducts. The operational problem is that infrastructure inspections are often labour-intensive, require specialist access arrangements, and may expose inspectors to safety risks when structures are difficult to reach. Public infrastructure managers need reliable ways to detect deterioration, document structural conditions and prioritise maintenance without closing assets unnecessarily or deploying extensive human resources for every inspection. The implementation uses drones to capture visual data from bridges and viaducts, allowing inspection teams to review high-resolution imagery of structural elements that would otherwise require physical access. At a conceptual level, the approach can combine UAV-based image capture, georeferenced inspection records, visual analytics and, where developed further, computer-vision models for recognising cracks, corrosion, deformation or other signs of damage. The expected impact is faster inspection, lower operational burden, improved safety for inspection staff and more consistent documentation of asset condition. If validated, the pilot could support more risk-based infrastructure maintenance by helping authorities identify which structures require closer expert review and which can be monitored remotely.

title: Intelligent traffic control systems (I-VRI's) - Better traffic flow
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Urban traffic intersections must balance the needs of private vehicles, buses, emergency services, cyclists and pedestrians while reducing congestion and improving journey reliability. In Gelderland, existing traffic lights at eight intersections in Arnhem and Velp were replaced with intelligent traffic-control systems, or iVRIs, to support better traffic flow. The objective was to move beyond fixed or locally reactive signalling by using digital information from road users and connected systems. The implementation uses mobile data and vehicle-to-infrastructure communication so that road users and traffic-control installations can exchange information. Buses and emergency services can receive priority when approaching an intersection, while other road users may receive up-to-date information about routes and speed advice. At a conceptual level, iVRIs combine connected traffic-light controllers, data exchange standards, road-user messages, priority rules and adaptive signal control. This allows the intersection to respond more dynamically to current traffic conditions and to support policy priorities such as public transport reliability or emergency response. The expected impact is smoother traffic flow, reduced waiting times, better journey predictability and more efficient use of existing road infrastructure. Dutch public portals continue to provide national visibility on iVRI deployments, while Gelderland’s own public material refers to implementation and execution documents for the Arnhem and Velp iVRIs.

title: Use of scan cars for underground containers - Determining type of waste
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Municipal waste management services struggle with contamination of waste streams when incorrect materials are deposited in underground containers, leading to higher processing costs and reduced recycling rates. In The Hague and other cities, scan cars were introduced to monitor underground containers and improve waste separation. Stakeholders include municipal waste services, residents and environmental authorities. The objective is to detect incorrect waste disposal early and support targeted interventions. Vehicles equipped with cameras periodically capture images of open or overfilled containers. Image analysis techniques are applied to identify visible waste types, such as bulky items or mixed waste placed in recycling containers. The system integrates with municipal waste management platforms, allowing services to prioritise clean-up operations and identify recurring problem locations. The pilots have improved operational efficiency by reducing manual inspections and enabling faster responses to misuse. Municipalities report cleaner collection points, better data on citizen behaviour and more effective communication campaigns. While still limited in scope, the approach demonstrates scalable potential for data-driven waste management and supports broader circular economy objectives.

title: iRN_iColumbo
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Police investigations increasingly involve large volumes of online information, making manual monitoring of digital sources time-consuming and inconsistent. iColumbo was developed within the Dutch police’s Internet Research & Investigation Network (iRN) to support systematic online searches for suspicious material. Stakeholders included law enforcement investigators, digital forensics units and judicial authorities. The objective was to enhance investigative capacity by automating parts of open-source intelligence collection while preserving legal oversight. The service crawled publicly accessible online sources and forums using predefined search strategies, keywords and behavioural patterns. Collected material was indexed and presented to investigators for assessment, rather than triggering automatic enforcement actions. The project improved consistency and speed in early-stage investigations and reduced reliance on ad hoc manual searches. Although the specific iColumbo project has since been concluded, its concepts informed later police tooling for digital investigations. The main impact lies in professionalisation of online investigative practices and improved methodological consistency in handling internet-based evidence.

title: Artificial Intelligence Knowledge System for the judiciary searches for similar lawsuits
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Artificial Intelligence Knowledge System for the judiciary was developed to support legal professionals in identifying comparable lawsuits more efficiently. The operational challenge is that courts and judicial staff work with large volumes of case material, and finding relevant precedents or similar disputes can be time-consuming when searches rely only on keywords or manual legal knowledge. The District Court of East Brabant tested a system that allows users to enter text and receive the ten most similar lawsuits. The implementation is based on textual similarity search, likely combining natural language processing, document representation and ranking techniques to compare an input text with a database of past cases. Conceptually, the tool transforms legal documents into searchable representations, calculates similarity between the user’s text and available case records, and returns a ranked list of relevant results. The expected impact is faster legal research, more consistent retrieval of comparable cases and better support for judicial preparation. By assisting users in navigating case material, the system can improve internal efficiency without replacing judicial reasoning. Its value depends on the quality of the underlying case database, the transparency of similarity criteria and careful use by trained legal professionals.

title: LAA - Address quality in Personal Records Database (BRP)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Public authorities depend on accurate address records to deliver services, administer rights and obligations, and prevent misuse of public systems, but incorrect registrations in the Personal Records Database can undermine these functions. LAA - Address quality in Personal Records Database (BRP) supports the Dutch Ministry of Interior in improving address quality by using data analysis to recognise patterns that may indicate incorrect addressing. The underlying problem is that inaccurate address data can affect administrative decisions, public-service delivery and fraud prevention, particularly where residence information is used to determine eligibility, correspondence, enforcement or access to benefits. The initiative aims to help bring the BRP into better order by identifying records that may require verification or correction. The technological implementation applies analytical methods to administrative data in order to detect combinations, deviations or patterns associated with possible address-registration problems. These outputs can then guide further checks by competent authorities, who assess whether a registration is indeed incorrect and what follow-up is required. The system therefore functions as a risk-identification and prioritisation tool within a broader governance process. The expected impact is improved data quality, more targeted verification work, stronger reliability of the population register and better support for fraud prevention. Given the sensitivity of population data, the value of the system depends on clear legal safeguards, proportionality, transparency and appropriate human oversight.

title: Using smart algorithms to map whether building or demolishing certain homes improves liveability
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Housing policy can affect liveability through tenure mix, housing type, density, neighbourhood composition, public-space quality and access to services, but the relationship between physical interventions and social outcomes is difficult to assess with simple indicators. Breda’s use case concerns the application of machine-learning methods to investigate whether building or demolishing certain types of homes could improve neighbourhood liveability. The operational problem is that urban-planning decisions often involve long-term effects and many interacting variables, making it hard for decision-makers to isolate which housing interventions are likely to improve local conditions. The implementation concept uses historical and spatial data to detect patterns between housing stock, neighbourhood characteristics and liveability outcomes. At a conceptual level, the model would compare combinations of housing and contextual indicators, identify correlations with liveability measures and support planners in evaluating possible redevelopment scenarios. The expected impact is more evidence-based housing policy, better targeting of regeneration measures and stronger analytical support for decisions on demolition, new construction or housing mix. The system should be understood as a planning-support tool rather than a substitute for political, social and participatory decision-making. Its value depends on combining model outputs with local knowledge, resident engagement and policy judgement.

title: Tackling undermining using AI
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Municipalities and safety-domain partners can lose valuable intelligence on subversive crime when suspicions are reported through fragmented channels or fail to reach the right professionals quickly. Tackling undermining using AI builds on Milvum’s “Report a Suspicion” platform, which is already used by more than 300 professionals to share signals of undermining, such as illegal prostitution or drug production, directly with the relevant municipal actors. The operational challenge is to improve communication between municipalities and chain partners so that local safety information is not lost, delayed or handled inconsistently. The existing platform combines a mobile app and web portal, enabling professionals to submit and route suspicions in a structured way. The planned or added AI functionality strengthens this model by applying big-data analysis to identify, categorise and prioritise signals of subversive crime more effectively. At a conceptual level, the system can analyse reports and related data to detect patterns, cluster similar cases, highlight urgent risks and support prioritisation for follow-up. The impact is improved information flow, faster routing of relevant signals, better coordination between municipal and safety partners, and more systematic handling of local crime intelligence. For public authorities, the platform offers operational value by turning dispersed observations into structured knowledge that can support earlier intervention and more targeted action against undermining.

title: Detecting 'unknown' companies with environmental risk
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Environmental supervision depends on knowing which businesses operate in a municipality, what activities they carry out and whether those activities may create inspection or permitting risks. Eindhoven’s use case focused on mapping “unknown” companies that could pose a potential environmental risk by using data more intelligently. The operational problem is that companies may be invisible to inspectors because records are incomplete, activities change, addresses are inconsistent or information is distributed across multiple administrative sources. This creates the risk that environmentally relevant businesses are not prioritised for supervision or included in the appropriate regulatory process. The implementation uses data matching and analytical screening to identify companies that may fall outside established inspection lists but show characteristics associated with environmental risk. At a conceptual level, the system combines business-register information, location data, sector classifications, permit or enforcement records and risk indicators to generate candidate companies for further human review. The expected impact is better coverage of environmental supervision, earlier detection of potentially risky activities, more efficient targeting of inspections and improved data quality in municipal environmental registers. The system should be understood as a prioritisation and discovery tool: it does not determine guilt or non-compliance, but helps inspectors find entities that may require attention. Public case material records the project as an Eindhoven initiative to make otherwise hard-to-find companies visible through smarter data use.

title: Detecting welfare fraud - Prediction of the likelihood of unlawful behavior on the House Market
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Totta Datalab, municipality of Nissewaard, municipality of Brielle
source_description: Municipalities administering welfare benefits face pressure to prevent fraud while ensuring fair and lawful treatment of beneficiaries. The Municipality of Nissewaard introduced a predictive model to identify cases with a higher likelihood of unlawful behaviour in the housing market, such as undeclared cohabitation or subletting. Stakeholders included social services, case officers and welfare recipients. The objective was to prioritise investigations and reduce random or unnecessary checks. The model analysed historical administrative data, identifying patterns associated with confirmed fraud cases and assigning risk scores to current clients. These scores informed decisions on whether further investigation was warranted, always requiring human review. While the system aimed to improve efficiency, concerns emerged around transparency, bias and legal safeguards. Following national scrutiny of similar systems and evolving legal standards, Nissewaard discontinued the model in 2021. The case significantly influenced Dutch policy discussions on automated risk profiling, reinforcing the need for strict governance, explainability and proportionality in data-driven public services.

title: Detecting welfare fraud in the municipality of Deventer and Goirle (SyRI system)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Municipality of Deventer, Municipality of Goirle
source_description: The Deventer and Goirle welfare-fraud detection pilot used risk profiling to identify welfare recipients whose files might require additional investigation. The administrative problem was the need to target limited enforcement capacity towards cases considered more likely to involve irregularities, while managing public funds and ensuring compliance with welfare rules. The stakeholders included the municipalities of Deventer and Goirle, welfare recipients, municipal social-service staff, enforcement teams and citizens affected by decisions based on risk scores. The implementation generated risk profiles for welfare recipients, with the resulting score used to decide whether a dossier should be examined more closely. At a conceptual level, such a system links administrative datasets, applies risk indicators or algorithmic scoring rules, and routes selected cases to additional human investigation. The intended impact was more efficient fraud detection, better prioritisation of municipal control resources and earlier identification of possible unlawful behaviour. However, because SyRI-style systems involve sensitive personal data and profiling of welfare recipients, they raise significant concerns around transparency, discrimination, proportionality and legal accountability. These concerns are particularly relevant given the broader Dutch SyRI judgment, where the system’s legal basis was found incompatible with privacy protections.

title: Detection of crime and subversion in the Municipality of Leudal (SyRI system)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Local authorities may seek to detect organised or “subversive” crime where administrative records suggest unusual patterns around buildings, businesses or permits. The Leudal use case concerns the reported use of algorithmic profiling to identify locations where paperwork or administrative signals may indicate possible criminal or irregular activity. The operational problem is that suspicious activity may not be visible through a single inspection file, but may emerge from combinations of property records, business information, permits, registrations, enforcement history or other municipal data. At a conceptual level, the system would combine multiple administrative indicators and generate risk signals for further investigation by officials. The intended impact is to help local government and enforcement partners prioritise inspections, detect hidden misuse of premises and support more coordinated action against organised crime. However, this type of system is high-risk because it can involve profiling of people, addresses or businesses without clear visibility for those affected. It therefore requires strict legal basis, transparency, proportionality, data-quality controls and human review. The use case should be treated cautiously because “subversion” is a broad policy category and algorithmic indicators may produce false positives or reinforce biased inspection patterns.

title: Detection of crime and subversion in the municipality of Dronten (SyRI system)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Dronten’s pilot examined whether algorithms could help identify patterns associated with subversive crime at municipal level. The municipality therefore explored how algorithmic analysis could support earlier detection and prioritisation of cases requiring further attention. The implementation is described as an experiment using algorithms to detect subversive crime. Conceptually, the system may combine municipal data sources, risk indicators, pattern detection and case-selection workflows to flag locations, activities or dossiers that appear to warrant additional scrutiny. The expected impact would be improved situational awareness for local enforcement actors, more targeted investigation and better use of limited municipal capacity. At the same time, the use of predictive or profiling tools in public-order contexts requires strong safeguards. Risks include opaque criteria, inaccurate suspicion, disproportionate targeting of specific groups or areas, and weak routes for contesting decisions. The pilot therefore needs careful legal, ethical and operational governance if algorithmic signals are used to trigger further enforcement action.

The system’s role should be framed as risk signalling for human review, not as automatic proof of wrongdoing. The use case therefore raises strong requirements around explainability, proportionality, auditability and safeguards against discriminatory targeting of neighbourhoods, businesses or residents.

title: Detection of crime and subversion in the municipality of Nederweert (SyRI system)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Smaller municipalities can face complex enforcement challenges when criminal or improper activity is hidden behind legal-looking administrative structures, property records or business registrations. Nederweert was reported as using algorithmic methods to support detection of subversive crime. The operational problem is that municipal datasets may contain weak signals of irregularity, but individual records may not be meaningful unless combined with other information. A risk-based system can help identify buildings or cases where paperwork “smacks of suspicious cases”, allowing limited inspection capacity to be focused where further review appears justified. At a conceptual level, such a system would aggregate administrative indicators, score or classify cases and provide signals to officials for follow-up. The expected impact is more efficient local enforcement, earlier identification of hidden misuse of property and better support for multi-agency responses to organised crime. However, the system can also create legal and ethical risks if residents, owners or businesses are profiled through opaque combinations of data. The case therefore needs to be presented as an enforcement-support system requiring human verification, rather than an automated determination of criminal conduct. Transparency and safeguards are particularly important because flagged persons may not know that algorithmic profiling influenced official attention.

More broadly, the project creates value by changing how municipal services are organised around public-space maintenance, reducing unnecessary effort and supporting a more data-driven, responsive and scalable approach to keeping urban environments clean.

title: Enforcement of social policy laws with AI

The administrative problem is that several public bodies are responsible for schemes, payments, registrations and enforcement processes that may involve overlapping information on citizens, benefits, education, taxation, vehicles and justice-related records. Coordinated analysis can help authorities understand enforcement risks, identify inconsistencies and evaluate how social-security rules are implemented. The implementation involves organisations including UWV, SVB, the Tax and Customs Administration, DUO, Justid, CJIB and RDW. Conceptually, the system can combine cross-agency data analysis, risk indicators, policy evaluation and compliance monitoring to support enforcement of social-policy laws. The expected impact is more structured insight into enforcement practice, better targeting of checks and improved understanding of where errors, omissions or potential fraud may occur. title: Speaker Tracking in Time and Space
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Dutch Police, with Speech lab B.V.
source_description: Speaker Tracking in Time and Space supports police analysis of audio recordings by separating and labelling speech from different speakers. The operational issue is that investigations can involve lengthy recordings with multiple voices, requiring officers or analysts to listen manually to identify who is speaking and when. This is time-consuming and can also expose investigators to conversations unrelated to the subject of interest, creating unnecessary privacy intrusion. Spraaklab develops technology that can largely disassemble, distinguish and label speech from different speakers, allowing police teams to work more efficiently and with higher analytical quality. The implementation uses speech-processing techniques, likely including speaker diarisation, voice-separation, audio segmentation and speaker-labelling models. Conceptually, the tool structures raw audio into speaker-specific segments, helping analysts locate relevant parts of recordings without reviewing unrelated material repeatedly. The expected impact is faster audio review, improved investigative productivity, better-quality evidence handling and stronger privacy protection for people whose conversations are not relevant to the investigation. Its value depends on accuracy in difficult acoustic conditions, careful validation and appropriate human review, since mistaken speaker attribution could affect investigative interpretation.

title: Road safety model The Hague - Providing a risk score for all road sections and intersections
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Urban road authorities require proactive tools to reduce traffic accidents and prioritise safety interventions across complex road networks. The Municipality of The Hague developed a road safety model to assess and compare risk levels for all road sections and intersections within the city. Stakeholders include municipal traffic engineers, urban planners, and road safety policymakers. The objective is to move from reactive accident analysis to preventive, data-driven traffic safety management. The model combines historical accident records with a comprehensive dataset describing traffic conditions, infrastructure characteristics, environmental factors, and usage patterns. Each road segment and intersection is described using approximately 250 variables, enabling systematic comparison across the network. These datasets are processed to generate a relative risk score that highlights locations with a higher likelihood of future accidents. The results are visualised through analytical dashboards used by traffic experts to prioritise inspections, redesigns, and enforcement measures. According to official government documentation, the model is actively used as a decision-support instrument rather than an automated enforcement mechanism. The approach has improved the municipality’s ability to identify high-risk locations before accidents occur, allocate resources more effectively, and justify infrastructure investments transparently, contributing to a more systematic and preventive road safety strategy.

source_description: The Municipality of Rotterdam faces similar challenges to other large cities in managing road safety across a dense and diverse transport network. Key stakeholders include municipal traffic authorities, safety analysts, and infrastructure planners. The objective is to identify hazardous road locations proactively and guide targeted interventions. The model links accident records with data describing road geometry, traffic intensity, surrounding land use, weather conditions, and environmental characteristics within the influence area of each accident location. These combined datasets are analysed to identify patterns associated with elevated accident risks, allowing the municipality to generate predictive insights rather than relying solely on past accident counts. The results are used internally by experts to prioritise safety audits, redesigns, and policy measures. According to sector knowledge platform documentation, the model is operational as a decision-support tool and does not replace expert judgement. Its use has strengthened Rotterdam’s capacity to focus safety investments where they are most needed, improved transparency in traffic safety planning, and supported a shift towards data-informed preventive road management.

title: Movable Traffic Predictor
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Movable Traffic Predictor pilot was designed to support traffic-management decisions by forecasting traffic conditions before congestion becomes visible in real time. The operational problem is that traffic-control centres often react to current data, while non-recurrent congestion caused by incidents, sudden bottlenecks or unusual flows may require earlier warnings to deploy effective measures. File radar B.V. developed a new type of AI-based traffic forecaster capable of predicting traffic up to about one hour ahead, with testing carried out in collaboration with traffic-control centres, particularly the national VCNL centre near Utrecht. The implementation applies predictive analytics to traffic data to generate short-term forecasts in the range of approximately 20 to 60 minutes. Conceptually, the system analyses current and historical traffic conditions, identifies emerging disruptions and provides predictive information for operational decisions such as congestion detection, deployment of mobile assets or traffic-management measures. The expected impact is earlier intervention, improved traffic flow, reduced delay and better use of transport-management resources. By shifting traffic control from purely real-time monitoring to anticipatory decision support, the pilot can improve resilience to irregular and incident-driven congestion.

title: Reference Index Recherche Onderzoeken en Subjecten - Detection of unusual transactions
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Law enforcement agencies must efficiently identify suspicious financial transactions that may be linked to ongoing criminal investigations while operating within strict legal frameworks. In the Netherlands, unusual transactions are partly assessed through comparison with the Reference Index Recherche Onderzoeken en Subjecten (VROS), a database managed by the National Police. Stakeholders include financial institutions, law enforcement bodies, and investigative authorities. The objective is to support criminal investigations by identifying whether reported unusual transactions are linked to existing police investigations. Transaction data flagged by reporting entities is compared through a partly automated process with entries in the VROS. A positive match indicates a potential connection between the transaction and an active investigation, triggering further human-led assessment. The system does not autonomously label transactions as criminal but acts as an investigative signal within a broader legal process. VROS is formally embedded in Dutch legislation and remains operational as part of the national framework for combating financial crime. Its use has improved investigative efficiency by enabling faster cross-referencing of financial intelligence, reducing manual searches, and supporting coordinated law enforcement action, while maintaining procedural safeguards and human oversight.

title: Viralcom Egg - accidents in the water

source_description: Viralcom Egg is a prototype designed to detect accidents in water and communicate relevant alerts to rescue services. The safety problem is that drownings or underwater incidents can be difficult to identify quickly, especially where visual monitoring from the shore is limited or delayed. The Municipality of Dordrecht is linked to the pilot context, with Viralcom seeking to test the Egg remotely from the quay in Zwijndrecht to the opposite quay in Dordrecht. The implementation uses artificial intelligence and neural networks for pattern recognition and drowning detection. Conceptually, the system monitors activity in or around the water, analyses visual or sensor patterns that may indicate an accident, and sends information to emergency or rescue services when a potential incident is identified. The expected impact is faster detection of water accidents, shorter response times and improved public safety in areas where people may fall into or become distressed in water. The prototype’s value depends on reliable detection under varying environmental conditions, low false-alarm rates and effective integration with rescue-service workflows. If validated, it could strengthen prevention and emergency response in urban waterfront areas.

title: Predict which residents have a higher risk of care or debt problems in Twenterand (SyRI)

source_description: Residents experiencing debt, care needs or social vulnerability often interact with multiple services, but early warning signs may remain fragmented until problems become acute. The operational problem is that social problems often develop gradually and may only become visible once enforcement, crisis care or intensive support is required. A predictive system can bring together administrative indicators and historical patterns to identify households or individuals whose situation resembles earlier cases of debt escalation or care need. At a conceptual level, the system would classify or prioritise residents according to risk signals, enabling municipal professionals to consider preventive outreach or support. The expected impact is earlier intervention, better coordination between social services, reduced crisis escalation and more efficient targeting of limited municipal capacity. The use case must be handled carefully because it involves potentially sensitive social and financial data, and because predictive profiling can unintentionally stigmatise residents or neighbourhoods. Its legitimacy depends on clear purpose limitation, strong human oversight, transparency to affected people and safeguards ensuring that the system is used to offer support rather than punishment.

title: Early school leavers in the municipality of Amersfoort - Estimation of students at risk
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Preventing early school leaving requires timely identification of pupils whose educational trajectory suggests a higher risk of dropping out before completing their programme. The Amersfoort and Dordrecht use case concerns the use of an algorithm to estimate which students may be at risk of becoming early school leavers. The operational problem is that schools and municipalities may hold relevant signals, such as school changes, grade repetition or attendance-related patterns, but these signals may not be systematically combined for early intervention. At a conceptual level, the algorithm compares current pupils with patterns observed among previous early school leavers and assigns an indication of risk. Professionals can then decide whether additional guidance, counselling or follow-up is appropriate. The intended value is preventive: the model is meant to help education and youth-support services act before disengagement becomes irreversible. The expected impact is better targeting of support, lower dropout rates, more efficient use of guidance capacity and improved educational outcomes. However, the case also raises important governance issues because educational-risk profiling can affect young people’s opportunities and may be difficult to understand or contest. It should therefore be presented as decision support for human professionals, with transparent explanation of the indicators used and safeguards against discriminatory effects.

title: Wabo assistant - Automated environmental permits

source_description: The municipality of The Hague needed a more efficient way to manage the intake of environmental-permit applications governed by the Environmental Law General Provisions Act, known as Wabo. The stakeholders include municipal permit teams, applicants and environmental-administration staff, with the objective of automating part of the intake process and improving the speed and quality of early-stage handling. The solution is implemented through a Wabo assistant that uses natural language processing to support permit-related tasks. At a conceptual level, the system analyses incoming textual information, identifies relevant content and helps structure or route permit applications so that initial handling requires less manual intervention. This creates a more standardised intake workflow and allows staff to spend less time on repetitive front-end processing. The expected impact is faster handling of permit submissions, reduced clerical burden and improved efficiency in the administration of environmental permits. More broadly, the Wabo assistant creates value by modernising a document-heavy municipal process, supporting better service for applicants and enabling a more scalable model for managing regulatory intake under environmental law.

source_description: Cities increasingly face pressure to manage water sustainably while reducing reliance on potable water for non-drinking purposes. Rainwater from the surrounding area is collected and filtered through a series of natural purification layers before being stored for reuse. Sensors continuously monitor system performance, rainfall volumes, and storage levels. Operational data is analysed to optimise purification processes and forecast water availability, supporting adaptive system management. According to reporting on the project, the water fields are fully implemented and integrated into Breda’s water infrastructure. The initiative has improved water efficiency, reduced operational costs, and enhanced resilience to drought and heavy rainfall. It also demonstrates how data-driven monitoring can support sustainable urban water systems while maintaining transparency and reliability.

source_description: Welfare administrations need to ensure that people who are entitled to benefits receive support while also detecting improper use or abuse of public funds. WIL Lekstroom, a cooperation of municipalities in the Utrecht region, was reported as using algorithms to support detection of abuse and improper use of social-assistance benefits. The operational problem is that benefit-control processes are labour-intensive, and staff may need to identify which cases deserve additional review without checking every file manually. At a conceptual level, the system would use historical benefit, case-management or administrative data to detect patterns associated with previous improper use, then generate signals or risk scores for officials. The expected impact is more targeted investigation, reduced unnecessary checks, improved administrative efficiency and better protection of public resources. However, welfare-fraud prediction is a high-risk area because historical data may reflect biased enforcement patterns and flagged residents may not know that an algorithm influenced additional scrutiny. The system should therefore be understood as decision support only, not as automatic sanctioning or benefit withdrawal. Any responsible use would require clear documentation, explainability, human review, appeal routes and monitoring for discriminatory impact, especially because the affected population may already be socio-economically vulnerable.

title: Poverty prevention - Identification of poverty and debt early

title: INZNAK Project - Intelligent road signs for adaptive vehicle traffic control
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The INZNAK project responds to the need to improve road safety and traffic management by providing drivers with timely, location-specific warnings about hazards, disruptions and recommended speeds. Many highway collisions are linked to speed that is not adapted to current weather, road-surface or traffic conditions, particularly during sudden braking, congestion, fog, storms, blizzards or black ice. In Gdańsk, the project aims to develop a network of autonomous intelligent road signs capable of warning drivers earlier and supporting adaptive traffic control. The emerging technology implementation includes three types of signs: standing, hanging and mobile. Each sign has a display showing text and image messages, including suggested speeds and information on current disruptions. The signs communicate with each other through LoRaWAN and with the traffic control centre through LTE, creating a two-level communication architecture that improves resilience if telecommunications infrastructure fails. Each sign is equipped with sensors such as Doppler radar, lidar, acoustic probes, RGB cameras, Bluetooth receivers and a local weather station. This multimodal approach allows the system to combine different detection methods, for example using lidar when standard cameras are less effective at night. The expected impact is earlier hazard detection, more reliable traffic information and better adaptation of driver behaviour to real-time road conditions, with potential benefits for safety, traffic flow and operational resilience.

title: Virtual Clerk - Assistance with search for information
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Municipal offices that serve large numbers of residents and beneficiaries must provide clear procedural information quickly, even when enquiries concern many different services, administrative routes and eligibility conditions. Virtual Clerk helps the Municipality of Chorzów optimise service processes for hundreds of thousands of beneficiaries by offering an intuitive digital channel for finding information about the office and the procedures it manages. The operational challenge is that citizens often need guidance outside office hours or may not know where to look for the correct administrative information, while staff can spend considerable time responding to repetitive enquiries. The system uses artificial intelligence to support natural and user-friendly searches across institutional information. At a conceptual level, it interprets user questions, identifies the relevant procedural content and returns guidance in a form that is easier to access than navigating multiple static pages or contacting the office directly. The service is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, improving accessibility for users who need information at different times. Its impact is faster access to public-service information, reduced friction for beneficiaries, lower pressure on front-office staff and more consistent communication on municipal procedures. For the municipality, Virtual Clerk contributes to a more modern, scalable and citizen-oriented model of administrative service delivery.

title: Intelligent Management Systems
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: County-office buildings require coordinated management of security, utilities, technical infrastructure and room equipment, yet these systems are often operated separately, making monitoring and optimisation more difficult. The case responds to the need for a more integrated approach to public-building management, covering access control, external roller shutters, monitoring, water and electricity consumption, PIAPs, IT networks, an intelligent conference room and the fire-protection system. The technological implementation consists of interconnected building-management systems that enable centralised monitoring and control of different technical installations. Sensors, controllers and digital interfaces can be used to gather information on building conditions, resource use and system status, while management software supports supervision and operational decisions.
