By integrating these functions, the administration can obtain a clearer view of how the building performs and respond more quickly to faults, security issues or inefficient consumption patterns. The expected impact includes improved energy and water management, stronger security, more efficient use of office infrastructure, better continuity of building operations and reduced manual effort for technical staff. In organisational terms, the project supports the modernisation of local-government facilities and provides a more resilient foundation for public administration services delivered from those buildings.

title: The use of game theory in the process of modeling the development of smart city
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Warsaw smart-city modelling pilot aims to represent the development and functioning of a smart city through a participatory game based on game-theory principles. The policy and planning problem is that urban development involves multiple actors with different objectives, resources and constraints, including city authorities, developers, environmental organisations and residents. A conventional planning model may struggle to capture these interactions, particularly where cooperation, conflict, negotiation and shared benefits influence outcomes. The implementation seeks to develop a participatory game model using artificial intelligence methods, with cooperative game theory providing the formal basis for representing smart-city processes. A key element is parameterisation: defining the number of players, assigning their roles and modelling how their decisions affect urban development scenarios. Conceptually, the system combines simulation, stakeholder modelling, strategic interaction and AI-supported analysis to illustrate how smart-city choices may evolve under different assumptions. The expected impact is better understanding of urban governance dynamics, stronger support for participatory planning and improved capacity to test policy options before implementation. By translating complex city-development processes into a structured game model, the pilot can help public authorities explore trade-offs, incentives and cooperation mechanisms in smart-city policy design.

title: Monitoring of a Water Treatment Station
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Municipal water operators need accurate and continuous information on flow, pressure, intake operations and distribution volumes to maintain reliable supply and detect losses within the network. This use case in the Municipality of Kartuzy addresses this need by introducing monitoring for the local water treatment plant and the associated water-supply system. The operational problem is that insufficient visibility over network parameters can make it harder to control the amount of water sent into the system, identify abnormal losses or regulate intake operations efficiently. The case focuses on measuring flow rate, monitoring network pressure, controlling and regulating intake activity, and balancing the volume of water distributed through the network. The technological implementation relies on sensors and monitoring equipment installed across key points of the treatment and distribution process. These devices collect operational measurements and transmit them to management systems that allow staff to observe conditions, compare distributed volumes and identify potential inefficiencies or losses. The resulting information supports more precise operational control and better evidence for maintenance or intervention decisions. The expected impact is improved reliability of water supply, faster identification of pressure or flow anomalies, better control of water intake and distribution, and stronger capacity to detect water losses. For the municipality, the system contributes to more efficient utility management and a more transparent view of essential water infrastructure.

title: Intelligent water and sewage network management system
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Water and sewage network operators face increasing complexity in managing ageing infrastructure, fluctuating demand, and rising maintenance costs. To address these challenges, an intelligent water and sewage network management system was developed to support real-time monitoring and optimisation of network operations. Stakeholders include utility operators, municipal authorities, and service recipients. The objective is to improve reliability, reduce losses, and optimise maintenance through better visibility of network performance. The system integrates hydraulic models with real-time sensor data collected across the network, including flow, pressure, and load information, alongside data on consumers and infrastructure assets. Analytical tools process this information to support dynamic resource allocation, predictive maintenance, and operational planning. According to official innovation mapping documentation, the project aligns with international smart grid trends and is being implemented incrementally, combining pilot deployments with gradual scaling. Expected impacts include lower operational costs, improved service continuity, faster fault detection, and more efficient use of water resources, supporting long-term sustainability of public utility networks.

title: Lupine Intelligent lighting system
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Municipalities must provide safe and reliable street lighting while limiting energy consumption, maintenance costs and response times when failures occur. Lupine Intelligent lighting system introduces centralised control of street lighting based on motion sensors and sensors that analyse weather conditions, allowing the municipality to adapt lighting more precisely to local needs. The operational challenge is that conventional lighting systems are often switched according to fixed schedules and provide limited real-time information on individual lamp performance. In this case, each lamp can be individually controlled and monitored, enabling different switching times and more flexible lighting patterns. The technological implementation combines sensor-based detection, central management software and remote monitoring of luminaire parameters. Motion and weather data inform when lighting should be activated or reduced, while lamps near pedestrian crossings can be switched on earlier and turned off later than others to improve visibility and safety. Continuous monitoring also allows technical teams to detect failures more quickly and plan maintenance before problems become more costly. The expected impact includes significant energy savings, increased safety at pedestrian crossings, fewer interruptions in lighting operation and shorter response times when faults occur. The availability of luminaire-performance data also supports earlier maintenance planning and cost minimisation, creating a more efficient and safety-oriented approach to local lighting management.

title: Development of the Electronic Flood Warning System
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The project concerns the expansion of the Electronic Flood Warning System in the Biała Tarnowska River catchment area, where recurring floods and flash floods pose significant risks to residents, infrastructure, agriculture and local authorities. Existing monitoring mechanisms provide limited predictive capacity, making it difficult for crisis management services, water management authorities and municipalities to anticipate when and where flooding may occur, and with what intensity. The objective of the initiative is to strengthen early warning capabilities by delivering reliable, location-specific flood risk forecasts that support timely decision-making, resource allocation and public safety measures. The system integrates advanced data analytics and machine learning models to analyse correlations between historical and real-time meteorological and hydrological data. Supervised learning algorithms are trained on long-term precipitation records, river water level measurements and flood wave dynamics to model patterns leading to river overflow or flash floods. The solution combines sensor networks, weather radar data and hydrological stations with predictive models deployed within the existing warning infrastructure, enabling automated risk assessments and scenario simulations. The enhanced system improves forecasting accuracy and lead time, enabling earlier alerts and more targeted emergency responses. It strengthens operational reliability, reduces potential damage to property and infrastructure, and enhances public safety. Improved scalability and automation lower long-term monitoring costs while increasing resilience in the catchment area.

title: Gliwice & Poznan Integrated Public Transport Management System - ITS
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Growing cities need to manage traffic, public transport, emergency movements, parking and traveller information in an integrated way, because fragmented systems can reduce punctuality, safety and network efficiency. Gliwice & Poznan Integrated Public Transport Management System brings together several intelligent transport functions to improve mobility management in the municipalities of Gliwice and Poznań. The case addresses multiple operational objectives: giving green-light priority to public transport, prioritising emergency-service vehicles at signalised intersections, informing drivers through road information systems, supporting road users through a mobile application and expanding traffic measurement points with vehicle identification. The technological implementation includes traffic-light priority systems, variable message signs showing journey times, video analytics for intersection monitoring, sensors or detection systems for free parking spaces, meteorological monitoring and pre-selection vehicle weighing at city inlets in Gliwice. Video analytics can automatically inform operators about dangerous road incidents, while traffic and weather data support better management of urban mobility conditions. The expected impact is improved punctuality of public transport, faster emergency-vehicle passage, better information for drivers, stronger incident detection, more efficient parking guidance and improved enforcement of vehicle-weight rules. Overall, the integrated system supports safer, more predictable and more data-informed urban transport management, while giving municipal authorities a broader operational picture of mobility across the city.

title: Cracow Virtual Clerk
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Cracow’s Virtual Clerk was introduced on the new POP website to improve access to information for entrepreneurs and people interested in setting up a business. The administrative issue is that business users often need to navigate dispersed information on registration procedures, municipal services and entrepreneur support, which can slow down decision-making and increase demand for front-office assistance. The Municipality of Cracow therefore launched a virtual clerk to make information retrieval more intuitive, rapid and continuously available. The implementation uses a conversational interface supported by artificial intelligence, allowing users to search for information in the field of entrepreneur services through natural-language interaction rather than manual browsing. At a conceptual level, the tool combines question interpretation, information retrieval, guided assistance and digital service personalisation. Its 24/7 availability is particularly relevant for users who need support outside office hours or who prefer self-service channels. The expected impact is faster access to reliable municipal information, reduced pressure on staff handling repetitive enquiries and a more user-friendly experience for entrepreneurs. By simplifying the first stages of business-related interaction with the municipality, the pilot can contribute to more efficient local economic-service delivery and better support for people seeking to start or manage business activities.

title: AI-based timetables
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Public transport authorities need timetables that reflect real operating conditions, because planned travel times that do not match actual journey patterns can reduce punctuality and passenger confidence. AI-based timetables in the Municipality of Poznań supports the creation of more accurate timetables by using historical data collected from vehicles after completed services. The operational problem is that public transport schedules are often affected by traffic conditions, route characteristics, time of day and recurring delays, and manually adjusting timetables may not fully capture these patterns. The software enables historical trip data to be projected onto timetable planning, allowing planners to analyse how long vehicles actually take on specific route sections. Its technological implementation applies statistical analysis to vehicle data from completed journeys in order to determine optimal travel times for individual sections. By identifying recurring deviations between planned and actual performance, the system helps create schedules that are better aligned with observed conditions. The expected impact is improved punctuality, more realistic timetable planning, better use of vehicle and driver resources, and a more reliable passenger experience. For the municipality, the system provides a stronger evidence base for transport planning and helps shift timetable design from assumption-based scheduling towards continuous improvement based on operational data.

title: Poznan: Improving the flow of electric bus traffic
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Poznań’s electric-bus traffic-flow pilot was designed to support the introduction of electric buses on route No. 174 by improving bus priority at traffic lights. The transport-management problem is that electric buses require reliable scheduling and sufficient charging time at terminal loops, while delays caused by traffic signals can reduce operational efficiency and affect service regularity. The Municipality of Poznań therefore equipped traffic lights along the route with signal receivers from buses and adjusted signal programmes to prioritise bus movement. The implementation combines vehicle-to-infrastructure communication, traffic-signal priority and timetable-sensitive operational planning. Conceptually, buses transmit their presence or approach to the signal system, which can then adapt traffic-light phases to improve journey smoothness and reduce unnecessary waiting time. The objective is not simply to reduce travel time, but also to maximise the time available for vehicle charging at the end loop, which is critical for electric-bus reliability. The expected impact is smoother public transport operation, improved punctuality, better energy-management conditions and stronger passenger service quality. By aligning traffic-control infrastructure with the needs of electric fleets, the pilot supports the transition to cleaner public transport while reducing the operational risks associated with battery charging and route delays.

title: Ioom Intelligent lighting system
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Municipalities need street-lighting systems that reduce energy use and maintenance costs while still providing safe lighting conditions for pedestrians, drivers and public-space users. Ioom Intelligent lighting system addresses this requirement through centralised street-lighting control based on motion sensors and sensors that analyse weather conditions. The service context is local infrastructure management, where lighting must respond to changing levels of movement, visibility and safety need rather than operating only according to fixed schedules. In the current model, each lamp can be individually controlled and monitored, allowing the responsible authority to define different switching times and lighting behaviours for specific locations. The implementation combines connected luminaires, sensor data, central management software and remote monitoring of lighting parameters. Lamps near pedestrian crossings can be activated earlier and switched off later than surrounding lights, increasing visibility in areas where road-safety risks are higher. Continuous technical monitoring also enables faster detection of failures and supports earlier planning of maintenance work. The expected results include significant energy savings, reduced interruptions in lighting operation, shorter response times when faults occur and lower maintenance costs through better planning. The wider public value is a more adaptive and safety-oriented lighting service that uses local conditions to guide infrastructure operation.

title: Smart lighting in urban space
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Urban residential areas require lighting that improves safety and liveability while limiting electricity costs and making better use of existing infrastructure. Smart lighting in urban space in Wrocław responds to this challenge through the installation of remotely controlled LED lighting in the WUWA 2 estate. The case focuses on replacing conventional lighting with a more flexible system that can adjust to changes in movement and local conditions, rather than maintaining the same level of illumination throughout the night. The implementation combines LED technology with a remote-control system and traffic-sensitive operation, enabling the lighting intensity to change when the system detects variations in use of the space. This supports safer movement for residents, pedestrians and other users while reducing unnecessary electricity consumption during periods of lower activity. A further technical feature is the permanent power supply to street-lighting circuits, which creates opportunities to use lighting infrastructure for additional urban services. These may include electric-vehicle charging or internet provision, turning lighting poles into multifunctional public assets. The expected impact is lower energy expenditure, improved safety and comfort in the estate, and greater flexibility in how urban infrastructure is used. For the municipality, the project also demonstrates how lighting networks can become a platform for broader smart-city services.

title: Wroclaw Intelligent lighting system
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Cities need to modernise lighting poles so that they do more than illuminate streets, especially where existing infrastructure can support new data services for mobility, safety and urban planning. Wroclaw Intelligent lighting system is a research project aimed at combining the basic function of lighting poles with additional functions designed for residents and municipal management. The operational problem is that traditional street-lighting infrastructure often represents a costly but underused urban asset, while authorities require better data on pedestrian, cyclist and vehicle flows to understand how public space is used. The project therefore adds new sensing and analytical capabilities to lighting infrastructure. Devices installed on selected poles count pedestrians, cyclists and vehicles, including the identification of vehicle types. At the same time, the lighting itself has been replaced with LED luminaires that can adjust light intensity to external conditions. The technological implementation combines traffic-counting devices, adaptive LED lighting and infrastructure-level monitoring, creating a platform that supports both illumination and data collection. The expected impact is improved energy efficiency, better adjustment of lighting to real-world conditions and richer information on mobility patterns in the city. For Wrocław, the system provides a practical testbed for multifunctional urban infrastructure, helping the municipality explore how existing assets can support safer, more responsive and more evidence-based local services.

title: Wroclaw Intelligent parking system
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Residents and visitors often lose time searching for parking spaces in busy urban areas, while municipalities lack precise and timely information on parking availability at street level. Wroclaw Intelligent parking system addresses this problem by developing a prototype that collects data from multiple sources, including sensors and cameras, to estimate the likelihood of finding a free parking space in the area towards which a driver is travelling. The operational objective is to reduce uncertainty for road users and improve the management of scarce parking capacity in the city. The system focuses on recognising how many spaces are occupied or available in a given street area, transforming dispersed observations into information that can be used by residents. Its technological implementation combines physical sensors, camera-based detection and data-processing components that analyse occupancy signals and generate parking-availability estimates. As part of the project, a mobile application is planned to show users both the travel time to a car park and the availability of spaces. The expected impact is a better user experience for drivers, reduced unnecessary circulation in search of parking, more efficient use of available spaces and potentially lower congestion and emissions in dense areas. For the municipality, the system can also provide valuable data for parking policy, infrastructure planning and traffic-management decisions.

title: Resident's Virtual Advisor
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Residents searching for municipal information can struggle to find the correct answer on public administration websites when procedures, forms and official notices are dispersed across many pages. Resident's Virtual Advisor helps the Municipality of Wrocław improve access to information on the Public Information Bulletin by guiding users towards the relevant content through a chat-based dialogue system. The service responds to the need to optimise customer-service processes for a large user base, including administrations and thousands of customers who require quick and reliable information. Rather than asking residents to navigate the website independently, the system simulates a conversation with a real person and leads the user to the appropriate answer. The technological implementation belongs to the field of intelligent customer-interaction solutions and uses artificial-intelligence mechanisms integrated with sound and video functions. At a conceptual level, the advisor interprets user queries, identifies the most relevant BIP content and presents guidance through a conversational interface. The service is available online, improving access beyond traditional office interactions. The expected impact is faster information retrieval, reduced pressure on municipal staff, more intuitive use of public information resources and greater consistency in how residents are directed to official answers. For Wrocław, the solution supports a more accessible and user-oriented model of digital municipal administration.

title: Katowice Intelligent Monitoring and Analysis System (KISMiA)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Urban safety services need to monitor public spaces effectively and coordinate responses across different operational units, but conventional video surveillance can become difficult to manage when large numbers of cameras produce continuous streams of footage. Katowice Intelligent Monitoring and Analysis System (KISMiA) addresses this challenge by integrating video management, video analytics and operational support into a single monitoring environment for the Municipality of Katowice. The system is built around three components: a Video Materials Management System, a Video Analytics Component and an Operational Support Component. The video management system administers the video data supplied to the platform, while the analytics layer, based on IBM Intelligent Video Analytics, continuously analyses streams and generates descriptive information from each camera. The operational support component is designed to provide the right people with the right information, helping them coordinate actions and follow results. The main integration point is the IOC platform, which gathers all system elements and supports coordination with other integrated systems, including IVA and VMS. With 260 cameras currently in the system, KISMiA enhances the city’s ability to detect relevant events, manage situational information and support decision-making by public services. Its expected impact is faster operational awareness, improved coordination, more effective use of video data and stronger support for urban safety management.

title: Integrated Public Transport Management System - ITS
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Public transport networks require reliable passenger information, safety monitoring and coordination with wider traffic-management systems to maintain service quality and user confidence. Integrated Public Transport Management System in Lublin complements the existing traffic-management system by adding functions that support travellers, operators and municipal transport management. The operational challenge is to provide timely information and improve safety at stops and interchange points, particularly where passengers depend on accurate updates to plan journeys and where public transport infrastructure must be monitored continuously. The system includes an information service for travellers, such as electronic information boards and online systems, as well as safety-monitoring systems installed at stops and transfer hubs. Technologically, it combines digital passenger-information displays, online data services, monitoring devices and integration with the city’s traffic-management environment. These components allow transport information to be communicated more clearly and enable responsible services to observe conditions at key public-transport locations. The expected impact is improved passenger experience, better access to real-time or updated transport information, enhanced safety at stops and hubs, and stronger operational coordination within the urban mobility system. For the municipality, the project supports a more integrated approach to public transport management and helps align passenger services with broader traffic-control capabilities.

title: Chojnice Virtual clerk
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Chojnice’s Virtual Clerk was launched through the Biznes Chojnice portal as part of a wider project to promote the poviat as attractive, innovative and investment-friendly. The service problem is that residents, visitors, entrepreneurs and potential investors may require rapid access to information on local matters, tourism and business opportunities, while municipal staff can face repeated enquiries on standard topics. The chatbot is intended to optimise the servicing of large numbers of beneficiaries by providing a digital first point of contact. The implementation uses a virtual assistant on the bizneschojnice.eu website to answer general questions connected with the poviat, including tourism and business-related information. Conceptually, the system combines chatbot interaction, local information retrieval, structured knowledge content and self-service access to administrative or promotional material. The expected impact is faster access to information, greater availability of support, reduced repetitive workload for staff and improved visibility of the local business and tourism offer. By embedding the assistant in an investment and promotion portal, the municipality can also strengthen external communication with potential partners and visitors. The pilot’s value lies in making local government information easier to navigate while supporting economic-development objectives through a more accessible digital channel.

title: Introduction of autonomous electric vehicles for urban transport
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Rzeszów’s autonomous electric vehicle pilot focuses on connecting different transport nodes through driverless public transport vehicles. The mobility challenge is to improve first- and last-mile connectivity between local, long-distance, railway and air stations, where passengers often need convenient transfers across different transport modes. The Municipality of Rzeszów and MPK are associated with the planned introduction of autonomous, driverless electric vehicles that would carry passengers between these transfer points. The implementation is based on autonomous electric shuttle technology, combining vehicle automation, electric propulsion, route planning, passenger-transfer management and integration with the wider urban transport network. Conceptually, such a system uses sensors, navigation software, control systems and predefined operating routes to move passengers safely between nodes without a conventional driver. The expected impact is improved intermodal connectivity, reduced dependence on private cars for short transfer journeys, lower local emissions and a more innovative public transport offer. If successfully tested, the pilot could provide evidence on the feasibility of autonomous shuttles in Polish urban mobility, including their operational reliability, passenger acceptance and integration with existing public transport services. Its long-term value would depend on safety performance, regulatory approval, infrastructure readiness and clear service integration.

title: Chatbot SAM - Virtual Community Assistant
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Chatbot SAM is a solution that is being introduced to the Kielce Technology Park. It enables communication between tenants and guests with KPT employees. SAM runs mainly on the platforms that users know best, such as Facebook Messenger and Facebook. Using Messenger, the virtual assistant is able to precisely locate its user, helping it find an event, office, or specific company, and even lead and navigate inside and outside the building. Using it, tenants have ongoing contact with guardians, and it is easier for them to find business partners. Artificial Intelligence is being used here to present the offer and stimulate the activity of the KTP community.

title: Kąty Wrocławskie Virtual clerk
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: The Kąty Wrocławskie Virtual Clerk is designed to modernise interactions between the municipal administration and residents by expanding digital public services and making routine communication with the office more efficient. The underlying problem is that citizens often need to access information, submit requests, or follow administrative procedures through channels that can be fragmented, time-consuming, or dependent on office opening hours. For the municipality and commune administration, this creates workload pressures and can reduce the quality and timeliness of responses. The main stakeholders are inhabitants of the Kąty Wrocławskie commune, municipal employees, local decision-makers, and service providers supporting the eK@ty Wrocławskie mobile application. The objective is to improve and rationalise administrative work while giving residents a practical digital assistant for local public services. The implementation is based on a mobile application that acts as a citizen-facing service interface, combining digital forms, information access, service notifications, guided support, and communication features. Conceptually, the virtual clerk can be integrated with municipal back-office systems, case-management workflows, resident databases, and e-service portals, enabling users to interact with the administration through a single digital entry point. The expected results include faster handling of standard enquiries, reduced pressure on front-office staff, improved transparency for residents, and better continuity in communication between the office and the citizen. The initiative can also increase the accessibility of local services, support administrative standardisation, and improve satisfaction by making municipal procedures easier to navigate.

title: BOSCO - Distribution of financial aid
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Energy-price vulnerability requires public authorities to determine quickly and consistently whether households qualify for financial support with electricity bills. BOSCO was introduced in Spain by the Secretary of State for Energy to help electricity suppliers assess eligibility for the bono social eléctrico, a social tariff that reduces bills for eligible consumers. The stated rationale was to simplify the process for applicants and make eligibility checking more efficient for reference electricity suppliers. The implementation is an automated decision-support or rule-processing system that checks whether applicants meet legal and regulatory conditions for the social tariff. At a conceptual level, BOSCO translates eligibility rules into software logic, receives or verifies applicant information and returns an outcome that determines whether the supplier can apply the discount. The expected administrative benefit was faster processing, standardised eligibility checks and reduced burden on utility companies. However, the system became controversial after reports that eligible applicants were wrongly denied support. Civio investigated the problem and requested access to the source code to understand the causes. In 2025, Spain’s Supreme Court ordered the administration to provide access to the BOSCO code, making the case a major example of algorithmic transparency in public-service decision-making. Its significance therefore lies both in welfare automation and in the legal debate over accountability for automated public decisions.

title: Pred Crime Pilot Rivas-Vaciamadrid
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Pred Crime pilot in Rivas-Vaciamadrid addressed the challenge of supporting local police in anticipating where and when common offences and misdemeanours were more likely to occur. In 2016, the local police of Rivas-Vaciamadrid, a municipality of around 86,000 inhabitants in the Madrid region, tested the Pred-Crime software developed by the Spanish company EuroCop. The operational objective was to use historical policing information to support prevention-oriented deployment decisions, particularly in relation to offences such as robberies and traffic violations. The emerging technology implementation relied on analytical software that processed historical crime and incident data to identify spatial and temporal patterns associated with different categories of offences. At conceptual level, the system generated predictions on likely locations and timeframes for future incidents, which could then inform police planning and patrol allocation. The pilot was reportedly intended for full implementation during 2016; however, after nine months of testing, the municipality decided not to continue using the software. The available information therefore points to limited operational impact in this specific municipality. While EuroCop states that it has numerous municipal customers across Spain, it is not clear whether those authorities use Pred-Crime or other non-predictive EuroCop tools. The case is therefore particularly relevant as an example of a tested but discontinued predictive policing application, highlighting issues of adoption, validation and long-term suitability.

title: Automated analysis of social media content
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The automated analysis of social media content in Catalonia was introduced to help public authorities better understand public reactions to policy initiatives and communication campaigns. In January 2018, the regional Government of Catalonia launched a pilot to assess the public impact of STEMcat, a policy initiative aimed at promoting scientific and technological vocations among young people. The objective was to move beyond traditional consultation and survey methods by analysing online conversations at scale, while supporting the SmartCAT strategy to position Catalonia as a smart region. The emerging technology implementation used Citibeats, a text-analysis software developed by Social Coin, a Barcelona-based start-up. During the pilot, the system collected and analysed around 12,000 tweets concerning STEM disciplines in Catalonia, using machine-learning techniques to classify content and identify patterns in public attitudes. Authorities reported insights such as different levels of responsiveness among women to messages on natural sciences compared with technology, which were then used to optimise strategy and propose further initiatives. Citibeats had also been used by Barcelona municipality in December 2017 to analyse around 30,000 comments from more than 15,000 people on public transport and mobility, and by Navarra from March 2019 to detect online hate speech across Facebook, Twitter and Instagram. The main reported value is faster, lower-cost analysis of large volumes of online content, although the representativeness of the samples, methodological transparency, oversight mechanisms and actual policy influence remain unclear.

title: IBM Watson: Automated assistance in tax filing in Spain
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: The Spanish Tax Authority’s use of IBM Watson responds to a specific administrative challenge in VAT filing, particularly for large companies dealing with complex reporting obligations. Before the deployment, civil servants received a substantial volume of email enquiries related to VAT issues, creating repetitive workload and slowing down support for taxpayers. The operational context therefore involved a national tax administration seeking to provide more continuous, consistent, and scalable assistance, while reducing the burden on staff responsible for answering technical questions. The objective was to offer automated support on a defined aspect of VAT filing, allowing companies to obtain guidance outside standard office hours and helping public servants concentrate on more complex cases. The implementation used IBM Watson as an automated assistance tool, applying natural language processing and question-answering capabilities to interpret written queries, retrieve relevant information, and provide responses linked to tax-filing requirements. At system level, the solution would rely on curated tax knowledge, structured guidance, conversational interfaces, and integration with the Tax Authority’s service channels. Public communications emphasised its 24/7 availability and its capacity to absorb repeated enquiries. Reported results indicate a marked operational effect: between July 2017 and February 2018, weekly emails to civil servants on VAT matters fell from 900 to 165, while the assistant’s use rose from around 200 questions per week at launch in July 2017 to approximately 2,000 by November 2017. These figures suggest improved scalability, lower administrative pressure, and greater availability of taxpayer support.

title: REACHOUT: Smart Cities: from smart waste to smart tourism
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Logroño municipality and the La Rioja and Cantabria regional governments
source_description: The REACHOUT-related Smart Waste example reflects the broader effort of Spanish local and regional authorities to use data-driven tools to improve municipal service planning. Waste management is a complex operational area in which authorities must decide where, when and how services are needed, while responding to changing urban patterns, citizen behaviour and resource constraints. The Smart Waste platform was first piloted in 2018 by Logroño municipality and the regional governments of La Rioja and Cantabria. Its objective was to support more informed waste-management decisions by combining multiple sources of data rather than relying only on fixed collection schedules or fragmented local knowledge. The emerging technology implementation was developed by The Circular Lab, the innovation centre of Ecoembes, with support from Minsait, a division of Indra. The platform gathers data from sensors installed in waste bins and collection trucks, and combines these with information from social media, surveys, census sources and satellite data. At conceptual level, the system supports automated analysis and decision-support outputs that help authorities estimate service needs by location and time. The platform is now described as available to local and regional authorities across Spain. Its potential impact includes improved targeting of waste services, better planning, more efficient resource allocation and increased scalability across municipalities. However, the available information does not explain the software’s internal functioning, the exact outputs it produces, or the concrete decisions adopted by authorities as a result of its use.

title: Briefcam - Smart video surveillance by the local police
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Local police in the cities of Kortrijk, Kuurne, and Lendelde (VLAS)
source_description: The Briefcam use case concerns the adoption of smart video surveillance by the local police serving Kortrijk, Kuurne, and Lendelede, known as VLAS, from 2019 onwards. The operational issue was the need to process large amounts of video footage more efficiently, particularly when police services had to search for people, vehicles, animals, or other objects appearing in recorded images. Traditional manual review of surveillance footage can be slow, resource-intensive, and inconsistent, especially where many cameras or long recordings are involved. The stakeholders include local police forces, municipal authorities, residents, people captured by surveillance systems, and the technology provider. The objective was to make video analysis faster and more searchable for policing and security purposes. The implementation uses Briefcam’s video analytics system, which stores objects detected in footage and classifies them into categories such as people, small vehicles, large vehicles, and animals. The system then performs additional categorisation: for people, it may distinguish between men, women, and children, and further identify visual attributes such as sleeve length, trousers, clothing colour, hats, handbags, or backpacks; comparable categorisation is applied to vehicles. At a conceptual level, the system combines object detection, image classification, metadata extraction, and searchable video indexing. The expected impact is faster investigation support, improved ability to identify relevant footage, and reduced time spent on manual review. However, the use case also raises important issues regarding proportionality, accuracy, transparency, and the monitoring of people in public spaces.

title: Algorithmic school registrations
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Algorithmic school registration systems in Belgian cities emerged in response to persistent problems in allocating school places fairly when demand exceeded capacity, particularly where parents sought admission to the same popular schools. In some cases, families spent nights in tents outside schools to secure early registration, which was widely seen as inequitable and administratively unsustainable. The stakeholders include children, parents, schools, municipalities, education authorities, and communities concerned with equal access to education. The objective was to replace first-come, first-served practices with centralised online registration procedures capable of allocating places according to defined criteria. In primary education, the Leuven system considers variables collected from parents, including the mother’s education level and whether the student receives a grant, to classify children as “indicator” or “non-indicator” students. Further allocation is based on distance between home and school and the stated school preference, with schools able to assign different weights to these two criteria, such as 30%, 50%, or 70%. In Antwerp, distance must receive at least 50% weight. For secondary schools, some cities use a different algorithm because distance can be discriminatory where not all municipalities have secondary schools; instead, priority students and indicator students are considered, with random allocation based on first choice across three rounds. The expected benefits include less queuing, greater procedural order, and more transparent allocation. Yet the system has also produced contested outcomes, such as pupils living near a school not receiving a place while others from farther away were admitted.

title: Predictive ADM systems for healthcare and upbringing
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: This use case brings together two related applications of predictive automated decision-making in Belgium: health risk prediction and possible future support for child-related public services. In healthcare, the operational problem concerns the early identification of atrial fibrillation, a heart rhythm disorder associated with serious cardiovascular events, including heart attacks. Earlier detection could support preventive care, clinical prioritisation, and better risk management. Stakeholders include patients, clinicians, researchers, healthcare providers, and technology developers such as the Brussels start-up Kantify and the AI Lab at Université Libre de Bruxelles, Iridia. The implementation described for atrial fibrillation involves a predictive model trained to identify patterns linked to the condition, using health-related data and machine-learning techniques to estimate risk. A second, less concrete strand concerns the Flemish Agency for Upbringing, where public discussion indicated interest in using predictive systems to anticipate whether problems may emerge for a particular child, based on existing information. However, the Agency stated that there were no concrete plans at that stage and that it was preparing a policy note. The potential impact in healthcare includes earlier detection, better targeting of interventions, and improved clinical efficiency. In child and family services, possible benefits could include earlier support and more proactive case management, but the absence of a defined implementation makes results uncertain. The use case therefore illustrates both the promise of predictive tools and the need for caution, legal clarity, transparency, and strong safeguards in sensitive domains.

title: Taxation and the automatization of property evaluation
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Denmark’s automated property valuation initiative addresses a long-standing administrative challenge in tax governance: how to assess property values consistently, efficiently, and at national scale. Property valuation is central to taxation, but manual or fragmented approaches can be slow, costly, uneven, and difficult to update across large numbers of properties. The Danish government has therefore sought for several years to centralise and automate parts of tax administration, with property assessment becoming one of the key initiatives. The relevant stakeholders include the Danish Tax Authority, property owners, taxpayers, legislators, administrative law experts, and system developers. The objective is to establish a more standardised valuation process capable of calculating property values through a national automated system. The legal basis is the Ejendomsvurderingslov, the 2017 law on property assessment, which mandates the use of an automated valuation system. The planned implementation is expected to use machine learning to develop a statistical predictive model, drawing on property characteristics, market information, geographic variables, and other administrative datasets to estimate values. At a system level, this requires integration with tax databases, cadastral information, valuation workflows, and channels for administrative review. The intended impact is greater scalability, more consistent assessments, lower long-term processing costs, and faster updates. However, the system has faced delays, rising cost concerns, doubts about accuracy, and questions over compatibility with Danish administrative law, meaning that the expected benefits remain dependent on technical reliability and legal robustness.

title: Exam control in schools: fighting fraud or profiling students?
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: This use case concerns the use of digital examination-monitoring tools in Denmark to detect suspected exam fraud in schools and universities. The operational problem is the need to protect the integrity of assessments while managing large numbers of students and increasingly digital forms of examination. Education authorities and institutions sought ways to identify plagiarism, unauthorised collaboration, or manipulation of exam conditions more efficiently than through manual review alone. However, students, schools, universities, and public authorities became involved in a wider debate about proportionality, privacy, accuracy, and fairness. The implementation relied on digital monitoring and analytical tools designed to observe or assess student behaviour, device activity, and written submissions. One strand involved The Digital Exam Monitor, while another example came from students at Copenhagen University, who developed a machine-learning system for plagiarism detection using around 130,000 student assignments. Such systems can conceptually combine text comparison, behavioural monitoring, statistical similarity detection, and data-driven anomaly identification. The expected impact would be stronger fraud detection, more consistent enforcement, and reduced administrative effort in checking exams. Nevertheless, the use case generated substantial resistance because students considered the tools invasive and potentially discriminatory. Concerns also emerged around the unauthorised use of assignment data, the risk of false positives, and the profiling of particular groups of students.

title: The Youth Guarantee Support System (YGSS) to identifying young people not in education or employment
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Young people who are not in education, employment or training can be difficult for municipalities to identify early, especially when information about education, work, residence and social support is held in separate registers. Estonia’s Youth Guarantee Support System helps municipal case managers identify residents aged 16–26 who may need support to return to education or enter the labour market. The objective is to turn existing administrative data into an outreach mechanism for youth support, while keeping the intervention anchored in municipal casework. The implementation works through the STAR social-services and benefits information system. Twice a year, municipalities that have joined the programme can receive a list of young people registered in their locality who appear, based on data from multiple registers, to be in a NEET situation and potentially in need of help. At a conceptual level, the system combines register-based screening, local-authority access controls, case-manager review, youth contact and consent-based follow-up. Young people can restrict analysis, and where support proceeds, they are contacted and asked to complete a survey before individual assistance is planned. The expected impact is earlier identification of unsupported youth, more proactive municipal outreach, better targeting of employment and education services, and stronger prevention of long-term exclusion. Current European and Estonian policy sources continue to describe youth-guarantee support and NEET-targeted measures as active policy areas.

title: Prediction model for the healthcare needs of patients with chronic illnesses
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: This use case addresses the need to strengthen primary care in Estonia by helping family physicians identify patients with selected chronic conditions who are at higher risk of hospital admission or other adverse health outcomes. The operational challenge is that health systems often hold substantial administrative and billing data but may struggle to use it proactively to support prevention, care planning, and earlier intervention. Stakeholders include the Estonian Health Insurance Fund, family practitioners, patients with chronic illnesses, the World Bank, and international partners contributing comparative data. The objective is to provide a practical prediction model that can support physicians in prioritising patients who may require closer monitoring or tailored care. The implementation draws on medical invoice data held by the Estonian Health Insurance Fund to identify relevant diagnoses and patient characteristics. The pilot also involved Costa Rica, which provided access to its medical billing database to examine clinical and socio-economic data not included in EHIF datasets. At a conceptual level, the model applies predictive analytics to administrative health records, seeking the algorithm that best estimates the likelihood of hospital admission or further health problems. Training and reinforcement were supported through webinars for family practitioners, led by a local pilot coordinator acting as a World Bank consultant. The expected impact is better targeting of primary care, earlier identification of high-risk patients, and improved use of existing health data for prevention-oriented service planning.

title: Checking of data Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The initiative was developed to address concerns on the automation of data verification during the registration of unemployed citizens in Estonia. The operational problem is that unemployment registration requires public authorities to validate applicant information against multiple administrative sources before granting formal status and determining the next procedural step. Manual checks can be time-consuming, repetitive, and vulnerable to inconsistent handling, particularly where high volumes of applications are processed. The key stakeholders are unemployed citizens, the Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund, public databases holding relevant administrative records, and case officers responsible for employment services. The objective is to make registration faster and more standardised by allowing the system to verify the applicant’s data after online submission and determine which document should be sent to the person concerned. The implementation uses automated background checks across different databases once a citizen registers as unemployed through the Fund’s website. Conceptually, the solution combines data-matching, rule-based validation, automated decision workflows, and document-generation mechanisms. It checks whether submitted information is correct, processes the result, and initiates the appropriate communication with the applicant. The expected impact is a more efficient registration process, reduced administrative workload, quicker confirmation for eligible citizens, and more consistent handling of standard cases. By automating routine data checks, the Fund can allocate staff attention to more complex situations requiring human judgement or additional clarification.

title: Checking entitlement of umemployment aid
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: This use case concerns the use of automated decision-making by Estonia’s Unemployment Insurance Fund to determine what unemployed persons are entitled to receive, including the amount and duration of unemployment aid or unemployment insurance benefits. The operational problem is that benefit entitlement assessment requires the processing of eligibility rules, personal employment histories, insurance records, and other administrative data, often under time pressure and with direct consequences for citizens’ income security. Stakeholders include unemployed applicants, the Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund, public employment-service staff, and the wider social protection system. The objective is to accelerate and standardise the calculation of benefit rights while reducing manual workload in routine cases. The implementation uses automated systems to assess entitlement on the basis of available applicant data and predefined legal or administrative criteria. At a conceptual level, the system likely combines data retrieval from official registers, rule-based eligibility checks, automated calculation modules, and case-routing functions for decisions requiring further review. The information provided indicates that 50% of these decisions are made entirely through automated means. The expected impact includes faster processing, improved administrative scalability, and more uniform application of entitlement rules. At the same time, because the decisions affect access to financial support, the use case raises important requirements around explainability, contestability, accuracy, and human oversight, especially where applicants may need to challenge or correct the data used in the assessment.

title: Automatic identification of individual risk factors in social care and healthcare
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Social exclusion among young adults can arise from interacting health, social, educational and economic factors, making it difficult for professionals to identify early patterns using service records in isolation. Eksote, the South Karelia social and healthcare district, worked with Fujitsu on an AI model to identify factors associated with social exclusion and related risks. The operational problem was to understand which combinations of service-use patterns, health records or social-care indicators were associated with later adverse outcomes, so that welfare professionals could improve prevention. The implementation used pseudonymised data from Eksote services and machine-learning methods to identify risk factors defined by professionals. At a conceptual level, the model analyses historical service data, identifies statistical relationships with social-exclusion outcomes and produces an overview of factors associated with increased risk. Its expected value is to support service planning, professional awareness and research on early intervention. Importantly, the system was constrained by Finnish rules on secondary and combined use of healthcare data: the model could not be used to identify individual young adults at risk without additional legal or consent arrangements. The case is therefore best framed as a modelling and risk-factor analysis project rather than a fully operational individual risk-identification system.

title: Predicting youth problems - Identifying youth problems and providing support
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: In South Karelia, Eksote developed a predictive welfare model to help social, health and education professionals identify children and young people who might need support before difficulties became more severe. The operational problem was that warning signs are often dispersed across maternity clinics, kindergartens, schools, healthcare, mental healthcare and social services, making it difficult for authorities to intervene early and coordinate support for families. The objective was to detect emerging risks linked to school performance, attendance, behavioural issues, psychiatric care, custody decisions and substance abuse, so that preventive action could be taken sooner. The implementation used a model developed with the Finnish IT firm Avaintec, combining administrative data from several public-service systems and analysing predefined undesirable outcomes. It identified 1,340 risk factors, including examples such as dental problems, missed maternity-clinic appointments by parents and bullying behaviour among siblings. At a conceptual level, the system used cross-sector data integration, pattern detection and risk-factor modelling to follow indicators at individual level. The expected value was earlier identification of children requiring support, better coordination between services and more targeted preventive intervention. However, the use case also raised serious questions about proportionality, data quality, family profiling and whether administrative indicators can reliably capture complex social and educational needs.

title: Face recognition at schools - Face recognition at the building’s entrance
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The use case concerns a proposed access-control system for selected high schools in Nice and Marseille, where local authorities sought to manage entry to school buildings more efficiently while strengthening perimeter security and monitoring the flow of pupils. The operational issue was centred on verifying that only authorised students could enter school premises, with school administrations, municipal authorities, students, parents, and technology providers all affected by the initiative. The intended objective was to replace or complement existing manual checks at the building entrance with a faster identity-verification process. The proposed implementation relied on facial recognition technology installed at school entrances, under a programme to be funded and delivered by Cisco. In conceptual terms, the system would have compared live facial images captured at entry points against enrolled biometric templates associated with authorised pupils, using image-processing models, biometric matching algorithms, controlled access infrastructure, and secure storage mechanisms. Integration would likely have involved entry gates, local school databases, and identity-management workflows. The expected benefits included shorter queues, more consistent access control, reduced administrative burden for staff, and improved perceived security. However, the project was placed on hold after the French data protection authority considered it illegal, underlining that operational efficiency gains could not outweigh concerns around proportionality, consent, children’s rights, and compliance with data protection rules.

title: RADAAR-iTE Predictive policing - risk assessment of militant Salafitsts
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: RADAR-iTE is a German risk-assessment tool used to support police evaluation of persons already known to the authorities in relation to militant Salafist extremism. The operational problem is that security agencies must prioritise attention and resources across individuals who may present different levels of threat, while ensuring that assessments are structured, documented, and comparable. Stakeholders include the Bundeskriminalamt, caseworkers, other security authorities, assessed individuals, and the research partner involved in development. The objective is to classify known persons into threat levels that can inform subsequent operational decisions. The implementation is based on a standardised questionnaire completed by a caseworker using observable behaviour and data already gathered by the police, as well as information the police are legally authorised to access. The system then produces a categorisation into three levels: high, conspicuous, or moderate. Conceptually, RADAR-iTE functions as a structured professional judgement and risk-scoring tool, combining behavioural indicators, case information, and predefined assessment criteria rather than acting as a fully autonomous policing system. Once the threat level is generated, the responsible caseworker or department decides what action should follow. The expected impact is greater consistency in risk classification, clearer prioritisation of security resources, and more systematic documentation of assessments. However, the use case also requires careful safeguards due to its sensitivity, including legality, proportionality, non-discrimination, and accountability for decisions based on risk categorisation.

title: PRECOBS - Predictive policing in German administrations
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Baden Wurttemberg, Hesse, Berlin and North Rhine-Westphalia
source_description: PRECOBS and related predictive policing systems in German administrations address the challenge of preventing burglary and other property crime through more targeted operational planning. Several German Länder and cities have tested or deployed tools designed to identify locations where break-ins are more likely to occur, allowing police forces to incorporate forecasts into prevention and patrol strategies. In Bavaria, PRECOBS, developed by the Institut für musterbasierte Prognosetechnik, has been used to calculate areas with higher predicted burglary risk. Similar approaches have been adopted elsewhere: Hesse uses KLB-operativ, Berlin uses KrimPro, North Rhine-Westphalia developed SKALA based on IBM products, and Lower Saxony uses PreMAP. The emerging technology implementation is based on analytical systems that process historical crime data and related contextual variables to identify recurring spatial and temporal patterns. These systems generate forecast areas or hot spots, which police authorities can use in action plans and resource deployment. The impact is intended to be more proactive burglary prevention, better allocation of police capacity and improved operational situational awareness. However, implementation outcomes vary across jurisdictions. In Baden-Württemberg, use of PRECOBS was discontinued in 2019 due to data-quality issues, showing that predictive policing tools depend heavily on the reliability, completeness and suitability of the underlying data. The case therefore illustrates both the operational promise and the governance limitations of algorithmic forecasting in police work.

title: AI to combat child pornography online
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: the Zentral- und Ansprechstelle Cybercrime (Contact Office for Cyber Crime, ZAC NRW)
source_description: Investigations into child sexual abuse material impose a severe workload and psychological burden on investigators, who may need to review large numbers of harmful images while identifying victims, suspects and links between cases. North Rhine-Westphalia’s cybercrime contact office, ZAC NRW, collaborated with Microsoft and researchers to explore AI-supported analysis methods for this investigative context. The operational objective was to reduce manual exposure to harmful material and accelerate the identification of relevant evidence, while complying with strict rules on data protection and child protection. The implementation used software to anonymise or protect data before analysis, with cloud-based algorithms examining images, detecting illegal content indicators and supporting comparison with profiles or known material. At a conceptual level, the system combines content classification, face or feature matching, secure data handling and investigative review workflows. The technology is intended to support police and prosecutors by triaging and structuring evidence, not to replace human legal assessment or investigative responsibility. The expected impact is faster case analysis, reduced psychological strain for officers, better detection of recurring victims or perpetrators and more efficient allocation of specialist investigative resources. Public material from North Rhine-Westphalia describes the work as a research cooperation at ZAC NRW using AI analysis methods to combat child sexual abuse material.

title: Suicide Prevention in Jail - Detecting of suspicious objects in a cell
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Ministry of Justice of the State of North Rhine-Westphalia
source_description: North Rhine-Westphalia’s prison suicide-prevention programme was launched to reduce suicide risk among detainees classified as medium to high risk. The operational problem is that conventional in-person checks at 15-minute intervals can be resource-intensive and may increase emotional strain on inmates, while prison staff still need reliable ways to detect dangerous objects or situations promptly. The Ministry of Justice of North Rhine-Westphalia commissioned FusionSystems GmbH to build a video surveillance system able to identify suspicious objects in a cell, such as a knotted rope or a firelighter, and alert officers on duty. The implementation uses video analytics and object-recognition techniques to monitor defined visual indicators associated with suicide risk. Conceptually, the system combines camera-based observation, automated object detection, risk-specific alerting and staff response workflows. The expected impact is earlier warning of potential self-harm situations, reduced need for intrusive repeated checks and better allocation of staff attention towards cases requiring intervention. However, because the system operates in a prison environment and concerns highly vulnerable individuals, it requires strict safeguards around privacy, necessity, accuracy, proportionality and human oversight. Its value depends on whether automated alerts can improve safety without creating excessive surveillance or false reassurance.

title: PRE-VIEW - Identification of international crisis
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Foreign ministries need early signals of instability so that diplomatic, stabilisation and humanitarian responses can be planned before crises escalate. Germany’s Federal Foreign Office uses PRE-VIEW, short for Prediction, Visualization, Early Warning, as a data-analytics tool to support crisis early warning and stabilisation planning. The operational problem is that political, social, economic and conflict-related developments produce large volumes of open data, but analysts need structured insight rather than unfiltered information. The implementation analyses publicly available data on current trends and conflicts, then produces maps, infographics and trend analyses for officials working on international stabilisation and crisis engagement. At a conceptual level, PRE-VIEW combines data collection, machine-learning or AI-supported processing, conflict indicators, geospatial visualisation and analyst-facing dashboards.
