source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: OpenGovIntelligence sought to modernise public administrations by using Linked Open Statistical Data to co-produce innovative public services with citizens, businesses and public-sector actors. Public administrations hold substantial statistical information, but its value is often limited by fragmented formats, weak interoperability and insufficient mechanisms for external reuse. The project therefore focused on new processes, policies and tools that would enable society and businesses to participate actively in data sharing and service co-production. Its implementation used Linked Open Statistical Data technologies and ran pilot studies in six countries, testing how structured, interoperable data could support new public-service models. Conceptually, the project combined linked data, semantic technologies, statistical datasets, co-creation methods and public-administration process redesign. It followed an iterative approach, using development and evaluation cycles to refine the OpenGovIntelligence framework and associated tools. The expected impact was greater transparency, more innovative public services, improved reuse of official statistics and stronger collaboration between administrations and external stakeholders. By treating data as a shared resource for service design, the project aimed to stimulate innovation and creativity while strengthening evidence-based administration.

title: RECAP - Reliable Capacity Provisioning and Enhanced Remediation for Distributed Cloud Applications
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: RECAP supported the implementation of the Common Agricultural Policy by developing personalised public services for farmers, agricultural consultants and administrations responsible for monitoring compliance. CAP rules create complex obligations, particularly around cross-compliance, and public authorities need efficient ways to monitor whether requirements are being met across diverse agricultural contexts. Farmers and consultants also benefit from clearer, more transparent information on obligations and potential breaches. The project implemented a cloud-based Software-as-a-Service platform using open Earth Observation data, user-generated information and geospatial data to support compliance monitoring. Conceptually, the system extracted relevant features from satellite and other open data, correlated them with information available to public organisations and modelled potential breaches of CAP requirements. This enabled authorities and inspectors to focus attention on likely non-compliance while giving users more personalised support. The expected impact was more efficient administrative control, lower monitoring burden, greater transparency for farmers and better targeting of inspections. By combining Earth Observation with cloud services and user-generated data, RECAP demonstrated how agricultural public services can shift from document-heavy compliance checks towards more continuous, data-supported monitoring.

title: SIMPATICO - Platform for PS - Italian Usecase
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: SIMPATICO was developed to improve the way citizens and companies interact with online public services, addressing a common weakness in digital administration: many services are standardised replicas of offline procedures, designed mainly around internal organisational logic rather than the needs, language and behaviour of users. In the Italian use case, the Municipality of Trento provided a public-service context in which administrative procedures could be simplified and adapted through continuous feedback. The objective was to make digital services easier to understand, reduce the distance between users and administrations, and identify why online procedures remain difficult or underused. The implementation combined language-processing technologies, machine-learning techniques and community contributions. Public administrations supplied formal knowledge about procedures, while citizens, companies, civil servants and professionals contributed questions, doubts, explanations and improvement suggestions. At a conceptual level, the platform linked service interfaces, text simplification, workflow guidance, user feedback and collaborative knowledge creation, allowing interactions to be progressively refined. The expected impact was improved usability of online services, fewer errors during administrative procedures, better citizen satisfaction and stronger capacity for administrations to learn from recurring difficulties. By combining institutional knowledge with bottom-up input, SIMPATICO treated service improvement as a continuous, participatory process rather than a one-off redesign of digital forms.

title: WeGovNow: Collective and participative approaches for addressing local policy challenges
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Empirica Gesellschaft für Kommunikations- & Technologieforschung mbH.
source_description: WeGovNow explored how local public services and policy challenges could be addressed through collaborative digital participation, treating citizens as partners in public-service delivery rather than passive users or customers. Local authorities often need to respond to issues such as neighbourhood improvement, service quality, environmental concerns or community planning, but conventional consultation channels can be fragmented, episodic and disconnected from day-to-day civic action. The project therefore aimed to provide public administrations, citizens, civil-society organisations and local businesses with digital tools for co-production, collective proposition development and shared problem-solving. Its implementation integrated emerging civic technologies into a pilot platform tested under day-to-day conditions in the London Borough of Southwark, the City of Turin and San Donà di Piave. Conceptually, the platform combined participatory mapping, issue reporting, discussion, collective proposal development and community coordination functions. The project also examined legal, ethical and organisational conditions to ensure democratic legitimacy and practical exploitability. The expected impact was stronger citizen engagement, more responsive local services and improved evidence on how digital co-production works in real administrative contexts. During the final project year, 9,976 pilot user accounts were registered across the three pilot municipalities, showing meaningful uptake in real-life settings.

title: REBUILD - ICT toolbox providing support to both migrants and refugees
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: REBUILD aimed to improve how migrants and refugees access services in Europe while helping local service providers manage integration support more effectively. The operational challenge was two-sided: newcomers often face fragmented information, language barriers, unfamiliar administrative systems and difficulties identifying relevant opportunities, while public authorities and support organisations need better tools to understand needs, coordinate services and evaluate impact. The project adopted a user-centred and participatory design approach, involving migrants, refugees and service providers from the early stages so that ethical, cultural and practical requirements could shape the solution. Its implementation developed an ICT toolbox using user profiling, skills-and-needs matching, chatbot functions and accessible service interfaces. Conceptually, the ecosystem connected information about individuals’ needs, skills and preferences with local service offers, guidance pathways and administrative workflows. It also included mechanisms to monitor and validate socio-economic impact. The expected value was more personalised support, easier access to services, improved communication between users and administrations, and better evidence for integration policies. By combining digital tools with co-design, REBUILD sought to avoid imposing a generic integration platform and instead build services around the lived experience of migrants and refugees and the operational realities of local providers.

title: NADINE - platform to promote migrant inclusion
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: NADINE was designed to support migrant inclusion by improving the way public authorities and guidance professionals understand skills, needs and available services. Migration brings significant human capital to Europe, yet integration systems may struggle to match people’s abilities, career ambitions, educational requirements and social or cultural needs with real opportunities in host societies. The project therefore aimed to build a platform that could support employability, career guidance and service matching on the basis of richer evidence about both migrants and local environments. Its implementation used open data, large-scale data repositories and analytical tools to create two main information banks: one concerning host societies and services, and another concerning migrants’ profiles, needs and skills. As users interacted with the platform, further data could be collected to refine the system and improve recommendations. Conceptually, NADINE combined skills assessment, labour-market intelligence, local-service mapping, guidance tools and personalised support interfaces. The expected impact was more tailored assistance for migrants, better use of skills, improved decision support for professionals and stronger alignment between integration services and actual needs. By linking social, educational, cultural and employment dimensions, NADINE approached inclusion as a multidimensional process rather than only a labour-market matching exercise.

title: WELCOME(Multiple Intelligent Conversation Agent Services for Reception, Management and Integration)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: WELCOME focused on supporting the reception and integration of third-country nationals, migrants and refugees through personalised digital assistance for both newcomers and public administrations. Reception and integration processes often involve complex registration steps, orientation needs, language barriers, civic education, access to local services and social inclusion challenges, while administrations must provide guidance across diverse profiles and contexts. The project aimed to create a psychologically and socially competent support environment that could help users navigate these processes in a more accessible and personalised way. Its implementation developed intelligent multilingual conversational agents, including embodied assistants, designed for contexts such as registration, orientation, language learning, civic education and community integration. The system used personalisation techniques so that agent behaviour could adapt to the user’s profile and situation, and it also explored immersive virtual and augmented reality technologies to make interaction more realistic and engaging. Conceptually, WELCOME combined conversational interfaces, multilingual processing, user profiling, interaction adaptation and immersive service design. The expected impact was better access to integration guidance, reduced pressure on frontline administrations, more consistent information provision and improved user experience for migrants and refugees. The services were validated through pilot use cases in Catalonia, Spain, Germany and Greece.

title: DPER Robotic Process Automation (RPA) Pilot
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Department of Public Expenditure and Reform
source_description: The DPER Robotic Process Automation pilot examined whether routine, stable and fully computer-based administrative processes in Irish central government could be automated to improve efficiency and service delivery. Public bodies often manage high-volume tasks that require staff to copy, check or transfer information between digital systems, even when the rules are clear and human judgement is limited. In 2017, the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform coordinated a pilot in which four government departments selected suitable processes to test the potential of robotic process automation. The implementation used software robots to operate existing applications at user-interface level, automating labour-intensive, rules-based tasks without requiring wholesale replacement of legacy systems. Conceptually, RPA was applied as a non-invasive automation layer that could log into systems, follow predefined steps, transfer data, validate entries and generate outputs consistently. The expected impact was improved accuracy, fewer manual errors, faster processing and the release of staff time for higher-value work. The pilot also helped the Irish public service understand which process characteristics make automation feasible and what governance, procurement and implementation arrangements would be needed for wider adoption. A later government RPA framework indicates that the pilot contributed to a broader national approach to automation services.

title: Housing Assistance Payment Robotics Pilot
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Housing Assistance Payment Shared Service Centre
source_description: The Housing Assistance Payment Robotics Pilot addressed the operational pressure faced by the HAP Shared Service Centre, operated by Limerick City and County Council on behalf of the local government sector. The centre manages very large payment and tenancy volumes, including more than 47,000 tenancies, 27,000 landlords, over €400 million in payments and more than €100 million in rent collection, with projected growth to 80,000 tenancies, 55,000 landlords and €600 million in payments by 2021. These volumes create substantial administrative workload and a strong incentive to identify processes that can be automated safely. In 2018, Agilisys carried out a proof-of-concept pilot examining three micro-processes within the centre. The implementation used robotic process automation to test whether repeatable, rule-based activities could be executed by software robots across existing business systems. Conceptually, the pilot assessed process suitability, automation feasibility, savings potential and opportunities for wider business-system integration. The results demonstrated that efficiencies and savings could be achieved, and the subsequent business case suggested that replacing 10 complex processes with RPA could generate considerable savings while improving services for tenants, landlords and administrative stakeholders. The use case therefore provided a practical basis for identifying further immediate automation opportunities within the HAP SSC.

title: Artificial intelligence finds disease-related genes
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: This use case addresses a central challenge in biomedical research: disease mechanisms are often distributed across large numbers of interacting genes, making it difficult for researchers to identify meaningful patterns in high-dimensional gene-expression data. Scientists at Linköping University led a study exploring how these complex datasets could be used to discover groups of genes associated with disease and, in the longer term, support more precise diagnosis and treatment. The objective was not to replace biological interpretation, but to give researchers a stronger exploratory method for finding structures that may otherwise remain hidden in very large molecular datasets. The implementation used an artificial neural network trained on extensive gene-expression information, allowing the system to learn patterns without relying only on predefined disease categories or manually selected markers. At a conceptual level, the model processed expression profiles, detected relationships between genes and organised them into groups that could reveal disease-relevant biological signals. The expected impact is improved discovery of candidate genes, better understanding of disease pathways and stronger foundations for precision medicine and individualised treatment. Although the work remains research-oriented, its value lies in showing how neural-network methods can support biomedical knowledge discovery by extracting interpretable signals from datasets that exceed the capacity of conventional manual analysis.

title: Estonia to give citizens Alexa-like access to public services
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Digital public services can still be difficult to use when citizens must navigate multiple portals, forms and institutional websites to complete a life event or obtain an answer. Estonia’s Bürokratt initiative aims to create a network of public-sector virtual assistants that allow people to interact with the state in natural language. The operational problem is that even highly digital government systems can remain fragmented from the user’s perspective, especially when a request requires cooperation between different agencies. The implementation concept connects chatbots across public-sector institutions into a shared assistant network. At a conceptual level, a citizen can ask a question or request a service through a conversational interface, while the system identifies the relevant institution, retrieves information and, where possible, supports service routing or administrative action. The longer-term vision is for personalised AI agents to cooperate across domains and help citizens solve problems without navigating complex portals or repeating information. The expected impact is simpler access to public services, better customer support, reduced administrative friction and more human-centred digital government. The initiative is significant because it moves beyond isolated chatbots towards an interoperable assistant layer for the public sector, building on Estonia’s wider digital-state infrastructure.

title: Artificial intelligence "Wuhan model"" at the biomedical campus in Rome"
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: During the early COVID-19 emergency, hospitals needed rapid tools to support diagnosis and monitoring of pneumonia from lung imaging, especially when clinical pressure was high and radiology teams faced urgent triage demands. Campus Bio-Medico University Hospital in Rome acquired an imaging system originally used in Wuhan to assist with early diagnosis and monitoring of COVID-19 pneumonia. The objective was to help radiologists interpret lung CT scans more quickly and consistently, while supporting clinical assessment rather than replacing specialist judgement. The implementation used an artificial-intelligence system trained to analyse chest CT images and identify patterns associated with COVID-19 pneumonia. Public reporting described a response reliability of 98.5% in around 20 seconds, and the system was tested successfully on anonymised patients by radiologists at the Rome hospital. At a conceptual level, the software processes CT image data, identifies relevant lung abnormalities and provides a rapid diagnostic support output for clinicians. The expected impact was faster radiological triage, improved monitoring of disease progression and better allocation of clinical resources during pandemic peaks. Its longer-term significance lies in demonstrating how emergency deployment of image-analysis systems can support hospital workflows, although public sources describe this primarily as a COVID-era installation and test rather than an enduring, general diagnostic platform.

title: Against the infection comes Minerva, a "robot"" invented by an engineer from Noci (IT)"
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The early pandemic period generated intense demand for reliable information, while misinformation and rapidly changing rules made it difficult for citizens to know which guidance to follow. Minerva was created as a chatbot intended to share information about coronavirus using data drawn from the Italian Ministry of Health website. The objective was to provide a simple digital assistant that could answer recurring questions and direct users towards official public-health information. Although described publicly as a “robot”, the use case was essentially a conversational information service rather than a physical robot or clinical diagnostic tool. The implementation relied on an automated interface that processed user queries and returned relevant content based on official sources. At a conceptual level, the system acted as a bridge between citizens and institutional information, reducing the need to search manually through government webpages and helping standardise the messages received by users. Its expected impact was faster access to trusted information, improved public awareness and reduced confusion during a period of high uncertainty. The case was connected to a specific emergency context and should be interpreted as a lightweight crisis-communication tool rather than a long-term health-service platform. Its value lay in rapid deployment, official-source orientation and accessibility for users seeking immediate guidance.

title: E-health 4.0, chatbots at the service of diagnostic units
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Italian National Institute for Insurance against Accidents at Work (INAIL)
source_description: Healthcare facilities faced extraordinary pressure during the COVID-19 emergency, especially where citizens needed preliminary symptom guidance and hospitals had to manage information demand at scale. Through collaboration between Microsoft and INAIL, Italian healthcare organisations were able to use the Healthcare Bot solution free of charge to create digital assistants for self-assessment of coronavirus symptoms. The initiative supported facilities such as Spallanzani, San Giovanni Addolorata Hospital and ASL Napoli 3 Sud, giving them a rapid way to deploy online symptom-checking and orientation tools. The implementation used a healthcare chatbot configured for COVID-19 self-assessment, allowing users to answer questions about symptoms and receive guidance through the healthcare provider’s portal. At a conceptual level, the service translated triage and public-health information into a conversational workflow, supporting preliminary risk orientation and directing users towards appropriate next steps. Its expected impact was reduced pressure on phone lines and diagnostic units, faster information access for citizens, and more consistent communication from healthcare organisations. The service did not replace medical evaluation; it provided a first layer of digital interaction at a time when health systems needed to reserve human capacity for urgent or complex cases. The use case demonstrates how a reusable cloud-based bot platform could be rapidly adapted to emergency public-health needs.

title: Management of the emergency at Hospital Gemelli - Rome
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Major hospitals faced exceptional operational pressure during the COVID-19 emergency, requiring rapid decisions on intensive-care capacity, ward planning, patient pathways and resource allocation. Fondazione Policlinico Universitario Agostino Gemelli IRCCS used SAS analytics to support management of the emergency by transforming clinical and organisational data into actionable insight. The practical problem was that many important data relating to COVID-19 patients were unstructured, particularly information contained in clinical notes and hospital documentation, while managers and clinicians needed timely intelligence on patient flows, complications and expected organisational impact. The implementation used SAS analytics, visual analytics and text-mining techniques to extract information from unstructured clinical data, support prediction of intensive-care demand, understand possible medical complications and plan hospital operations. At a conceptual level, the system combines data integration, text mining, predictive analytics, dashboards and operational planning. Its expected impact was faster access to clinical information, better forecasting of admissions and hospitalisation needs, more efficient resource allocation and support for personalised patient pathways. SAS describes Gemelli as using its solutions to predict ICU admissions, understand medical complications, plan ward work and manage COVID-19 vaccine administration.

title: Artificial intelligence and video surveillance to control the distance at the airport
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: COVID-19 restrictions severely limited in-person contact in hospitals, isolating patients from families and complicating communication between healthcare staff. Hospitals in Turin launched a pilot to explore how remote presence technologies could mitigate social isolation while maintaining safety protocols. Stakeholders included patients, relatives, healthcare professionals, hospital administrators, and telecom providers, with the objective of preserving human interaction and collaboration despite physical distancing requirements. From 2020 to 2021, the pilot deployed Double Robotics Double3 mobile robots connected via a 5G network. These remotely controlled robots enabled high-definition video communication and autonomous movement within hospital wards. Secure network connectivity ensured low latency and reliable audio-visual interaction, while simple user interfaces allowed staff and families to connect without specialised training. The robots integrated with hospital connectivity infrastructure and operated under strict data protection policies. The pilot improved patient well-being by restoring contact with families and supported collaboration among medical staff across wards. It reduced unnecessary physical movement within hospitals and demonstrated the value of high-bandwidth connectivity for healthcare environments. The solution proved reliable and scalable, highlighting potential long-term applications for telepresence in clinical care, training, and hospital operations beyond emergency contexts.

title: Natural language processing for Land Registry documentation in Sweden
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Land-registry authorities manage large collections of historical legal documents, including handwritten records that can be difficult to search, interpret and reuse in modern digital workflows. The Swedish Land Registry used natural language processing to handle land-registry requests more efficiently by extracting and structuring information from low-quality handwritten documentation. The operational problem was that staff received many requests from citizens for information about properties, but older records were difficult to process because image quality and resolution were poor and handwriting recognition was challenging. The implementation first pre-processed handwritten documents to improve input quality, then used handwritten text recognition to extract text. A neural network then applied word corrections and associations to complete sentences where the recognition process missed words, after which an AI model highlighted key features such as locations, names and summaries. At a conceptual level, the system combines image pre-processing, handwritten text recognition, neural language correction and information extraction. The expected impact is faster handling of citizen requests, reduced manual search effort, better access to historical property information and more time for case handlers to focus on urgent decisions.
supporting_source_urls: Natural language processing for Land Registry documentation in Sweden

title: How the Ministry of Justice used AI to compare prison reports
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Prison oversight produces large volumes of inspection and monitoring reports, but staff may struggle to locate relevant patterns when information is buried in unstructured text. The UK Ministry of Justice developed an intelligent search tool to compare prison reports and identify trends across more than 500 documents containing over 250,000 sentences. The source material included reports from HM Inspectorate of Prisons, the Independent Monitoring Board, the Prisons and Probation Ombudsman, and Ofsted reports on secure training centres. The implementation trained a neural network on prison-report text so that it could track how particular words are used in prison contexts and group words with similar meanings. At a conceptual level, this creates semantic search rather than simple keyword search: users can uncover related concepts, identify recurring themes and compare language across institutions or report types. New reports are automatically added to the tool’s library, helping the information base remain current. The expected impact is faster retrieval of relevant information, better trend detection, improved policy and operational analysis, and reduced staff time spent manually reading large numbers of reports. The tool’s value lies in surfacing evidence for human analysts, not in making prison-management decisions automatically.

title: AI-for-Covid Predictive diagnostics made in Italy
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Hospital Centro Diagnostico Italiano di Milano
source_description: During the Covid-19 pandemic, hospitals faced significant pressure to rapidly assess newly admitted patients and prioritise clinical resources. Clinicians needed early, reliable indicators to identify which patients were at higher risk of respiratory deterioration and might require intensive care or mechanical ventilation. This use case addresses this challenge by supporting radiologists and hospital physicians with a decision-support service based on chest X-ray examinations performed at admission. The objective is to improve early risk stratification, optimise care pathways, and enable timely clinical interventions for patients with Covid-19–related pulmonary involvement. The service is implemented through advanced machine learning techniques applied to diagnostic imaging. Predictive models trained on large datasets of chest X-ray images and associated clinical outcomes analyse radiological patterns linked to disease progression. The system processes imaging data captured at hospital admission and generates a risk score indicating the likelihood of pulmonary worsening. The platform is integrated into existing radiology and hospital information systems, enabling seamless access for clinicians without disrupting established diagnostic workflows. The solution improves the timeliness and consistency of clinical decision-making by providing early insight into disease progression risk. This supports more effective allocation of intensive care resources, reduces uncertainty in patient triage, and enhances overall care quality. By enabling earlier interventions for high-risk patients, the platform contributes to better patient management, increased operational efficiency, and improved resilience of healthcare services during periods of high demand.

title: Using deep learning to structure GOV.UK's content
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Large government websites contain thousands of pages that must be organised consistently so users can find information through topic structures, navigation and search. GOV.UK faced a content-organisation problem because many pages were not tagged to the correct “sub-branches” of the site taxonomy, while manual classification at scale would have required substantial editorial effort. The Government Digital Service used natural language processing to make page text machine-readable and combined this with metadata such as publication date and department to learn patterns associated with existing content tags. The implementation used a multilabel deep-learning model because some GOV.UK pages belong to more than one sub-branch. At a conceptual level, the system transformed unstructured text into features, learned from already-tagged pages and predicted the most appropriate content categories for untagged pages. Predictions were then used selectively: where training examples were too few or categories too diverse, the team did not rely on model outputs. The expected impact was better content structure, improved user journeys, reduced manual tagging work and more consistent organisation across GOV.UK. GDS reported that machine learning helped tag 96% of untagged GOV.UK pages, corresponding to roughly 100,000 pages, while user researchers and content designers reviewed the outputs before wider rollout.

title: How the Department for Transport used AI to improve MOT testing
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Vehicle roadworthiness depends on MOT garages applying testing standards consistently, but inspection authorities cannot manually examine every garage and tester with the same intensity. The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency used artificial intelligence to improve risk-based oversight of MOT testing across Great Britain. The operational problem was that the agency had very large volumes of garage and tester data, but no labelled dataset that directly identified all problematic behaviour. The implementation therefore applied a clustering model to garage test data from the previous three months, grouping MOT centres according to patterns in how they conducted tests. The agency then created a risk score by combining the clustering output with historical information on how often garages had been disciplined for failing to apply MOT standards correctly. At a conceptual level, the system uses unsupervised learning to identify behavioural similarity, then enriches those groups with compliance history to prioritise inspection and enforcement resources. The expected impact is more effective targeting of garage visits, better identification of regional trends, stronger protection of road safety and improved use of examiner time. DVSA updated garage test data every three months, balancing model freshness with stable inspection windows.

title: How DFID used satellite images to estimate populations
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Population estimates are essential for census planning, vaccination campaigns, humanitarian response and service delivery, but countries affected by conflict, rapid growth or limited statistical capacity may lack accurate small-area data. DFID supported GRID3, a geospatial programme that combines satellite imagery, settlement mapping, administrative boundaries and demographic modelling to estimate population distribution. The objective was to help countries such as Nigeria, Zambia, Mozambique and the Democratic Republic of Congo plan censuses and public services using fine-grained gridded population data. The implementation uses remote sensing and geospatial modelling to identify settlements and produce population estimates for small, uniform grid cells, combining observed geographic features with available census or survey data. At a conceptual level, the system transforms satellite-derived settlement and infrastructure information into spatial population layers that can support government and development planning. In conflict-affected or hard-to-reach areas, this can provide a safer and more practical basis for estimating population than traditional enumeration alone. The expected impact is better vaccination microplanning, improved census preparation, more accurate service-location decisions and stronger evidence for development investment.

title: Whatsapp InfoCenter City of Milan (020202)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The City of Milan manages a very high volume of citizen enquiries, particularly during periods of regulatory change and public health or mobility restrictions, when residents need fast and reliable information across multiple service areas. Traditional channels such as phone lines and counters risk congestion and long waiting times. This use case addresses the need to provide immediate, accessible guidance through a familiar digital channel, involving the municipal administration and citizens, with the objective of improving responsiveness and reducing pressure on frontline services. The service is implemented as a virtual assistant available via WhatsApp, guiding users through structured menus covering key topics such as citizenship services, economic activities, mobility rules, health information, parking, accessibility, and official decrees. User selections trigger predefined conversational flows connected to up-to-date municipal content, integrated with existing information systems and communication processes. The solution improves accessibility by meeting citizens on a widely used platform and ensures consistency of official information. It delivers faster responses, reduces call volumes, and enhances user experience through simple, mobile-first interaction, strengthening the city’s capacity to communicate effectively at scale.

title: A unique artificial intelligence system now directs Ülemiste City drivers to available parking spots
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Large business districts can lose time, capacity and user satisfaction when drivers circulate looking for parking spaces without reliable real-time information. Ülemiste City introduced an AI-powered smart parking system to guide drivers directly to available spaces and reduce the uncertainty of parking in a busy urban campus. The implementation combines cameras, AI video analysis, signposts, LED displays and a web interface. Instead of relying on individual in-ground sensors for every bay, the system analyses camera feeds to estimate occupancy and communicate availability to drivers. At a conceptual level, computer-vision models detect vehicles and available spaces, aggregate occupancy information and distribute it through digital displays or interfaces so that drivers can decide where to go before entering or circulating through parking areas. The expected impact is shorter parking-search time, improved use of available capacity, lower unnecessary vehicle circulation and better experience for employees and visitors. The supplier, Pixevia, describes the underlying smart-parking technology as using precise mapping from security cameras, with one camera able to cover up to around 100 parking spots, and information on available places delivered to displays or applications.

title: Detection of mowing events on grasslands from Sentinel-data
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Estonian Agricultural Registers and Information Board (ARIB)
source_description: Agricultural payment agencies must verify whether farmers comply with land-management requirements, but manual on-the-spot checks are costly, time-consuming and difficult to scale nationally. Estonia’s Agricultural Registers and Information Board applied satellite-data analysis to automate detection of mowing events on grasslands, supporting compliance checks for agricultural subsidies. The operational problem is that mowing is one of the conditions for receiving certain government grants, yet field inspections can only cover a limited sample of parcels. The implementation uses time series from Sentinel-1 radar and Sentinel-2 optical imagery, allowing the system to observe vegetation changes over the growing season even under frequent cloud cover. A deep-learning model with a reject option detects likely mowing events and can flag uncertain cases for further attention. At a conceptual level, the system converts satellite observations into a national monitoring layer for agricultural practice: changes in vegetation and surface characteristics indicate whether a field has probably been mown. The expected impact is fewer unnecessary field inspections, earlier reminders to applicants, better compliance monitoring and more efficient use of administrative resources. Public case records describe Estonia’s system as the first nationwide automated monitoring system for agricultural practices in the EU, operational from 2018, with reported mowing-detection accuracy of around 85%.

title: “Connected” robots in Turin hospitals
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Hospitals of Regina Margherita and Sant’Anna (Turin)
source_description: Job seekers often struggle to navigate complex information on occupations, training pathways, and reskilling opportunities, particularly in a rapidly changing labour market. Austria’s Public Employment Service (AMS) developed Berufs-Infomat to provide accessible, personalised career information to support informed decisions. The use case involves job seekers, students, career advisors, and AMS staff, with the objective of improving access to labour-market information and supporting lifelong learning. The solution is implemented as an interactive digital assistant that responds dynamically to user questions about professions, qualifications, and further education opportunities. It draws on structured labour-market data, occupational profiles, and training catalogues to generate tailored responses aligned with user interests and backgrounds. Integrated into AMS digital services, it complements human counselling rather than replacing it. The impact includes faster access to relevant career information, improved user engagement, and better alignment between individual aspirations and labour-market needs. AMS benefits from more scalable service delivery, while users gain clearer guidance and increased confidence in career planning, supporting employability and workforce adaptability.

title: eTranslation: Machine translation for public administrations
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: European public administrations need to exchange information across many languages, but manual translation can be too slow or expensive for routine documents, datasets, forms and digital services. eTranslation provides the European Commission’s machine-translation service for EU institutions, public administrations, academia, SMEs, NGOs, Digital Europe Programme projects and other eligible users. The objective is to make multilingual public-sector communication faster and more accessible while relying on infrastructure aligned with European institutional needs. The implementation uses neural machine translation built on the EU’s long history of professional translation and is available both through a web interface and machine-to-machine APIs. At a conceptual level, the service receives text, documents or integrated system requests, translates them across official EU languages and selected associated languages, and returns raw machine translation that can be used for understanding, publication support or professional refinement. Public systems can integrate the API directly into services, such as portals that need to translate metadata or user-facing content across multiple languages. The expected impact is reduced translation turnaround, greater multilingual accessibility, easier cross-border public-service delivery and more efficient reuse of public data. Current Commission material presents eTranslation under AI-based multilingual services in the Digital Europe framework and confirms that both web pages and APIs are available for machine-to-machine access.

title: Frag-den-Michel! Innovativer Online-Bürgerservice in Betrieb
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Hamburg authorities receive a wide range of general enquiries from citizens, many of which fall outside normal office hours and place pressure on telephone services. Citizens expect timely access to reliable information regardless of time or channel. This use case addresses the need to extend access to public information while complementing existing contact centres, involving city authorities and residents. The objective is to provide a continuous, digital entry point for common questions about administrative services. Frag-den-Michel is implemented as a text-based dialogue system available online, designed to answer frequently asked questions using structured knowledge bases maintained by the city. The chatbot operates alongside the central authority telephone number, offering an alternative self-service channel and integrating with official content repositories. The service improves availability of information beyond business hours, reduces waiting times on phone lines, and supports more efficient allocation of human resources. It enhances user satisfaction by offering immediate responses and strengthens the city’s multi-channel service strategy through a scalable and low-cost digital solution.

title: Municipality Welcome Manager (L2B2 Service Robot) in Ludwigsburg
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Visitors to municipal service offices often need orientation before reaching the correct desk, department or waiting area, especially in buildings where multiple citizen services are delivered. Ludwigsburg introduced L2B2 as a speaking service robot in the entrance area of its citizen office, making it the first German municipality to use this type of welcome robot in a city administration. The objective was to provide first information and guidance for citizens visiting the service department while demonstrating how robotics could support public-facing administration. The implementation uses a mobile robot that welcomes visitors, moves autonomously through corridors and accompanies them to relevant departments. At a conceptual level, the robot combines speech interaction, indoor navigation, visitor guidance and service information. It does not make administrative decisions or process applications; its role is to reduce uncertainty at the first point of contact and provide a visible, interactive guide within the municipal building. The expected impact is improved visitor experience, faster orientation, reduced routine guidance burden on staff and public familiarity with service robotics. Public material describes strong media and citizen interest, and the robot’s name was chosen through a public call, giving the project a participatory communication dimension as well as a technical one.

title: Swedish municipality deploys robots for safer recruitment
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Recruitment processes can reproduce unconscious bias when candidates are screened through CVs, informal impressions or inconsistent interview questions. Upplands-Bro Municipality used Tengai’s AI interview system to support more structured and resume-free candidate screening, particularly during urgent recruitment needs in care and welfare roles during the COVID-19 period. The objective was to scale early-stage recruitment while reducing the influence of irrelevant background characteristics and ensuring that applicants were asked comparable questions. The implementation uses a conversational AI interview tool that conducts structured screening interviews, asking candidates identical or standardised questions and producing information for recruiters to review. At a conceptual level, the system separates initial candidate assessment from CV cues, applies consistent interview protocols and provides structured data that HR staff can use in later selection stages. The expected impact is faster screening of large applicant pools, reduced unconscious bias at the early interview stage, greater consistency across applicants and more time for HR staff to focus on qualitative follow-up and final hiring decisions.

title: London Police Facial Recognition System
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Metropolitan Police Service in London seeks to enhance its capacity to identify individuals of interest in public spaces in order to prevent crime, safeguard vulnerable persons and support ongoing investigations. Traditional identification methods rely on post-event analysis or manual recognition, which can delay interventions and limit operational effectiveness. The deployment of live facial recognition aims to support frontline officers by automatically identifying individuals who appear on pre-defined police watch lists, such as wanted suspects or missing persons. Stakeholders include law enforcement officers, public authorities, oversight bodies and members of the public whose data may be processed in public settings. The objective is to enable rapid identification in real time while operating within the UK legal and regulatory framework. The system uses computer vision and deep learning models trained on large facial image datasets to extract biometric templates from live video feeds. These templates are compared against encrypted watch-list databases using pattern-matching algorithms. The solution is integrated with existing police camera infrastructure and operational command systems, generating alerts for officers when similarity thresholds are met. The technology supports high-speed processing of video streams in dynamic environments. The intended impact is improved response times, enhanced public safety and more efficient deployment of police resources. Operational benefits include automation of identity checks in crowded areas and support for targeted interventions, although the system also requires strict governance, oversight and accuracy monitoring to maintain reliability and public trust.

title: The Municipality of Oslo explores chatbots to respond to citizen requests
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Municipality of Oslo sought to improve the efficiency and accessibility of internal and external administrative services by reducing response times to routine enquiries. Municipal employees and citizens frequently require confirmations, certificates and standard information, which traditionally involve manual processing and significant administrative effort. In collaboration with Capgemini, the municipality established an interdisciplinary team to develop proof-of-concept chatbot solutions capable of handling structured service requests. The objective was to test whether conversational interfaces could automate repetitive tasks while maintaining service quality and reliability. The initial pilot focused on an internal chatbot that allowed employees to request confirmation of employment through a chat interface. The solution uses natural language processing models to interpret user queries, classify intent and trigger backend workflows. When a request is validated, the chatbot interacts with existing automated document generation systems to produce confirmation documents and delivers status updates within the chat window. The system integrates with municipal HR and document management platforms through secure APIs. The pilot demonstrated the feasibility of conversational automation, reducing processing times and administrative workload. The approach improves user experience by providing immediate acknowledgement and faster turnaround, while offering scalability for broader deployment in citizen-facing services and other municipal processes.

title: Chatbot - City of Vienna
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Residents and visitors often need quick answers to practical city questions while on the move, such as where to find a service, how long parking rules apply, when public transport departs or where the nearest public facility is located. Vienna developed WienBot as a digital assistant that complements the city website by providing concise answers through chat and voice. The objective is to make municipal information easier to consume in everyday situations, without requiring users to navigate long web pages or search-result lists. The implementation connects the chatbot to city information and open government data, including geospatial data, the city events database and real-time public-transport interfaces from Wiener Linien. At a conceptual level, the bot interprets a user’s question, retrieves relevant structured or editorial information and returns a direct answer, sometimes supported by map or route data. It can answer in standard language and has also been known for a local Viennese tone. The expected impact is faster access to municipal information, improved usability on mobile devices, greater accessibility through voice search and reduced friction for routine enquiries.

title: London TravelBot
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Transport users need immediate and reliable information about service status, disruptions and arrivals, particularly when travelling through a large multimodal network. Transport for London launched TravelBot as an automated Facebook Messenger service to provide quick journey information through a familiar social-media channel. The objective was to improve customer service by allowing users to ask for Tube, rail, tram and bus updates without navigating separate status pages or waiting for social-media staff to respond manually. The implementation used an AI-powered chat function connected to TfL’s latest operational data. It could answer questions about bus arrival times, service updates and Tube maps, and link users directly to a customer-service agent where escalation was required. At a conceptual level, the bot combined conversational intent recognition, transport-status data, route or line lookup and social-media messaging integration. The expected impact was faster customer information, reduced pressure on manual social-media response teams, more convenient travel updates and better accessibility for users already using Messenger. TfL’s 2017 launch described TravelBot as its first such social-media tool, and a 2018 London Assembly response reported that TfL had enhanced TravelBot’s technology to provide step-free access information more simply.

title: Virtual assistant equipped with artificial intelligence for Parkinson's patients and their families
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Patients living with Parkinson’s disease and their families often need practical information outside scheduled clinical appointments, especially when questions concern symptoms, therapies, daily management and the relationship between medical recommendations and everyday care. Campus Bio-Medico University Hospital in Rome and IBM developed “Parkinson bot” to provide a virtual assistant capable of answering Parkinson’s-related questions at any time. The service was designed to improve access to reliable information and strengthen continuity between specialist expertise and patients’ day-to-day needs. The implementation used IBM Watson Assistant, configuring a conversational interface around clinically relevant content prepared for people affected by Parkinson’s, caregivers and family members. At a conceptual level, the system interprets user questions, matches them to a structured knowledge base and returns answers in natural language, reducing the need for users to search manually through multiple sources or wait for routine information. Its expected impact is easier access to medical guidance, stronger patient and caregiver support, reduced burden on staff for repetitive questions and a more responsive digital communication channel around chronic neurological care. The case also illustrates how conversational AI can be used in hospital services when the subject matter requires a careful balance between accessibility and clinical reliability: the bot supports information delivery but does not replace medical evaluation or personalised decisions by clinicians.

title: Sohjoa - Baltic Sea Region transitioning into eco-friendly autonomous last mile public transport
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Urban areas across the Baltic Sea region face growing pressure to provide sustainable, accessible, and efficient last-mile public transport. Cities need solutions that reduce emissions while maintaining safety, reliability, and public trust in new mobility services. This use case addresses these challenges by piloting eco-friendly autonomous minibuses on real urban routes, involving local authorities, transport operators, technology providers, and passengers, with the objective of evaluating the feasibility of autonomous last-mile public transport, supporting the transition to greener mobility, and generating evidence to inform future transport policies and deployments. The service is implemented through autonomous driving technologies that enable small electric buses to operate on predefined demonstration routes, using a combination of sensors such as cameras, lidar, and radar to continuously scan their surroundings, detect obstacles, and make driving decisions including slowing down or stopping when required. Control software processes sensor data in real time to support safe navigation in mixed traffic environments, while a trained operator remains on board during all pilot operations to supervise the system, intervene if necessary, and ensure compliance with safety regulations, with operational data collected to support system evaluation and refinement. The pilots provide valuable insights into the technical, operational, and regulatory aspects of autonomous public transport, demonstrating potential reductions in environmental impact, improved last-mile connectivity, and increased efficiency in urban transport networks, while the supervised deployment model helps build public confidence and supports the development of scalable, low-emission mobility solutions for cities planning future autonomous transport services.

title: Finland Migration Service Chatbot
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Finnish Immigration Service faced sustained pressure to respond to large volumes of repetitive public enquiries related to residence permits, application processing times, and contact information, particularly during periods of high migration demand. Citizens and applicants required timely, consistent information in both Finnish and English, while staff resources were limited. This use case addressed the need to improve access to basic immigration information and reduce pressure on customer service channels, involving the Finnish Immigration Service, applicants, and the general public. The objective was to provide a scalable, always-available information service integrated into the migri.fi website. The solution was implemented through a rule-based and language-processing chatbot embedded across all website pages, designed to recognise common user queries and retrieve predefined responses from official information sources. The chatbot supported bilingual interaction and was integrated with existing web content management systems. During its pilot phase, the service improved accessibility to information, reduced simple enquiries handled by staff, and enhanced user convenience. Although the chatbot has since been decommissioned, it demonstrated the value of automated digital front-line services in public administration and informed later approaches to online service design.
supporting_source_urls: New chatbot answers questions about processing times and contact details

title: Virtual Digital Assistant with the Revenue Commissioners of Ireland
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Revenue Commissioners of Ireland handle large volumes of telephone enquiries related to tax clearance certificates, creating operational pressure and delays for both staff and taxpayers. Many of these requests are repetitive and transactional in nature. This use case addresses the need to streamline telephone-based services while maintaining accuracy and trust, involving Revenue, taxpayers, and contact centre staff. The objective is to improve efficiency in handling general information requests and simple applications. The service is implemented as a voice-driven virtual assistant that recognises spoken queries, retrieves relevant information, and in some cases processes tax clearance certificate applications directly. It integrates with Revenue’s back-end systems to verify eligibility and status, operating within existing telephony infrastructure. The pilot demonstrates improved call handling efficiency, shorter response times, and reduced workload for human agents. It enhances accessibility for users who prefer voice interaction and supports more consistent service delivery, while freeing staff to focus on complex cases with higher added value.

title: University La Sapienza launches the first voice "assistant"": Infostud-Watson"
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Large universities manage complex administrative interactions with students, including exam bookings, certification requests, and general study-related enquiries, which can overwhelm traditional service desks. Sapienza University sought to simplify access to student services and modernise interaction channels. This use case involves the university administration, students, and technology partners, with the objective of improving usability and reducing administrative friction. Infostud-Watson is implemented as a mobile application that enables students to interact with university systems through voice commands and natural language dialogue. The assistant is connected to existing academic and administrative systems, allowing actions such as exam booking and certificate generation, and continuously adapts its responses based on usage patterns. The solution improves convenience by enabling hands-free interaction, reduces queues and manual processing, and enhances the overall student experience. It supports scalable service delivery across a large student population and strengthens digital engagement within the university ecosystem.

title: Project “Sibyl A.I. Virtual" with Regione Puglia"
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Public administrations increasingly need efficient and accessible channels to manage interactions with citizens, respond to enquiries, and deliver services in a timely manner. Regional institutions face high volumes of requests, fragmented communication channels, and rising expectations for digital public services. This use case addresses these challenges by creating a unified digital platform to support interactions between the Regione Puglia and citizens, involving public sector staff, local businesses, and end users, with the objective of improving access to information and services, streamlining communication processes, and enhancing the overall quality and responsiveness of institutional services. The platform is implemented through a virtual assistance system based on natural language processing and conversational interfaces, with language models trained on institutional content, public service information, and frequently asked questions to understand user requests and generate accurate, context-aware responses. The system integrates with existing public administration information systems and digital service portals, enabling automated handling of routine enquiries while allowing escalation to human operators when required, and using interaction data to continuously refine the knowledge base and improve response accuracy. The solution improves the efficiency and scalability of citizen support services by reducing response times and relieving administrative staff from repetitive tasks, while enhancing user experience through consistent, always-available access to information. For the administration, it supports cost-effective service delivery, greater transparency, and improved capacity to meet growing demand for digital public services, contributing to the modernisation of public sector operations in the region.

title: Artificial intelligence: high technology and innovation to make life easier for citizens
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Municipality of Trieste sought to modernise citizen interaction with local administration by simplifying access to demographic services, such as registry information and administrative procedures. Prior to the initiative, citizens relied heavily on in-person visits or phone calls, leading to queues, delays, and fragmented communication. The use case involved the Municipality of Trieste, regional authorities, and citizens, with the objective of providing real-time information through the institutional website and improving service efficiency. The solution was implemented as a conversational chatbot developed by Insiel SpA and co-financed by the Friuli Venezia Giulia Region. It was connected to municipal information systems and structured knowledge bases covering demographic services, enabling automated responses to common questions. During its initial operation in early 2020, the chatbot improved response times, increased transparency, and reduced manual workload for staff. However, the service was later discontinued. Despite this, the project provided valuable insights into citizen expectations, system integration challenges, and the organisational changes required to sustain digital assistance services in local government.

title: Robots to be used in UK care homes to help reduce loneliness
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Loneliness and social isolation are persistent challenges in residential care homes, particularly among older adults with limited mobility or family contact. A UK pilot explored whether social robots could complement care staff by providing companionship and daily interaction for residents. Stakeholders included care home residents, carers, management, families, and technology providers, with the objective of improving emotional well-being without replacing human care. Conducted between 2019 and 2020, the pilot introduced “Pepper” wheeled humanoid robots into selected care homes. The robots were pre-programmed and gradually adapted to residents’ preferences, enabling simple conversations, music playback, reminders, and interactive activities. Sensors and speech interfaces supported autonomous navigation and engagement, while learning components allowed the robots to personalise interactions over time. The systems operated locally within care facilities and were supervised by staff. The pilot showed positive effects on resident engagement and mood, particularly for individuals with limited social contact. Care staff reported that robots supplemented, rather than replaced, human interaction and could be deployed flexibly. While not a substitute for personal care, the solution demonstrated potential to scale as a supportive tool to reduce loneliness and enhance quality of life in long-term care settings.

title: Caterina, the first (virtual) municipal employee for identity cards and changes of residence
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Municipality of Siena aimed to reduce administrative burdens on citizens and improve access to essential municipal services such as identity cards, change of residence, and electoral card renewals. Long queues and office visits were a source of frustration, particularly for elderly residents. This use case involved the municipality, residents, and service providers, with the objective of enabling citizens to complete administrative procedures remotely. Caterina was implemented as a virtual assistant accessible online, designed to guide users through specific administrative workflows and provide procedural information. The system relied on structured process logic, predefined decision trees, and integration with municipal service information. While active, Caterina reduced unnecessary in-person visits, improved convenience, and demonstrated strong public interest in digital municipal services. The service has since been discontinued, but it highlighted the potential of virtual assistants to support administrative simplification and informed subsequent digitalisation efforts within Italian municipalities.
