The university is the first organisation to implement this functionality, financed by the NTNU digitalisation program. The functionality is not available anymore.

title: Clean Air Optimisation in Madrid Metro
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Madrid Metro (Department of Public Works, City Planning, and Transportation)
source_description: Ensuring good air quality in underground transport systems is essential for passenger health and comfort, yet traditional ventilation systems often operate on static rules that do not respond efficiently to real conditions. Madrid Metro sought to improve air quality while optimising energy consumption. This use case involves the metro operator, passengers, and technology providers, with the objective of dynamically managing ventilation to maintain high air quality standards. The solution is implemented through a self-learning ventilation control system that processes environmental sensor data from stations to adjust airflow in real time. The system integrates with existing ventilation infrastructure and continuously adapts to changing conditions such as passenger density and external air quality. The result is improved air quality, more efficient energy use, and reduced operational costs. Passengers benefit from a healthier environment, while the operator gains a more sustainable and responsive infrastructure management approach.

title: Bebot – Vienna AirportCity Virtual Assistant
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Airports must provide clear, up-to-date information to diverse users, particularly during disruptions such as public health emergencies, while managing high volumes of enquiries. Vienna AirportCity introduced a digital assistant to support visitors navigating transport, facilities, and Covid-19-related requirements. This use case involves airport operators, travellers, and businesses, with the objective of improving information access and reducing pressure on staff. Bebot is implemented as a web-based chatbot accessible via mobile and desktop through on-site Wi-Fi and the airport website. It delivers structured responses on transport options, directions, facility services, and health regulations, integrated with airport information systems. The service enhances user experience by providing immediate guidance, improves operational efficiency by reducing routine enquiries, and supports consistent communication in a complex, high-traffic environment.

title: AI technology speeds up historical image handling at Hungary's National Archive
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Hungary’s National Audiovisual Archive (NAVA) faced the challenge of organising and preserving millions of historical images and audiovisual records forming the country’s twentieth-century cultural memory. Manual classification was slow, costly, and unable to keep pace with digitisation efforts. Stakeholders included archivists, historians, public broadcasters, and citizens, with the objective of accelerating cataloguing while maintaining archival quality. Between 2019 and 2021, a pilot deployed cloud-based image analysis services to classify large image collections automatically. Visual recognition models were trained to detect objects, scenes, and contextual features, generating metadata to support indexing and retrieval. The system integrated with existing archive databases and digitisation workflows, enabling human archivists to validate and refine outputs rather than start from scratch. The pilot significantly reduced processing time for image classification, allowing millions of records to be indexed efficiently. It improved searchability and long-term preservation planning while lowering operational costs. Archivists retained editorial control, ensuring trust and reliability. The approach demonstrated strong scalability and laid the foundation for sustainable management of national audiovisual heritage.

title: Unlocking the potential of crowdsourcing for public decision-making with artificial intelligence
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Public administrations increasingly use online participation platforms to collect citizen input, but processing thousands of contributions manually limits their impact on decision-making. This use case addresses the challenge of transforming large-scale citizen feedback into actionable insights, involving civil servants, policymakers, and citizens. The objective is to support evidence-based public decisions while maintaining inclusive participation. CitizenLab’s platform implements advanced text analysis techniques to automatically classify, cluster, and summarise citizen contributions by topic, location, and demographic traits. Dashboards present emerging trends and patterns, integrated into participation workflows used by public authorities. The solution significantly reduces analysis time, improves insight quality, and enables officials to respond more effectively to citizen priorities. It strengthens trust in participatory processes, enhances transparency, and scales citizen engagement without proportional increases in administrative effort.

title: Artificial intelligence dives into thousands of WWII photographs
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Researchers in history, computer science, and the social sciences face significant challenges when analysing large collections of historical photographs, as manual examination is time-consuming and limits the scale of inquiry. Understanding patterns of authorship, perspective, and visual style in wartime imagery is important for historical interpretation, archival research, and cultural analysis. This use case addresses these challenges through an interdisciplinary study that examines thousands of Second World War photographs, involving academic researchers and cultural heritage institutions, with the objective of uncovering latent patterns in visual content and advancing new methods for large-scale historical image analysis. The study is implemented using computer vision and pattern recognition techniques applied to extensive datasets of digitised wartime photographs, with models trained to extract visual features related to composition, subject matter, and contextual elements. These models analyse similarities and recurring visual signatures across images, enabling the system to distinguish and attribute photographs to individual photographers based solely on image content, without relying on metadata. The results demonstrate that large-scale automated image analysis can reveal meaningful stylistic and contextual patterns in historical archives, including the ability to identify photographers with a high degree of accuracy. This approach significantly expands the analytical capacity of historical research, supports more systematic exploration of visual archives, and opens new opportunities for interdisciplinary collaboration and data-driven insights in the study of cultural heritage.

title: U.K. to use AI to spot dangerous side effects in the COVID-19 vaccinations
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: U.K. Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA)
source_description: Large-scale vaccination programmes generate vast volumes of safety reports that regulators must review to identify potential adverse effects and protect public health. During the Covid-19 vaccination rollout, the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) faced the challenge of monitoring tens of thousands of reports within tight timeframes, far beyond what could be efficiently handled through manual analysis alone. This use case addresses the need for timely and reliable pharmacovigilance by supporting the MHRA in detecting early safety signals from reported side effects, involving regulators, healthcare providers, and the public, with the objective of ensuring vaccine safety while maintaining public confidence in the vaccination programme. The solution is implemented through a machine learning system developed under a $1.96 million contract awarded to the UK arm of Genpact, which ingests large volumes of reported side-effect data from multiple sources and applies statistical learning and pattern-recognition techniques to identify unusual trends, correlations, or clusters that may indicate potential safety concerns. Models are trained on historical vaccination and adverse-event data to distinguish normal background reporting patterns from signals requiring further investigation, and the platform integrates with existing regulatory reporting systems to enable continuous monitoring and prioritisation of cases for expert review. The approach significantly improves the scalability and responsiveness of vaccine safety monitoring, enabling the MHRA to manage an expected volume of 50,000 to 100,000 reports of suspected side effects per 100 million doses administered over a six- to 12-month period, while reducing manual workload, accelerating the identification of potential risks, supporting faster regulatory decision-making, and strengthening the overall reliability of pharmacovigilance processes to deliver safer vaccination campaigns and improved public health outcomes.

title: Aurora, the new virtual assistant of the South East Tuscany AUSL is online
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Azienda USL Toscana Sud Est (Regional Health structure)
source_description: Healthcare organisations face high demand for reliable public information, particularly across large geographic areas. The South East Tuscany Local Health Authority aimed to improve access to health-related information for citizens in Siena, Arezzo, and Grosseto. This use case involved the health authority, technology providers, and residents, with the objective of delivering easy-to-use digital information services. Aurora was implemented as a 3D virtual avatar accessible via web and mobile devices, providing scripted responses to health service enquiries through a conversational interface. The system integrated visual interaction with structured information repositories. During its pilot phase, Aurora improved accessibility and visibility of health information and showcased innovative digital communication methods. The service has since been discontinued, but it demonstrated early experimentation with virtual interfaces in healthcare communication and contributed to organisational learning on digital citizen engagement.

title: Self-driving buses roll into Gothenburg
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Cities seeking to modernise public transport must balance sustainability goals, service accessibility, and the safe introduction of new mobility technologies. In Gothenburg, local authorities and transport operators aimed to explore innovative solutions that could enhance connectivity within key employment and innovation districts while reducing environmental impact. This use case focuses on the trial deployment of autonomous electric shuttles to provide public transport services within the Lindholmen Industrial and Science Park, involving the city, the transport operator Keolis, and passengers, with the objective of assessing the feasibility, safety, and operational value of self-driving buses in an urban setting. The service is implemented through autonomous electric shuttle vehicles operating on a dedicated 1.8-kilometre route, using onboard sensors, navigation systems, and control software to perceive their environment and drive without direct human control. The shuttles operate under supervised conditions during a 4.5-month trial period that began on 18 January, allowing for real-world testing, data collection, and system validation while ensuring passenger safety and regulatory compliance. The trial provides insights into the performance, reliability, and user acceptance of autonomous public transport, demonstrating the potential for low-emission, flexible mobility services in urban areas. It supports evidence-based decision-making on future deployments, contributes to innovation in public transport provision, and helps position Gothenburg as a testbed for sustainable and scalable autonomous mobility solutions.

title: Data-Driven Risk Analysis to Prevent Tax Evasion in Italy
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Tax authorities face persistent challenges in identifying and preventing tax evasion, particularly as economic activities and financial relationships become increasingly complex. Traditional risk assessment methods often struggle to detect sophisticated patterns of non-compliance early enough to support effective enforcement and voluntary compliance. This use case addresses these challenges by modernising tax evasion risk analysis for the Italian Revenue Agency, involving the Ministry of Finance, its in-house technology partner SOGEI, and European Union funding bodies, with the objective of strengthening preventive identification of taxpayers at high risk of non-compliance and improving the effectiveness of fiscal oversight. The initiative is implemented through a data-driven system that applies machine learning, network analysis, and advanced data visualisation techniques to large volumes of fiscal, administrative, and economic data. Analytical models examine relationships between individuals, companies, and transactions to uncover hidden networks and anomalous behaviours associated with evasion risks, while visualisation tools support analysts in interpreting complex results and prioritising cases. The system integrates with existing tax administration processes and information infrastructures, enabling experimentation, validation, and gradual operational adoption. The project enhances the accuracy and timeliness of risk assessments, enabling more targeted controls and more efficient use of investigative resources. By shifting towards preventive and evidence-based analysis, it supports reduced tax evasion, improved compliance, and stronger public finances, while increasing the transparency, scalability, and analytical capacity of the Revenue Agency’s risk management processes.

title: Autonomous Tram Depot (AStriD) – Digital Depot Operations in Potsdam
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Urban transport operators face rising pressure to increase efficiency while maintaining safety and reliability in depot operations. The ASTRiD project addresses this challenge by developing a digital tram depot capable of supporting autonomous vehicle movements within controlled environments. Stakeholders include Verkehrsbetrieb Potsdam (ViP), Siemens Mobility, transport authorities, and national research funders. The objective is to automate routine depot manoeuvres, such as moving trams through washing facilities or into sidings, reducing manual labour and operational risk. The project integrates autonomous vehicle control systems, depot infrastructure sensors, digital signalling, and safety supervision mechanisms. Trams are equipped with perception and navigation systems that interpret depot layouts and execute predefined manoeuvres under supervision. The system interfaces with depot management software and safety controls to ensure compliance with operational constraints. According to public reporting, a key demonstration phase was successfully completed as part of the three-year research project funded under Germany’s mFund programme. While the project remains at pilot level, it has validated the technical feasibility of autonomous depot operations and provided a foundation for future scaling in urban rail systems.

title: Manchester uses artificial intelligence to gain more insight into active travel
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: City regions face increasing pressure to promote walking and cycling while ensuring that investments in active travel infrastructure are evidence-based. Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) planned a regional monitoring initiative to gain better insight into how pedestrians and cyclists use segregated routes, junctions, and priority corridors. Stakeholders included TfGM, local authorities, urban planners, and residents. The objective was to obtain continuous, anonymised data on active travel flows to support infrastructure planning, safety interventions, and evaluation of policy measures without relying on manual surveys. The planned solution involved the installation of around 100 roadside sensors supplied by Vivacity Labs. These sensors combine optical and signal-based detection to count pedestrians, cyclists, and vehicles in real time while processing data locally to avoid personal identification. Aggregated flow data would be transmitted to central dashboards and combined with contextual information such as time of day and location. According to public reporting, elements of the sensor deployment were initiated, but the programme was framed as an exploratory pilot rather than a fully institutionalised system. The initiative demonstrated the potential for scalable, low-intrusion monitoring of active travel, supporting more responsive transport planning and contributing to wider smart mobility strategies, even though full regional rollout was not confirmed at the time.

title: Creating an AI-driven mobile virtual assistant and common public services platform
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Croatian pilot in the inGOV project focuses on the City of Bjelovar and demonstrates how digital public services can be made more accessible through an AI-driven mobile virtual assistant. The idea is to create a unified platform that allows citizens to access all local government services through a simple, mobile-first interface, reducing the complexity of navigating multiple disconnected systems. The pilot specifically targets around 32,000 citizens, with a strong emphasis on inclusivity, especially for older or less digitally experienced users. It aims to replace fragmented service portals with a conversational assistant (similar to messaging apps), improving usability, accessibility, and awareness of available public services. The solution also supports co-creation with stakeholders and is intended to reduce the need for helpdesk support by enabling more direct and intuitive interactions with government services.

title: AI-SCORE, a project to calculate prognostic risk from Covid-19
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The AI-SCORE project (Artificial Intelligence – SARS-CoV-2 Risk Evaluation) is an Italian research initiative led by IRCCS San Raffaele Hospital in Milan, developed in collaboration with academic and industrial partners. Its goal is to build an AI-based system capable of predicting the risk of severe outcomes in COVID-19 patients. The platform uses machine learning to analyze a combination of clinical data, laboratory results, and medical imaging to estimate the probability that an infected patient will develop serious complications. This helps doctors identify high-risk patients early, improve triage decisions, and optimize hospital resource allocation during the pandemic. Beyond COVID-19, the project is designed as a broader model for predictive medicine, showing how artificial intelligence can support clinical decision-making in future infectious disease outbreaks and other high-risk health conditions.

title: Computer vision e-scooter technology to be trialled in UK city
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The pilot is a UK trial of computer vision–enabled e-scooters designed to improve safety and urban mobility management in shared micromobility systems. The scooters are equipped with on-device AI and camera-based perception systems that can analyse the surrounding environment in real time. This allows them to detect where they are being ridden (for example, on roads, cycle lanes, or pedestrian areas) and whether they are being parked appropriately. When risky or non-compliant behaviour is identified, the system can trigger automated responses such as warnings or speed adjustments, helping encourage safer riding habits. At the same time, it collects anonymised mobility data that cities can use to understand travel patterns, identify conflict zones, and improve infrastructure planning for pedestrians, cyclists, and scooter users. Overall, the pilot explores how embedded AI in micromobility vehicles can support safer behaviour, better compliance with regulations, and smarter urban transport management.

title: Dublin to host AI-powered e-scooter research project
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Dublin faces growing challenges in managing shared micro-mobility services, particularly e-scooters, as their rapid adoption raises concerns around road safety, pavement congestion, parking compliance, and integration with existing transport systems. City authorities, transport planners, mobility operators, researchers, and citizens all have a stake in ensuring that e-scooters contribute positively to sustainable urban mobility rather than creating new risks or inefficiencies. The objective of this use case is to improve how e-scooters are deployed, used, and regulated across the city by generating evidence-based insights that support safer operations, better infrastructure planning, and more effective policy decisions. The project applies advanced data analytics and machine learning techniques to data collected from e-scooters, including location, speed, braking events, trip duration, and interaction with the urban environment, combined with contextual data such as road layouts, traffic conditions, and weather. Computer vision and predictive models are used to analyse rider behaviour, identify unsafe patterns, optimise parking zones, and simulate different regulatory or infrastructure scenarios. These models are integrated into a research platform that connects mobility operators, city systems, and analytical tools to enable continuous experimentation and evaluation. The initiative supports improved rider safety, reduced pavement clutter, and more efficient use of public space, while providing the city with robust evidence to guide regulation and investment. It enhances service reliability and user experience, enables scalable management of micro-mobility, and delivers long-term value by helping Dublin design safer, more sustainable urban transport systems.
