title: Blockchain-based Land Registry
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Public authorities responsible for land and geo-information management must ensure that datasets are accurate, current, and used in the correct legal and administrative context, as outdated or misapplied data can lead to regulatory errors and disputes. In Eindhoven, the municipal department and the national land registry faced challenges in guaranteeing that users always accessed the most up-to-date datasets when completing processes such as environmental law applications. This use case addresses these issues by improving the reliability and traceability of land ownership and geo-information data, involving the municipality, the Kadaster, and data users, with the objective of ensuring data integrity, transparency, and trust across administrative processes. The solution is implemented by publishing open datasets on a distributed ledger with cryptographic timestamps that clearly identify the latest valid version of each dataset. This enables all participants to verify that the data they are using is current and authoritative, while supporting reuse across multiple applications and services. The prototype serves as an initial, low-complexity implementation to explore the feasibility of distributed ledger technology in land administration, informed by international experiments. The approach reduces the risk of errors caused by outdated information, improves confidence in shared data, and provides a foundation for more advanced applications of trusted digital land registries.

title: Truck Driver Tracking
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Road transport regulation requires accurate monitoring of truck drivers’ working and resting hours to ensure safety, compliance with labour laws, and fair competition within the logistics sector. Traditional tracking and reporting methods can be fragmented, prone to manipulation, and burdensome for drivers, employers, and regulators. This use case addresses these challenges by improving the transparency and reliability of driver hours registration, involving transport companies, drivers, and supervisory authorities, with the objective of ensuring compliance while reducing administrative friction. The system is implemented through a blockchain-based register that records driving and rest periods in a shared, tamper-resistant ledger. Time-stamped entries create an immutable log that can be accessed by authorised parties, reducing disputes and manual reconciliation. The solution improves trust in reported data, simplifies compliance checks, and enhances road safety by supporting more consistent enforcement of working time regulations.

title: Financing New School Buildings
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The development of new school buildings involves complex financial and administrative processes that span multiple governmental bodies, financial institutions, and project stakeholders. These processes are often slow and opaque, leading to delays and coordination challenges. This use case addresses these issues by improving the way school construction projects are financed, involving public authorities and a national banking partner, with the objective of increasing transparency, efficiency, and coordination in public infrastructure financing. The prototype is implemented on the Ethereum platform, where financial commitments, approvals, and project milestones are recorded in a shared digital environment accessible to authorised stakeholders. This enables clearer tracking of responsibilities and funds across institutions and supports automation of administrative steps. The initiative demonstrates the potential to reduce processing time, lower administrative costs, and improve accountability in the financing of public education infrastructure.

title: Electric Vehicle Subsidy Registry
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Governments seeking to accelerate the adoption of electric vehicles must manage subsidy schemes that are efficient, transparent, and resistant to fraud, while handling high volumes of applications and payments. Existing subsidy processes are often manual and administratively heavy, limiting scalability and increasing the risk of errors. This use case addresses these challenges by redesigning the regulation and administration of electric vehicle subsidies, involving public authorities, applicants, and service providers, with the objective of delivering a highly automated and reliable subsidy system. The solution is implemented through a digital registry based on distributed ledger technology, where eligibility checks, subsidy approvals, and payments are recorded and validated in a shared system. Automation reduces manual intervention and enables consistent enforcement of subsidy rules. The result is a more scalable and transparent subsidy programme, with faster processing times, reduced administrative burden, and increased trust in the management of public funds.

title: Medical Instrument Registration
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (CIBG)
source_description: The Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport manages multiple national registers related to healthcare professionals and medical instruments, requiring high levels of accuracy, reliability, and public trust. Although these registers are largely digitised, questions remain about how to further strengthen data integrity, interoperability, and long-term trust in sensitive health-related information. This use case explores whether distributed ledger technology can add value to the registration of medical instruments and related data, involving the ministry, healthcare stakeholders, and regulatory bodies, with the objective of enhancing the robustness and transparency of health information management. The proposed approach examines the use of a blockchain-based register to record key registration events and updates in a tamper-resistant manner, complementing existing digital systems. By providing a shared and verifiable source of truth, the solution has the potential to improve auditability, reduce disputes over data accuracy, and reinforce confidence in national health registries, while supporting future innovation in healthcare data governance.

title: Employment and Identity Fraud
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: The Inspectorate of the Ministry of Employment
source_description: Public authorities responsible for employment, welfare, and income support must detect and prevent fraud while coordinating across multiple organisations that each hold partial and sensitive data. Fragmented information sharing limits the ability to identify identity fraud, labour exploitation, and organised crime within the work and income chain. This use case addresses these challenges by improving secure data sharing between governmental organisations involved in employment and social services, with the objective of strengthening fraud detection, protecting vulnerable workers, and improving enforcement effectiveness. The solution is implemented through a shared data-exchange framework supported by distributed ledger technology, where relevant events and verified data points from participating organisations are recorded and made accessible to authorised parties under agreed governance rules. The ledger provides a trusted, tamper-resistant reference that improves consistency across datasets while preserving institutional autonomy. The approach enhances the timeliness and accuracy of fraud detection, reduces duplication of investigations, and supports more coordinated and effective public-sector responses to complex employment-related crime.

title: Multi-stakeholder Financial Arrangements
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Complex public and private projects often involve financial arrangements between multiple stakeholders, creating challenges in coordination, transparency, and accountability. Disparate financial records and approval processes can lead to delays, misunderstandings, and increased administrative effort. This use case addresses these issues by improving the management of multi-stakeholder financial arrangements, involving public authorities, financial institutions, and other partners, with the objective of creating clearer oversight and more efficient financial coordination. The solution is implemented through a shared digital financial framework based on distributed ledger technology, where agreements, commitments, and transactions are recorded in a single, verifiable environment accessible to authorised stakeholders. Smart contract mechanisms can be used to automate predefined financial steps and conditions. The result is improved transparency, reduced administrative overhead, and greater trust between parties, supporting faster decision-making and more reliable execution of complex financial arrangements.

title: Large Event Permitting
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Municipalities of Barendrecht, Albrandswaard and Ridderkerk
source_description: Municipalities are responsible for issuing permits for local events, but the process often requires consultation with multiple authorities such as police and fire services, resulting in lengthy procedures and high administrative burden. In the municipalities of Barendrecht, Albrandswaard, and Ridderkerk, even small-scale events such as street parties required complex coordination and repeated information exchange. This use case addresses these inefficiencies by redesigning the event permitting process, involving municipalities and advisory authorities, with the objective of simplifying workflows and reducing processing time. The proof of concept models the permitting process on a blockchain, where applications, advice, and approvals are shared in a common environment and standard procedures are automated using smart contracts. All involved agencies gain real-time visibility into each other’s input without relying on manual coordination by the municipality. The solution significantly reduces administrative workload, accelerates permit issuance, and makes the process more resilient by minimising manual communication and duplication.

title: Waste Sector Data Sharing
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Waste management involves multiple actors, including municipalities, transporters, intermediaries, and processors, each maintaining separate records that must align for regulatory compliance and billing. This fragmentation increases the risk of discrepancies and reduces transparency across the waste processing chain. This use case addresses these challenges by improving data sharing and integrity in the waste sector in the City of Utrecht, with the objective of creating a reliable end-to-end overview of waste flows. The proof of concept is implemented through a blockchain-based shared administration that links waste weight data per container with information from transporters, intermediaries, and final processors. Smart contracts automate selected control and verification steps, while each party retains its own operational systems. The approach improves trust in data accuracy, reduces reconciliation effort, and provides clear visibility from waste collection to final processing, supporting more efficient and accountable waste management.

title: Blockchain-based Digital Identity: Do-it-Yourself Marriage
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
task: Authentication of self-sovereign Digital ID services
source_description: Civil status processes such as marriage traditionally rely on trusted third parties to verify identities and formalise agreements, which can limit flexibility and increase administrative involvement. The National Office for Identity Data explored whether emerging digital identity approaches could simplify such processes while maintaining legal certainty. This use case examines the concept of a “do-it-yourself” marriage, involving citizens and civil registration authorities, with the objective of understanding how identity verification and consent could be managed digitally. The concept is implemented through a blockchain-based digital identity framework in which the identities and intentions of both partners are verified and recorded, and smart contracts are used to formalise the agreement without the need for an intermediary registrar. While primarily exploratory, the use case illustrates how decentralised identity and automated trust mechanisms could reduce administrative steps, increase citizen autonomy, and inform future redesign of civil registry processes, subject to legal and regulatory considerations.

title: Aid Subsidy Collection
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Municipalities are responsible for administering social support schemes efficiently while ensuring that public funds are used correctly and reach their intended beneficiaries. In Zuidhorn, the implementation of the national Kindpakket programme, which provides financial support for children from low-income families, required a solution that reduced administrative burden, improved transparency, and involved local businesses and associations in a simple and trustworthy way. Around 150 children in the municipality are eligible for the scheme, which supports participation in sports, cultural activities, and school-related initiatives. The objective of this use case is to enable fast, user-friendly subsidy collection for families, ensure correct spending of public funds, and simplify coordination between the municipality, beneficiaries, and local entrepreneurs. The solution is implemented through a digital subsidy platform based on distributed ledger technology, where entitlements are securely issued to eligible families and linked to specific spending purposes. Beneficiaries use a unique digital code at participating local businesses to pay for approved goods or services, such as a bicycle, while transaction records are validated and stored in a shared system. Payments are settled directly with entrepreneurs without manual intervention by the municipality, and the platform integrates with existing municipal administrative processes for eligibility and oversight. The approach significantly reduces administrative complexity and processing time, improves transparency and traceability of subsidy use, and enhances user experience for families and businesses. It also strengthens local economic participation, increases trust in subsidy management, and provides a scalable and cost-effective model for delivering targeted social support.

title: TrustForWills
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Ministry of Economy Tourism and Digital Agenda (MINETAD)
source_description: The management of digital assets after death or temporary incapacity presents legal and practical challenges, as traditional testamentary processes often do not adequately address online accounts, cryptocurrencies and other digital property. TrustForWills was developed as a government-supported initiative to facilitate the secure and automated execution of digital wills, ensuring that users’ digital assets are managed in accordance with their instructions. Stakeholders include individuals, legal professionals, public authorities and emerging digital service providers. The objective is to modernise inheritance management and stimulate new business models within the legal sector by addressing digital patrimony. The platform uses blockchain technology to record testamentary instructions in a tamper-resistant distributed ledger. Smart contracts are designed to execute predefined actions when specific conditions are met, such as verified notification of death or incapacity. Cryptographic mechanisms secure user identity and asset references, while integration with digital asset platforms enables controlled transfer or access. The system supports transparency, auditability and automated compliance with predefined rules. The expected impact includes greater legal certainty for digital asset succession, reduced administrative disputes and improved efficiency in estate management. By leveraging distributed ledger infrastructure, the initiative enhances trust, security and innovation in the management of digital legacies.

title: Distributed Open Data Portal
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Open data initiatives aim to improve transparency and civic participation, but centralised portals can face challenges related to data integrity, persistence, and accountability of changes. The City of Valls sought to strengthen trust and resilience in its open data publication. This use case involves the municipality, developers, and citizens, with the objective of publishing open data in a secure, verifiable, and participatory way. The solution is implemented through a distributed open data portal where datasets are published both on a traditional web interface and on a decentralised storage network based on IPFS, ensuring long-term data persistence. All changes to datasets are logged on an immutable distributed ledger, enabling full traceability of updates. This hybrid architecture improves reliability and transparency of open data. It enhances citizen trust, supports reuse of data, and strengthens participation, while providing a scalable model for accountable open government data publishing.

title: Decentralised Energy Trading Marketplace
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Municipal and national energy markets rely on centralised trading platforms that can be costly to operate and may limit flexibility and transparency for market participants. Vattenfall and 22 European energy trading firms sought to explore whether wholesale energy trading could be organised in a more efficient, decentralised way while maintaining the reliability of existing market operations. The objective of this use case is to assess whether a peer-to-peer trading model can match current trading platforms, reduce operational costs, and increase resilience by removing dependence on a single central intermediary. The pilot is implemented through a decentralised digital trading infrastructure based on distributed ledger technology, where participating firms exchange buy and sell orders directly via an encrypted, shared order book. Software provided by a specialised B2B solutions provider enables secure submission, matching, and settlement of trades without the need for a third-party exchange or broker, while integrating with participants’ existing trading and risk management systems. The trial allows real-time testing of decentralised order handling, transaction integrity, and system performance under market conditions. The project provides insight into the feasibility of decentralised wholesale energy trading, with potential benefits including lower transaction costs, reduced operational complexity, increased transparency, and improved scalability. It also supports innovation in energy markets by exploring alternative trading architectures that could enhance competition and efficiency in the long term.

title: PROCIVIS e-Government Pilot Project
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
task: Authentication of self-sovereign Digital ID services
source_description: Citizens increasingly expect secure and convenient access to public services via mobile devices, while governments seek to reduce reliance on multiple logins and paper documents. The Canton of Schaffhausen aimed to simplify digital access to public services through a trusted mobile identity. This use case involves cantonal authorities and residents, with the objective of enabling secure, user-friendly e-government services. The solution is implemented through the Schaffhauser eID+ mobile application, which allows citizens to install a verified electronic identity validated by the residents’ registration office. The app enables authentication for multiple public services and secure storage of digital documents on smartphones. It integrates with existing government systems while maintaining high security standards. The solution improves usability, reduces administrative friction, and increases uptake of digital services. It delivers operational efficiency, enhances citizen experience, and provides a scalable foundation for mobile-first e-government.

title: City of Zug Blockchain Voting Trial
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Cities are increasingly seeking secure and trustworthy digital channels to engage citizens in democratic processes, while ensuring transparency, data integrity, and voter confidence. The City of Zug aimed to test whether electronic voting could be delivered in a way that strengthens trust and protects voter identity, as part of its broader strategy to experiment with innovative digital public services. This use case focuses on a municipal voting trial conducted between 25 June and 1 July 2018, involving residents and city authorities, with the objective of evaluating the feasibility and acceptance of digital voting at local level. The proof of concept is implemented through a blockchain-based e-voting platform that records voting transactions and voter credentials in a tamper-resistant system. Resident identities are verified digitally, and votes are securely stored to ensure integrity, traceability, and protection against manipulation, while preserving voter confidentiality. The platform operates alongside existing administrative systems and is limited in scope to enable controlled experimentation. The trial demonstrates that digital voting can be carried out securely and transparently at municipal level, providing a positive user experience for participants. It offers valuable lessons on governance, security, and citizen trust, and supports informed decision-making on the future use of digital voting technologies in democratic processes.

title: e-Auction 3.0
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Privatisation and leasing of state assets are vulnerable to corruption, lack of transparency, and public mistrust. Ukraine sought to reform these processes by introducing a more open and verifiable auction mechanism. This use case involves public authorities, bidders, and oversight bodies, with the objective of ensuring fair, transparent asset auctions. The solution is implemented through a decentralised electronic auction platform based on blockchain technology, supporting the sale and lease of state and regional property, land, and enterprises. The platform provides open APIs for monitoring and embeds transparency by design, making auction data publicly auditable. The system reduces opportunities for manipulation, increases competition, and improves public confidence. It accelerates privatisation processes, lowers administrative costs, and delivers strong governance value through transparency and accountability.

title: R3 Project Maison
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Regulatory reporting of mortgage transactions involves complex data exchanges between financial institutions and supervisory authorities, often relying on fragmented reporting systems and manual reconciliation processes. These inefficiencies can increase operational risk, reporting errors and compliance costs for banks, while limiting real-time oversight capabilities for regulators. R3, in collaboration with the UK Financial Conduct Authority and major banks, launched Project Maison to explore how distributed ledger technology could improve mortgage reporting. The objective was to create a shared, secure infrastructure that streamlines data submission and enhances transparency in regulatory reporting workflows. The project utilises blockchain-based platforms to record mortgage transaction data in a shared ledger accessible to authorised participants. Cryptographic validation ensures data integrity, while consensus mechanisms synchronise updates across participating institutions. Smart contract logic can standardise reporting formats and automate compliance checks. The prototype integrates with banks’ internal systems through secure interfaces, enabling structured data exchange between institutions and regulators. The anticipated impact includes reduced duplication of reporting processes, improved data accuracy and enhanced regulatory visibility. By creating a common data layer, the initiative aims to lower compliance costs, strengthen trust between regulators and banks and support innovation in supervisory technology.

title: GovCoin Proof of Concept
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: HM Treasury (HMT) and the Department of Work and Pensions
source_description: Public welfare systems face ongoing challenges in distributing financial support efficiently while preventing fraud, reducing administrative costs, and ensuring that vulnerable citizens can access benefits easily. In the United Kingdom, HM Treasury and the Department for Work and Pensions sought to explore new payment models that could modernise the delivery of government grants and welfare support. The objective of this use case is to improve the registration and payment of benefits, strengthen control over public expenditure, and support broader policy goals such as financial inclusion and poverty reduction. The proof of concept is implemented through a digital payment and registration framework based on distributed ledger technology, often referred to as GovCoin. The system records benefit entitlements and transactions in a shared, secure ledger, enabling automated checks, traceability of payments, and reduced reliance on intermediaries. Integration with existing government systems supports eligibility verification and compliance, while digital wallets enable recipients to receive and use funds more efficiently. The approach demonstrates potential to reduce losses from fraud and error, lower administrative overhead, and increase transparency in welfare payments. It also improves user experience for beneficiaries by supporting faster and more reliable access to support, while offering better value for money and a more sustainable footing for public expenditure.

title: RMGA The New Digital Gold Standard
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Trading and holding physical gold traditionally involves high costs, intermediaries, and operational complexity. The Royal Mint and CME Group sought to modernise gold markets by combining physical security with digital efficiency. This use case involves institutional investors, traders, and market operators, with the objective of enabling secure, efficient gold trading and settlement. The solution is implemented by issuing digital records of ownership for gold stored in The Royal Mint’s vaults, with transactions executed and settled through integrated market infrastructure. Each digital unit represents allocated physical gold, secured cryptographically and backed by trusted custody. The system reduces settlement risk, lowers costs, and improves market access. It enhances liquidity, transparency, and efficiency, delivering a modern alternative to traditional spot gold markets. However, the project has been discontinued in 2018.

title: Distributed Ledger-based Gross Settlement System
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: The Bank of England recognised the need to modernise its ageing Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system to ensure long-term financial stability and accommodate emerging financial technologies. As interbank settlement forms the backbone of the UK’s payment infrastructure, the central bank sought to design a replacement system capable of interfacing with innovative technologies without compromising resilience or security. Stakeholders include commercial banks, financial market infrastructures, fintech providers and regulatory authorities. The objective was to create a next-generation RTGS platform that safeguards monetary stability while enabling future integration with distributed ledger systems. The proposed architecture considers interoperability with distributed ledger technologies by enabling secure APIs and messaging interfaces that allow external platforms to connect with the central settlement core. While not replacing the RTGS with a blockchain system, the design incorporates modular components capable of interacting with tokenised assets or ledger-based platforms if these achieve industry maturity. Advanced encryption, real-time processing engines and high-availability infrastructure underpin the system. The impact is a more flexible, resilient and innovation-ready settlement infrastructure that maintains systemic stability while supporting future technological evolution. This approach enhances scalability, ensures regulatory compliance and positions the UK payment system to adapt to industry developments.

title: Food Standards Agency
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
task: Tracking of goods and assets along the supply chain
source_description: The Food Standards Agency (FSA), the UK’s food safety regulator, faces the ongoing challenge of ensuring transparency, traceability and regulatory oversight across complex meat supply chains, where fragmented records and limited data sharing can slow inspections and reduce trust. In the context of meat production and inspection, the FSA worked with an unnamed cattle slaughterhouse to address the need for consistent, verifiable and timely access to production and inspection data. Key stakeholders included the regulator and the slaughterhouse operator, with the shared objective of improving end-to-end visibility of meat movements and compliance information while aligning industry practices with regulatory requirements. Emerging Technology Implementation: The solution was implemented using a blockchain-based supply chain monitoring system, piloted through a proof of concept. Standardised data relating to meat inspection and production events were recorded on a shared distributed ledger accessible to both the FSA and the slaughterhouse. The approach focused on developing common data standards in collaboration with industry, enabling secure, tamper-evident data sharing and integration with existing operational systems at a conceptual level. Impact and Results: The trial demonstrated that the technology functions effectively within this segment of the food industry, delivering improved transparency and shared visibility across the supply chain. It validated the feasibility of real-time data access for regulators, strengthened trust between industry and government, and highlighted opportunities to scale the approach. The results showed clear potential for more efficient inspections, improved compliance assurance, and a collaborative model that can be expanded across the wider food sector.

title: Aragon General Directorate of Contracting, Blockchain Project
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Public procurement transparency posed significant challenges for Spain's regional governments, with traditional vendor selection processes lacking auditability and creating opportunities for disputes over contract awards. The Government of Aragon implemented a pioneering hybrid blockchain solution combining Ethereum and Hyperledger Fabric technologies through the Alastria Consortium to automate and secure public tender evaluations. The system, developed in partnership with Oesia and Open Canarias, uses smart contracts to process vendor submissions whilst maintaining civil servant oversight for final decisions. Since launching in 2019, the platform has processed over 25 contracts, establishing Aragon as Spain's first regional government to deploy blockchain in public procurement. The initiative has demonstrated measurable improvements in processing times and transparency, with all evaluation criteria and scoring permanently recorded on the distributed ledger for public verification.

title: Basque Government Blockchain project
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Bilbao's municipal administration required a secure infrastructure for inter-institutional data exchange that could integrate with the Basque government's existing digital systems whilst enabling innovative citizen services. The city launched a €150,000 tender to develop a public blockchain network built on JPMorgan's Quorum platform, designed for compatibility with the regional EJIE technological infrastructure. The resulting platform employs smart contracts to facilitate secure data sharing between government institutions, with initial applications including digital power of attorney services that allow citizens to authorise representatives online. The system operates as a permissioned network ensuring that sensitive administrative data remains accessible only to authorised public bodies. This initiative positioned Bilbao among Spain's early municipal adopters of distributed ledger technology for government operations.

title: V-ICT-OR Blockchain Project
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Belgian public procurement processes faced challenges with document integrity verification and timestamp reliability for tender submissions, requiring a solution that could provide immutable evidence of submission times without compromising confidentiality. Digipolis Antwerp, the IT agency for the City of Antwerp, developed a blockchain-based procurement tool in partnership with BallistiX that timestamps tender metadata on a private distributed ledger. The system operates nodes at Digipolis, the Belgian federal agency BOSA, and the Port of Antwerp, creating a trusted network for procurement documentation. Integrated within the Antwerp City Platform as a Service (ACPaaS), the solution received recognition as Belgian ICT Project of the Year. The platform demonstrates how blockchain can enhance public procurement integrity without requiring fundamental changes to existing administrative workflows.

title: Smart procurement tool in Antwerp
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The City of Antwerp, through its municipal IT agency Digipolis, explored ways to enhance public procurement processes by introducing greater transparency, reliability and trust in how requests for quotations and vendor offers are exchanged and recorded. Traditional procurement systems can be vulnerable to data tampering and lack robust, tamper-evident records of submissions, which may undermine confidence among procurers and bidders and lead to disputes or compliance challenges. The tool was developed in the context of public procurement stakeholders including municipal procurement officers, IT administrators, and suppliers, with the objective of testing whether distributed ledger technology could strengthen the integrity of procurement transactions while respecting existing procurement regulations. The solution developed combines blockchain-based and conventional components: procurers publish requests for quotations via a user interface linked to a customer relationship management system, and metadata from published requests and vendor submissions are recorded on a permissioned blockchain to provide immutable time-stamped attestations that documents have not been altered. The blockchain component, using a proof-of-authority configuration hosted by Digipolis and the Belgian Federal Government Procurement Organization (BOSA), underpins the process alongside smart contracts that log key events such as contract award outcomes. Integration with the CRM system ensures award notifications and non-award communications can be automated following on-chain events. The tool has been implemented as part of the BLING (Blockchain in Government) programme of proof-of-concept projects, and the early experience indicates the system is stable enough to support procurement workflows, offering enhanced transparency and tamper resistance compared to legacy systems while remaining compliant with public procurement law

title: Malta Information Technology Agency (MITA), Smart Public Contracts
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: COVID-19 vaccine distribution required unprecedented cold chain monitoring, with Pfizer vaccines demanding storage at -70°C and any temperature deviation potentially compromising entire batches worth thousands of doses. NHS South Warwickshire partnered with Everyware Ltd and Hedera Hashgraph to deploy IoT sensors across Stratford Upon Avon and Warwick hospitals that continuously monitor refrigeration units and record encrypted temperature data on a distributed ledger. The blockchain-based audit trail provides tamper-proof evidence of compliance with storage requirements, supporting regulatory accountability and enabling rapid identification of any cold chain breaches. Following successful vaccine monitoring, the system has been expanded to track chemotherapy drugs, blood products, and other temperature-sensitive medical assets. Everyware was subsequently selected for the Digital Catapult 5G programme to further develop healthcare IoT applications.

title: Data embassy - Estonian Blockchain Technology
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Estonia's comprehensive digital government services created an unprecedented national dependency on data infrastructure, raising concerns about continuity in the event of cyber attacks or physical disasters affecting domestic systems. The government established the world's first data embassy in Luxembourg, housing backup copies of critical national databases including land registry, population register, business register, and health records within a Tier 4 datacenter in Betzdorf. The facility operates under a bilateral agreement providing diplomatic immunity equivalent to a physical embassy, ensuring data sovereignty regardless of its physical location. Built with €2.2 million in funding (85% from EU ERDF), the infrastructure employs Guardtime's KSI Blockchain for data integrity verification alongside solutions from Cybernetica, Dell EMC, Ericsson, OpenNode, and Telia. The initiative has since inspired similar projects, with Monaco replicating the model in 2021.

title: Signaturit - The smartest e-Signature solution to send and sign documents on the go
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: International credential recognition in Italy faced challenges with verification delays and document fraud, creating barriers for qualified professionals seeking employment or further education. CIMEA, the Italian ENIC-NARIC centre responsible for foreign qualification recognition, developed Diplome as a private permissioned blockchain platform for automatic notarisation of Statements of Comparability and Verification. Italy became the first country to use blockchain technology specifically for credential evaluation processes, providing holders with a digital wallet containing their verified qualifications. In March 2024, CIMEA Diplome attestations were accepted as equivalent to the Declaration of Value for EU Blue Card applications, significantly streamlining immigration procedures for skilled workers. The CIMEA Diplome Chain infrastructure continues to expand, supporting European mobility initiatives and international recognition frameworks.

title: Obrir Girona - system of certifications of vaccinations and Covid19 tests
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Andorra's small higher education system required modernisation to ensure academic credentials would be readily verifiable by international employers and institutions, supporting graduate mobility in the European region. The government implemented blockchain technology to store all academic qualifications issued by Andorran higher education institutions, creating tamper-proof digital credentials that can be verified independently without contacting issuing institutions. This digital transformation aligned with broader national strategies to position Andorra as an innovative jurisdiction embracing emerging technologies. The system provides graduates with internationally recognisable proof of their qualifications, reducing verification delays and eliminating risks of credential fraud. The initiative demonstrates how smaller nations can leverage blockchain to enhance the international recognition of their educational systems.

title: Decentralised Social Security System
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Academic and professional credential verification has traditionally relied on centralised institutions, creating administrative burdens for universities, graduates and employers who must repeatedly authenticate certificates and qualifications. To address inefficiencies in credential issuance and verification, the University of Nicosia pioneered the use of blockchain infrastructure to issue tamper-evident academic certificates that can be independently verified without requiring direct institutional confirmation. The initiative sought to modernise trust mechanisms in academic certification while supporting innovation in digital currency and blockchain education. Stakeholders include students, employers, academic institutions and accreditation bodies. The system records cryptographic hashes of academic certificates on the Bitcoin blockchain, enabling third parties to validate authenticity through decentralised verification processes. Secure digital signatures and blockchain time-stamping ensure document integrity while preserving personal data off-chain. The solution is integrated into the university’s academic administration systems and supports issuance for large-scale online programmes, including the Digital Currency MOOC and specialised MSc degrees. The initiative has been implemented and operational for several years, positioning the university as an early adopter of blockchain credentials. It has improved efficiency in verification, reduced administrative overhead and enhanced global accessibility of academic records while strengthening trust in digital certification frameworks.

title: Digital vehicle registration
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Malta's rental housing market suffered from widespread informal contracts and limited regulatory oversight, creating problems for tenants lacking legal protections and enabling tax evasion through unreported rental income. In June 2019, the Cabinet approved regulations requiring all property rental contracts to be registered on blockchain, making Malta the first country to mandate distributed ledger technology for residential tenancy agreements. The system uses smart contracts to ensure documents cannot be tampered with after registration whilst maintaining controlled access for authorised parties including landlords, tenants, and regulatory authorities. Ledger Projects, with developers David Schranz and Anthony Mamo, created a supporting application for property transfer management. The initiative aims to eliminate informal rental arrangements, protect tenant rights, and improve tax compliance in the housing sector.

source_description: Italian universities faced increasing challenges with diploma verification requests and credential fraud, whilst graduates required faster proof of qualifications for job applications and further study. This approach enables independent verification by employers or other institutions without requiring contact with the university, reducing administrative burden whilst providing tamper-proof evidence of qualification authenticity. The system supports European Higher Education Area mobility objectives by facilitating cross-border credential recognition. The initiative established a model subsequently adopted by other Italian institutions seeking to modernise their credential issuance processes.

title: Staffing the Public Sector – The Case of Greece
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Supreme Council for Civil Personnel Selection (ASEP)
source_description: Citizens interacting with Antwerp's digital services lacked control over their personal data stored across multiple government databases, whilst GDPR requirements demanded new approaches to consent management and data portability. Digipolis Antwerp launched the Blockchain on the Move project in partnership with Jolocom (Berlin), V-ICT-OR, and the Flemish Government under the Programme for Innovation Procurement to develop Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) infrastructure. The system enables citizens to manage their own identity data and control which government agencies can access specific information, with initial applications focusing on change of address processes. The initiative forms part of Digipolis's broader ACPaaS (Antwerp City Platform as a Service) ecosystem and includes GDPR management tools and a Business Rules Engine for access rights. By returning data control to citizens, the project demonstrates how blockchain technology can support privacy-by-design principles in public services.

title: Staffing the Public Sector – The Case of Portugal
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Swiss institutions required secure and transparent methods for managing digital assets and credentials that met the country's high standards for financial services and data protection. Swiss Ledger was established as a private, institutional, and non-profit blockchain infrastructure providing distributed ledger services to Swiss organisations across sectors including finance, government, and academia. The platform enables secure credential management, asset tokenisation, and data integrity verification whilst maintaining compliance with Swiss regulatory requirements. Operating since 2021, Swiss Ledger provides a permissioned blockchain environment where participating organisations can issue and verify digital credentials, track assets, and maintain auditable records. The infrastructure supports Switzerland's broader digital transformation objectives whilst preserving the privacy and security standards that characterise Swiss financial and institutional services.

title: Provision of Recruitment & Competency Management Services
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Traditional air quality monitoring relies on expensive governmental stations providing limited geographic coverage and delayed data publication, leaving many pollution hotspots undetected and populations without timely warnings. PlanetWatch, a French startup and CERN spin-off, developed a global air quality monitoring network using the Algorand blockchain to create the first immutable ledger for environmental data. The platform incentivises individuals and organisations to deploy low-cost sensors through PLANET token rewards, with over 25,000 sensors deployed globally by late 2021. Initial deployments in Milan and Taranto, Italy, demonstrated the system's capability to provide dense, real-time monitoring complementing official stations at a fraction of the cost. Data collected undergoes validation through CERN's C2MON acquisition framework before blockchain recording, ensuring reliability. The Algorand Foundation supported the initiative through grants, recognising its environmental and public health potential.

title: DECODE - Digital Democracy and Data Commons
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Barcelona Digital Democracy and Data Commons pilot explored how citizens could participate in online democratic processes while retaining greater control over their personal data. The operational problem was that digital participation platforms often require users to disclose personal information for authentication, even when the democratic action itself does not require full identity exposure. Barcelona City Council tested the pilot through Decidim, the city’s digital democracy platform, which had more than 60,000 users. The objective was to enable people to sign petitions anonymously while still meeting legitimate authentication requirements, such as proving place of residence. The implementation integrated a DECODE module into Decidim, supported by privacy-preserving data-sharing tools, the DECODE app, the BCNOW dashboard and a distributed ledger for transparency. Rather than relying on conventional identity checks, the system allowed users to disclose only the attributes needed for participation. The pilot also included a deliberative process on the politics and economics of data and on how Barcelona could develop a democratic city data commons. The expected impact was stronger trust in digital participation, more privacy-respecting civic engagement and a practical demonstration of how public authorities can enable democratic processes without unnecessary personal-data exposure.

title: DECODE - Citizen Science Data Governance
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Ideas for Change and FabLab Barcelona
source_description: The Barcelona Citizen Science Data Governance pilot focused on enabling residents to collect and share environmental data while maintaining control over how their information was used. The urban challenge was that citizen-generated sensor data on issues such as pollution and noise can be valuable for local decision-making, but it also raises questions about privacy, ownership, consent and secure data sharing. Residents used environmental sensors placed in their homes and neighbourhoods to record factors including noise levels and pollution. DECODE technology enabled them to share encrypted data anonymously with communities and public actors, according to conditions they could define. The implementation addressed both a technical and governance problem: how to collect and store continuous streams of citizen-sensed data while allowing individuals to decide what to share, with whom and under which terms. The pilot also included training and support sessions to help participants install sensors, gather data, analyse results and use the evidence to influence city-level decisions. Its expected impact was to strengthen citizen science, improve the evidence base for urban policy and demonstrate a privacy-preserving model for community data sharing. By linking environmental monitoring with citizen-controlled data governance, the pilot offered a practical route towards more democratic and accountable smart-city services.

title: DECODE - Amsterdam Digital Register - age check with municipal census data
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
task: Authentication of self-sovereign Digital ID services
source_description: The Amsterdam Digital Register pilot examined how citizens could use personal data held in municipal databases to prove specific attributes without revealing their full identity. The operational problem was that many public, civic or online interactions require proof of eligibility, such as age, but traditional verification often exposes more information than necessary, including name, full identity details or social security numbers. The pilot gave participants access to personal data stored in the municipal database and enabled them to reuse it in other contexts, both online and offline. Its specific use case was age verification, allowing citizens to prove that they were over 16 or 18 without disclosing broader personal information. The implementation used Attribute-Based Credentials, a data-minimising authentication mechanism that certifies only the required attribute. Conceptually, the system separated the proof of eligibility from the disclosure of identity, supporting selective and privacy-preserving data sharing. The expected impact was to demonstrate how municipalities can act as trusted custodians of citizen data while giving individuals more agency over its reuse. The pilot showed how public registers could support digital identity functions in a way that reduces unnecessary data exposure and strengthens privacy by design.

title: DECODE - Gebiedonline (Neighbourhood Online)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The GebiedOnline pilot in Amsterdam tested how a local neighbourhood social network could operate with stronger privacy protections and less dependence on commercial login systems. GebiedOnline was already used as a community platform, but access was managed through email and password credentials or Facebook login, creating security concerns and unwanted dependency on an external private platform. The pilot addressed the need for a more open, inclusive and privacy-preserving model for community interaction, where users could participate without unnecessarily sharing personal data. The implementation introduced Attribute-Based Credentials as an alternative login and access mechanism. This allowed communities using GebiedOnline to define which credentials they would accept, while giving users more granular control over the data they shared with the platform and with other members. Conceptually, the pilot combined decentralised identity, selective disclosure and community-governed access rules. The expected impact was to reduce platform dependency, improve security and strengthen trust in neighbourhood-level digital participation. By allowing each community to determine acceptable credentials, the pilot also supported local autonomy and flexibility. It demonstrated how small-scale civic platforms could adopt privacy-enhancing identity infrastructure while remaining inclusive, open-source oriented and aligned with the needs of community users.

title: Public administration employee skills cerification
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Italian National Institute for Insurance against Accidents at Work (INAIL)
source_description: Catalonia's Open Administration Consortium (AOC) receives over 91,000 annual support requests, with citizens struggling to navigate complex e-government procedures for digital identification and certificate management. The AOC deployed La Paula (January 2021) and La Rita (April 2021) as AI-powered chatbot assistants supporting the VALid identification service and idCAT Certificate respectively, developed in partnership with 1MillionBot. The chatbots use natural language processing to interpret citizen queries and provide instant responses 24/7, achieving over 95% accuracy rate. In 2022, Paula supported 62,588 people with 127,454 messages whilst Rita assisted 43,520 people through 100,606 messages. The AOC has pioneered algorithmic transparency in Spain, publishing detailed documentation of chatbot operation, governance, and limitations. In May 2024, the AOC upgraded to generative AI chatbots, serving 11,575 monthly users with 88% success rate and 90% cost savings per query.

title: Buying and selling property with blockchain
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Italy loses over €99 billion annually to tax evasion, with €30 billion from VAT alone, whilst traditional enforcement methods struggled to identify non-compliant taxpayers among millions of returns. The Agenzia delle Entrate developed VeRa (Verifica dei Rapporti finanziari), an AI-powered algorithm that cross-references taxpayer filings with data from the Financial Relations Archive, property registries, bank accounts, and electronic payments to identify compliance risks. In 2022, VeRa flagged one million high-risk cases and helped prevent over €6.8 billion in fraud. The system assigns risk scores enabling targeted audits rather than random checks, whilst EU-funded projects through Sogei introduce network analysis, machine learning, and data visualisation for complex evasion schemes. In 2023, the agency recovered €18.1 billion, increasing to projected €19.6 billion by 2025. A complementary AI chatbot launched in 2023 analyses VAT returns in real-time, flagging irregularities for immediate investigation.

title: The European Blockchain Services Infrastructure (EBSI)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Global mangrove mapping relied on infrequently updated datasets that could not capture the dynamic changes affecting these critical coastal ecosystems, limiting understanding of carbon sequestration, biodiversity, and natural coastal protection. The UK Hydrographic Office (UKHO) developed the ADMIRALTY Global Mangrove Data Set using deep learning applied to European Space Agency Sentinel-2 satellite imagery, creating the world's highest resolution, most up-to-date global view of mangrove forests. The neural network was trained on over 7,000 coastal images and achieves geo-generalisability across diverse global locations through collaboration between UKHO's Data Science, Data Engineering, and Remote Sensing teams. The system automatically updates every six months, processing new cloud-free satellite imagery to detect mangrove extent changes. This serverless architecture enables scalable analysis supporting marine navigation, coastal sustainability planning, and climate change research on these vital carbon sinks that sequester 3-5 times more carbon than inland tropical forests.

title: Voting Trial Using NEM's Blockchain
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Italy's education system faced the annual challenge of assigning approximately 100,000 teachers to schools across diverse regions, a complex optimization problem that had historically relied on manual processes prone to errors and delays. The Ministry of Education implemented an algorithmic system to automatically assign teachers to schools based on preferences, qualifications, and regional needs, processing massive datasets to generate placements within compressed timeframes. However, the 2020 deployment generated significant controversy when thousands of teachers received assignments to schools far from their preferences or in regions they had not selected, with some relocated hundreds of kilometres from their homes. The algorithm's logic and decision criteria remained opaque, preventing affected teachers from understanding or effectively challenging their placements. The case became a prominent example in debates about algorithmic accountability in public administration, highlighting tensions between efficiency gains and transparency requirements in automated government decision-making.

source_description: Germany's customs authority receives high volumes of citizen inquiries about import duties, customs procedures, and international trade regulations, creating significant workload for staff and variable response times for users. title: Sustainability: rewarding best practices
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Consumers in Germany are increasingly purchasing food and cosmetics online, with a rising trend in online purchases of various items including kitchen utensils, toys, clothing, and tobacco products. The Federal Office of Consumer Protection and Food Safety (BVL) hosts a central unit called G@ZIELT, jointly managed by federal states, to regulate internet trade in products covered by the Food and Feed Code and tobacco. The G@ZIELT unit searches the internet to identify risky food offers, misleading labels, and unregistered businesses, reporting findings to appropriate authorities.

title: PoSeID-on - Protection and control of Secured Information by means of a privacy enhanced Dashboard
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: International airport border control in Germany faced growing passenger volumes requiring faster processing whilst maintaining security standards and compliance with Schengen external border regulations. The Federal Police implemented EasyPASS, an automated border control system using biometric facial recognition developed by Bundesdruckerei, secunet, and Cognitec to verify travellers' identities against their e-passport chip photos. The system is deployed at Frankfurt, Munich, Hamburg, Hannover, Düsseldorf, Stuttgart, Berlin Brandenburg, and Cologne/Bonn airports, available to EU/EEA citizens aged 12+ and registered third-country nationals from the USA, Hong Kong, South Korea, Taiwan, and the UK. Travellers place their e-passport on the document reader, then proceed through gates where cameras capture facial images for 1:1 comparison against stored biometric data, with information also checked against Schengen databases. Data is stored for 48 hours (extendable to 30 days for police investigations), and the system strictly limits facial recognition to identity verification purposes under the Passport Act.

title: Identity system to combat child trafficking
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
task: Authentication of self-sovereign Digital ID services
source_description: The Office of Integration of the Ministry for Social Affairs, Health, Family, Youth, and Senior Citizens integrated a chat bot into its website in February 2020. This chat bot is being further developed in a follow-on project. Using the chat bot, people can call up general information, arrange for callbacks, and determine time windows for contact purposes. It is also possible to use the chat bot to submit an initial application for accompanying assistance.

title: Safeguarding the integrity and accessibility of digital government records of national archives
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: School districts should be designed in such a way that schools have as even a capacity as possible and the distances to school for children are short. At the same time, it is important to achieve a social mix among the students. In order to achieve these goals, school office employees in the Berlin district of Tempelhof-Schoeneberg have invested a lot of time. Streets had to be walked through one by one, information was recorded in Excel spreadsheets. This work is now done by an algorithm that automatically outputs a first draft of the cut based on the available data from the State Statistical Office.

title: Blockchain Verified Certificates
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Academic institutions worldwide lacked practical mechanisms for issuing credentials that could be independently verified without institutional involvement, creating inefficiencies for employers and graduates alike. The University of Nicosia became the first university globally to issue academic certificates verified on the Bitcoin blockchain, pioneering a model subsequently adopted by institutions worldwide. The university launched the world's first Digital Currency MOOC in 2014, which has reached over 145,000 students across 120 countries, taught by leading experts including Andreas Antonopoulos and Professor George Giaglis. In 2024, marking the MOOC's 10th anniversary, the programme was restructured into two levels covering introductory and advanced blockchain concepts. The university also established the first MSc in Blockchain and Digital Currency and first MSc in Metaverse, whilst becoming the first accredited institution to accept Bitcoin for tuition payments.

title: Electronic voting system
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Robot Automation Plan has created a new service for robotic process automation. The aim behind the project is to provide the City Council with innovative solutions, such as increasing the quality of citizen help and information services and reducing human error in processes that are repetitive and with little added value, increasing the Council’s production capacity, for example in processing licences for café terraces, and increasing the guarantee and transparency of processes and ensuring coherency in the data processed. The purpose of this initiative is to free up the time that workers currently spend on manual, repetitive tasks that are of little added value, so they can devote their time to providing real value to the organisation and reduce the time it takes to respond to requests.

title: Registration of Property Rental Contracts
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Malta's rental housing market suffered from widespread informal contracts and limited regulatory oversight, creating problems for tenants lacking legal protections and enabling tax evasion through unreported rental income. In June 2019, the Cabinet approved regulations requiring all property rental contracts to be registered on blockchain, making Malta the first country to mandate distributed ledger technology for residential tenancy agreements. The system uses smart contracts to ensure documents cannot be tampered with after registration whilst maintaining controlled access for authorised parties including landlords, tenants, and regulatory authorities. Ledger Projects, with developers David Schranz and Anthony Mamo, created a supporting application for property transfer management. The initiative aims to eliminate informal rental arrangements, protect tenant rights, and improve tax compliance in the housing sector.

title: Solution for welfare payments in the UK
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Public transport affordability is crucial for social inclusion, yet fixed-price ticketing can exclude low-income residents from mobility services essential for employment, healthcare access, and social participation. Nantes Métropole implemented an algorithmic system for solidarity transport pricing (Tarification Solidaire Transports) on its Naolib public transport network. The algorithm determines eligibility for free travel or discounts up to 50% on unlimited annual passes based on household income and family composition. All households with a family quotient of 900 or below qualify for solidarity pricing. Users apply at their local town hall, where agents collect supporting documents and enter information into Deltas, software developed by Nantes Métropole. The algorithm processes data in real time, immediately notifying applicants of their entitlement level. Benefits apply to all household members regardless of age. Since May 2023, the eligibility threshold was raised from 600 to 900 family quotient, significantly expanding coverage. The solidarity pricing programme extends beyond metropolitan residents to include commuters from surrounding areas who travel within Nantes Métropole. This ensures transport affordability for the most vulnerable populations whilst supporting labour market access and social cohesion across the metropolitan region.

title: Decentralised identity platform
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
task: Authentication of self-sovereign Digital ID services
source_description: Citizens across Europe increasingly interact with online public services that require secure identity verification, yet centralised identity systems raise concerns about data control, privacy and cross-border interoperability. The Government of Catalonia initiated the IdentiCAT pilot to give residents control over their own digital identities and enable secure engagement with online services without the government collecting personal data centrally. The objective is to align regional e-identification with EU eIDAS standards, enabling citizens to authenticate and transact with confidence not only within Catalonia but across other EU member states. The solution uses distributed ledger technology to establish a decentralised identity platform where the Catalan government acts as validator rather than data custodian. Personal identity claims and attestations are anchored on the ledger, ensuring transparency and immutability while supporting user-controlled consent for data disclosure. The platform integrates with public service portals and service providers to enable access, proof of identity, and electronic transactions under recognised standards. By decentralising identity management, IdentiCAT enhances privacy, reduces dependency on central databases, and supports cross-border recognition of digital identities. As a pilot, the project demonstrates scalable infrastructure for citizen empowerment, secure online interactions and compliance with EU digital identification frameworks.

title: Digitallisation of surety policies' management process
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Public administrations traditionally manage surety policies through paper-based and fragmented procedures that are slow, error-prone and difficult to verify, exposing municipalities to fraud and administrative inefficiencies. The Municipality of Bari, together with banks, financial intermediaries, insurance companies and SIA as technology partner, launched this pilot to modernise the issuance and validation of surety guarantees required in public procurement and administrative processes.
