INPS developed an AI decision engine upstream of the customer-service process to assess the complexity of incoming web requests. At a conceptual level, the system analyses the text of a citizen’s request, identifies topic and complexity signals, and recommends whether the request can be treated by first-level support or should be routed to a specialised operator. The expected impact is faster response time for citizens, fewer duplicate handling steps, improved workload distribution and more efficient use of expert staff. The use case is closely related to INPS’s broader strategy of applying natural language processing to high-volume citizen communication channels while preserving human responsibility for substantive responses. The online INPS Risponde service itself remains a key channel for submitting and monitoring requests for information, clarifications and case updates.

title: Virtual Assistant based on generative AI at INPS
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Citizens using social-security services often struggle to find the correct information among many pages, circulars, administrative messages and service sheets, especially for complex benefits such as pension schemes. INPS began experimenting with a generative-AI virtual assistant to improve search and orientation on its website. The objective is to allow users to ask follow-up questions conversationally after searching for a service, receiving clearer explanations and guidance without having to interpret multiple documents independently. The implementation uses a large language model through Microsoft Azure and OpenAI technologies, integrated into the INPS digital environment. In the first experimental area, the assistant supported questions on the “Opzione Donna” pension measure, drawing from service pages, circulars, messages and internal acts. At a conceptual level, the system combines retrieval of institutional knowledge sources with conversational generation, maintaining dialogue context so that users can ask additional questions and receive more precise answers. The expected impact is improved accessibility of social-security information, more intuitive navigation of INPS services, reduced friction for citizens and better use of institutional documentation. The assistant is designed as an information and orientation tool, not as a decision-maker on eligibility or benefits. Its significance lies in the movement from traditional keyword search towards conversational access to complex public-administration knowledge.

title: Talk with Arianna - the chatbot of the Italian National Institute for Social Security
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Citizens using INPS digital services often need immediate help with access credentials before they can complete personal procedures online. Arianna was designed as a virtual assistant dedicated to questions about the INPS PIN, a credential historically used to access services on the institute’s website. The operational problem was that users frequently needed guidance on how to request, manage, recover or understand their PIN, and these recurring enquiries could generate avoidable pressure on help desks and service channels. The implementation uses a conversational chatbot interface that allows citizens to interact through a guided dialogue rather than searching manually across support pages. At a conceptual level, the assistant recognises the user’s question, connects it to the relevant support content and provides a direct answer or orientation on the next step. The expected impact is faster access to credential-related information, reduced repetitive support requests, improved usability for citizens and a more efficient first level of digital assistance. Although the use case is narrow, it is significant because identity and access management are preconditions for many welfare and social-security services. By making support available continuously and in a conversational format, Arianna helped reduce friction at a critical entry point to INPS online services.

title: Quantum Catalyst Fund in the UK
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
source_description: The use case was developed to accelerate the use of quantum technologies across the public sector and help government departments understand where quantum solutions can create practical value. Quantum technologies can offer capabilities beyond conventional computing, sensing and measurement systems, but public-sector adoption requires testing, evidence and clear use cases rather than abstract technological promise. The fund therefore supports government-facing projects in policy areas such as transport, health, space, energy and net zero, including applications from drug discovery and dementia diagnosis to navigation, infrastructure monitoring and grid optimisation. Its implementation operates through a £15 million competition funded and delivered by the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and Innovate UK. Phase 1 selected 30 projects to explore the benefits of quantum technologies for government, and later funding rounds supported projects progressing towards applied demonstrations. Conceptually, the programme acts as an innovation-procurement and adoption mechanism: it links public-sector problems with companies and researchers able to test quantum sensing, quantum computing or quantum-enabled algorithms. The expected impact is faster learning inside government, reduced adoption barriers, stronger UK quantum supply chains and earlier identification of high-value public-sector applications. It also supports the UK ambition to build a quantum-enabled economy by 2033.

title: COMo - CO2 monitoring in publicly accessible indoor spaces
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Technology Foundation Berlin and the Berlin University of Applied Sciences (HTW)
source_description: Publicly accessible indoor spaces such as cultural venues, educational buildings and hospitality settings needed practical ways to manage air quality during the pandemic, when ventilation was closely linked to infection-risk reduction. COMo used carbon dioxide concentration as a proxy indicator for indoor air quality and aerosol accumulation, helping operators understand when rooms needed ventilation. The initiative built on the earlier Clair Berlin work and focused on connected sensors that could collect, process and publish CO₂ readings from indoor environments. The implementation combined networked CO₂ sensors, an Internet of Things platform, data processing and public visualisation. At a conceptual level, sensors measured indoor air conditions, transmitted readings to a digital platform, and converted them into actionable information for operators and visitors. Facility managers could use the information to decide when to ventilate, while visitors could consult published data before entering a space. The expected impact was more objective management of indoor air, improved confidence in public venues, better infection-prevention behaviour and a replicable model for low-cost environmental monitoring. The value of the case lies in translating an invisible risk factor into visible, operational information that could support everyday decisions without requiring specialist technical knowledge from building users.

title: London Electric Vehicle Charge Points Dashboard
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Electric-vehicle charging infrastructure in London is delivered by many public and private actors, creating a coordination problem for boroughs, the Greater London Authority and infrastructure providers. The London Electric Vehicle Charge Points Dashboard was developed to provide a shared view of what charging infrastructure exists, how it is used and where future installations may be needed. The operational challenge is that charging-point data can be fragmented across operators and boroughs, while investment decisions require evidence on utilisation, location, coverage and demand. The implementation brings together data on charge-point locations and usage into a dashboard that supports planning and analysis. At a conceptual level, the system aggregates infrastructure and utilisation data, presents it spatially and analytically, and helps public authorities compare provision across places. This enables better strategic deployment of new EV charging infrastructure rather than relying on isolated local datasets or assumptions. The expected impact is more coordinated infrastructure planning, improved understanding of charging behaviour, better targeting of investment and stronger support for London’s transition to cleaner transport. The dashboard also demonstrates how data collaboration can make a fragmented smart-city service area more manageable, particularly where delivery depends on many organisations rather than a single municipal provider.

title: Air-purifying billboard in Skopje
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Severe urban air pollution in Skopje has posed persistent public health and environmental challenges, with limited large-scale institutional interventions. The air-purifying billboard was introduced as a pilot civil society initiative to demonstrate a visible, scalable mitigation concept and stimulate broader institutional engagement. Stakeholders include local communities, environmental groups and public authorities. The billboard incorporates filtration materials and airflow mechanisms designed to capture particulate matter from surrounding air. In a second prototype phase, air quality sensors and Internet of Things components are integrated to collect real-time environmental data, enabling data analytics, monitoring dashboards and predictive modelling of pollution trends. Although still at prototype and testing stages, the initiative has raised public awareness and demonstrated the feasibility of modular, low-cost air purification installations. No evidence suggests large-scale municipal deployment to date; the project remains developmental and exploratory.

title: Use of Public Lighting System to Deploy a Comprehensive Smart City Platform
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Public lighting is one of the most extensive forms of urban infrastructure, making it a strong foundation for smart-city services when it is connected, centrally managed and technically scalable. Paris used its public-lighting system as the basis for a citywide smart-city platform, with the aim of reducing energy consumption, improving public safety and creating infrastructure that could support future digital services. The operational problem was not limited to lighting: the city needed a networked urban grid that could minimise environmental impact while also enabling new functions across the public realm. The implementation modernised and connected the lighting grid, transforming it from a standalone utility into a smart-city-ready infrastructure layer. At a conceptual level, connected lighting points can provide power, location, communication and mounting capacity for additional sensors, actuators or urban services. This makes it easier to scale future applications without rebuilding infrastructure from scratch. The expected impact is lower electricity consumption, better maintenance, improved user experience, enhanced public-space safety and a reusable platform for other smart services. The case is important because it treats lighting not simply as an energy-efficiency target, but as a strategic physical and digital backbone for urban innovation.

title: Blockchain to distribute government saving bonds in Poland
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Retail government bonds are distributed through intermediaries, which means several actors need consistent data on sales, transactions and reporting. Poland’s Ministry of Finance, together with PKO Bank Polski and the National Clearing House, implemented a blockchain-based reporting system for treasury savings bonds. The objective was to improve the collection and reporting of transaction data related to the sale and distribution of government savings bonds to consumers. The implementation uses an enterprise blockchain architecture, based on Hyperledger Fabric, to record relevant transaction lifecycle information and allow authorised parties to access consistent data. At a conceptual level, the platform creates a shared ledger for bond-distribution reporting, reducing reconciliation problems between the Ministry, banks and intermediaries. Rather than functioning as a retail cryptocurrency or public token market, the system supports administrative and reporting processes around conventional government savings bonds. The expected impact is better transparency between institutions, more reliable reporting, reduced duplication of records and improved operational oversight of bond distribution. The use case is notable because it applies blockchain to a public-finance reporting problem where shared data integrity and multi-party access are more relevant than speculative digital assets. It demonstrates a pragmatic form of distributed ledger adoption in the public sector, focused on back-office coordination.

title: Experimenting settlement of French government bonds in Central Bank Digital Currency with blockchain technology
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Post-trade financial markets depend on secure settlement, liquidity management and reliable interoperability between institutions that operate under strict regulatory and operational constraints. In France, Banque de France commissioned a consortium led by Euroclear to test whether French government bonds could be settled using central bank digital currency on a blockchain platform. The experiment involved Agence France Trésor, BNP Paribas CIB, Crédit Agricole CIB, HSBC, Société Générale and IBM, and its objective was to assess whether a broad range of securities-settlement operations could be executed on distributed ledger infrastructure from a user perspective. The implementation used wholesale CBDC in a test blockchain environment to process securities issuance, primary-market and secondary-market trades, repo-based liquidity optimisation and interest payments. At a conceptual level, the platform linked tokenised securities, central bank money, privacy-preserving tokens, hybrid cloud capabilities and interfaces with existing market infrastructure. This allowed the consortium to test not only individual transactions, but the feasibility of an end-to-end securities lifecycle on blockchain. The experiment demonstrated that distributed ledger systems could coexist and interoperate with conventional market infrastructure while supporting several core post-trade functions. Its main value was evidential rather than operational: it provided Banque de France and market participants with practical insight into the technical, functional and institutional conditions under which CBDC-based settlement might become viable.

title: Green Assets Wallet - tracking the impact of green bonds
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Green-bond markets rely on investor confidence that proceeds are genuinely linked to environmental objectives, but impact claims can be difficult to verify when reporting formats differ and supporting evidence is dispersed. The Green Assets Wallet initiative was developed to strengthen trust in sustainable finance by creating a shared digital environment for issuers, investors and validators to record, review and communicate the environmental impact of green debt instruments. The initiative aimed to increase both the supply of credible green investment opportunities and demand from investors seeking transparent climate-aligned assets, especially in markets where verification capacity may be limited. Its implementation used blockchain to create an immutable record of green-bond information and impact data. At a conceptual level, the platform combined distributed ledger technology, impact validation workflows, reporting tools and access for market participants, allowing green-investment claims to be checked against traceable evidence. The system was launched by Stockholm Green Digital Finance and brought together climate-finance and digital-technology expertise, including ChromaWay, CICERO, Öhman and SEB, with support connected to Swedish and German public actors. The expected impact was greater transparency, reduced verification friction, improved investor confidence and stronger scalability for credible green finance. By making impact data more auditable, Green Assets Wallet sought to reduce greenwashing risks and support capital allocation aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals and the Paris Agreement.

title: AI-based device for parkinson patients
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Fondazione IRCCS Ca' Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico Hospital and the University of Milan
source_description: Parkinson’s disease patients undergoing deep brain stimulation often receive continuous stimulation at fixed parameters, which may not optimally respond to fluctuating symptoms and can affect quality of life. The objective of this project is to develop an adaptive neurostimulation device capable of adjusting stimulation in response to real-time neural activity, involving patients, clinicians and medical device manufacturers. The system uses implanted electrodes to record brain signals and applies machine learning models to detect pathological patterns associated with motor symptoms. Control algorithms dynamically adjust stimulation parameters, creating a closed-loop system integrated with clinical programming tools. Clinical studies indicate improved symptom control, reduced side effects and more personalised therapy compared with conventional constant stimulation. The device remains under clinical development and regulatory processes in several markets, with ongoing trials and staged commercialisation rather than universal availability.

title: Chatbot - Lad Va
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Rural Support Service of the Republic of Latvia
source_description: Farmers, rural businesses and applicants for agricultural support often need guidance on funding schemes, application procedures, permits, registers and deadlines outside ordinary office hours. The Rural Support Service of Latvia introduced the LAD virtual assistant to make information about agricultural and rural support services easier to access online. The operational problem is that the agency provides a large number of services, while its users often work seasonally and may need answers when consultants or regional offices are not available. The implementation uses an AI-powered chatbot that answers general enquiries and helps users navigate support programmes, rural development measures, funding opportunities and administrative procedures. At a conceptual level, the assistant interprets a user’s question, maps it to the relevant institutional information and provides guidance in conversational form. It reduces the need for users to search across many pages or contact staff for routine questions. The expected impact is quicker access to information, reduced workload for agency employees, better support for applicants and improved accessibility of rural-support administration. The chatbot also helps standardise answers in a service area where rules, deadlines and funding conditions can be complex. Its role is informational and navigational, supporting users before formal application, assessment or decision-making processes take place.

title: AI to increase the efficiency of fiscal audit at the Greek General Directorate of Financial Controls (GDDE)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Public financial oversight bodies face limited resources and cannot audit all government entities annually, increasing the risk of inefficiency, fraud, and corruption. Greece’s General Directorate of Financial Controls sought to improve audit coverage and effectiveness. This use case involves central government bodies and auditors, with the objective of automating fiscal assessment and enabling targeted controls. The solution is implemented through a digital financial control system that consolidates audit data into a central database and applies risk analysis to prioritise audits. Automated evaluation supports online assessments and policy analysis per institution. The system increases audit coverage, supports targeted interventions, and saves at least 20% of staff time previously spent on manual checks. It improves efficiency, transparency, and governance, delivering measurable public sector value.

title: Municipality of Palaio Faliro: Development of IOT Platform - Energy Upgrade
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Municipalities increasingly need continuous visibility over how buildings, facilities and urban assets consume energy and other resources, rather than relying on fragmented readings or periodic manual checks. In Palaio Faliro, the administration developed a centralised IoT management platform to monitor, control, record and analyse consumption data across municipal infrastructure. The local context includes a diverse estate of municipal buildings, schools, social facilities, sports facilities and street lighting, with further potential sources of data across urban services. The objective is to give the municipality a single operational layer for understanding its energy footprint and progressively improving the performance of public assets. The implementation uses the SenseOne IoT platform, connecting sensors, meters and infrastructure data sources so that information can be collected, processed and displayed through dashboards. At a conceptual level, the platform can extend beyond electricity monitoring to environmental indicators, waste bins, parking spaces, gas meters, smart water meters, tanks, wells and electric-vehicle chargers. This makes the system a scalable smart-city architecture rather than a narrow energy-accounting tool. The expected impact is improved decision-making, lower consumption, earlier detection of anomalies and better prioritisation of energy-efficiency interventions. By consolidating operational data, Palaio Faliro can shift from reactive infrastructure management to continuous, evidence-based monitoring of its municipal footprint.

title: Chatbot Poseidon - Municipality of Palaio Faliro
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Residents and visitors to a municipality often need quick answers about local services, procedures, facilities, events and community resources. Poseidon was introduced as a virtual assistant on the Municipality of Palaio Faliro’s digital portal to make municipal information more accessible through an automated conversational channel. The operational problem is common in local government: useful information may exist online, but users do not always know where to find it, which department is responsible or which procedure applies to their situation. The implementation uses a chatbot interface embedded in the municipal website, allowing users to ask questions and receive automated guidance rather than navigating only through static pages. At a conceptual level, the system recognises common municipal-service queries, retrieves or maps the relevant information and directs users towards appropriate content or service pathways. The expected impact is faster access to municipal information, fewer routine enquiries for staff, better availability outside office hours and improved user experience for people interacting with the municipality online. The chatbot’s function is primarily informational and navigational: it does not replace formal applications, permits or administrative decisions, but provides a more convenient first point of contact. The case fits into Palaio Faliro’s wider digital-service approach, where municipal online channels are used to improve citizen support and access to local services.

title: Pollinator Highway Augmented Reality Application - Avalinn AR
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Urban-planning projects can be difficult for residents to imagine when future public spaces exist only as drawings, plans or technical descriptions. AvaLinn AR was created in Tallinn to support citizen engagement around the Pollinator Highway, a green corridor and public-space project in North Tallinn. The objective is to help people experience proposed landscape-architecture solutions through augmented reality, making the future intervention more understandable and inviting. The implementation combines mobile augmented reality, murals, map-based interaction and visualisations of future public space. Users download the application and scan wall paintings along the Pollinator Highway, each linked to themes such as species richness, sustainable mobility, reuse of garages and leisure activities. At a conceptual level, physical murals become digital entry points: the app overlays additional information, future visions and interactive content onto the urban environment. The expected impact is more accessible planning communication, stronger citizen participation, better understanding of biodiversity and mobility goals, and increased engagement with a major green-infrastructure project. The case is significant because it uses AR not as a novelty, but as a participatory planning tool that connects local art, environmental strategy and spatial imagination. It allows residents to experience potential future changes in the place where those changes would occur.

title: Crowdsorsa - City of Helsinki
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Municipalities need up-to-date information on the condition of roads, cycle lanes, public infrastructure and environmental assets, but comprehensive field surveys can be costly and slow. Crowdsorsa applies gamification and crowdsourcing to urban data collection, allowing citizens to complete location-based missions through a mobile app while collecting GPS-tagged photos or videos. In Helsinki, the approach has been used for tasks such as surveying road and cycle-lane conditions, mapping infrastructure assets and supporting environmental missions. The implementation turns data collection into a game: participants move through assigned areas, collect virtual objects, record evidence and upload material for analysis. At a conceptual level, the system combines citizen participation, location tracking, smartphone sensing, AI-based asset analysis and municipal asset-management workflows. Data gathered by participants can be evaluated by AI and converted into condition assessments or maintenance intelligence. The expected impact is faster infrastructure inventories, lower survey costs, improved coverage of physical assets and more participatory maintenance of the urban environment. The model also creates a direct incentive for residents to contribute, because missions can include monetary rewards. Its value lies in combining human mobility, local knowledge and automated analysis to update infrastructure data at a scale that would otherwise require dedicated survey teams.

title: Tackling urban heat through data, paying attention to our citizens' perception
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Rising urban temperatures require local authorities to understand not only where heat is physically concentrated, but also how inhabitants experience discomfort, exposure and relief in everyday public spaces. Bordeaux Métropole developed this initiative to support climate-adaptation policies with indicators that combine environmental measurement and citizens’ perceived thermal comfort. Technical services need evidence on the conditions under which trees, fountains, urban design or surface materials reduce heat-island effects, while elected officials and planners also need to know whether residents actually feel improvements in liveability. The project began with a data-collection phase across eight cities in the metropolitan area, installing sensors in places with varied topographical and urban characteristics, including public squares, alleys, dense districts and wooded areas. The implementation combines environmental sensing, spatial analysis and typologies of urban spaces to compare temperature differences and evaluate the effects of local interventions. It also incorporates subjective perceptions, recognising that physical measurements alone cannot capture vulnerability, behavioural adaptation or citizen satisfaction. The expected impact is better targeted climate-adaptation planning, stronger evidence on which measures work, and greater legitimacy for public investment in cooling strategies. By connecting measurable heat conditions with lived experience, the initiative helps Bordeaux Métropole design responses that are both technically informed and socially meaningful, with possible replication across the wider metropolitan territory.

title: The Chatbot of the Austrian Federal Ministry of Justice
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Justice services can be difficult for citizens, companies and legal professionals to navigate because procedures, forms, court contacts and digital submissions are distributed across many legal-administrative pathways. The Austrian Ministry of Justice’s JustizOnline portal provides a digital access point for court services, case information, electronic submissions and justice-related documents, and the chatbot functions as an interactive assistant within this environment. The operational objective is to help users identify the correct procedure, form or information source before engaging with a court or public prosecutor’s office. The implementation uses a conversational interface to guide users through simple legal-administrative questions and direct them to relevant digital services on JustizOnline. At a conceptual level, the chatbot interprets user intent, links questions to justice-service content and provides orientation for self-service tasks. It supports transparency and accessibility by making the justice portal easier to use, particularly for users who are unfamiliar with legal terminology or administrative structures. The expected impact is quicker navigation, fewer misdirected enquiries, improved access to online justice services and better availability outside office hours. The tool remains informational and procedural: it does not provide binding legal advice or make decisions in judicial proceedings, but helps users reach the appropriate official channel.

title: AI for anonymisation of court decisions in Croatia
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Publishing court decisions is essential for transparency, legal certainty and consistency of case law, but it requires strong safeguards for personal data and confidential information. Croatia’s AI anonymisation initiative addresses this problem by preparing judicial decisions for online publication while protecting the identities of parties and other individuals mentioned in the text. The operational challenge is that courts produce large volumes of decisions, and manual anonymisation can be slow, inconsistent and resource-intensive. The project therefore uses AI-powered tools to support automatic pre-anonymisation, helping identify personal names, addresses and other sensitive elements before decisions are reviewed and published. At a conceptual level, the system combines document analysis, named-entity recognition, anonymisation rules, search functionality and publication workflows. Its purpose is not only to remove personal data, but also to preserve the legal meaning of the decision so that judges, lawyers, researchers, businesses and citizens can search and understand case law. The expected impact is greater transparency, faster publication of judgments, improved consistency in anonymisation and stronger public access to judicial information. The initiative also sits within a wider digital-justice agenda, including e-communication between courts, prosecutors, litigants and other justice stakeholders.

title: Judicial Anonymisation Tool
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Courts must publish judicial decisions to ensure transparency and legal certainty, while strictly complying with personal data protection requirements. Manual anonymisation of court rulings is time-consuming, resource-intensive and prone to inconsistencies, particularly given the volume and complexity of decisions issued by public courts. Stakeholders include judicial authorities, court clerks, data protection officers, legal professionals and citizens accessing published rulings. The objective of this use case is to streamline and standardise the anonymisation process prior to publication, ensuring legal compliance while preserving the substantive content and readability of decisions. The solution combines rule-based expert systems with natural language processing techniques to automatically detect and classify personal data elements such as names, addresses and identifiers within judicial texts. Predefined legal rules guide masking, redaction or pseudonymisation, and the tool integrates with court document management and publication platforms to support human validation workflows. Expected impacts include significant reductions in manual workload, faster publication cycles, improved consistency in anonymisation practices and strengthened compliance with data protection legislation, thereby enhancing trust in digital justice services.

title: AI to anonymise judicial courts in Denmark
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Judicial transparency depends on publishing court judgments in a form that is accessible to the public, while privacy law requires that parties and other individuals are protected from unnecessary identification. Denmark’s court judgment anonymisation project supports publication of decisions in Domsdatabasen, the Danish courts’ judgment database, by using machine learning to pseudonymise judgments before they are made public. The operational problem is that judgments contain names, pronouns, descriptions, contextual details and other linguistic elements that can reveal identity directly or indirectly. The implementation uses a machine-learning system to pre-screen documents and suggest text passages that may need anonymisation or pseudonymisation. At a conceptual level, the solution combines named-entity recognition, privacy-risk detection, text marking and human quality control. Each judgment is reviewed by human participants after the software has identified potentially sensitive content, creating a hybrid workflow in which AI accelerates the process but does not make publication decisions alone. The expected impact is faster preparation of judgments, more consistent protection of personal data, broader access to case law and better public understanding of judicial practice. The system is particularly important because anonymisation quality affects both privacy and the usefulness of judgments for legal analysis.

title: AI to plan meeting dates, times and locations for prosecutors
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Court and prosecution services depend on effective scheduling, because hearings, meetings and procedural events must bring together busy professionals, appropriate locations and case-specific priorities. Denmark’s meeting-planning AI use case focused on allocating meeting dates, times and locations for prosecutors according to profile and logistical constraints. The administrative problem is that meeting organisation can consume staff time, generate inefficient schedules and make it difficult to distinguish between urgent or high-priority meetings and less critical coordination tasks. The implementation concept uses profile-based allocation, prioritisation and scheduling logic to reduce manual planning effort. At a conceptual level, the system would combine information about prosecutors’ roles, calendars, availability, meeting importance, location constraints and procedural requirements. It could then propose suitable meeting slots and venues, helping administrative staff organise work more efficiently. The expected impact is reduced clerical burden, fewer scheduling conflicts, better use of court and prosecution resources, and more consistent prioritisation of important meetings. The use case is administrative rather than adjudicative: it does not assess legal merits or influence prosecutorial decisions, but supports the logistics around justice work. This distinction is important because automation in scheduling can improve efficiency while leaving professional judgement and procedural responsibility with human officials.

title: Automatic anonymisation and content description of documents containing personal data
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Judicial and administrative documents contain information that is valuable for transparency, research and decision-making, but wider electronic availability is constrained by the need to protect personal data. In Finland, the Ministry of Justice led the Anoppi project to address this challenge for court decisions and other official decisions issued by public authorities. Manual anonymisation can be slow, costly and inconsistent, particularly when large collections of documents must be prepared for publication, research use or legal-information services. The objective was therefore to provide tools that help authorities make documents more accessible while preserving privacy and legal safeguards. The implementation uses language-technology and semantic-computing methods to support two functions: automatic or semi-automatic anonymisation and pseudonymisation of personal data, and content description or annotation of legal documents. At a conceptual level, the system applies natural language processing, named-entity recognition, semantic annotation and document-structuring techniques to identify sensitive elements and generate metadata that improves searchability and reuse. The expected impact is faster document processing, broader access to legal information, improved support for research and more efficient publication workflows. By reducing the burden on courts and authorities, Anoppi strengthens digital justice services while maintaining data-protection requirements. It also supports the wider development of open, anonymised legal data for intelligent legal applications and the Semantic Finlex environment.

title: Robot process automation (RPA) in Finnish judicial system
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Judicial administrations handle many repetitive financial and register-based tasks that require accuracy but do not necessarily require complex human judgement. Finland’s Ministry of Justice applied robotic process automation in the enforcement-of-fines area to improve administrative efficiency and reduce manual handling. The operational problem concerns recurring enquiries, overpayment checks and payment allocation tasks linked to fines and other financial sanctions. The implementation uses software robots to carry out structured actions such as sending enquiries by email to banks and the Finnish Population Centre, reviewing data to identify erroneous overpayments and supporting the return or allocation of payments to citizens. At a conceptual level, RPA interacts with existing administrative systems by following predefined rules, retrieving information, comparing records, triggering messages and flagging cases that require human attention. The expected impact is faster processing, fewer manual errors, better handling of overpayments, more consistent financial administration and reduced staff time spent on routine clerical activity. The use case shows how justice-system digitalisation is not limited to courtrooms or judicial decisions: substantial value can come from automating back-office processes that support the enforcement and correction of financial sanctions.

title: DataJust
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Compensation for bodily injury is a legally sensitive field because victims, parties, lawyers and judges need reliable information on comparable cases while preserving the independence and discretion of judicial decision-making. In France, the Ministry of Justice launched DataJust to explore whether past civil and administrative liability decisions could support a more consistent understanding of compensation levels. The project aimed to carry out retrospective and prospective evaluations of public policies, develop an indicative framework for bodily-injury compensation, inform parties during amicable settlement discussions and provide documentation for judges ruling on damages claims. The implementation was authorised by Decree No. 2020-356 of 27 March 2020, following CNIL review, and involved automated processing of personal data from relevant judicial decisions. At a conceptual level, the system was intended to extract compensation-related information, structure legal and factual variables, conduct statistical analysis and generate decision-support or information outputs. The expected value was greater transparency for parties, better-informed settlement negotiations and more documented policy evaluation in civil liability. However, the initiative raised concerns because it involved sensitive personal and judicial data and could influence perceptions of standardisation in damages assessment. The project ultimately did not reach operational deployment, showing the difficulty of applying algorithmic tools in domains where individual harm, legal nuance and institutional legitimacy are closely intertwined.

title: Land register analysis component in the project Development of a federal database land register
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Commission for information technology in the judiciary
source_description: Digitising land-register information requires converting legally important legacy documents into structured, accurate and reusable data without weakening the certainty attached to property records. In Germany, this project component focused on automating the analysis of existing PDF files containing land-register information so that their contents could be fragmented, interpreted and assigned to appropriate database fields. The operational problem is that land-register material may exist in document formats that are difficult to search, integrate or process electronically, creating manual workload for justice administrations and limiting interoperability between systems. The objective was to support the development of a federal land-register database by transforming unstructured or semi-structured documents into structured records. The implementation is based on expert systems and rule-based techniques, reflecting the formalised structure of land-register documents and the need for deterministic interpretation rather than open-ended prediction. At a conceptual level, the tool analyses document content and layout, separates relevant sections, recognises values according to predefined rules and maps them into corresponding database fields. The expected impact is reduced manual transcription, improved consistency of digitised records, faster migration of legacy information and stronger support for electronic workflows involving courts, land-registry authorities, notaries and other authorised users. The case demonstrates that rule-based automation remains valuable where legal formats are stable and accuracy requirements are high.

title: Application of AI for early recognition of criminal offences that relate to hate crime
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Online hate crime creates a difficult enforcement problem because potentially criminal content circulates at high volume, changes quickly and may be embedded in ambiguous linguistic, social or political contexts. In Germany, the Federal Criminal Police Office participated in a research project examining how police organisations could use automated support to detect, prevent and prosecute hate crime while respecting legal, ethical and organisational constraints. The objective was not only to classify online statements, but to define the conditions under which such tools could be responsibly adopted by law-enforcement bodies. The implementation investigated technical approaches for classifying hate speech according to criminal-law categories, hate-speech phenomena and thematic content. At a conceptual level, the project combined natural language processing, supervised classification, domain-specific annotation, organisational analysis and legal-ethical assessment. This holistic design was intended to ensure that any prototype would be evaluated not only for technical accuracy, but also for its suitability within police workflows and fundamental-rights safeguards. The expected impact was faster identification of potentially criminal hate messages, better prioritisation of police review, and stronger evidence on how automated tools can support, rather than replace, human legal judgement. FRA records the output as reports and a technical prototype to be evaluated by police, while later project reporting indicates that a tool recognising criminal hate messages from social media posts was developed through KISTRA.

title: Future criminal court rooms
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Criminal proceedings increasingly rely on digital evidence, remote participation, audio-visual material and complex case records, while many courtrooms remain organised around paper-based or manually documented hearings. In North Rhine-Westphalia, the Central Cybercrime Department developed a pilot project aimed at modernising criminal courtrooms through technologies that could reduce the time and effort required to record, review and present proceedings. The objective was to create a courtroom environment in which hearings could be videotaped, speech could be converted into written transcripts, and participants could access both the transcription and embedded audio material. The implementation concept combined audio recording, video recording, speech-to-text recognition and digital document production inside the courtroom workflow. A further element under consideration was the 3D projection of crime scenes, which could support the presentation of spatially complex evidence in cybercrime or other criminal cases. At a conceptual level, the system would connect hearing capture, automated transcription, evidentiary presentation and case-file integration, allowing judges, prosecutors, lawyers and other authorised participants to work with richer digital records. The expected impact was reduced administrative effort, faster review of hearings, more accurate documentation and broader modernisation of criminal justice infrastructure. The available European Commission study records the project as a pilot within the wider mapping of innovative technologies in justice, but does not confirm full operational roll-out.

title: Speech recognition and transcription
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Court proceedings generate spoken information that must be transformed into written minutes, decisions and procedural records, but manual transcription can be time-consuming and places a heavy burden on clerical staff. Hungary’s National Office for the Judiciary examined the use of speech-recognition and transcription software in courts to accelerate the production of written judicial documents. The operational challenge is that hearings and procedural events contain substantial spoken content, and delays in putting decisions or minutes into writing can affect court efficiency. The implementation applies automatic speech recognition to convert audio from proceedings into text, creating a draft transcript or written basis for further review. At a conceptual level, the system combines audio capture, speech-to-text processing, language modelling, transcription correction and integration into court workflows. It is intended to assist court staff rather than replace the official validation of minutes or decisions. The expected impact is reduced transcription time, better compliance with procedural deadlines, more efficient use of clerical capacity and faster availability of written records. For courts, the quality of such tools depends heavily on legal vocabulary, acoustic conditions, speaker variation and the ability to correct outputs reliably. The use case therefore illustrates both the potential and the implementation challenges of applying speech technology to judicial administration.

title: Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Road-policing and law-enforcement operations often require rapid identification of vehicles without manual reading or recording of registration plates. Ireland’s Automatic Number Plate Recognition use case concerns deployment of ANPR technology by justice and policing authorities to support traffic and law-enforcement operations. The operational problem is that officers may need to identify vehicles of interest, verify registration information or process large numbers of passing vehicles quickly and accurately. The implementation uses optical character recognition, later capable of being augmented by artificial-intelligence techniques, to read and record vehicle registration plates automatically from camera feeds. At a conceptual level, the system captures an image of a vehicle plate, converts it into text, compares it with relevant records or alert lists, and produces information for policing or administrative follow-up. The expected impact is faster identification of vehicles, more efficient enforcement, reduced manual input, and stronger operational capacity in roads policing. The technology also raises privacy and governance questions because vehicle movements can reveal sensitive information about individuals’ behaviour. For that reason, legal authorisation, retention rules, access controls and oversight are important elements of responsible deployment. The tool should be understood as an investigative and traffic-management support capability rather than an autonomous sanctioning system.

title: Evaluate the potential of facial matching technologies as an aid to the intelligence gathering process
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Law-enforcement and justice authorities face recurring challenges in identifying persons of interest, comparing image material and supporting intelligence processes, but facial-matching technologies raise significant questions about accuracy, proportionality, bias and fundamental rights. In Ireland, the Department of Justice and Equality developed a 2019 project to evaluate whether facial matching could assist intelligence gathering as part of a broader European mapping of innovative technologies in justice. The objective was exploratory: to assess potential use rather than to present a fully deployed policing system. The implementation concerned facial-matching technologies, which compare facial images to identify possible similarities or candidate matches. At a conceptual level, such a tool would require image inputs, biometric feature extraction, similarity scoring, human review and governance controls to ensure that any result remains investigative support rather than automatic identification or evidentiary determination. The expected value would be faster screening of image material, better support for intelligence workflows and improved prioritisation where large visual datasets are involved. However, the use case also sits in a high-risk area, because biometric matching in justice and policing contexts requires a clear legal basis, strict necessity and proportionality assessment, data-protection safeguards and transparency. The European Commission study records the Irish project as an evaluation initiative, and I found no evidence that it progressed to full operational deployment.

title: Predictive justice - a database to provide predictable guidelines and timing in particular areas
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Judicial users, lawyers and citizens often need to understand how similar cases have been decided and how long proceedings may take, especially in areas where case-law orientation can affect litigation strategy and settlement decisions. In Brescia, the Court of Appeal developed a predictive justice initiative to organise selected decisions from the Brescia Court of Appeal and Ordinary Court into a navigable database. The objective was to provide predictable guidelines, relevant precedents and procedural orientation in particular legal areas, while supporting legal professionals rather than automating judicial decisions. The implementation uses a structured jurisprudence database supported by natural language processing and rule-based or expert-system logic. At a conceptual level, users choose a legal area and follow a guided path that progressively identifies the judicial situation most similar to their own issue, using essential linguistic and graphical presentation to make the case-law material easier to consult. The platform focuses on legal similarity, orientation and knowledge access rather than on generating binding outcomes. The expected impact is improved transparency of local case-law, faster retrieval of relevant decisions, better preparation by lawyers and parties, and greater consistency in understanding judicial tendencies. Current online material shows that the Brescia predictive justice platform remains publicly accessible and presents selected decisions grouped by thematic areas, notably labour and business law.

title: ITA.CA (Italian Case-Law On Private Antitrust Enforcement )
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Private antitrust enforcement depends on access to specialised case law, but judgments in this field can be difficult to locate, compare and analyse across courts. ITA.CA was developed to collect and systematise Italian case law on private enforcement of competition law, initially around the Milan courts and later with broader contributions. The operational problem is that practitioners, judges, scholars and public stakeholders need a coherent view of decisions relating to damages actions, competition infringements and related civil litigation. The implementation uses a structured online database hosted by the Eurojus scientific journal, collecting judgments and organising them so that users can search and analyse relevant material. At a conceptual level, the system combines legal information retrieval, classification, expert curation and rule-based structuring of case-law content. It is not an autonomous legal decision-maker; rather, it supports legal knowledge management by making decisions easier to find and compare. The expected impact is improved legal transparency, better access to antitrust jurisprudence, stronger doctrinal analysis and more consistent understanding of private enforcement across Italy. The case is relevant to digital justice because curated and searchable databases are a foundation for more advanced legal analytics, even when the underlying technology is primarily rule-based or expert-system oriented.

title: Voice recognition in court administration
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Court and prosecution services generate large volumes of spoken material, including hearings, interviews, procedural acts and internal administrative communication. Latvia’s voice-recognition use case for the Prosecutor’s Office applied AI-based speech technology to support court-administration or prosecution-office workflows. The operational problem is that transcription and document preparation can be labour-intensive, especially where staff must convert spoken material into structured written records. The implementation uses voice-recognition technology to transform speech into text, reducing the need for purely manual typing and helping legal-administrative staff prepare records more efficiently. At a conceptual level, the tool combines audio capture, automatic speech recognition, language processing and human correction or validation. Its expected impact is faster production of written records, reduced clerical burden, more efficient use of prosecution staff and better standardisation of documentation. In justice settings, such systems must handle legal vocabulary, speaker variation, Latvian-language recognition requirements and confidentiality constraints. Human review remains essential, because transcript errors can have procedural consequences. The use case should therefore be understood as an administrative support tool: it can improve efficiency in preparing and managing documents, but it does not replace prosecutorial judgement or court decision-making.

title: Just - virtual assistant of the State Unitary Computerized Land Book
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Land-register services can be difficult for citizens and professionals to navigate because users must understand property identifiers, cadastral information, service categories and procedural steps. Latvia’s Court Administration introduced the virtual assistant Justs into the Land Register portal to help users find their way around the services of the State Unified Computerised Land Book. The objective was to provide a conversational guidance layer for people seeking land-register information or digital services. The implementation uses a virtual assistant on the land-register portal, allowing users to ask questions or obtain orientation without relying only on static navigation menus. At a conceptual level, the assistant maps user questions to service information, helps identify relevant procedures and supports navigation through the portal. Its expected impact is easier access to property-information services, fewer routine support enquiries, better digital self-service and improved user experience for citizens, businesses and legal professionals. Because land-register data are legally significant, the assistant’s role is informational: it supports navigation and service access, while formal registry records, rights and procedural acts remain governed by official systems and staff. The case is a useful example of conversational support in a specialised justice-administration domain where users may not know the correct terminology or route to obtain information.

title: Automatic Ship Classification from Optical Aerial Images with Convolutional Neural Networks
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Maritime surveillance, coastal monitoring and aerial reconnaissance generate large volumes of visible-spectrum imagery in which ships or small unidentified floating objects may be difficult to identify quickly and consistently. Traditional approaches to ship detection have often relied on manually designed image-processing features, followed by conventional supervised classifiers, which can be sensitive to changing image conditions and may not capture complex visual patterns. Researchers at the University of Alicante addressed this challenge by developing a method to determine whether an optical aerial image contains a ship. The implementation used a convolutional neural network architecture adapted to visible-spectrum aerial imagery. At a conceptual level, the model extracted neural visual codes from images and combined them with a k-nearest neighbour method to improve classification performance. This approach moved feature extraction away from manually engineered descriptors and towards representations learned from image data. The expected impact is faster and more accurate screening of aerial image collections, reduced manual inspection effort and stronger support for maritime monitoring applications such as traffic surveillance, search and rescue, environmental control or security tasks. The work is research-oriented, but it demonstrates how deep-learning methods can improve remote-sensing image interpretation when the operational question is binary and clearly framed: whether a ship is present or absent in the observed scene.

title: LoRaWAN - The IoT network for Zurich
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: EWZ - Service Division of the Department of Public Utilities and Transport of the City of Zurich
source_description: Chronic-disease care requires continuity across hospitals, community services, clinicians, patients and caregivers, especially where repeated outpatient visits or avoidable hospitalisations can reduce quality of life and increase pressure on health systems. COReHealth was developed in Puglia as a regional telemedicine operations centre for chronic diseases and clinical networks, with a particular role in turning the Apulian Oncological Network into a digitally enabled care ecosystem. The operational problem is that patients with chronic conditions often need monitoring, therapeutic adherence support, clinical follow-up and timely intervention without necessarily being physically present in hospital. The implementation provides a telemedicine platform through which patients can be cared for from home, send measurements, monitor their therapeutic plan, receive support for self-management and access remote-care services. At a conceptual level, the system connects patients, clinical networks and regional operational coordination through digital tools, enabling data collection, monitoring, communication and escalation where intervention is needed. The expected impact is reduced hospitalisation, fewer outpatient visits, better continuity of care, improved patient comfort and more proactive disease management. COReHealth is also significant because it positions telemedicine as a regional operating model rather than a single disease-specific application, creating infrastructure that can support chronic-care pathways and clinical networks across multiple territories.

title: Sen4Weeds: automatic detection in-field weeds
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Farmers need timely and reliable information on weed pressure, because uncontrolled weeds reduce yields, increase inspection workload and often lead to broad herbicide use even when infestation is spatially uneven. Sen4Weeds was developed within AI4Copernicus to create an automated system for detecting and mapping weed patches at large scale, using Earth-observation data rather than relying only on field scouting. The objective is to support earlier, more targeted interventions that improve productivity while reducing environmental impact and input costs. The implementation combines high-resolution and super-resolved Sentinel-2 imagery, automated field delineation, weed classification and AI-based spectral unmixing of multi-spectral satellite data. At a conceptual level, the system identifies field boundaries, enhances satellite-image detail, detects spectral patterns associated with weeds and produces maps showing where weed pressure is likely to be concentrated. These outputs can then help farmers, advisers or agri-tech platforms decide where treatment is needed. The expected impact is more efficient crop monitoring, reduced manual inspection, lower herbicide use and improved scalability across different crops, weed species and regions. By linking Copernicus data with machine-learning models, Sen4Weeds demonstrates how satellite-based precision agriculture can move from general vegetation monitoring towards actionable, within-field weed-management intelligence.

title: Scaviho: scalable vegetation index and harvesting forecaster
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Precision agriculture already uses NDVI widely to monitor crop condition, but intermediate NDVI values during the growth stage can be difficult for farmers to interpret despite containing important information on crop development. In Spain, Scaviho was developed to make vegetation-index information more actionable for vineyards and other agricultural contexts, helping users assess growth evolution, anticipate hidden problems and forecast harvesting dates. The operational problem is not the absence of satellite data, but the difficulty of translating seasonal vegetation signals into practical decisions for field management and harvest planning. The implementation uses historical Sentinel-2 NDVI data, crop phenological information and artificial-intelligence methods to broaden the interpretation of intermediate vegetation-index values. At a conceptual level, the solution builds a scale that links NDVI patterns to crop-growth stages and uses past satellite observations to identify deviations or signals relevant to expected harvest timing. The project involves ENCORE LAB and Castillo de Maetierra, combining digital-agriculture capabilities with vineyard operational experience. The expected impact is better crop monitoring, earlier detection of hidden stress, improved harvest planning and more precise use of remote-sensing information in everyday farm decisions. AI4Copernicus and the AI-on-demand platform describe Scaviho as an Open Call success story whose results have been developed in a consortium already using satellite images in daily agricultural operations.

title: Planning for flexible manufacturing with robots
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Heavy-vehicle axle production involves many machining stages, machine constraints, stock dependencies and planning decisions that are difficult to automate when they rely heavily on human expertise. In this Swedish use case, the challenge is to support flexible manufacturing of front axles by transforming expert production knowledge into a form that automated planning and scheduling systems can use. Human planners understand which operations are possible, which machines can perform them, how available stock affects production routes and how orders should be sequenced, but this knowledge is often implicit and hard to scale. The implementation combines planning and scheduling techniques to generate machining plans from three main inputs: expert knowledge extracted from human planners, incoming order requirements and available stock. At a conceptual level, the system formalises production rules, links them to machine capabilities and uses scheduling-based reasoning to identify feasible and efficient machining sequences. This allows planning decisions to be produced more systematically while remaining grounded in operational know-how. The expected impact is faster production planning, better use of machinery, reduced dependence on individual planners and improved ability to respond to changing orders or stock availability. By combining knowledge representation with automated scheduling, the use case demonstrates how industrial planning systems can support flexible, small-batch or variable manufacturing without requiring a complete redesign of production infrastructure. (aiod.eu

title: Planning and execution for a mobile indoor robot
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence
source_description: Indoor mobile manipulation requires a robot to act in environments where object positions, task conditions and execution outcomes may not be fully known in advance. This German use case explores how task planning and execution can control a mobile robot performing manipulation tasks in such settings. The practical challenge is that a robot may need to find boxes or other objects placed on tables, move through the environment, decide which actions to perform and adapt when observations differ from the initial model. The implementation combines task-planning methods with execution control on a mobile robotic platform. In the demonstration scenario, the robot starts without knowing where objects are located and must plan, perceive, move, manipulate and update its knowledge as the task progresses. At a conceptual level, symbolic planning represents goals, actions and preconditions, while execution modules dispatch actions to the robot, monitor results and trigger replanning if expected conditions fail. This creates a loop between high-level reasoning and low-level robotic control. The expected impact is more robust service robotics, improved ability to operate in uncertain indoor environments and a clearer path from planning research to physical deployment. The use case is valuable because it demonstrates not only plan generation, but also the operational challenge of making plans executable on real robots. (research.aiodp.eu

title: AI planning for integrated urban traffic control
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Connected and autonomous vehicles create new possibilities for traffic management because they can exchange information with infrastructure rather than only reacting independently to road conditions. In Kirklees and related research settings, this use case examines how urban traffic control could combine conventional signal management with route guidance for connected vehicles. The operational problem is that urban networks experience congestion, emissions, delays and safety risks, while traffic-control systems often act through limited instruments such as traffic-light timing. Vehicle-to-infrastructure communication adds a further control channel: vehicles can provide information about traffic conditions and receive guidance about preferable routes. The implementation uses planning techniques to coordinate traffic-light decisions and connected-vehicle routing so that the two mechanisms work together rather than separately. At a conceptual level, the system represents the traffic network, vehicle movements, signal states and possible interventions, then generates control strategies able to respond to expected or unusual conditions. The expected impact is reduced congestion, lower emissions, time savings, improved accident prevention and more integrated management of urban mobility. Research linked to this area shows that model-based planning can address both normal patterns and unexpected traffic conditions in real time, making it relevant for future traffic-control systems as connected vehicles become more common. (aiod.eu
