title: CSAI: Cyber Security Artificial Intelligence
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Cybersecurity teams operate in environments where attacks evolve quickly, alerts are numerous and purely rule-based systems may struggle to distinguish meaningful threats from routine activity. CSAI responds to this challenge by exploring how more intelligent models and techniques can support cybersecurity technology beyond automated analytics alone. The project, funded by Flanders’ innovation and entrepreneurship agency, brings research and industry actors together to investigate methods that can improve detection, reasoning and response across cybersecurity contexts, from devices and networks to compliance. The implementation combines symbolic and sub-symbolic approaches, using domain-specific cybersecurity knowledge, mechanisms to acquire new knowledge and techniques that can apply that knowledge to operational tasks. At a conceptual level, CSAI seeks to connect machine-learning models, knowledge representation, threat intelligence and security workflows so that systems can reason more effectively about risks and incidents. The expected impact is stronger cyber-threat detection, more robust decision support for analysts, and improved ability to apply research advances in practical security products and services. By focusing on hybrid intelligence rather than only statistical detection, the project aims to make cybersecurity tools more explainable, adaptable and aligned with professional expertise. Its public value lies in strengthening digital resilience in a domain where both technical sophistication and trustworthiness are essential.

title: EV Charging Optimiser
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The rapid electrification of vehicle fleets creates a practical energy-management problem: charging many vehicles at the same time can overload local capacity, increase costs and make operations difficult to coordinate, especially in unpredictable real environments. VUB and Energis developed the EV Charging Optimiser to test how an entire fleet of electric vehicles could be charged in a coordinated and controlled way, both in laboratory settings and in operational contexts. The objective is to move beyond static charging schedules and create a controller that remains robust when vehicles arrive late, leave early, require different charging levels or face changing electricity and infrastructure constraints. The implementation applies reinforcement learning to charging scheduling, allowing the system to learn policies that balance fleet requirements, grid constraints and operational uncertainty. At a conceptual level, the controller observes charging demand, vehicle availability, battery states and environmental constraints, then selects charging actions that improve long-term outcomes rather than optimising only the immediate moment. The expected impact is more efficient fleet charging, lower peak demand, improved use of charging infrastructure and better integration of electric mobility into energy systems. By testing the approach in real environments, the project emphasises robustness and practical viability, which are critical for fleet operators that cannot rely on perfectly predictable charging behaviour.

title: Driving collective data governance through smart engagement platforms (COLLIBRA)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Data governance often remains distant from the everyday contexts in which business users create, interpret and reuse data, leading to weak adoption, unclear ownership and limited trust in datasets. This project sought to bring governance closer to actual workplaces by embedding support into the systems of engagement where decisions are already discussed, such as boardrooms, design workshops, Confluence, Slack and other collaboration tools. The objective was to help users make better low-level decisions when interacting with data, while generating richer contextual information on how datasets are used. The implementation developed a platform that uses artificial intelligence to learn bottom-up data-usage context and provide reliable, machine-accurate recommendations for the next best action inside core business applications. At a conceptual level, the system combines data-governance metadata, engagement traces, workflow context, recommendation logic and integration with collaboration environments. This allows governance guidance to appear at the point of use rather than as a separate administrative obligation. The expected impact is better data stewardship, stronger trust in datasets, more efficient governance decisions and more time for users to focus on substantive business problems. The project also supports dataset promotion by helping users build credibility around data generated through collaborative engagements, making governance more participatory and embedded in practice.

title: Competence based matching - a success story from Flanders to Malta
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Flemish Employment and Vocational Training Service (VDAB)
source_description: Public employment services often struggle to match jobseekers and vacancies accurately due to vague job descriptions and inconsistent skill profiling. This leads to inefficient labour market matching and prolonged unemployment. This use case involves the Flemish employment service (VDAB), employers, jobseekers, and later the Maltese Public Employment Service, with the objective of improving match quality and labour market efficiency. The system is implemented through structured competency frameworks that require employers to define vacancies in detailed, standardised skill terms, while jobseekers build equally comprehensive competency profiles. Matching algorithms compare these profiles to generate higher-quality matches based on skills rather than job titles alone. The concept was successfully transferred from Flanders to Malta in 2016, demonstrating cross-border applicability. The solution improves placement accuracy, reduces mismatch, and shortens recruitment times. It supports mobility of best practices across Europe and delivers measurable value through more effective employment services and better labour market outcomes.

title: Managing vacancies - Recommender: the amazon of the labour market
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Flemish Employment and Vocational Training Service (VDAB)
source_description: Public employment services face challenges in efficiently matching jobseekers with suitable vacancies, particularly as labour markets become more dynamic and digitally mediated. Traditional keyword-based search functions often fail to capture skills proximity, transferable competences and evolving job profiles. Stakeholders include jobseekers, employers and public employment agencies. The objective is to enhance matching quality and labour market efficiency through personalised vacancy recommendations. The system leverages big data analytics to process vacancy descriptions, candidate profiles and historical placement data. Collaborative filtering, content-based recommendation algorithms and skills ontology mapping are used to infer relevance scores and suggest vacancies aligned with a jobseeker’s competences and preferences. Integration with the public vacancy platform enables real-time recommendations upon user login, supported by feedback loops to continuously refine model accuracy. Expected benefits include improved placement rates, reduced job search duration, better utilisation of transferable skills and enhanced user experience comparable to leading e-commerce recommendation systems.

title: A DIGITAL BUILDING PERMIT SYSTEM FOR THE SMART CITY in Wien
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: City of Wien - Municipal Directorate of Strategic ICT
source_description: Building-permit procedures are often slow, document-heavy and difficult for applicants and administrations to navigate, especially in a growing city that receives high volumes of construction applications. Vienna’s BRISE project rethinks this process by replacing paper-based, two-dimensional submissions with a more integrated digital workflow for construction approvals. The City of Vienna’s objective is to make permit procedures faster, more transparent and less costly, while creating a model that can later be transferred to other fields of public administration. The implementation combines Building Information Modelling, artificial intelligence, augmented reality and robotic process automation. Instead of submitting 2D plans, applicants use digital 3D building models that can be checked against relevant building regulations. At a conceptual level, the system connects BIM data, automated rule checking, administrative workflows, AR-supported inspection and digital collaboration between applicants, experts and public officials. This creates an end-to-end basis for managing a construction project from planning and submission to site inspection and acceptance of the completed structure. The expected impact is faster processing, improved project quality, greater transparency and reduced administrative effort. OECD OPSI reports 50% time savings, while Vienna’s project material notes approximately €4.8 million in EU Urban Innovative Actions funding and implementation by March 2023.

title: Facebook chatbot connected to NoiPA services
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Direzione dei Sistemi Informativi e dell'Innovazione of the Minitry of the Economics and Finances
context: Transfers of a general character between different levels of government.
source_description: NoiPA manages payroll and administrative services for a large number of Italian public employees, generating frequent enquiries related to payslips, allowances, and administrative procedures. Traditional support channels faced congestion and delays. This use case involves the Ministry of Economy and Finance, public employees, and service administrators, with the objective of improving communication and assistance. The solution is implemented as a chatbot integrated into Facebook Messenger, providing automated responses to frequently asked questions about NoiPA services. The chatbot draws from official knowledge bases and guides users through common issues in a conversational format. It operates alongside existing support channels, offering immediate assistance through a widely used social platform. The service improves accessibility, reduces call centre workload, and speeds up resolution of simple enquiries. It enhances user satisfaction and demonstrates effective use of social messaging channels for public sector service delivery.

title: Stadio di Domiziano - visita con realtà aumentata
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Sovrintendenza ai Beni Culturali di Roma Capitale
source_description: Archaeological sites can be difficult for visitors to interpret when only partial remains are visible and the original urban context has disappeared beneath modern layers of the city. The Domiziano Virtual Experience uses virtual and augmented reality to help visitors understand the ancient Stadium of Domitian beneath Piazza Navona in Rome. The operational objective is to make the site’s historical significance more accessible by reconstructing the stadium’s original appearance, spatial organisation and role in Roman public life. The implementation provides an immersive digital reconstruction that can show the ancient monument as it may have appeared, supporting interpretation through visualisation rather than text panels alone. At a conceptual level, XR technology overlays or recreates missing architectural elements, allowing users to move from fragmentary remains to a fuller understanding of the original structure and its urban setting. The expected impact is improved heritage interpretation, broader educational outreach, greater accessibility for users who struggle to imagine lost spaces and stronger public engagement with protected archaeological assets. The use case demonstrates how immersive technologies can support cultural management by making conservation-compatible interpretation possible without physically reconstructing the monument.

title: Duomo di Milano 4.0
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Historic monuments often contain stories, materials and construction processes that visitors cannot easily access through a normal tour, especially when key places such as quarries or technical workspaces are physically distant or restricted. Duomo di Milano 4.0 uses virtual reality and augmented reality to reveal the cathedral’s history, material origins and construction techniques. The programme includes a VR journey to the Candoglia Quarry, where the marble used for the cathedral was extracted, and AR-guided experiences that use smart glasses to enrich the visitor route with reconstructions, images and videos. At a conceptual level, the technology creates an immersive interpretative layer: visitors can visualise quarry environments, historical stages and sculptural processes that would otherwise remain abstract. The expected impact is deeper public understanding of the cathedral’s long construction history, more inclusive and engaging heritage education, and a stronger connection between the monument, its material supply chain and the craftsmanship behind it. The use case is particularly relevant because it applies XR to a major cultural site not only for spectacle, but also to explain geological origin, artistic labour, conservation and historical continuity. It supports cultural-management objectives around accessibility, learning and innovation in heritage interpretation.

title: Chatbot Duomo di Milano official website
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Visitors planning a visit to a major cultural and religious monument often need fast answers about tickets, opening hours, guided tours, accessibility, services and institutional information. The Duomo di Milano website chatbot supports this need by providing a conversational assistance layer within the official digital environment of the Veneranda Fabbrica del Duomo. The operational problem is that users may arrive with very different needs: some are tourists planning a route through the Cathedral, terraces and museum, while others are researchers, worshippers or users looking for information about the institution, events or visitor rules. The implementation uses an integrated chatbot interface to help users navigate site content and find practical information more quickly than by browsing all pages manually. At a conceptual level, the assistant interprets the user’s question, maps it to available visitor-service content and directs the user towards the relevant page, ticketing option or information area. The expected impact is improved digital visitor experience, reduced friction in planning a visit, fewer repetitive enquiries for staff and better online accessibility of the Duomo’s cultural and administrative information. The use case is part of a broader digital-service ecosystem around the cathedral, which also includes official apps, video guides and immersive visitor experiences.

title: Colosseum Archeologic Park - Domus Area Virtual Experience
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Ministry of Culture (MiBACT) - Parco Archeologico del Colosseo
source_description: Archaeological remains can be difficult for visitors to interpret when the surviving structures only partially convey the scale, decoration and spatial logic of the original monument. The Domus Aurea Virtual Experience addresses this challenge by using immersive virtual-reality technology to reconstruct Nero’s palace and help visitors understand its architectural and decorative richness. The operational objective is to translate complex archaeological knowledge into an accessible visitor experience within a fragile heritage environment. The implementation combines an educational guided tour with VR content that reconstructs lost spaces, decorations and spatial relationships that are no longer visible in the physical remains. At a conceptual level, the system overlays scholarly interpretation onto the site through immersive visualisation, helping users move between the surviving archaeological fabric and a scientifically informed reconstruction of the original palace. The expected impact is stronger public understanding of the Domus Aurea, better interpretation of fragmentary remains, increased cultural participation and more sustainable heritage presentation because digital reconstruction can communicate lost elements without physical rebuilding. The use case is particularly relevant for conservation because it enhances visitor experience while respecting the vulnerability of the archaeological site. It demonstrates how XR can support both education and preservation in high-value cultural assets.

title: Colosseum Archeological Park - "Speak with Nerone"" chatbot"
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Ministry of Culture (MiBACT) - Parco Archeologico del Colosseo
source_description: Cultural institutions increasingly need digital tools that help visitors access historical interpretation and practical information in a more engaging format than static web pages. The “Speak with Nerone” chatbot was introduced by the Colosseum Archaeological Park as an AI-based conversational assistant embodied as Emperor Nero. The operational objective is to help users obtain information about opening hours, monuments and the park’s historical context while also creating a more memorable and playful interaction with cultural heritage. The implementation uses chatbot technology to simulate dialogue with Nero, enabling users to ask questions and receive answers through a conversational interface. At a conceptual level, the tool combines visitor assistance, public-history storytelling and automated information retrieval: a historical figure becomes the interface through which users navigate content about the Colosseum Archaeological Park and related sites. The expected impact is improved online engagement, better access to practical visitor information, stronger appeal for younger audiences and broader cultural literacy around the park’s monuments. The system does not replace curatorial or guide-led interpretation; rather, it provides an additional digital channel that makes introductory information more accessible and interactive. Its value lies in combining service support with historical characterisation, turning an administrative chatbot into a cultural-education tool.

title: Virtual tour of the Acropolisin Athens
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens (NKUoA)
source_description: Access to major archaeological sites is often limited by distance, mobility, cost, crowding or conservation constraints, while educational users may need detailed visual material that goes beyond conventional photographs. The Acropolis Virtual Tour provides an immersive digital environment through which users can explore the Acropolis and its principal monuments, including the Parthenon, Propylaia, Erechtheion and Temple of Athena Nike. The operational objective is to widen access to one of Greece’s most important cultural-heritage sites and support learning through interactive 360-degree exploration. The implementation uses panoramic high-resolution imagery, virtual navigation and descriptive historical content linked to selected monuments and points of interest. At a conceptual level, the system converts the archaeological site into a structured digital experience: users can move between viewpoints, examine architectural details and read contextual information that explains the significance of the monuments. The expected impact is broader public access, stronger educational use, better support for users unable to visit physically and enhanced understanding of the Acropolis’ historical and architectural value. The use case is important because it demonstrates how digital heritage platforms can complement physical visitation, providing a conservation-friendly channel for interpretation and remote learning.

title: EKOME Greece - chatbot
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: National Centre of Audiovisual Media and Communication
source_description: Audiovisual-sector organisations must guide producers, educators, researchers and citizens through incentives, administrative procedures, digital-media initiatives and institutional services. The EKOME chatbot was designed as a digital assistant on the website of Greece’s National Centre of Audiovisual Media and Communication, supporting users seeking immediate guidance on the organisation’s activities. The operational problem is that audiovisual production incentives, education programmes, archive initiatives and administrative processes can be difficult to navigate for users with different levels of expertise. The implementation provides a conversational interface that can answer general enquiries and direct users to relevant information areas. At a conceptual level, the chatbot recognises user intent, retrieves institutional service information and presents concise responses or pathways through the website. The expected impact is faster access to public information, reduced pressure on staff for repetitive enquiries, improved service accessibility and better user experience for the audiovisual sector. The case fits within a broader public-service trend in which specialised agencies add automated assistants to help users navigate complex policy and funding environments. It also reflects the role of digital service design in creative-industry support, where efficient access to information can affect production planning and participation in public programmes.

title: ACCUDIRE - export tracking based on blockchain
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Agenzia delle dogane e dei Monopoli (ADM)
task: Tracking of goods and assets along the supply chain
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: International freight documentation remains heavily dependent on paper, repeated signatures and fragmented exchanges between exporters, freight forwarders, customs authorities, ports and importers. ACCUDIRE addresses this problem by digitising logistics documentation and creating trusted interoperability between public and private actors in export processes. The July 2021 pilot concerned a shipment from Italy to Turkey and involved Benetton Group, the Port of Trieste, the Italian Customs and Monopolies Agency, a global freight forwarder and a Turkish importing company. The implementation used the ACCUDIRE platform to create an electronic CMR consignment note, verify the identities of participants through two-factor authentication, geolocate signatures and store relevant information on a permissioned Hyperledger Fabric blockchain. The platform interoperated with AIDA, the Italian Customs Agency’s system, and transmitted pre-arrival goods information to the Port Community System. At a conceptual level, the solution combines blockchain-based immutability, digital identity, e-signature, customs integration and logistics-document workflows. The expected impact is lower paperwork, faster export procedures, better traceability, stronger anti-counterfeiting protection and improved coordination across the supply chain. Subsequent material shows that ACCUDIRE’s ExAc platform continues to support e-CMR and supply-chain document digitalisation, including further pilots connected to eFTI and customs interoperability.

title: Giotto OnChain blockchain-based Notarisation Service for digital assets
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Public bodies, companies and organisations increasingly need to prove the integrity, authorship and existence of digital documents, especially where fraud, counterfeiting or later disputes could undermine trust. Giotto OnChain is a blockchain-based notarisation service developed by Almaviva to certify digital assets such as documents, letterheads, presentations and press releases. The operational problem is that digital content can be copied, altered or misrepresented, making it useful to create an independent proof that a given asset existed at a certain time and has not been changed. The implementation generates a digital fingerprint of the asset and records notarisation evidence on a public blockchain, while also supporting ownership certification through electronic signature. At a conceptual level, the service does not store the full document on-chain; instead, it anchors cryptographic evidence that can later be used to verify integrity and authenticity. The expected impact is stronger protection against fraudulent use, clearer evidentiary value for documents, easier verification by third parties and a reusable trust layer for digital communications. The service is also available in SaaS mode, making it suitable for organisations that need blockchain-based certification without building distributed-ledger infrastructure themselves.

title: Gibraltar Regulatory Agencies Trial Anti-money Laundering Platform for Crypto Asset Investigations
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Regulators and law-enforcement agencies face growing difficulty tracing illicit finance when crypto assets move quickly across wallets, exchanges and decentralised services. Gibraltar entered into an agreement with Coinfirm to trial an AML risk-management platform for crypto and blockchain assets, aiming to strengthen its ability to investigate money laundering and terrorist-financing risks in digital-asset markets. The implementation uses blockchain-native analytics capable of monitoring high-risk transactions, tracing misappropriated funds and visualising transaction pathways. At a conceptual level, the platform analyses source and destination of funds, wallet ownership indicators, transaction fingerprints, clustering patterns and e-discovery data to support investigative workflows. This allows regulators and enforcement agencies to move beyond isolated wallet checks towards network-based analysis of suspicious activity. The expected impact is improved detection of high-risk crypto transactions, better investigative intelligence, stronger supervisory capacity and support for Gibraltar’s positioning as a regulated digital-asset jurisdiction. Public statements described the 2021 initiative as the first use of such technology to support Gibraltar’s anti-money-laundering work. Because the source frames the initiative as a trial, its main value is best understood as controlled evaluation of RegTech capabilities rather than confirmed permanent deployment across all Gibraltar agencies.

title: Green Blockchain
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
task: Tracking of goods and assets along the supply chain
source_description: Climate-data trust is becoming increasingly important as cities, laboratories and environmental actors rely on low-cost sensors to monitor CO₂ concentrations and other indicators. Green Blockchain addresses this issue by notarising the processing of climatic data so that the public and third parties can verify that treatment steps have not been altered. The use case involves sensors deployed in urban areas, which send raw climatic data to a laboratory responsible for processing it into time series of CO₂ concentrations. The implementation uses blockchain anchoring rather than storing all raw data on-chain: hashes of treated data or processing outputs are written to smart contracts, allowing other laboratories or auditors to reproduce the treatment process and compare results with the recorded hashes. At a conceptual level, the system combines urban sensing, climate-data processing, web dashboards and low-energy blockchain approaches such as proof-of-stake or Byzantine fault-tolerant mechanisms. The expected impact is greater public trust in environmental data, stronger auditability between laboratories, and new trusted services for institutional or industrial environmental actors without requiring a central control body. Its participation in the European Blockchain Sandbox indicates regulatory and technical interest in the model. The use case remains particularly relevant because it connects blockchain not to speculative assets, but to data integrity and climate-monitoring accountability.

title: EBSI-VECTOR - EBSI enabled VErifiable Credentials & Trusted Organisations Registries - Education
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Cross-border education and employment processes still require people and institutions to verify diplomas, qualifications and organisational status through complex, document-heavy procedures. EBSI-VECTOR addresses this problem by applying the European Blockchain Services Infrastructure to verifiable credentials and trusted registries, with education as a major use case. The objective is to simplify how students, universities, employers and public authorities issue, hold, share and verify educational credentials across Europe. The implementation builds on the EBSI diploma use-case specifications and the wider EBSI Verifiable Credentials Framework, using W3C Verifiable Credentials, digital wallets and blockchain-based trust mechanisms. At a conceptual level, educational institutions issue tamper-resistant digital credentials; learners store them in wallets; and receiving organisations verify their authenticity through decentralised trust registries rather than repeated manual checks. EBSI-VECTOR extends existing EBSI capabilities by adding further functions such as trusted organisation registries, legal-person identity and revocation mechanisms. The expected impact is faster cross-border recognition of qualifications, less administrative burden for universities and employers, stronger user control over personal credentials and more reliable verification of academic records. The project involves 52 partners from 20 countries and is designed to deploy several cross-border journeys for education and social-security capabilities.

title: EBSI-VECTOR - EBSI enabled VErifiable Credentials & Trusted Organisations Registries - Social security
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
task: Authentication of self-sovereign Digital ID services
source_description: Cross-border social security procedures in Europe still require workers, employers and public administrations to exchange and verify documents across different national systems, which can slow down labour mobility and create administrative friction. The EBSI-VECTOR social security use case addresses this problem by applying decentralised digital identity and verifiable credentials to two key documents: the Portable Document A1 for posted workers and the European Health Insurance Card. The objective is to introduce EBSI-compliant infrastructure into social security processes so that citizens and institutions can issue, hold, present and verify trusted documents more efficiently across borders. The implementation builds on the European Blockchain Services Infrastructure, digital wallets, W3C-style verifiable credentials and trusted registries for issuers and organisations. At a conceptual level, a competent social security institution issues a credential, the citizen or worker stores it in a wallet, and another authority or relying party verifies authenticity through decentralised trust mechanisms rather than manual document checks. The expected impact is faster verification, less paperwork, stronger fraud prevention, better user control over credentials and more interoperable social security administration. The project is linked to ESSPASS, whose first phase focused on cross-border digital verification of the PDA1, and EBSI-VECTOR aims to bridge pre-production capabilities towards real-life adoption in education and social security.

title: EBSI-VECTOR - EBSI enabled VErifiable Credentials & Trusted Organisations Registries - Business registries
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Companies operating across borders often need to prove legal identity, authority, registration status or organisational credentials repeatedly to banks, public administrations, trading partners and digital-service providers. The EBSI-VECTOR business registries use case focuses on these frictions by exploring how digital wallets, national business registries and legal-entity verification systems can work together. The operational objective is to create a more trustworthy and interoperable way of recognising organisations across countries and sectors, reducing duplicated checks while improving confidence in business transactions. The implementation is based on EBSI-compliant verifiable credentials, trusted organisation registries and decentralised identity concepts for legal persons. In this pilot, digital-identity experts from 12 EU Member States collaborate to examine how national registries and wallet-based credentials can interact. At a conceptual level, a business registry or authorised issuer provides verifiable credentials for a legal entity, while relying parties verify that credential through EBSI trust frameworks and registry endpoints. The expected impact is faster cross-border onboarding, stronger legal-entity verification, reduced administrative burden and more secure business-to-government or business-to-business digital transactions. The wider EBSI framework also defines legal entity credential registry standards for publishing legal-entity verifiable credentials in an open and interoperable manner.

title: VR4CLIMATE - Virtual Reality (VR) in education for sustainable development
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Energy-transition concepts such as Power-to-X, hydrogen production and sector coupling are technically complex, yet public acceptance and workforce preparation depend on making their risks and opportunities understandable. VR4CLIMATE was developed from a virtual-reality experience commissioned by WWF Germany within the Kopernikus P2X project, with the aim of explaining grey, green and blue hydrogen worlds to a broad audience, especially young adults. The implementation uses immersive VR scenarios to make abstract energy-system transformations visible and experiential. At a conceptual level, learners enter a simulated hydrogen and Power-to-X environment, encounter different production pathways and explore how renewable electricity can be converted into gases, fuels, chemicals or other products. The solution is being further developed into “Green Experience Packages” that combine VR hardware, software and educational content for use in schools, digital hubs, innovation labs and similar settings. The expected impact is improved understanding of sustainable energy technologies, stronger engagement in climate education and more accessible communication of scientific findings from the Kopernikus P2X research programme. Its value lies in translating technical research into an educational format that can reach non-specialist audiences and support curricula in vocational and general education. Public Kopernikus and WWF material confirms the broader P2X education and outreach context, while product material frames VR4CLIMATE as a deployable learning package.

title: Ghent turns downtown traffic data into predictions during three-month pilot
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Busy city centres need better information on how pedestrians, cyclists and vehicles move through streets, especially when congestion affects shops, public space, safety and accessibility. Ghent’s three-month pilot tested whether anonymised traffic data from downtown streets could be converted into predictions about when and where crowding or congestion would occur. The municipality’s objective was both analytical and practical: to understand high-traffic areas better, provide useful intelligence for city officials and businesses, and identify which sensing technology would be most suitable for possible wider deployment. The implementation tested four types of cameras and sensors, each collecting anonymised counts or movement data on pedestrians, cyclists and vehicles. At a conceptual level, the system combined urban sensing, data anonymisation, time-series analysis and predictive modelling, using several months of observations to forecast likely pressure points in the city centre. These insights could support decisions on mobility management, public-space planning and retail-area operations. The expected impact was earlier anticipation of congestion, more evidence-based traffic and crowd management, and better understanding of sensor performance before scale-up. Ghent has since continued to experiment with data-driven mobility tools, including EIT Urban Mobility-supported work using AI and drones for road-safety analysis, indicating an ongoing smart-mobility trajectory beyond the initial pilot.

title: Aarhus Municipality creates an AI-enabled analytical tool for sustainable procurement decisions
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Public procurement has a major climate footprint, because everyday purchases of goods and services generate indirect emissions across large supplier chains. Aarhus Municipality worked with the local company Konsido to make these impacts more visible and actionable, helping public buyers understand how purchasing patterns could be redirected towards more sustainable options. The objective was to move sustainable procurement from broad policy ambition to concrete decision support, using municipal expenditure data to identify where emissions reductions might be achieved. The implementation developed Konsido CPO, an AI-based analytical tool that processes purchasing behaviour, supplier expenditure and climate-emissions information. GovLaunch reports that the tool divided municipal purchases into around 1,000 categories based on invoice analysis, while Aarhus describes the project as further developing Konsido CO2-focused Procurement Optimisation for automated Scope 3 climate accounting. At a conceptual level, the system links e-invoices, financial systems, supplier registers, category structures and emissions estimates to produce procurement intelligence. The expected impact is better prioritisation of green purchasing measures, more continuous follow-up on whether interventions work, and stronger ability to align procurement with climate-reduction targets. Konsido now presents itself as providing AI-based consumption and climate-emission analytics for public authorities and private companies, suggesting that the solution has moved beyond an isolated municipal experiment.

title: AI-enabled platform for reduced hospitalizations among senior residents
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Municipal eldercare services need to identify health deterioration early enough to prevent avoidable hospital admissions, while also allocating limited staff and resources where they are most needed. Køge Municipality’s planned AI-enabled platform uses information from municipal caregiver notes to support earlier disease detection among senior residents. The objective is to complement staff training in early diagnosis and patient communication with a data-supported tool that can detect warning signs in everyday care documentation. The implementation analyses text notes and care observations, looking for patterns that may indicate emerging illness or increased risk. At a conceptual level, the system processes caregiver documentation, identifies clinically relevant signals, and provides recommendations on local resource deployment so that officials and care managers can respond earlier. The expected impact is fewer preventable hospitalisations, better targeting of municipal care resources, improved continuity for older citizens and stronger evidence for preventive eldercare. The Danish Digitisation Agency funded the project and intended to use the Køge platform as a model for other municipalities, showing its role as a public-sector AI signature initiative. However, available public sources describe it as planned or project-based rather than as a fully embedded operational service, so the current maturity should be treated cautiously.

title: AI-enabled system for assistive technology requests
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Municipal welfare services must process large volumes of applications for assistive technologies while ensuring that urgent cases receive attention quickly and that documentation is complete. Sønderborg Municipality handles around 5,000 annual requests for body-worn aids, including items such as corsets, diabetes materials and orthopaedic footwear, with 15 to 20 applications arriving each day. The operational objective is to reduce processing time and improve prioritisation without weakening the individual assessment that each citizen’s situation requires. The implementation tests an AI-enabled system that reviews whether the necessary medical or administrative documentation is present and sorts applications according to urgency and condition. At a conceptual level, the system analyses application content, checks completeness against case requirements, identifies missing information and supports triage so that caseworkers can focus on the most urgent or complex files first. The expected impact is faster case handling, fewer delays caused by missing documents, better allocation of caseworker time and a more reliable application pathway for citizens needing assistive technology. GovLaunch reports that the municipality received a DKK 3.2 million grant for a pilot of AI-supported application review, indicating that the initiative was designed as a funded test rather than a fully mature service.

title: The LOVOT social AI robot in nursing homes to help people with dementia
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Dementia care often involves residents who experience loneliness, high arousal, withdrawal or difficulty sustaining social interaction, while care staff must balance emotional support with limited time and resources. Aalborg, Viborg and Skive municipalities piloted LOVOT in Danish nursing homes to investigate whether a social robot could contribute to quality of life for people with dementia. The target group includes residents in care centres who may benefit from comforting interaction, sensory stimulation or a non-demanding social presence. The implementation uses LOVOT, a small social robot designed to respond to touch, speech and eye contact through sensors, movement, warmth, sounds, facial expression and body language. At a conceptual level, the robot detects social cues, reacts in ways that resemble a living companion, and develops interaction patterns that may encourage residents to engage, calm down or seek contact. The technology does not replace professional care or relational work by staff; rather, it provides an additional welfare-technology tool that can be introduced where a resident’s needs and preferences make it appropriate. The expected impact is improved wellbeing, reduced loneliness or agitation, and richer activity options in dementia care. Ethical attention remains necessary, especially because lifelike robots can blur emotional boundaries for people with cognitive impairment, making staff assessment and transparent use essential.

title: The city of Tampere, in Finland, predicts future foot traffic in the city center with its Tamperen Pulssi tool
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: City-centre businesses, event organisers and municipal services need to anticipate pedestrian flows in order to plan staffing, maintenance, opening hours and operational resources. Tampereen Pulssi was developed by the City of Tampere and Wapice as an AI-powered tool that predicts visitor flows in the city centre. The operational problem is that footfall depends on multiple variables, including regular mobility patterns, weather, public holidays, events and local venue programming, making manual forecasting unreliable. The implementation collects anonymised data from downtown traffic cameras and combines it with weather forecasts, the Tampere event calendar and ticketing-related information. At a conceptual level, the system transforms mobility observations and contextual variables into short- and medium-term predictions of pedestrian activity. The results are shown through the Tampere.Finland app and a map-based interface, helping local businesses and agencies understand where and when higher flows are expected. The expected impact is better preparation for busy periods, more efficient retail and restaurant staffing, improved planning of street maintenance and stronger data-driven support for city-centre vitality. The case is significant because it turns smart-city sensing into a practical economic-development service for businesses, rather than keeping mobility analytics only inside municipal operations.

title: Kuusamo Municipality experiments with Kuusamo-Kati chatbot for tourism and health questions
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Municipal websites often serve multiple audiences, including residents, seasonal visitors and tourists, who may need guidance outside office hours on services, tourism, local events and health-related information. Kuusamo-Kati was introduced as an AI-enabled chatbot to provide automated support when live help was unavailable, especially during evenings and weekends. The operational problem was that many website visitors searched for recurring topics, and municipal staff could not offer continuous live support across all channels. The implementation began by training or programming the bot with knowledge about the most frequently searched website topics, then using real user conversations and feedback forms to refine future development. At a conceptual level, the system interprets a question, matches it to existing municipal content and returns an answer or direction to the relevant web page. The expected impact is better after-hours service, faster answers for residents and visitors, reduced repetitive staff workload and evidence on what topics users most often struggle to find. The case is also relevant because it combines tourism and municipal-service information in a single assistant, reflecting the needs of a destination municipality where visitors interact with local public services as well as tourism providers.

title: Järvenpää is piloting Kunta-Kati the AI chatbot as its new customer service representative
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The City of Järvenpää sought to modernise customer service by providing residents with faster access to information while managing limited staff resources. Citizens often had questions outside office hours or on topics spanning multiple departments. This use case involves the city administration, residents, and technology partners, with the objective of improving service availability and efficiency. Kunta-Kati is implemented as a digital customer service representative embedded on the city’s website, capable of answering questions about municipal services and local issues. When unable to resolve a query, it seamlessly redirects users to human customer service staff. The solution improves first-contact resolution, extends service availability, and reduces routine workload for employees. It enhances citizen experience through clear, immediate guidance and supports a hybrid service model combining automation and human expertise.

title: Porvoo Municipality integrated the Kunta-Kai AI virtual customer advisor into the city's website
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Porvoo Municipality aimed to improve navigation and information access on its website while reducing repetitive enquiries to city departments. This use case involves municipal services, residents, and visitors, with the objective of providing more intuitive digital support. The Kunta-Kati virtual advisor is integrated into the city’s website to handle frequently asked questions and support search functionality. It connects users to relevant information and, when necessary, directs them to the appropriate department. The city is exploring extensions such as voice interaction to further enhance accessibility. The solution improves website usability, reduces administrative burden, and strengthens digital service delivery. It delivers scalable customer support and supports continuous improvement of municipal digital channels.

title: Turku Municipality breaks down language barriers to COVID-19 outreach and later Ukrainian refugee crisis with Åbot chatbot
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The City of Turku faced urgent communication challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic and later during the Ukrainian refugee crisis, requiring rapid dissemination of reliable information across language barriers. This use case involved city authorities, residents, refugees, and volunteers, with the objective of ensuring inclusive access to public information. Åbot was implemented as a multilingual conversational service capable of responding in over one hundred languages. It provided up-to-date guidance on health measures, city services, and support for Ukrainian refugees and those wishing to help them. Integrated with official information sources, the service ensured accuracy and consistency. Åbot improved accessibility, reduced misinformation, and supported social inclusion during crises. It strengthened community resilience and demonstrated the value of multilingual digital services in emergency and integration contexts.

title: Bordeaux partners with Superpedestrian on micro-mobility service featuring AI-enabled scooters
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Shared e-scooter services can improve short urban trips, but they also create safety, parking and sidewalk-riding challenges for municipalities. Bordeaux partnered with Superpedestrian to deploy LINK e-scooters as part of a regulated micro-mobility service. The operational objective was to offer residents a low-emission mobility option while using embedded technology to improve compliance and vehicle safety. The implementation used Superpedestrian’s Vehicle Intelligence system, which continuously evaluates component status and can respond when scooters operate in restricted ways. At a conceptual level, the scooters combine sensors, microprocessors, diagnostics, geofencing and real-time control logic. The system can slow or stop vehicles when they are used on sidewalks or outside permitted areas, while operational teams use electric vans for lower-impact maintenance and collection. The expected impact is safer shared micro-mobility, better management of public-space rules, reduced maintenance risk and improved confidence for the city in permitting e-scooter operations. The use case is important because it shows how AI-enabled vehicle intelligence can be embedded directly into mobility devices, shifting enforcement from only after-the-fact regulation towards real-time operational controls that support local policy.

title: Municipality of Cologne improves the accuracy of its wastewater taxation system with a geospatial AI system
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Wastewater taxation often depends on the amount of impervious surface on private property, because paved or sealed areas increase rainwater runoff into the drainage system. Cologne’s municipal wastewater authority, Stadtentwässerungsbetriebe Köln, worked with Hexagon to improve the accuracy and efficiency of this process using a GeoAI solution. The operational problem was that earlier methods relied heavily on manual inspections and property-owner self-reporting, which made it difficult to detect changes in paved surfaces consistently across the city. The implementation uses aerial imagery, LiDAR mapping and AI-based classification to identify sealed and unsealed surfaces on private land. At a conceptual level, the platform analyses high-resolution geospatial data, detects changes since previous surveys and classifies surfaces that affect drainage-fee calculations. This provides a more accurate basis for wastewater-tax assessment and can also support simulations related to climate adaptation, such as renaturalisation or de-sealing of paved areas. The expected impact is fairer taxation, lower manual workload, improved data quality and better environmental planning. The case shows how GeoAI can support municipal finance and climate resilience at the same time: a taxation dataset becomes useful not only for billing, but also for understanding urban runoff and planning greener surfaces.

title: Rüsselsheim am Main enforces truck ban with AI to abate pollution
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Air quality and traffic-management measures can be difficult to enforce when they depend on distinguishing specific vehicle types without creating intrusive surveillance. Rüsselsheim am Main introduced an AI-enabled intelligent-infrastructure solution to support enforcement of a ban on trucks weighing 7.5 tonnes or more when they originate outside city limits. The operational problem was to identify vehicles subject to the ban at roads entering and exiting the city while protecting privacy and avoiding manual monitoring. The implementation installed sixteen Velodyne Ultra Puck lidar sensors on street lights along relevant routes. These sensors collect anonymised three-dimensional traffic data that allow an AI-enabled platform to distinguish heavy trucks from other vehicles. At a conceptual level, the system analyses vehicle shape, size and movement patterns rather than relying on facial recognition or licence-plate identification. This enables local officials to understand whether restricted vehicles are entering the city and to generate evidence for traffic-control and environmental-management decisions. The expected impact is improved enforcement of the truck restriction, reduced pollution and noise, better data on freight movement and a foundation for wider traffic and air-quality analytics. The same infrastructure can also support prediction-based traffic management and environmental monitoring, making it a broader smart-city tool rather than a single-purpose enforcement device.

title: Urban Intelligence-as-a-Service model for smart lighting upgrade
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Street lighting is essential for safety, accessibility and public confidence, but conventional lighting systems often waste energy and provide limited flexibility for environmental or situational needs. Bad Hersfeld used an Urban Intelligence-as-a-Service model to upgrade its public lighting and integrate smart technologies into a unified urban-management system. The operational challenge was to modernise lighting while balancing energy efficiency, safety, traffic conditions, weather, noise, temperature and ecological concerns such as wildlife-sensitive light colour and brightness. The implementation connects new LED lighting fixtures to sensors and digital controls that gather urban data and adjust lighting behaviour. At a conceptual level, the system links lighting infrastructure, real-time traffic information, weather data, environmental sensors and a central interface. This allows lighting levels, light distribution and colour temperature to be adapted according to conditions rather than remaining fixed. Residents can also request lighting changes through a mobile app, adding a participatory service layer to the infrastructure. The expected impact is reduced energy consumption, improved safety and visibility, better environmental compatibility and a reusable platform for future smart-city services. The case is significant because it treats lighting as both a utility and a data-enabled urban platform, where operational intelligence can be delivered as a service rather than through isolated infrastructure projects.

title: Messina online transparency platform for waste management services
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Waste-management services affect every household, yet residents often struggle to understand collection schedules, sweeping activities, transport responsibilities, washing services and waste-fee information. Messina adopted an online transparency platform to make the city’s waste-management service more visible and easier to use. The operational problem was to provide clear, accessible and regularly updated information about collection, transport, sweeping, washing and the application of the TARI waste-management service. The implementation makes this information available through a digital transparency platform and extends access through a voice-assistant skill for Amazon Alexa. At a conceptual level, the system turns structured service information into both web-based and voice-based interaction: citizens can ask what waste is collected, update their calendar, select or change their collection zone, request information about responsible entities and use a “rifiutologo” function to understand where a specific item should be disposed of. The expected impact is better resident compliance with collection rules, fewer information gaps, improved transparency of waste-service responsibilities and more convenient access for people who prefer voice interaction. The use case is relevant because it connects open municipal-service information with conversational AI, making waste-management transparency available through everyday domestic devices.

title: The Hague and The Routing Company develop on-demand public transit service
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Fixed-route public transport in low-density neighbourhoods often suffers from low occupancy rates and limited flexibility, resulting in operational inefficiencies and reduced service attractiveness. In The Hague’s Benoordenhout area, local transit operator HTM sought to replace underused fixed routes with a flexible, demand-responsive alternative. Stakeholders include passengers, municipal authorities, HTM and technology providers. The objective is to improve accessibility and service efficiency through dynamic routing. The service uses a digital platform accessible via passenger and driver applications, where ride requests are processed using optimisation algorithms and AI-enabled routing models that account for real-time traffic conditions, vehicle capacity and stop locations. The system dynamically assigns vehicles and calculates efficient shared routes between designated stops, integrating with existing ticketing and operational systems. Anticipated impacts include higher vehicle utilisation, reduced operational costs, shorter waiting times and improved user satisfaction, alongside data-driven service planning capabilities.

title: Rotterdam created digital twin to improve urban planning
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Urban planning in Rotterdam requires balancing growth, sustainability, and resilience, yet fragmented data limited predictive analysis and cross-domain optimisation. This use case involves the city administration, planners, infrastructure managers, and technology partners, with the objective of improving evidence-based urban planning. Rotterdam’s digital twin is implemented by integrating existing city maps, LiDAR-based 3D models, engineering blueprints, and real-time sensor data into a unified virtual representation of the city. The platform supports simulation and analysis across domains such as energy consumption, mobility, and subsurface infrastructure management. The solution improves planning accuracy, supports scenario testing, and enhances coordination across departments. It reduces risk, supports sustainability goals, and delivers long-term value by enabling smarter, data-driven urban development.

title: Borås Municipality assesses AI chatbot improvements to customer service during pilot
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Borås Municipality faces a high volume of routine enquiries from residents seeking information on municipal services, which can place pressure on customer service teams and slow response times. To address this, the municipality launched a six-month pilot to assess whether a virtual assistant could improve accessibility and service quality while supporting staff rather than replacing them. The use case involves municipal departments, customer service staff, and citizens, with the objective of providing faster answers to common questions and ensuring smooth escalation to human agents when needed. The solution is implemented through a conversational chatbot embedded on the municipal website, initially populated with frequently asked questions identified by staff. The system continuously expands its knowledge base by learning from user interactions and feedback, and it is integrated with existing customer service workflows to redirect unresolved queries to human operators. During the pilot, the chatbot increased first-contact resolution for routine enquiries and improved availability outside office hours. The municipality is evaluating user satisfaction, accuracy of responses, and operational impact. Early results indicate reduced workload for staff, faster access to information for residents, and valuable insights into citizen needs, supporting evidence-based decisions on future digital service delivery.

title: Birmingham City Council takes aim at illegal dumping with its AI-enabled CCTV camera pilot
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Illegal dumping creates environmental, financial and public-safety problems for local authorities, particularly when waste is left repeatedly in known hotspots and enforcement teams must review footage or respond after the fact. Birmingham City Council introduced an AI-enabled CCTV pilot to strengthen its response to fly-tipping in Aston, Erdington and North Edgbaston. The operational objective is to detect suspected dumped waste more quickly, support timely investigations and deter environmental offences alongside signage on penalties and online reporting channels. The implementation places AI-enhanced cameras near fly-tipping hotspots, where they are trained to identify waste placed anywhere other than public bins. When a suspected incident is detected, the system sends an alert to council officers with relevant imagery, reducing the need to manually review hours of footage. At a conceptual level, the system combines object detection, event-triggered notification, CCTV evidence capture and enforcement workflow support. The expected impact is faster officer response, improved investigation efficiency, better evidence for enforcement and reduced street-cleansing burden. The pilot was supported by a £45,000 national grant, and Birmingham’s own announcement described three AI CCTV cameras as an additional tool in the city’s effort to tackle environmental criminals. Its value lies in targeted hotspot monitoring rather than generalised citywide surveillance.

title: Derby City Council connects residents to city services with AI-powered digital assistants
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Residents contacting a council often need help with multiple service areas through web and telephone channels, but routine enquiries can absorb staff capacity that would be better directed to complex cases. Derby City Council introduced AI-powered digital assistants, Darcie for council customer services and Ali for Derby Homes housing enquiries, to create a more accessible digital front door for residents. The operational problem was to allow people to access services in one place, receive immediate assistance and avoid unnecessary transfer between channels or teams. The implementation uses conversational AI across website and phone interactions, replacing or augmenting traditional switchboard and interactive voice-response functions. At a conceptual level, the assistants interpret what the resident is asking, provide answers, route the query to the right service or escalate to staff where human support is needed. The expected impact is quicker access to information, reduced waiting times, lower handling cost and more staff capacity for issues that require professional judgement or personalised service. The case is also important because it applies AI to mainstream local-government customer contact, rather than limiting it to a specialist back-office process. It demonstrates how conversational tools can become part of an authority-wide operating model for resident interaction.

title: Project-A.I.R (Artificial Intelligence Guided Retrofit)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Housing decarbonisation is particularly difficult in social housing because retrofit measures must reduce emissions and energy costs while remaining practical, affordable and acceptable for residents. In Harrow, Project-A.I.R explored a solar-glass structure concept intended to support household energy transition and reduce fuel poverty. The concept centres on a standalone transparent garden structure or pergola-canopy in which photovoltaic glass serves both as construction material and power-generating surface. The implementation brings together retrofit analysis, solar PV glass, a three-kilowatt peak array and the wider transition from fabric-first improvements to electric-powered homes. Public descriptions frame the initiative as AI-guided because the concept was identified and assessed through an approach designed to target efficient decarbonisation measures in housing. At a conceptual level, the solution combines household retrofit intelligence, semi-transparent solar generation, structural design and social-housing energy planning. The expected impact is reduced household energy bills, lower carbon emissions and a visible demonstration of renewable technology integrated into domestic space. GovLaunch reported a potential annual bill reduction of up to 45% if implemented, while NewFrame reports that the three-kilowatt solar-glass array could deliver up to 68% of individual household energy bills throughout the year. The project was presented publicly at Grand Designs Live in 2023.

title: Dudley Metropolitan Borough Council creates smart intersection with AI-powered road sensors
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Traffic congestion and road-safety problems often require detailed information about how different users move through junctions, including cars, buses, cyclists and pedestrians. Dudley Metropolitan Borough Council deployed AI-powered road sensors with VivaCity to support smarter junction management and improve traffic flow in the Brierley Hill and Merry Hill area. The operational problem was to identify where congestion and active-travel demand were greatest, then use data to select and improve a specific junction. The implementation installed a network of sixty-five VivaCity sensors, with a cluster supporting a Smart Junction at Venture Way and Mill Street. At a conceptual level, the sensors use computer vision to classify and count road users, measure demand and journey times, and feed multimodal traffic data into a signal-control platform. This allows traffic lights to respond more dynamically to current motor-vehicle, cycling and pedestrian flows. The expected impact is reduced delay, better traffic flow, improved air quality, stronger support for active travel and more evidence-based local transport interventions. The case is significant because it combines monitoring and control: the same sensor data that helps diagnose congestion also supports real-time or near-real-time optimisation of traffic signals.

title: Cambridgeshire County Council, GB pilots AI-powered traffic sensors at East Road in Cambridge
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Signalised crossings must balance pedestrian safety and traffic flow, especially in busy urban locations where road users arrive in groups and demand changes throughout the day. At East Road in Cambridge, AI-powered traffic sensors were trialled to reduce waiting times for pedestrians and other road users while making crossings safer and more responsive. The operational problem was that conventional crossing systems do not always understand the number, type or behaviour of users waiting to cross. The implementation used Starling Technologies’ camera-based AI sensors, installed through collaboration between the Greater Cambridge Partnership and Cambridgeshire County Council’s traffic signals team. At a conceptual level, the system analyses road users in real time, identifies different types of movement, and learns when people are likely to want to cross. Linked signals can then adjust timings based on pedestrian and traffic conditions. The expected impact is safer crossings, shorter pedestrian waits, smoother traffic movement and improved support for active travel. Privacy is also relevant because the technology is designed to analyse movement patterns rather than identify individuals. The use case demonstrates how computer vision can improve local traffic infrastructure by making crossings more adaptive to actual street conditions.

title: Leeds City Council pursues smart traffic management with AI for Detection technology
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Busy urban junctions require accurate real-time detection of different transport modes if traffic signals are to support buses, cyclists, pedestrians and general traffic effectively. Leeds City Council deployed VivaCity’s AI for Detection technology across a network of junctions to improve smart traffic management and tackle congestion. The operational problem was that traditional detection infrastructure, such as induction loops, provides limited information and can be costly to maintain, while modern transport policy requires multimodal prioritisation.
