The implementation installed more than 180 AI for Detection sensors across twenty-five sites. At a conceptual level, the sensors use computer vision to classify road users, detect buses, cyclists, pedestrians and other vehicles, and communicate with existing traffic-signal controllers. This enables more dynamic signal responses, potentially including bus priority or active-travel support at critical times of day. The expected impact is reduced stop-start traffic, improved bus reliability, better cycling and pedestrian movement, and richer traffic datasets for future road projects. The case is important because it embeds AI into existing urban traffic-control infrastructure, showing how cities can upgrade junction intelligence without replacing the entire signal network.

title: Westminster City Council deploys AI-supported cameras in campaign against illegal dumping
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Illegal dumping creates costs for councils, damages the public realm and can become concentrated in specific hotspots where conventional enforcement is difficult. Westminster City Council deployed AI-supported CCTV cameras as part of a campaign against fly-tipping and wider anti-social behaviour. The operational problem was to detect suspected dumping incidents more systematically at locations where waste was repeatedly left and to support enforcement with usable evidence. The implementation placed cameras linked to an AI-enabled platform at three hotspots. When a suspected incident occurs, the system captures relevant footage and nearby licence plates, after which council or enforcement staff review the material and may pursue fines or further action using Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency data. At a conceptual level, the system combines event detection, CCTV evidence capture, vehicle-record linkage and human enforcement review. The expected impact is faster identification of suspected offenders, deterrence in problem areas, more targeted clean-street operations and better coordination under local anti-social-behaviour strategies. The technology does not issue penalties autonomously; it supports investigation by surfacing incidents and evidence for human review. Its value lies in increasing enforcement visibility and reducing the manual burden of watching footage continuously.

title: Powys County Council builds AI-enabled system for expedited Fuel Support Scheme reviews
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Emergency household-support schemes require fast payment, fraud control and simple application processes, particularly when residents face acute energy-cost pressures. Powys County Council built an AI-enabled platform to accelerate reviews of applications for the Welsh Government Fuel Support Scheme. The operational problem was to process high volumes of £200 support-payment applications without creating excessive manual workload or delaying assistance to eligible households. The implementation allowed applicants meeting all scheme criteria to receive automatic approvals, while duplicate applications were filtered out and potentially fraudulent or unclear applications were routed for council review. At a conceptual level, the system combines eligibility checking, duplicate detection, workflow triage and exception handling. This means automation handles straightforward applications, while human officers focus on cases where judgement or further investigation is required. The expected impact is quicker payment to residents, reduced administrative cost, better fraud prevention and a more user-friendly support process. The case shows how AI can support welfare administration when rules are structured and urgency is high, provided that human review remains available for flagged applications. It is best understood as a narrowly scoped administrative tool for a defined support scheme rather than a general welfare decision-making system.

title: Bournemouth, Christchurch & Poole Council monitors coastal water quality with AI sensors
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Protected coastal waters require continuous monitoring because pollution, nutrients, industrial discharges and changing environmental conditions can affect bathing water, shellfish beds and sensitive ecosystems. Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole Council worked with Poole Harbour Commissioners and UnifAI Technology to develop a more timely and affordable alternative to traditional laboratory-based monitoring. The objective was to provide real-time insight into water-quality changes so that authorities could identify risks earlier and target mitigation or clean-up activity more effectively. The implementation deployed low-cost wireless sensors on buoys and connected them to UnifAI’s analytical platform. At a conceptual level, the system collects raw water-quality measurements, transmits them remotely, and applies AI-enabled modelling to turn sensor readings into indicators, alerts and analysis of pollutant or discharge conditions. BCP Council described the first phase as live in October 2020 and as the first deployment of a low-cost remote and continuous sensor network using AI to monitor a protected water ecosystem in real time. A later council update states that BCP had partnered with UnifAI two years earlier to develop low-cost wireless sensors with AI for more timely monitoring. The expected impact is lower monitoring cost, reduced reliance on slow laboratory testing, earlier warning of deterioration and a reusable model for other councils managing coastal water quality.

title: Southampton City Council trains residents for the Future of Work with its Bodyswaps pilot
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Employment support increasingly needs to help residents build soft skills, confidence and communication abilities, not only provide job listings or formal training. Southampton City Council selected Bodyswaps as part of its Future of Work programme to help residents prepare for interviews, teamwork, leadership and workplace communication through immersive learning. The operational problem was to support people seeking jobs, apprenticeships or other work-related outcomes in a labour market shaped by digitisation and changing employer expectations. The implementation uses virtual reality and AI-enabled simulations in which learners practise communication scenarios, receive feedback and reflect on their performance. At a conceptual level, Bodyswaps creates a safe practice environment where users can experience realistic conversations, observe themselves from different perspectives and build confidence through repeated attempts. Employment-service providers host the technology, and employability professionals support learners alongside the digital training. The expected impact is improved interview performance, stronger soft skills, increased confidence and better access to innovative training for residents who may benefit from experiential learning. The case is significant because it connects immersive technology with local economic-development policy, using VR not as entertainment but as a practical tool for employability and workforce preparation.

title: Leicester City Council partners with university researchers on H2A: Lifestyle initiative
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Obesity prevention requires more than generic health messaging, because lifestyle choices are shaped by local environment, housing, employment, activity patterns, demographics and access to support. Leicester City Council partnered with De Montfort University on the H2A: Lifestyle initiative to develop more personalised weight-loss and health-improvement support for residents. The objective is to help practitioners and public-health officials understand which factors contribute to obesity risk in different parts of the city and to design interventions that respond to individual and neighbourhood conditions. The implementation uses artificial intelligence and machine learning to analyse multiple variables, including demographic, social, environmental and activity-related information. The planned tool recommends small, realistic lifestyle changes based on individual activity data and wider city health data, while dashboards can help officials target wellness campaigns by postcode. At a conceptual level, the system links personalisation, population-health analytics, behavioural insight and local policy planning. The expected impact is more relevant support for residents, better targeting of obesity-prevention campaigns, and stronger evidence for local strategies that reduce barriers to healthy living. The initiative also reflects a broader Local+ partnership between Leicester City Council and the university, using academic research to inform public-policy interventions. Public sources describe it as a research-led programme rather than a fully mature citywide health service.

title: Monmouthshire County Council monitors the success of new bike lanes with Vivacity Labs platform
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Active-travel infrastructure needs reliable evidence on how streets are used before and after design changes, especially where new cycle lanes alter traffic flow or reduce carriageway space for motor vehicles. Monmouthshire County Council used VivaCity sensors to evaluate protected contraflow cycling lanes introduced on one-way streets in Abergavenny. The operational problem was to understand whether the new arrangement improved cycling conditions and affected vehicle behaviour, rather than relying only on anecdotal feedback or occasional manual counts. The implementation placed sensors at three points on Lion Street to gather anonymised multimodal data on traffic density, user classification, paths and speeds. At a conceptual level, the sensors use AI-enabled computer vision to distinguish different road-user types, measure flows and produce indicators such as cyclist counts and average vehicle speed. This allows the council to monitor whether cycling becomes more popular and whether vehicle speeds change as a result of the new layout. The expected impact is more evidence-based active-travel planning, improved safety for cyclists and pedestrians, and better assessment of whether similar interventions should be used elsewhere. The use case is significant because it links policy evaluation directly to live street data, helping a local authority understand the real-world effects of infrastructure investment.

title: The City of Edinburgh Council continues smart city evolution with CCTV Control Centre
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Large urban centres need coordinated situational awareness across public safety, transport, major events and city operations. Edinburgh’s smart CCTV Control Centre was developed to modernise the city’s security and surveillance infrastructure while integrating it with traffic and transportation systems. The operational problem was that older CCTV and remote security systems were not fully connected, limiting rapid retrieval of footage, coordinated response and citywide operational insight. The implementation included high-definition CCTV cameras, expanded security coverage, advanced analytics and artificial intelligence capable of supporting situational awareness and alerts about emerging threats. North was selected to deliver the system and integrate the security environment with wider city platforms. At a conceptual level, the control centre consolidates camera feeds, analytics, transport data and operational workflows into a single environment where authorised staff can identify incidents, retrieve evidence and coordinate responses. The expected impact is improved public safety, faster issue resolution, better traffic and city-operations management, and richer understanding of how people move through the urban environment by foot, bicycle or vehicle. The case demonstrates how CCTV modernisation can become part of a wider smart-city operating model when video infrastructure is connected to urban analytics and service coordination.

title: Sunderland City Council converts data into improved services with AI-powered platform
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Local authorities hold large volumes of data across services such as anti-social behaviour, social care, taxation, health and environmental incidents, but fragmented datasets can prevent early intervention and coordinated action. Sunderland City Council adopted ConnexinOS as an integrated smart-city platform to pool council and third-party data and support more responsive public services. The operational problem was to move from isolated information systems towards a shared data environment that could reveal trends, risks and service demands across departments. The implementation uses artificial intelligence and machine learning to analyse raw datasets, identify patterns and suggest potential courses of action. At a conceptual level, the platform aggregates diverse operational data, applies analytical models, presents insights through dashboards and supports multi-agency decision-making. This can help staff detect issues such as vandalism patterns, environmental incidents or residents who may need support before problems escalate. The expected impact is earlier intervention, better coordination across agencies, improved service targeting and stronger evidence for local policy decisions. The case is important because it treats AI not as a single service chatbot or automation script, but as a cross-cutting urban intelligence layer that can inform multiple municipal service areas.

title: Wandsworth Borough Council tracks air quality and traffic patterns with Eco Census cameras
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Air-quality policy depends on understanding both pollution levels and the local traffic behaviours that contribute to them. Wandsworth Borough Council used Eco Census cameras to combine traffic monitoring with real-time air-quality measurement in Putney, supporting its wider Air Quality Action Plan. The operational problem was that the council needed better evidence on pollutants such as nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter, including PM2.5, while also understanding how pedestrians, cyclists and motorists used the monitored streets. The implementation installed AI-enabled cameras and environmental monitoring equipment at key locations, producing data on traffic patterns and pollutant concentrations through a dedicated dashboard. At a conceptual level, the system combines computer vision, road-user classification, pollutant sensing and place-based analytics. This allows officials to evaluate long-term trends, assess policy interventions, understand road-layout impacts and support measures to reduce pollution exposure. The expected impact is better air-quality management, more evidence-based street design, improved safety for pedestrians and cyclists, and clearer progress tracking against local and national objectives. The use case shows how environmental monitoring and mobility analytics can be joined in one street-level system, helping a borough understand not only air quality outcomes but also the traffic conditions behind them.

title: London Borough of Redbridge modernizes planning requests and services with Planbot
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Planning services in the London Borough of Redbridge handle complex regulations and high volumes of enquiries, often diverting specialist staff from higher-value work. Residents and developers require clear guidance on planning rules, applications, and documentation. This use case addresses the need to simplify access to planning information and improve service efficiency, involving the borough council, customer support teams, applicants, and residents. The objective is to streamline enquiries, reduce delays, and support faster planning decisions. Planbot is implemented as a mobile-friendly conversational assistant covering around 200 planning topics, connected to official guidance, forms, and documents. It supports both self-service use by the public and assisted use by customer support staff handling phone calls, ensuring consistent and accurate responses. The bot integrates with planning information systems and digital content repositories. As a result, routine questions are resolved more quickly, calls are handled more efficiently, and planning officers can focus on complex applications and strategic work. The solution improves user experience, shortens response times, and delivers operational savings, contributing to a more responsive and effective local planning service.

title: Dorset Council leverages 5G connectivity along the coast for Aquaculture Monitoring System
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Aquaculture businesses need continuous insight into marine growing conditions, yet coastal environments can be difficult to monitor because connectivity is limited and underwater data collection is technically demanding. Dorset Council’s 5G RuralDorset programme supported an Aquaculture Monitoring System for Jurassic Sea Farms in Portland Harbour, developed with JET Engineering System Solutions. The objective is to help a growing seaweed and shellfish sector improve productivity, sustainability and operational decisions through real-time environmental intelligence. The implementation uses 5G-connected buoys made from sustainable materials and underwater cameras that can stream live 4K video from marine sites. Real-time data are then fed into an AI-enabled platform that can support recommendations on how to maximise cultivation conditions for seaweed and shellfish. At a conceptual level, the system combines coastal connectivity, sensor buoys, underwater visual monitoring, data transmission and analytics for aquaculture decision support. The expected impact is better monitoring of stock and growing conditions, reduced need for manual inspection, improved responsiveness to environmental changes and stronger evidence for low-carbon aquaculture development.
vendor_reported: JET Engineering System Solutions; Jurassic Sea Farms

title: Bournemouth, Christchurch & Poole Councils turn litter maps into localized engagement
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Coastal destinations face intense litter pressure during visitor peaks, but effective interventions require knowing exactly what is being littered, where it accumulates and when behaviour changes. Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole Council worked with Ellipsis Earth and campaign partners to use AI-enabled litter mapping as the basis for localised engagement. The operational problem was to move beyond general anti-litter messaging towards evidence-based action tailored to specific places and waste types. The implementation used drone and camera-based surveys analysed by AI to identify and classify litter items, generating detailed maps of plastic, cigarette butts, tissues and other waste patterns. At a conceptual level, the system converts images into geolocated litter intelligence, showing hotspots, item types and temporal patterns. This data then informs practical interventions such as bin placement, street-cleaning routes, signage and behaviour-change campaigns. The expected impact is more targeted litter reduction, improved use of council resources, stronger environmental protection and better engagement with residents, visitors and businesses. The case is significant because it links advanced image analysis with public participation: the data does not remain a technical map, but becomes the basis for local action and communication designed to change behaviour.

title: Derby City Council embarks on next phase of using AI to streamline services
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Local authorities face rising demand, financial pressure and complex service backlogs, especially in adult social care and customer contact. Derby City Council entered a four-year AI transformation partnership with ICS.AI to expand digital assistants and staff copilots across council services. The objective is to support staff in day-to-day work while keeping human officers responsible for decisions that require professional judgement. In adult social care, copilots are intended to help review care packages and assess whether residents receiving support at home have the right level of care. In customer services, Derby’s Darcie and Ali digital assistants are being upgraded and expanded to handle web-based and telephone enquiries, while AI tools also support email triage and response. At a conceptual level, the system combines conversational AI, generative assistants, human-in-the-loop workflow support, knowledge retrieval and service-specific process integration. The expected impact is faster responses, reduced call transfers, more staff time for complex cases and improved service resilience.

title: Ministry of Labour and Social Policies chatbot
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Ministry of Labour and Social Policies
source_description: The chatbot replies to general enquiries from citizens in relation to social policies, such as the "bonus trasporti"" (Italian citizens could apply for a cash benefit of maximum 60 euros to buy transportation monthly passes)."

title: City Shark - Keeping Aarhus harbor clean with a robot
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Harbours and urban waterways collect floating waste that is difficult to remove continuously through manual cleaning alone. Aarhus Municipality developed the City Shark project to test robotic and drone-based methods for keeping the harbour cleaner. The operational problem was to collect waste from the water surface efficiently while also exploring how autonomous technology could support environmental management. The core solution was a WasteShark, a sailing drone designed primarily to collect floating rubbish. The project was organised in phases by Aarhus Municipality’s ITK department in collaboration with the Agency for Data Supply and Efficiency, the Port of Aarhus, the City of Aarhus and external suppliers. At a conceptual level, the water drone navigates the harbour, collects waste from the surface and can be combined with other sensor or drone systems to detect pollution such as oil or petrol from the air and guide the water drone to the affected area. The expected impact is cleaner harbour water, reduced manual cleaning effort, greater public visibility of marine litter problems and a testbed for autonomous environmental robotics. The use case demonstrates how relatively small autonomous systems can support municipal environmental services in constrained urban-water settings.

title: Italian central bank backs Decentralised Finance tokenisation project
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Institutional financial markets are exploring tokenisation, but regulated actors need evidence that digital-asset infrastructures can operate within existing supervisory, security and operational requirements. In Italy, the Bank of Italy’s Milano Hub selected an Institutional DeFi for Security Token ecosystem project promoted by Cetif Advisory, with partners including Fireblocks, Polygon Labs, Reply, Linklaters and DVRS. The initiative focuses on security tokens, understood as digital representations of ownership or rights over real-world assets, and examines how institutional players could access DeFi-like services while mitigating risks that would be unacceptable in retail or unregulated environments. The implementation is experimental and has no commercialisation purpose. At a conceptual level, it combines tokenised financial instruments, blockchain infrastructure, custody and security technology, legal structuring, compliance analysis and secondary-market workflows. The project extends analysis of how security tokens could circulate in institutional environments, including how regulated intermediaries might interact with decentralised infrastructures without losing control over identity, governance, investor protection and operational resilience. The expected impact is improved understanding of tokenised securities, clearer regulatory and technical requirements, and stronger Italian capacity to evaluate institutional digital-finance models. Its value is primarily exploratory: it gives public authorities and market participants a controlled setting to test opportunities and limits before any possible production-market use.

title: Romania plugs into Web3 with national NFT marketplace
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: ICI Bucharest (National Institute for Research and Development in Informatics)
source_description: Public institutions are beginning to experiment with Web3 tools as a way to create new forms of digital interaction, cultural promotion and trusted asset management. Romania’s National Institute for Research and Development in Informatics, ICI Bucharest, launched ICI D|SERVICES as an institutional platform for managing and trading digital assets, with an initial focus on non-fungible tokens. The objective is to connect public institutions, private actors and users through a government-backed digital marketplace that can support minting, management and trading of NFTs. The implementation operates on decentralised blockchain and Web3 technologies and was presented as the first European institutional platform for trading digital assets. At a conceptual level, the platform combines NFT issuance, digital-asset management, blockchain-based ownership records, user accounts and institutional collections, enabling organisations to publish digital assets while users can verify provenance and ownership. Its expected impact is to promote Web3 adoption in Romania, support new models of cultural and institutional engagement, and test how public-sector organisations can participate in digital-asset ecosystems. The initiative also provides an experimental bridge between national research infrastructure, government-backed digital transformation and private-sector blockchain communities. While the platform’s long-term public value depends on sustained institutional use and careful governance, its launch marked a concrete move from policy interest to operational Web3 experimentation.

title: Multiple chatbots on the spanish Agenzia Tributaria website
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Tax systems are procedurally complex, and citizens, companies and advisers often need interactive guidance on declarations, VAT, census obligations, collection, payment deadlines and classification of economic activities. Spain’s Agencia Tributaria provides a suite of virtual-assistance tools to help users answer common tax questions and complete or understand procedures. The operational problem is that many enquiries require structured interpretation of tax rules, but can still be handled through guided questions, calculators or virtual assistants before a user needs personalised support. The implementation includes virtual assistants, informants, economic-activity search tools, locators for goods and service transactions, real-estate transaction qualifiers, payment-term calculators, invoicing calculators, late-payment interest calculators and tools supporting VAT forms 303 and 390. At a conceptual level, these tools translate tax logic into interactive workflows: users provide relevant facts and the system returns guidance, classification or calculation results. The expected impact is improved taxpayer self-service, fewer avoidable errors, reduced demand for human assistance and greater consistency in first-level answers. The use case is significant because it combines several forms of automated assistance, from natural-language virtual assistants to rule-based calculators, within a single tax-administration support environment.

title: Chatbot - City of Rosealare
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The City of Roeselare receives frequent general enquiries from residents and visitors covering a wide range of municipal topics, from administrative services to local facilities. Managing these enquiries through traditional channels can be resource-intensive and limit availability outside office hours. This use case involves the municipal administration and citizens, with the objective of improving access to information and reducing pressure on staff. The solution is implemented as a general-purpose chatbot on the city’s website, designed to answer common questions using structured municipal information and predefined conversational flows. The chatbot is integrated with official content sources to ensure consistency and accuracy and acts as a first point of contact, guiding users to relevant information or services. The system improves responsiveness, provides immediate answers at any time, and reduces repetitive enquiries handled by staff. It enhances the overall digital experience for residents, supports more efficient use of municipal resources, and offers a scalable foundation for expanding digital citizen services over time.

title: Machine translation service of the justice system - Developing translation memory
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Ministerium der Justiz und für Europa (JUM)
source_description: Judicial authorities often need to understand foreign-language documents quickly, but legal translation is sensitive, time-critical and unsuitable for generic public translation platforms when quality, confidentiality and data protection are required. In the German justice context, the project responds to the recurring need for rapid work translations across many languages, where in-house expertise may not be available and manual translation can be too slow or costly for initial case assessment. The objective is to help justice staff search and understand foreign-language material more effectively, while preserving control over legal data. The implementation uses neural machine translation trained on translated texts relevant to the judicial environment. At a conceptual level, foreign-language documents are processed through a secure translation system that produces immediate work translations, enabling users to obtain an overview, search documents more precisely and decide whether certified or expert translation is needed. A further development goal is translation memory: texts already processed as input or output are recognised and reused, improving consistency and efficiency over time. In regular operation, the system is intended to shift towards a central translation platform. The expected impact is faster access to multilingual legal material, lower thresholds for preliminary translations, reduced dependence on external platforms and better support for time-critical judicial workflows. Because legal meaning is context-dependent, the service remains a support tool rather than a substitute for authoritative legal translation.

title: Asbestos suspect roofs from aerial imagery
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Identifying buildings with asbestos-containing roofing materials is essential for public health, environmental protection and safe renovation planning, yet manual inspections across large territories are costly and time-consuming. Public authorities require scalable methods to prioritise inspections and remediation efforts. Stakeholders include environmental agencies, municipal authorities and property owners. The objective is to detect and map roofs likely to contain asbestos using remote sensing data. High-resolution aerial imagery is processed using convolutional neural networks trained on labelled roof samples to classify material types based on texture, colour and spectral characteristics. Geospatial analysis techniques integrate detection outputs into geographic information systems, generating risk maps and inspection priority lists. The approach enhances coverage, reduces field survey costs and supports evidence-based environmental policy, enabling proactive risk management and more efficient allocation of inspection resources.

title: Smart Airports: Object detection and pose estimation for airport activity monitoring
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Airports manage complex ground operations involving aircraft, vehicles, equipment and personnel, where situational awareness and safety are critical. Manual monitoring through CCTV systems can be labour-intensive and reactive. Stakeholders include airport operators, ground handling services and safety authorities. The objective is to enhance operational efficiency and safety through automated activity monitoring. The system processes video streams using deep learning-based object detection models to identify aircraft, service vehicles and ground equipment, combined with pose estimation algorithms to interpret movement patterns and spatial relationships. Detected events are integrated into airport operational dashboards and alert systems, supporting real-time decision-making and post-event analysis. Expected impacts include improved safety compliance, faster incident detection, optimisation of ground handling processes and data-driven performance management across airport operations.

title: Mapping Vulnerable Populations with AI
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Policymakers require accurate, up-to-date insights into the spatial distribution of vulnerable populations to design targeted social, health and disaster response interventions. Conventional census-based methods may lack timeliness or granularity. Stakeholders include public authorities, social services and humanitarian organisations. The objective is to generate high-resolution vulnerability maps to support evidence-based policy and resource allocation. The approach integrates satellite imagery, demographic data and socio-economic indicators, applying machine learning models such as supervised classifiers and clustering algorithms to infer vulnerability proxies at fine spatial scales. Outputs are incorporated into geographic information systems and policy dashboards, enabling scenario analysis and targeted intervention planning. Anticipated benefits include improved targeting of public services, enhanced disaster preparedness and more equitable allocation of resources, supported by scalable data processing pipelines.

title: Deep learning-based mapping of tree density and species diversity in Flemish forests
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Forest managers require accurate, large-scale and up-to-date information on tree density and species diversity to support biodiversity conservation, climate adaptation strategies and sustainable timber management. Traditional field surveys are resource-intensive and limited in spatial coverage. Stakeholders include regional environmental authorities, forest agencies, researchers and land managers. The objective is to generate high-resolution forest structure and species diversity maps across Flemish territories to inform policy and operational planning. The solution processes multispectral and hyperspectral Earth observation imagery using convolutional neural networks trained on labelled forest plots to estimate tree density and classify species composition. Feature extraction techniques capture spectral, textural and structural patterns, while geospatial processing pipelines integrate outputs into geographic information systems for analysis and reporting. Expected impacts include broader spatial coverage than field surveys, reduced monitoring costs, improved ecological modelling and more precise targeting of conservation measures, supporting evidence-based forest governance.

title: Semi-Supervised Training to Improve Detection for Satellite Images
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Detecting objects and land features in satellite imagery often requires extensive labelled datasets, which are costly and time-consuming to produce. Limited annotated data can constrain model performance and scalability. Stakeholders include Earth observation analysts, public authorities and environmental monitoring agencies. The objective is to enhance detection accuracy while reducing dependency on fully labelled datasets. The approach combines supervised learning on annotated satellite images with semi-supervised techniques that leverage large volumes of unlabelled data. Methods such as pseudo-labelling, consistency regularisation and iterative retraining are applied to improve model generalisation. Detection models, typically based on deep convolutional architectures, are integrated into Earth observation processing workflows and evaluated against benchmark datasets. Anticipated benefits include improved detection performance, reduced labelling costs and faster deployment of monitoring applications across domains such as land use, infrastructure and environmental change.

title: AI-based compression on Sentinel 2 data
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The increasing volume of high-resolution satellite imagery places pressure on onboard storage, downlink bandwidth and ground processing infrastructure. Conventional image compression techniques may reduce file size but can limit downstream analytical value. Stakeholders include space agencies, data service providers and Earth observation users. The objective is to develop efficient onboard data reduction methods that preserve information relevant for analysis while reducing transmission requirements. The solution applies machine learning-based compression models, including autoencoder architectures, to learn compact feature representations of Sentinel-2 imagery. Additional onboard inference capabilities, such as cloud detection and information extraction, further reduce unnecessary data transmission. The compressed representations retain meaningful features suitable for lightweight downstream applications with reduced training data requirements. Expected impacts include lower data transmission costs, improved onboard processing efficiency and enhanced scalability of satellite missions without compromising analytical performance.

title: IADAS: project to identify individual tree and tree species based on EO and AI
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Monitoring forest ecosystems at individual tree level is essential for biodiversity assessment, carbon accounting and precision forestry, yet conventional surveys lack scalability. Stakeholders include environmental authorities, forestry services and research institutions. The objective is to identify and classify individual trees and their species using Earth observation data. The system integrates high-resolution satellite and aerial imagery with deep learning models for object detection and classification. Instance segmentation techniques isolate individual tree crowns, while classification networks assign species labels based on spectral and structural features. Outputs are georeferenced and incorporated into forest management systems, enabling detailed inventory mapping and change detection. Anticipated benefits include more granular forest inventories, improved carbon stock estimation and enhanced monitoring of ecosystem health, supporting data-driven environmental policy and sustainable land management.

title: Floodwater detection in urban areas powered by AI and SAR data
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Rapid and accurate detection of urban flooding is critical for emergency response, infrastructure protection and disaster risk management. Optical imagery is often hindered by cloud cover during extreme weather events. Stakeholders include civil protection authorities, municipalities and urban planners. The objective is to detect and map floodwater in near real time using synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data, which is resilient to weather conditions. The approach employs deep learning segmentation models trained on labelled SAR datasets to distinguish floodwater from urban surfaces, incorporating backscatter intensity and spatial texture features. Post-processing techniques refine boundaries and integrate outputs into geospatial platforms for emergency coordination. Expected impacts include faster situational awareness, improved targeting of response resources and enhanced resilience planning in flood-prone urban areas.

title: AI for Ethically Responsible Big Open Data (ETAPAS Case 1)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Publishing open datasets from public administration can create transparency and research value, but it can also expose privacy, fairness and re-identification risks when datasets are sensitive or can be combined with other information. The ETAPAS NoiPA use case examines these risks in relation to Italy’s NoiPA platform, which provides HR shared services to around 100 central and local administrations and is used by approximately 2.2 million civil servants. The objective is to identify ethical issues, legal risks and possible negative impacts linked to the analysis and publication of anonymised open datasets, then define mitigation actions consistent with the GDPR and public-sector accountability. The implementation applies the ETAPAS responsible-disruptive-technology framework to NoiPA open-data publication processes, focusing on privacy, fairness, transparency and risk management. At a conceptual level, the use case analyses how dataset combinations, proxy variables, biased sampling or apparently anonymised aggregates could reveal personal information or discriminatory patterns. The expected impact is a more robust procedure for publishing open data, stronger safeguards against re-identification, and better institutional awareness of ethical risks in public-data analytics. The use case is particularly relevant because it treats open-data governance not as a purely technical anonymisation task, but as an organisational process requiring continuous assessment, mitigation and documentation.

title: TrueBee (Digital forensics and blockchain tech against deceptive deepfake imaging in social media)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Synthetic and manipulated images can support fraud, harassment, disinformation and other harms, especially when they circulate rapidly on social platforms and users lack tools to assess provenance. TrueBees was created to help distinguish trustworthy images from deceptive deepfake or AI-generated visual content by combining forensic analysis with blockchain-based traceability. The project originated in 2022 through collaboration between U-Hopper and researchers from the University of Trento, with support from TruBlo, an EU-funded Next Generation Internet initiative. The implementation combines an AI module based on image-forensics methods with a blockchain registry. Users can upload an image through a web interface, receive a TrueBees score indicating trustworthiness, and have the image hash and corresponding score stored on a blockchain. At a conceptual level, the system links media-forensic classification, provenance recording, immutable timestamping and consultation of prior assessments. The expected impact is improved detection of deceptive images, stronger evidential trails for journalists or fact-checkers, and more trust in media verification workflows. The project white paper reports a prototype architecture and cites high classification performance, including a 97.99% figure in the publicly indexed summary, while the current TrueBees website presents the work as moving from research into a practical solution for AI-generated image detection.

title: ROXANNE – Real-Time Network, Text and Speaker Analytics for Combating Organised Crime
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Law enforcement agencies investigating organised and cross-border crime face large volumes of multilingual communications, multimedia content and complex relational data. Manual analysis can delay investigations and obscure network structures. Stakeholders include law enforcement authorities, judicial bodies and security agencies. The objective is to support the investigation and mitigation of organised crime through integrated analytical capabilities. The platform combines speech recognition, speaker identification, natural language processing and social network analysis to extract entities, detect relationships and generate visual maps of criminal networks. Interoperability mechanisms enable integration with existing investigative tools and databases. Expected impacts include accelerated investigations, reduced workload per case, improved identification of cross-border networks and enhanced analytical consistency within a defined legal framework.

title: EUIPO eSearch Plus
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Trade mark clearance depends on identifying earlier similar marks, including figurative marks whose similarity may arise from shapes, colours, textures and visual composition rather than text alone. EUIPO’s eSearch Plus image-search functionality supports users searching for similar-looking trade marks and designs in the European Union Intellectual Property Office’s databases. The operational problem is that manual image comparison and Vienna Classification searches can be time-consuming and may miss visually similar marks where keywords or classifications are incomplete. The implementation uses AI-based image-recognition technology to analyse uploaded or selected images and return visually similar trade marks or designs, which users can combine with criteria such as Nice and Vienna classifications. At a conceptual level, the system extracts visual features from an image, compares them with stored intellectual-property images and ranks results by similarity. The expected impact is more efficient trade mark clearance, better support for applicants and representatives, improved monitoring of potentially conflicting marks and stronger quality in IP-search workflows. The tool does not make legal decisions about likelihood of confusion or registrability; it supports human users by surfacing relevant prior rights and visual similarities for further legal assessment.

title: LEOS Case Study 1: Learning from examining corrigenda
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Legislative corrigenda reveal recurring drafting, formatting or reference problems that can undermine legal clarity and create costs when acts must be corrected and republished. This LEOS case study explored whether patterns in corrigenda could be identified and used to improve future legal drafting. The operational objective is to help drafters avoid avoidable errors, produce clearer legislation and reduce the administrative burden associated with post-publication corrections. The implementation uses legal-text analysis and hybrid AI methods applied to corpora of EU legislation and corrigenda, with particular attention to pattern detection and visualisation. At a conceptual level, the system clusters corrigenda, identifies recurring error types and translates those findings into possible smart functionalities for the LEOS legal drafting editor. These functionalities could warn drafters about risky structures, problematic references or repeated drafting patterns before publication. The expected impact is better regulation, clearer legislative texts, lower republication costs and faster availability of updated legislation. The case is part of a wider European Commission study on smart functionalities for LEOS, which piloted four use cases including corrigenda analysis, transposition, derogations and digital readiness. Public material describes the work as proof-of-concept research rather than a fully integrated production feature available across all EU legal drafting workflows.

title: LEOS Case 2: Transposition of EU directives
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Transposing EU directives into national law is legally complex because Member States must ensure that domestic provisions correctly reflect EU obligations while adapting them to national legal structures. This LEOS case study examines how AI-supported analysis could document and compare transposition more systematically. The pilot focuses on comparing selected directives with Italian domestic legislation to identify relationships between articles and detect where texts converge, diverge or omit relevant obligations. The implementation uses legal-text processing, similarity analysis, document comparison and visualisation tools within the broader LEOS smart-functionality framework. At a conceptual level, the system represents EU and national provisions, measures semantic or structural relationships between them, and highlights possible correspondences or gaps for legal experts to review. The expected impact is faster transposition analysis, improved documentation of legal implementation, better support for consolidation work and reduced risk that obligations are overlooked. Such functionality would not replace legal assessment, since transposition depends on legal interpretation, institutional context and national drafting conventions. Its value is to make comparison more systematic and navigable, helping experts focus on legally meaningful divergences. The European Commission’s LEOS smart-functionality study presents this case as one of four pilots exploring how hybrid AI can enhance legislative drafting and analysis.

title: LEOS Case 3: Derogations and transitory provisions
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Derogations and transitional provisions are essential in legislation, but they can make legal obligations difficult to understand because they modify when, where or under what conditions a rule applies. This LEOS case study explores how classification and legal-text analysis can help identify derogations, connect them to the obligations they modify, and extract temporal or conditional parameters. The operational problem is that drafters and users may struggle to trace the relationship between a general rule and exceptions that appear elsewhere in a legal act or in related legislation. The implementation uses AI classification, legal annotation and structured analysis of normative text. At a conceptual level, the system detects clauses that create derogations or transitional regimes, identifies the initial obligations affected, and extracts information such as dates, durations, conditions and applicability criteria. These outputs can then support drafting review, legal navigation and clearer presentation of exceptions. The expected impact is improved legal clarity, fewer interpretative errors, better traceability of temporal rules and stronger support for digital legal services. For policy and drafting teams, the value is not automatic legal interpretation but earlier visibility of how exceptions interact with obligations. The use case was included in the European Commission’s LEOS smart-functionality study alongside pilots on corrigenda, transposition and digital readiness.

title: LEOS Case 4: Checking for digital readiness
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Digital-ready legislation is increasingly important because laws and policies must be implementable through digital-by-default public services, data exchange and automated administrative processes. This LEOS case study investigates how smart drafting support could assess whether a legal act enables smooth digital implementation. The operational problem is that digital readiness is often assessed late or inconsistently, even though legislative wording can determine whether services can be automated, data can be reused and citizens can interact digitally with administrations. The proof of concept has three linked goals: calculate a digital-readiness index for a document, assess how normative citations and definitions propagate through the legal system, and develop a predictive model that estimates the index of new text fragments during drafting. The implementation uses legal-text analysis, citation analysis, modelling of definitions and predictive scoring. At a conceptual level, the system examines how a draft refers to other norms, how definitions affect implementation, and whether textual features support or hinder digital administration. The expected impact is earlier identification of provisions that may block digital-by-default services, better alignment between legal drafting and digital policy implementation, and more actionable feedback for drafters. The European Commission’s later LEOS work frames these cases as part of a broader move towards AI-based microservices that assist lawyers and policy developers while preserving human legal control.

title: Facial and official document recognition to deliver digital identities
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: AOC Consorci Administració Oberta de Catalunya
source_description: Digital public services require reliable remote identification, but traditional identity enrolment can depend on face-to-face registration that is inconvenient for citizens and difficult to scale. The Open Administration of Catalonia developed video-identification capabilities for obtaining digital identity credentials such as idCAT, using facial recognition and official-document recognition. The operational problem is to verify that the person applying remotely is the legitimate holder of the identity document and that the document is genuine, while maintaining security and privacy guarantees equivalent to in-person processes. The implementation asks the user to show both sides of an identity document, performs document checks, captures a selfie and compares the facial image with the image extracted from the document. The process also includes mobile-phone verification and later review by a trained operator. At a conceptual level, the system combines document image analysis, facial comparison, liveness or video evidence, consent capture, audit recording and human validation. The expected impact is easier access to digital identity credentials, reduced need for physical registration, improved inclusion for users who cannot attend offices and stronger uptake of digital public services. The case is relevant because it applies biometric matching in a controlled enrolment process, rather than in open-ended public-space surveillance.

title: Automating the energy poverty report
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: AOC Consorci Administració Oberta de Catalunya
source_description: Energy-poverty protection in Catalonia requires municipalities to determine whether households with unpaid utility bills are socially vulnerable before suppliers can cut off gas, water or electricity. This legal safeguard is essential for vulnerable citizens, but the administrative process is burdensome: utility companies send monthly lists in different formats, and municipal staff must manually check whether each person or household is at social or economic risk. AOC developed a pilot cloud service to standardise and automate the preparation of energy-vulnerability reports, improving interoperability between suppliers, municipalities and other administrations. The implementation validates and cross-checks data, manages requests through a single point and helps municipal social services process supplier consultations more efficiently. At a conceptual level, the system combines data reception, identity or case matching, rule-based verification, workflow automation and administrative interoperability to produce or support the required report. The expected impact is shorter processing time, fewer manual checks, more consistent treatment of households and better prevention of unlawful supply cuts. AOC reports that the pilot began in 2023 in the social-services areas of El Prat de Llobregat, Granollers and Amposta and validated technical and organisational feasibility in a real environment. The initiative’s public value is significant because it converts a rights-protection obligation into a more scalable and less error-prone administrative process.

title: JustizOnline
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Access to justice can be hindered when citizens and organisations must physically attend court offices or navigate several separate portals to find information, forms and register services. JustizOnline was created as Austria’s digital gateway to the judiciary, bringing together online information, procedural services and access to registers in a single service environment. The operational objective is to reduce unnecessary court visits and help users find relevant functions more quickly, whether they need information on proceedings, court services, forms, the Companies Register, the Land Register or judicial announcements. The implementation includes the chatbot “Justitia”, which guides users to the relevant information and can answer simple justice-related questions. At a conceptual level, the platform combines digital self-service, secure authentication, linked e-government interfaces, register access and conversational navigation. Integration with other Austrian e-government portals reduces duplication by allowing representation and authorisation information to be managed consistently across connected services. The expected impact is easier access to justice, faster completion of routine interactions, fewer administrative barriers and more efficient communication between the judiciary and the public. JustizOnline is important because it treats digital justice as a service ecosystem rather than a single online form, supporting both information needs and transactional access to judicial services.

title: AI for Weather Forecast in Trentino
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Local authorities need reliable warning systems for storms and fast-developing weather events because short lead times can affect emergency management, road safety, civil protection and public communication. In Trentino, the weather-forecasting AI use case focused on supporting MeteoTrentino and the Autonomous Province of Trento by improving the validation and use of weather-station data. The operational problem is that meteorological networks collect large volumes of real-time data from stations across the territory, but missing values, anomalous measurements and inconsistencies between nearby or similar-altitude stations can reduce the quality of warnings and forecasts. The implementation approach used artificial intelligence to identify errors or anomalies in weather data and improve the quality of archived and operational datasets. At a conceptual level, the system compares real-time station values with climatology, neighbouring stations and expected physical patterns, flagging values that may require correction or review before being used in alerts. The expected impact is more reliable weather warnings, better support for local administrators, improved emergency notifications and stronger data quality for climate and weather services. The use case is particularly relevant for mountain territories, where storms can develop rapidly and localised data quality is essential for timely action.

title: AI for Monitoring Glacier water flows
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Mountain water management depends on understanding how glacier melt contributes to downstream reservoirs, especially as climate change alters snow, ice and seasonal runoff dynamics. In Trentino, the Public AI Challenge applied artificial intelligence to the Careser Glacier in the Dolomites to reconstruct and forecast water flows towards reservoirs located downhill. The operational problem is that environmental monitoring datasets can contain gaps, missing measurements or discontinuities, making it harder for public authorities to understand hydrological conditions and anticipate changes in water availability. The implementation used dense neural-network techniques to estimate and reconstruct missing flow-rate data by learning relationships between available observations and expected water-flow patterns. At a conceptual level, the model supports prediction-measurement comparison: where sensor or historical data are incomplete, the neural network can infer plausible values and help reconstruct the hydrological series needed for environmental assessment. This creates a decision-support layer for monitoring glacier-fed systems, reservoir inflows and broader environmental status. The expected impact is improved continuity of hydrological monitoring, better evidence for water-resource planning and stronger public-sector capacity to use existing environmental datasets. The case is also relevant because it shows how an open-innovation challenge can introduce AI methods into provincial administration without requiring a full internal AI development team. Trentino Innovation describes the Public AI Challenge as a mechanism through which students develop predictive models and intelligent systems for public-administration needs.

title: AI for Water in Garda Lake area
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Wastewater-treatment and water-infrastructure operators need to manage variable inflows while controlling energy consumption, maintenance risks and service continuity. The Trentino / Garda-area AI for Water use case involved NIRIS and AI Challenge participants working on data from public water-treatment infrastructure to forecast incoming water variations using historical plant data and meteorological information. The operational problem is that treatment plants consume significant energy, and rainfall-driven changes in inflow can create operational peaks that are expensive or inefficient if not anticipated. The implementation used historical purifier data, weather data from the Stenico area and machine-learning methods to identify correlations between meteorological conditions, anthropic impact and plant behaviour. At a conceptual level, the system learns from past inflow, weather and operational patterns to forecast future water loads, enabling plant managers to prepare equipment and optimise energy use. The expected impact is lower energy consumption, better remote management, improved predictive maintenance and more resilient operation of depuration infrastructure. The use case is notable because it applies AI to a highly practical utility-management problem, where small percentage savings can matter because water-treatment systems operate continuously and at high energy intensity across many plants.

title: Fondo Caproni Project (AI for Culture)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Large cultural collections can become difficult to preserve and make accessible when the volume of material exceeds the capacity of manual cataloguing teams. The Caproni Collection contains approximately 200,000 historic photographs and aviation-related assets, including valuable images, memorabilia and documentation linked to Italian aeronautical history. The administrative challenge is to count, catalogue, classify, preserve, assess image quality and prepare selected materials for public exposure without imposing unsustainable labour requirements on cultural staff. The implementation explored the use of artificial intelligence to automate parts of the catalogue-building process, with particular emphasis on image-quality assessment and primary thematic classification. At a conceptual level, computer-vision models can identify damaged, blurred or low-quality photographs, group images into broad themes, support metadata generation and prioritise items requiring human review or conservation attention. This does not remove curatorial responsibility, but it can shift expert effort towards validation, interpretation and public presentation. The expected impact is faster digitisation, improved quality control, better searchability and broader public access to the Caproni heritage. Provincial material also confirms that the wider Caproni archive is being digitalised using PNRR funding, making the AI challenge part of a larger cultural-heritage digitisation trajectory. The case demonstrates how AI can support public cultural institutions when archive scale makes purely manual processes impractical.

title: ‘Outpost’ autonomous towers to monitor Greek islands for threats
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Remote island monitoring requires persistent situational awareness across land, sea and air, but continuous human surveillance can be costly, difficult and operationally limited. “Outpost” is an autonomous surveillance tower concept developed by Lambda Automata for monitoring Greek islands and other remote or sensitive areas. The operational problem is to detect and track diverse possible threats, including people, drones, vessels, aircraft, vehicles and smoke columns, across locations where infrastructure and personnel may be limited. The implementation uses autonomous towers equipped with sensors and artificial-intelligence software for geolocation, classification and tracking. At a conceptual level, the system observes the surrounding environment, processes sensor inputs, classifies detected objects or events and supports operators with alerts or situational information. The expected impact is stronger border and island surveillance, earlier detection of threats, reduced reliance on continuous manual observation and improved response coordination. The use case is security-focused and therefore distinct from civilian smart-city monitoring, but it illustrates a broader pattern in public-sector AI: distributed sensor infrastructure combined with automated classification to provide decision support in environments where rapid detection matters. It also raises typical governance issues around surveillance, oversight, proportionality and the human role in interpreting alerts.

title: I-CAN Police Crime Predictive System against Ndrangheta Network Crime
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Investigating organised and transnational criminal networks such as the ’Ndrangheta requires law enforcement agencies to analyse vast volumes of heterogeneous data, including communications, financial records, multimedia material and relational information. Traditional investigative tools struggle to cope with this complexity, leading to lengthy investigations and fragmented insights. INTERPOL launched the I-CAN initiative to strengthen the analytical capacity of police forces involved in combating Italian mafia-type organisations, supporting national and cross-border investigations. Stakeholders include INTERPOL, national police forces, judicial authorities and specialised organised crime units. The objective is to accelerate investigations, improve detection of hidden criminal relationships and enhance international cooperation. The system builds on technologies developed in EU-funded research projects such as ROXANNE, integrating network analysis, multilingual text and speech processing, and video analysis into a single interoperable platform. Data from multiple investigative sources are correlated to generate visual network graphs, behavioural patterns and relationship mappings, while remaining compatible with existing law enforcement databases and legal safeguards. I-CAN is operational as an INTERPOL cooperation framework, with tools progressively deployed to support investigations. Reported impacts include faster case analysis, improved situational awareness, reduced investigative workload per case and stronger cross-border intelligence sharing, contributing to more effective disruption of organised crime networks.

title: Venice Smart Control Room
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Managing Venice requires coordination across pedestrian flows, water traffic, road access, tourism pressure, public transport, weather, tides, security and parking. The Venice Smart Control Room was developed as an integrated urban “control tower” to aggregate information from sensors, video feeds, municipal systems and service operators. The operational problem is that Venice’s urban mobility is unusually complex: boats, pedestrians, road transport and tourist flows interact with weather and tidal risks in a fragile historic environment. The implementation, developed by the Municipality of Venice with TIM and local public-safety stakeholders, brings together data on people present in the city, types of boats in canals, water and road transport movement, tourist flows, forecasts and parking. At a conceptual level, the platform combines sensor networks, camera feeds, telecommunications data, urban analytics and predictive modelling to support monitoring and decision-making. It can help detect mobility issues, identify congestion, support public safety and provide evidence for planning. The expected impact is improved city management, faster operational coordination, better regulation of water and land mobility, and more informed decisions during high-pressure events. The case is significant because it combines heritage-city governance with smart-city operations in a territory where urban management has both everyday and exceptional-risk dimensions.

title: ChatGPT as a tool for Education
