title: AI4Gov - Trusted AI for Transparent Public Governance fostering Democratic Values (Spain)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Diputación Provincial de Badajoz (DPB) is a local government body coordinating municipalities to promote economic and social development across the province. As part of the AI4Gov project, the DPB pilot focuses on sustainable water cycle management, covering both drinking and wastewater. The council oversees 63 drinking water treatment plants serving 137,910 residents, along with wastewater treatment. The pilot aims to develop intelligent tools that leverage existing water management systems and data to identify inefficiencies—such as leaks, water losses, or off-hour energy use—enabling technicians to implement non-obvious, day-to-day solutions. The insights will also support policymakers in infrastructure planning, budget allocation, and optimising water services by training AI models to detect system malfunctions.
source_description: In the province of Badajoz, water-cycle management spans both drinking water and wastewater services, creating an operational challenge in identifying inefficiencies across a distributed infrastructure of treatment plants and networks. The provincial council oversees 63 drinking-water treatment plants serving 137,910 residents, alongside wastewater responsibilities, and needs better ways to detect leaks, losses, malfunctioning equipment and avoidable energy use. This pilot addresses that problem by helping technicians and policymakers use existing operational data more effectively in day-to-day management and long-term planning. The stakeholders include technical staff, infrastructure planners and provincial decision-makers, with the objective of improving service efficiency, targeting investment more intelligently and strengthening sustainable water management. The solution is implemented by building intelligent tools on top of existing water-management systems and datasets. At a conceptual level, the pilot uses analytical models to identify non-obvious inefficiencies, abnormal patterns and possible system malfunctions, translating these findings into operational insights for maintenance and service optimisation. The same evidence base can also inform budget allocation and infrastructure planning decisions. The expected impact is earlier detection of leaks and losses, more efficient energy use and better-informed technical interventions. More broadly, the pilot creates value by improving reliability in public water services, supporting sustainable infrastructure management and showing how existing municipal data can be turned into practical governance and operational benefits.

title: AI4Gov - Trusted AI for Transparent Public Governance fostering Democratic Values (Slovenia - Pilot1)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Many promising initiatives claim to contribute to the Sustainable Development Goals, but comparing them systematically and evaluating their ethical quality and practical impact at a global level is difficult. The Top100 Projects pilot, led by the Jožef Stefan Institute in partnership with UNESCO’s IRCAI, addresses this challenge by strengthening the application and evaluation process behind IRCAI’s annual showcase of one hundred initiatives linked to the 17 UN Sustainable Development Goals. The stakeholders include researchers, project applicants, evaluators and policymakers interested in socially beneficial innovation, with the objective of creating a more robust global platform that highlights projects not only for technical novelty but also for ethical practice and real-world value. The solution is implemented by enhancing the digital system through which initiatives are submitted, assessed and compared. At a conceptual level, the pilot applies structured analysis and evaluation support to make project selection more transparent, consistent and evidence-based, while giving greater visibility to considerations such as impact, fairness and responsible implementation. This transforms the showcase from a listing exercise into a stronger governance and learning instrument. The expected impact is improved quality and comparability of applications, better visibility for ethically grounded initiatives and more useful insights for organisations tracking innovation for the SDGs. More broadly, the pilot creates value by supporting a more credible and globally relevant framework for recognising technology-enabled projects with genuine societal benefit.

title: AI4Gov - Trusted AI for Transparent Public Governance fostering Democratic Values (Slovenia - Pilot2)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Policymakers and researchers need accessible ways to monitor progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals, yet relevant indicators are often dispersed across different sources and not always presented in a form that supports rapid understanding or action. The JSI SDG Observatory pilot addresses this challenge by creating a clearer and more usable evidence base for tracking sustainability progress. The stakeholders include researchers, policymakers and institutions working on SDG implementation, with the objective of making indicators easier to gather, visualise and interpret so that they can inform strategy, monitoring and public decision-making more effectively. The solution is implemented as a web-based toolkit that aggregates and displays SDG-related indicators in a structured and accessible format. At a conceptual level, the observatory combines data collection, harmonisation and visual analytics so that users can explore trends, compare indicators and identify areas requiring policy attention. This turns fragmented sustainability information into a more coherent monitoring environment and supports more timely use of evidence in governance. The expected impact is better visibility of SDG progress, improved usability of indicator data and stronger support for evidence-based policy discussions. More broadly, the pilot creates value by enhancing transparency in sustainability monitoring, reducing friction in the use of complex datasets and giving policymakers and researchers a more practical tool for understanding where action is succeeding and where additional intervention may be needed.

title: AI4Gov - Trusted AI for Transparent Public Governance fostering Democratic Values (Slovenia - Pilot3)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: National strategies on advanced digital technologies are now widespread, but understanding how these policy documents address issues such as bias, fairness and responsible governance remains a complex analytical task. The OECD AI policy-analysis pilot addresses this challenge by helping institutions examine national strategies in a more systematic way, with particular attention to how bias is treated in policy frameworks. The stakeholders include policymakers, governance researchers and organisations interested in responsible digital regulation, with the objective of improving understanding of policy quality, highlighting best practices and supporting more informed development of future governance approaches. The solution is implemented through analytical and visual tools that examine national policy documents and generate comparative summaries of how bias-related questions are addressed. At a conceptual level, the pilot combines policy-text analysis, thematic categorisation and visual presentation methods to reconcile large numbers of documents and make differences in emphasis, completeness and good practice easier to identify. These outputs can then support reflection and policy learning rather than replacing expert interpretation. The expected impact is clearer visibility of policy strengths and gaps, better benchmarking across national strategies and stronger support for more ethical policy development. More broadly, the pilot creates value by improving the transparency and usability of policy analysis, helping decision-makers move from broad strategy statements towards more concrete, informed and responsible approaches to governance.

title: AI4Gov - Trusted AI for Transparent Public Governance in Transport (Greece - Pilot1)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Vari-Voula-Vouliagmeni (VVV) is a municipality in eastern Attica with 50,585 residents and a significant influx of seasonal and weekend visitors drawn to its coastline, cultural sites, and events. The municipality faces the challenge of optimising policies across transportation, waste management, sanitation, healthcare, security, and public works to adapt dynamically to varying citizen flows, including spatiotemporal patterns and ad-hoc situations like severe weather. Coordinating updates across domains—for example, aligning parking management with waste collection—is crucial. Within AI4Gov, VVV proposed a use case focuing on parking ticket monitoring. The aim is to predict citizen flows and design efficient, multi-domain policies to manage people and vehicle movement effectively.

source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Vari-Voula-Vouliagmeni (VVV) is a municipality in eastern Attica with 50,585 residents and a significant influx of seasonal and weekend visitors drawn to its coastline, cultural sites, and events. The municipality faces the challenge of optimising policies across transportation, waste management, sanitation, healthcare, security, and public works to adapt dynamically to varying citizen flows, including spatiotemporal patterns and ad-hoc situations like severe weather. Coordinating updates across domains—for example, aligning parking management with waste collection—is crucial. Within AI4Gov, VVV proposed a use case focusing on waste management. title: Machine Learning towards a greener grid
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Electricity systems with high shares of wind and solar generation require more accurate forecasting because renewable output changes with weather and time of day. The “Towards a Greener Grid” project applied machine-learning and statistical forecasting to help National Grid Electricity System Operator balance the British electricity system more efficiently. The operational problem is that inaccurate renewable forecasts can force the system operator to procure more reserve or rely on backup generation, increasing costs and emissions. The implementation developed improved solar and wind forecasting approaches using data science methods created with researchers from the Alan Turing Institute. At a conceptual level, the models learn from historical generation, weather and system data to predict renewable output more accurately, especially for day-ahead operational planning. The expected impact is better balancing of supply and demand, reduced reliance on fossil-fuel backup, lower consumer costs and increased ability to integrate renewable energy into the grid. The use case is significant because it applies AI to a critical infrastructure function where forecast accuracy has direct operational, environmental and economic consequences. It demonstrates how machine learning can support decarbonisation not by producing energy directly, but by helping the grid absorb cleaner generation more reliably.

title: TrackIT Blockchain - The value chain for the traceability of Made in Italy
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Exporting companies often need to prove origin, quality, sustainability and production history to international buyers, while the “Made in Italy” brand is exposed to counterfeiting and misleading imitation. TrackIT Blockchain, promoted by the Italian Trade Agency, supports selected Italian exporters by providing blockchain-based supply-chain traceability connected to consumer-facing product information. The objective is to help companies, especially SMEs, communicate the authenticity and value of their products in sectors such as agri-food, fashion, cosmetics, furniture and design. The implementation records key production and provenance data on a blockchain and links that information to goods through QR codes or smart tags. At a conceptual level, the platform connects supply-chain events, company narratives, certification information and immutable distributed-ledger records, allowing consumers or business partners to scan a product and view its verified story. The expected impact is stronger consumer trust, better protection of the Made in Italy brand, improved export promotion and more transparent communication of quality and sustainability characteristics. Official ICE material presents TrackIT as a service that registers production data in blockchain and allows consumers to visualise the history of the product and company by scanning a smart tag. ICE also states that the project makes a standard traceability service available to 500 companies, with current participation deadlines extended into 2026.

title: Block4Mat - Blockchain technology for the ceramics and construction supply chain
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Construction-material supply chains involve multiple actors, technical certifications, environmental requirements and lifecycle information that can be difficult to trace reliably from raw materials to final use or disposal. BLOCH4MAT applies blockchain technology to strategic construction-material sectors in Emilia-Romagna, including ceramic tiles, bricks and composite materials. The project’s objective is to analyse where blockchain can bring effective advantages to producers and stakeholders, then develop a prototype platform able to make product information traceable, secure, unambiguous and non-falsifiable across the lifecycle. The implementation is coordinated by Centro Ceramico and involves scientific partners such as TEKNEHUB, CIRI-EC and Consorzio Futuro in Ricerca, together with companies including InnovationCHAIN and other industry actors. At a conceptual level, the platform records supply-chain information on materials, production steps, processing, certification and possibly end-of-life phases, while also exploring integration with BIM and other digital construction tools. The expected impact is greater transparency, anti-counterfeiting protection, process optimisation, improved coordination among construction actors and better availability of verified material data for digital building workflows. Public project material states that the central activity is the creation of a prototype blockchain platform for ceramic slabs, brick products and fibrous composite materials.

title: BIM-To-Digital Twin: towards predictive and intelligent management of real estate assets
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Large public real-estate portfolios require reliable information on buildings, maintenance needs, systems, spaces and performance, but asset data are often fragmented across static drawings, spreadsheets and facility-management systems. The University of Florence’s BIM-To-Digital Twin work explores how Building Information Modelling and Internet of Things data can support predictive and intelligent management of university real estate. The operational problem is to move from static building records to dynamic information environments that help managers understand current conditions and anticipate interventions. The implementation uses Infocad.FM and BIM tools to integrate property data, facility-management workflows and sensor information. At a conceptual level, BIM provides structured building geometry and asset information, while IoT data adds time-varying information on use, condition or performance. Combining these layers creates the basis for a digital twin that can support maintenance planning, data interoperability and lifecycle decision-making. The expected impact is more efficient facility management, safer and more reliable building data, improved maintenance scheduling and better long-term management of university assets. The use case is important because it applies digital-twin concepts to everyday building operations, where value comes from connecting existing asset knowledge with live data and predictive management.

title: Digital Twin of the City of Parma
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Urban administrations need reliable spatial data to evaluate planning decisions, manage public assets, support maintenance and assess environmental impacts before interventions are carried out. Parma’s Digital Twin creates a detailed three-dimensional representation of the city, including buildings, roads, green areas, infrastructure, technological networks and public assets. The operational problem is that many municipal decisions require field surveys, fragmented datasets or partial information, which can slow down planning and reduce transparency. The implementation uses panoramic surveys, geolocated point clouds and high-precision data acquisition across road and pedestrian areas, creating a shared digital model for municipal departments. At a conceptual level, the digital twin allows technical staff to inspect, measure, classify and simulate parts of the city from the office, while also supporting predictive analysis for weather events, flood risk, urban greenery and maintenance priorities. The expected impact is more efficient territorial management, faster asset inventories, better planning of public services, stronger climate-adaptation capacity and improved citizen participation. The project is also connected to Parma’s carbon-neutrality objectives, because a shared digital model can help administrators evaluate the environmental consequences of policies and infrastructure decisions before they are implemented.

title: BeTwin - Building Digital Twin for Built Heritage Performance-based Management
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Large building portfolios and heritage assets require management decisions that balance maintenance, energy performance, comfort, functional needs, costs and environmental impact. BeTwin addresses this challenge by developing digital-twin methods and tools for performance-based management of built heritage and complex real-estate portfolios. The operational problem is that facility managers often work with disconnected sources of information: BIM models may describe geometry and assets, energy simulations may model performance, IoT systems may capture real-time conditions, and financial or functional data may be managed separately. BeTwin proposes an integrated digital ecosystem that combines Building Information Modelling, Building Performance Simulation and Internet of Things data to support decision-making. At a conceptual level, the project creates digital twins that connect building characteristics, occupancy, comfort, energy use and performance indicators, making it possible to assess trade-offs between functional demand, environmental performance and operational cost. The expected impact is better building management, improved energy efficiency, more informed maintenance planning and easier use of advanced analytics by non-technical users. The use case is particularly relevant for universities, schools, museums, flexible offices and other multifunctional buildings where space use is intermittent and management decisions have both economic and sustainability implications.

title: 4D digital model for the archaeological site of Cencelle
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Archaeological sites require long-term monitoring because environmental exposure, structural decay and excavation activity can progressively change the condition of ruins. The Cencelle project develops a 4D digital model of the archaeological site near Tarquinia to support conservation, documentation and preventive management. The operational problem is that traditional site records may not capture change over time with enough precision to identify degradation patterns or plan interventions proactively. The implementation combines drone-based multisensor surveys, photogrammetry, thermal imaging, laser scanning, on-site documentation and historical-architectural analysis. At a conceptual level, the model creates a digital twin of the site that includes spatial and temporal dimensions: researchers can compare conditions across survey periods and identify changes in structures, materials or environmental impacts. The expected impact is better conservation planning, more precise monitoring, improved documentation for researchers and administrators, and a stronger basis for restoration or preventive maintenance decisions. The use case is significant because it applies digital-twin methods to cultural heritage management, where the objective is not only visualisation but also systematic safeguarding of fragile archaeological remains over time.

title: Milan Smart City Project: 2,500 km of roads surveyed by Cyclomedia mapping
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Smart-city governance depends on accurate, up-to-date information about the physical public realm, including roads, signage, lighting, traffic signals, street furniture, accessibility features and infrastructure assets. Milan worked with Cyclomedia and other geospatial partners to map approximately 2,500 kilometres of urban roads and establish the basis for a city digital twin. The operational problem was that planning, maintenance and street management require detailed spatial data, but urban information can become outdated quickly and may be distributed across multiple municipal databases. The implementation used mobile mapping technology, 360-degree panoramic imagery and geospatial data capture to record the city’s street environment at scale. At a conceptual level, the project creates an immersive, measurable digital representation of Milan’s road network and associated assets, enabling staff to inspect, update and analyse the city without always needing field visits. The expected impact is more efficient maintenance, better urban planning, improved management of public space, stronger support for mobility and safety projects, and a more complete foundation for future smart-city applications. The use case is relevant because it shows that a digital twin often begins with high-quality baseline mapping before advanced simulations or AI services can be built on top.

title: Digital twins in cultural heritage conservation: Notre-Dame Cathedral
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Major heritage monuments require detailed documentation for conservation, maintenance and public interpretation, especially where restoration history, structural complexity and visitor pressure create long-term management challenges. The Notre-Dame digital twin project aims to create a highly detailed virtual replica of the cathedral using AI-supported processing of imagery and spatial data. The operational objective is to build an accurate digital record of the cathedral’s interior and exterior, including roof, vaults, stonework, stained glass and architectural details, so that heritage professionals can support conservation and future maintenance. The implementation combines drone imagery, laser scanning, photogrammetry, high-resolution photographs and AI algorithms to integrate the data into a coherent digital model. At a conceptual level, the digital twin acts as both a conservation record and an immersive access tool: it can document physical condition, support analysis of the building fabric and allow remote users to explore the monument virtually. The expected impact is improved heritage preservation, more informed maintenance planning, broader public access and stronger resilience against future damage or loss. The case illustrates how AI and digital twins can support cultural heritage by making complex architectural information usable for both specialists and the public.

title: Digital Twin in the City of Matera
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: House of Emerging Technologies of Matera (CTE Matera)
source_description: Urban governance requires integrated knowledge of mobility, infrastructure, energy, waste, environmental risks, built heritage and public services, but these domains are often managed through separate datasets and systems. The Digital Twin of Matera creates a virtual representation of the city to support planning, management and sustainable regeneration. The operational problem is to provide city authorities, researchers, businesses and citizens with a shared digital environment where real-time and historical urban information can be analysed together. The implementation is developed through the Casa delle Tecnologie Emergenti di Matera and the Italian National Research Council, integrating sensors, geospatial information, software modules, data storage, computational services and user interfaces. At a conceptual level, the digital twin functions as a living lab: it combines data and models to simulate urban phenomena, monitor conditions and support decisions about mobility, buildings, energy efficiency, waste flows, extreme weather and cultural heritage. The expected impact is more proactive city management, better forecasting of urban dynamics, improved resource efficiency and stronger public understanding of the city’s systems. The use case is significant because it links digital-twin technology with a UNESCO heritage urban environment, where innovation must also support cultural and environmental stewardship.

title: Digital Twin of the Italian soil
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Italian Ministry of Environment and Energy Security (MASE)
source_description: Land and soil management require detailed information on terrain morphology, surface features and subsurface characteristics, especially in a country exposed to landslides, floods, erosion and complex geological risks. The Digital Twin of the Italian Soil project aims to create a high-resolution national model of Italy’s territory through collaboration between Leonardo, its subsidiary e-GEOS and the Italian Ministry of Environment and Energy Security. The operational problem is that environmental planning and risk prevention depend on consistent, accurate and up-to-date geophysical data, but such data are often fragmented across surveys, agencies and local systems. The implementation uses aerial LiDAR, aerogravimetric surveys and geospatial processing to build detailed maps of terrain elevation, ground surfaces and subsurface features. At a conceptual level, the digital twin becomes a national monitoring and prediction layer that can support analysis of land stability, hydrogeological risk, environmental conditions and territorial change. The expected impact is stronger prevention of natural hazards, better planning of mitigation measures, more informed land-use policy and improved resilience of infrastructure and communities. The use case is significant because it applies digital-twin thinking at national territorial scale, moving from city or building models to a strategic environmental data infrastructure.

title: DESIGN-IT (DEcision Science desIGN platform for digItal Twins)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Industrial organisations increasingly need to model products, machines and processes while integrating simulation, optimisation, machine learning and predictive maintenance into operational decision-making. DESIGN-IT was created to develop a Decision Science Design Platform that enables users to build and manage digital twins through a low-code approach. The operational problem is that advanced digital-twin and AI applications often require programming expertise, limiting adoption by engineers, designers and industrial professionals who understand the process but cannot build complex software pipelines. The implementation aims to provide a drag-and-drop platform where users can combine modelling, simulation, data management, optimisation and explainable AI components. At a conceptual level, the system acts as a configurable environment for creating digital twins at product, component and process levels, then connecting them with AI pipelines for prediction, maintenance and operational optimisation. The expected impact is faster development of industrial AI applications, greater accessibility for non-programmers, improved human-machine collaboration and smarter decision-making in automated manufacturing and robotics contexts. The use case is relevant because it treats digital-twin design itself as a serviceable workflow, making advanced analytics easier to reuse and adapt across industrial domains.

title: Adriano - first robot employee of the Italian Public Administration
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Public-facing offices and cultural-institutional venues often need to welcome visitors, provide orientation and answer routine questions while also presenting public administration as innovative and accessible. Adriano was introduced by the Rome Chamber of Commerce on 28 march 2025 as an embodied AI robot designed to support reception and information services at the Temple of Vibia Sabina and Hadrian. The operational problem is to assist citizens and tourists in a high-profile public setting through a system that can recognise surroundings, communicate naturally and guide users towards relevant information. The implementation combines robotics, computer vision, artificial intelligence, conversational capabilities and advanced robotic hands or actuators. At a conceptual level, Adriano perceives people and objects, adapts its movement and behaviour in real time, and interacts with users in Italian and English to provide information about the Chamber of Commerce, the building and related services. The expected impact is improved visitor reception, experimentation with embodied public-service AI, stronger accessibility of institutional information and public demonstration of robotics within administration. The use case is significant because it moves AI assistance from a website or call centre into a physical public space, testing how humanoid robots can support service interaction and cultural communication.

title: RePAIR – Reconstructing the Past: Artificial Intelligence and Robotics meet Cultural Heritage
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Archaeological restoration can involve thousands of damaged fragments whose manual reassembly is extremely slow, uncertain and resource-intensive. RePAIR addresses this problem by combining artificial intelligence, computer vision and robotics to support the reconstruction of fragmented artefacts such as frescoes, vases and amphorae. The operational challenge is that many cultural objects are excavated as large collections of worn, incomplete or irregular pieces, making traditional puzzle-solving methods impractical at scale. The implementation develops technologies that digitise fragments, analyse their shape and visual features, identify possible matches and physically assist reconstruction through robotic systems. At a conceptual level, the project creates a human-in-the-loop restoration workflow: AI helps reduce the search space and propose fragment relationships, while archaeologists and conservators retain expert control over interpretation and validation. The expected impact is faster restoration, recovery of artefacts that would otherwise remain inaccessible, improved documentation and new research capacity for cultural heritage institutions. The project’s significance lies in bringing together advanced robotics and archaeological expertise, demonstrating how automation can support restoration without replacing scholarly judgement or conservation ethics.

title: EBB_AI : Co-creation-as-a-Service
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Cultural institutions and artists face growing demand to use generative AI creatively while protecting copyright, attribution and fair compensation. EBB_AI proposes a Co-creation-as-a-Service platform that allows museums, art schools, contemporary artists, film producers and other cultural partners to create AI-assisted outputs while maintaining rights-holder traceability. The operational problem is that generative AI can remix or derive value from cultural datasets without clear governance, making it difficult for institutions and artists to control use, monetise outputs or ensure recognition. The implementation combines co-creation tools, cultural partner databases, AI content-generation workflows and a blockchain- or NFT-based copyright-management layer. At a conceptual level, users interact with curated cultural assets through AI tools, while the platform records rights information, supports automated compensation and enables digital merchandise or poster creation under controlled conditions. The expected impact is more responsible use of AI in the cultural sector, new revenue models for institutions and artists, improved user engagement and stronger safeguards against untraceable reuse of protected works. The case is important because it addresses one of the central tensions in creative AI: enabling experimentation while embedding mechanisms for copyright, inclusivity, bias reduction and stakeholder compensation.

title: IT4LIA – Italy for Artificial Intelligence
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Advanced AI development requires large-scale computing infrastructure, high-quality data services and technical support that many public administrations, SMEs, start-ups and research organisations cannot build independently. IT4LIA is Italy’s AI Factory initiative, designed to provide national and European users with AI-optimised supercomputing capacity, data-processing tools and related services. The operational problem is that AI adoption in strategic sectors depends on access to high-performance infrastructure and expert support, not only on algorithms. The implementation centres on the CINECA data centre in Bologna, where a new AI-optimised supercomputer is being integrated with existing high-performance computing and cloud systems. At a conceptual level, the factory provides a shared infrastructure layer for developing, training, testing and deploying AI applications in sectors such as agritech, cybersecurity, manufacturing, climate, earth sciences and public administration. The expected impact is stronger Italian and European AI competitiveness, wider access to advanced computing, accelerated innovation by SMEs and start-ups, and better translation of research into operational AI services. The initiative is significant because it treats AI capacity as public strategic infrastructure, linked to EuroHPC and national industrial-policy objectives.

title: 5G4LIVES – 5G for a Better Tomorrow: Protecting Lives and the Environment in Riga
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Riga State City municipal Agency “Riga Digital Agency”
source_description: Public-safety and environmental-monitoring teams need rapid situational awareness across beaches, parks, waterways and other large open areas, but manual patrols cannot continuously cover all locations. 5G4LIVES applies 5G-enabled automated drone operations to support the Riga Municipal Police and improve emergency detection, prevention and response. The operational problem is that accidents, dangerous behaviour or environmental risks can develop quickly in public spaces, while response teams may lack real-time visibility over wide zones. The implementation uses drones equipped with high-resolution and thermal cameras, connected through 5G infrastructure to transmit data and support automated or semi-automated flights. At a conceptual level, the system combines UAVs, high-bandwidth connectivity, remote monitoring, image capture and command-centre workflows. This allows authorities to inspect areas more efficiently, detect incidents faster and coordinate response without relying exclusively on ground patrols. The expected impact is improved public safety, faster emergency response, better environmental monitoring and reduced workload for municipal police. The case is relevant because it links 5G deployment to concrete public-interest services rather than connectivity as an abstract infrastructure upgrade.

title: 5G4LIVES – 5G for a Better Tomorrow: Protecting Lives and the Environment in Torino
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Urban emergency management in hilly and environmentally exposed areas requires rapid situational awareness, especially where floods, landslides, fires or missing-person incidents can evolve faster than conventional ground patrols can respond. In Turin, 5G4LIVES applies next-generation connectivity, drones and remote-sensing technologies to improve public safety and environmental monitoring. The operational problem is that emergency teams need reliable real-time information from difficult or risky areas, while drone missions require secure, low-latency communication, accurate tracking and integration with other data sources. The implementation uses 5G-enabled UAV operations, infrared sensors, satellite-data interoperability and anti-drone-hacking technologies to support aerial monitoring and vulnerability assessment. At a conceptual level, the system creates an aerial situational-awareness layer: drones collect visual, thermal and environmental information, while 5G connectivity supports command and control, mission planning, real-time tracking and rapid transmission of evidence to emergency operators. The expected impact is faster search-and-rescue response, better fire and hazard detection, improved assessment of vulnerable areas and stronger preparedness for natural disasters. The case is significant because it links 5G deployment to concrete municipal resilience needs, demonstrating how advanced connectivity can support both emergency operations and environmental protection.

title: 5GENIUS – A Next-Generation Network for the University College of Ghent
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Universities increasingly need connectivity infrastructure that can support data-intensive research, immersive teaching and experimentation across multiple applied domains. 5GENIUS creates a private 5G network at University College Ghent, turning the campus into a smart laboratory for education, research and innovation. The operational problem is that advanced applications in healthcare, agriculture, logistics, mobility, Geo-ICT and 3D prototyping require reliable bandwidth, low latency and secure local connectivity that conventional campus networks may not always provide. The implementation deploys a private 5G non-standalone network at the Schoonmeersen campus, enabling researchers, students and innovation partners to test digital services under realistic conditions. At a conceptual level, the campus becomes an experimentation environment where 5G supports connected sensors, drones, augmented and virtual reality, data-intensive laboratory work, e-health applications and smart-farming use cases. The expected impact is improved training, stronger applied research capacity, faster testing of digital services and closer links between education, technology providers and sectoral innovation. The case is relevant because it treats university infrastructure as a platform for wider regional innovation, allowing students and researchers to work with connectivity conditions similar to those required in future industrial and public-service environments.

title: 5G-TERRA – 5G infrastructure and services for public interest and social inclusion
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: WINGS ICT Solutions Technologies Pliroforikis Kai Epikoinonion Anonymi Etaireai
source_description: Remote rural areas and islands often face weaker connectivity, making it harder to provide modern healthcare, education and civil-protection services. 5G-TERRA addresses this digital divide by deploying 5G infrastructure in sparsely populated areas of central Greece and Greek islands. The operational problem is that communities with limited broadband access may struggle to benefit from telemedicine, remote monitoring, immersive learning or real-time emergency-alert systems. The implementation combines new 5G radio access equipment, upgraded backhaul links, cloud and edge resources, and a transition from non-standalone to standalone 5G architecture. At a conceptual level, the network becomes an enabling layer for three public-interest domains: digital healthcare, smart and green schools, and public protection. In healthcare, it supports wearable monitoring, video links for paramedics, remote medical support, electronic records and clinical decision support. In education, it enables connectivity, environmental monitoring and AR/VR learning. In civil protection, it supports wildfire and flood detection through IoT, AI, cameras, drones and risk-prediction tools. The expected impact is more equal access to essential services, better emergency preparedness, improved educational quality and stronger social inclusion for communities that would otherwise remain digitally underserved.

title: Hola 5G Oulu - Private 5G network at an operating European Hospital
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Hospitals require secure, resilient and high-capacity wireless connectivity to support real-time clinical information, wearable devices and advanced visualisation in sensitive environments such as operating theatres and wards. Hola 5G Oulu establishes a private 5G network at Oulu University Hospital to create a healthcare environment where wireless wearable solutions and data-sharing applications can be safely tested and used. The operational problem is that clinicians often need to retrieve patient data, imaging and vital-sign information through fixed terminals or fragmented systems, which can reduce time spent with patients and complicate workflows during procedures. The implementation provides a robust private network initially covering selected operating theatres and a patient-ward floor, supporting research and development of wearable and visualisation solutions. At a conceptual level, the network acts as a secure wireless backbone for AR/VR devices, live patient-data access, medical imaging retrieval and remote specialist guidance. The expected impact is faster clinical information access, reduced workload for nurses and doctors, improved support during surgery and stronger resilience for digital hospital operations. The case is important because it tests private 5G in a functioning hospital, where connectivity must meet strict safety, reliability and continuity requirements.

title: SmartPort Ploce - Enchancing public services through a private 5G network
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Ports need reliable real-time information on cargo, vehicles, vessels, safety risks and environmental conditions, but traditional communications infrastructure may not provide the latency, resilience or coverage needed for advanced smart-port applications. SmartPort Ploče aims to transform the Port of Ploče into a 5G-enabled smart port through a dedicated private standalone network across the port area. The operational problem is that port authorities and operators must coordinate logistics, safety, security and environmental monitoring across a complex industrial space with moving assets and high operational risk. The implementation combines private 5G connectivity with real-time location systems, video analytics, sensor-based monitoring, smart cameras, thermal imaging and weather-monitoring tools. At a conceptual level, the network becomes a secure digital layer connecting port assets, vehicles, vessels, cargo operations and safety systems. The expected impact is more efficient cargo handling, better traffic coordination, faster incident detection, improved fire and pollution monitoring, and stronger operational resilience. The case is relevant because it applies 5G not only as general connectivity, but as an enabling infrastructure for port automation, safety management and environmental supervision in a strategic maritime-logistics setting.

title: 5G in Healthcare – Northern Region (PT) (5G Healthcare (PT))
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Healthcare systems need rapid information exchange between emergency vehicles, hospitals, specialists and remote patients, particularly where time-critical decisions depend on video, imaging or live vital-sign data. The 5G Healthcare project in Portugal’s Northern Region deploys standalone 5G infrastructure to support advanced clinical services across the Porto district and surrounding healthcare network. The operational problem is that ambulances, helicopters, hospitals and remote-care environments require secure, high-capacity and low-latency communication for medical data, video streaming and specialist input. The implementation supports connected emergency vehicles, robotic-surgery live streaming, telemedicine, remote patient monitoring, virtual-reality therapy in intensive care and off-site anatomical pathology diagnosis. At a conceptual level, the 5G network acts as a clinical connectivity layer: it enables real-time data exchange, supports medical training, connects IoT monitoring devices and allows high-resolution diagnostic material to be transmitted to specialists. The expected impact is better emergency triage, faster diagnosis, improved patient monitoring, reduced avoidable hospitalisation, more effective medical training and enhanced recovery support for conscious ICU patients. The case is significant because it combines emergency medicine, hospital innovation, remote diagnostics and immersive therapeutic applications within one regional 5G healthcare ecosystem.

title: 5G.RURAL - Rural connectivity
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Rural communities often face persistent connectivity gaps that affect access to healthcare, education, business development, tourism, cultural services and smart-agriculture applications. 5G.RURAL addresses this problem by deploying shared 5G connectivity in parts of the Alentejo region of Portugal, with the objective of reaching villages and low-density areas that lack adequate digital infrastructure. The operational problem is that conventional operator-led deployment may be commercially difficult in sparsely populated territories, while public services and local businesses increasingly require reliable high-speed connectivity. The implementation is based on a neutral-host model, allowing infrastructure to be shared by multiple operators or service providers rather than duplicated. At a conceptual level, 5G becomes a common rural-service backbone supporting telemedicine, remote care for older people, immersive learning, smart farming, livestock monitoring, energy-efficiency tools, tourism and local economic development. The expected impact is reduced territorial inequality, improved access to essential services, stronger rural innovation and better conditions for digital public-service delivery in areas that would otherwise remain underserved. The case is important because it frames 5G as an inclusion and territorial-cohesion tool, not only as an urban or industrial technology.

title: 5GMHI – Smart healthcare
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Urban healthcare and hospital-estate management both require fast, reliable and secure data exchange, from ambulance triage and equipment tracking to smart-building control and emergency response. 5GMHI deploys a private 5G network in Stockholm to support medical services, emergency response and building-management use cases. The operational problem is that hospitals and emergency services need low-latency video, real-time asset location, resilient communication and connected sensors, while hospital buildings also require better monitoring of energy and indoor-air conditions. The implementation enables five main use cases: drone delivery of automated external defibrillators, real-time location of hospital beds and infusion pumps, video communication between ambulances and emergency departments, AR/VR integration of BIM and GIS for building management, and connected HVAC monitoring through IoT and digital twins. At a conceptual level, the private 5G network supports both clinical and infrastructure intelligence, linking people, equipment, vehicles, buildings and emergency responders through a secure connectivity layer. The expected impact is improved patient safety, faster emergency response, better hospital preparedness, reduced staff time spent locating equipment and more efficient management of buildings and energy use. The case is relevant because it integrates healthcare innovation with smart-estate management rather than treating them as separate digital-transformation tracks.

title: TUKE 5GSC - TUKE 5G Infrastructure for Smart Communities
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Research and industrial environments need connectivity that can support real-time location, automated workflows, energy monitoring and low-latency data exchange. TUKE 5GSC deploys a private standalone 5G network at the Technical University of Košice to support smart-community applications in logistics and energy management. The operational problem is that manufacturing and campus environments require accurate tracking of assets, production flows and energy consumption, but conventional networks may not provide the performance and reliability required for industrial-grade automation. The implementation uses C-band spectrum, indoor radio units, antennas, basebands, network controllers and cloud-based management to create a dedicated 5G environment. At a conceptual level, the network enables two principal use cases. The smart-logistics use case uses real-time location systems to optimise manufacturing and delivery processes, while the smart-metering use case provides real-time analytics on energy use, efficiency and automated workflows supported by machine learning. The expected impact is more efficient production logistics, better visibility of energy consumption, improved reliability of monitoring systems and a replicable 5G model for university-industry experimentation. The case is significant because it positions a technical university as a testbed for industrial 5G applications that can later inform smart-community or manufacturing deployments.

title: ED5GE - 5G Edge Enabled Smart Communities for Green Transformation in the North Project
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Cities of Luleå, Boden, Skellefteå and Uppsala
source_description: Northern Sweden’s green and digital transition requires connectivity that can support emergency response, port logistics, waste management, city traffic monitoring and precision agriculture across different types of communities. ED5GE deploys a 5G edge network across Luleå, Boden, Skellefteå and Uppsala to enable smart-community applications where low latency and local data processing are important. The operational problem is that many public-safety, transport and environmental services need real-time data from cameras, drones, sensors, autonomous machines and digital twins, but cloud-only architectures may introduce delay or reduce resilience. The implementation combines 5G connectivity, edge-computing nodes, local traffic breakout, public network integration and smart applications across five use-case areas. At a conceptual level, edge processing brings computation closer to data sources, allowing video streams, sensor data and machine-learning outputs to be analysed rapidly for operational decisions. The expected impact is improved emergency response in port areas, more efficient port traffic, better waste and recycling management, real-time traffic intelligence, and stronger support for sustainable farming through drones, autonomous machinery, digital twins and AR. The case demonstrates how 5G and edge computing can underpin multi-sector smart-community services rather than a single isolated application.

title: PIAST-Q - First European Quantum Computer
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: European research and industry need access to quantum-computing resources to explore problems that may be difficult for classical computers alone, including optimisation, materials science, chemistry, machine learning and complex simulation. PIAST-Q is a EuroHPC quantum computer hosted at the Poznań Supercomputing and Networking Center in Poland. The operational objective is to provide a European quantum-computing capability integrated with high-performance computing resources, so users can test hybrid classical-quantum workflows. The implementation is based on trapped-ion technology, using electromagnetic fields to trap charged atoms and precision lasers to perform quantum operations. At a conceptual level, the system operates as a gate-based quantum computer connected to the wider EuroHPC infrastructure, allowing researchers and eventually industrial or public-sector users to access quantum resources through a shared European framework. The expected impact is stronger European sovereignty in quantum technologies, broader access to advanced computing, faster experimentation with quantum algorithms and support for future scientific and industrial breakthroughs. The use case is significant because it is not a single research prototype in isolation, but part of a distributed European quantum-computing infrastructure designed to complement existing supercomputers.

title: EDITO-Infra project: EU Public Infrastructure for the European Digital Twin Ocean
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Ocean governance requires integrated knowledge about climate change, biodiversity, pollution, coastal pressures, marine resources and human activity, but marine data are distributed across many observation, modelling and service systems. EDITO-Infra develops the core public infrastructure for the European Digital Twin Ocean, providing a shared foundation for local and thematic ocean twins. The operational problem is to integrate ocean observations, forecasts, modelling tools, data services and computational capacity into a framework that can support interactive simulations and science-based decision-making. The implementation builds on Copernicus Marine Service and EMODnet, combining existing and emerging data sources with next-generation ocean modelling, artificial intelligence and high-performance computing. At a conceptual level, the infrastructure creates a digital environment where users can explore ocean data, simulate scenarios, build specialised digital-twin applications and assess the impacts of climate change or human activity. The expected impact is better marine-policy design, stronger support for restoration and conservation, improved public understanding of ocean systems and more accessible tools for researchers, policymakers and innovators. The use case is significant because it treats the ocean as a complex dynamic system requiring shared European digital infrastructure, rather than isolated datasets or individual models.

title: EDITO-ModelLab - European Digital Twin Ocean
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: EDITO-Model Lab is a Horizon Europe project launched in 2022 which forms a central component of the European Digital Twin Ocean initiative. Its purpose is to develop the next generation of ocean numerical models and the software infrastructure that will power a highly detailed, interactive digital representation of the ocean. The project combines state-of-the-art ocean modelling, artificial intelligence, satellite and in situ observations, and high-performance or cloud computing to create a “Virtual Ocean Model Lab” where advanced simulations can be built, tested and shared. This environment will allow users to explore a wide range of scenarios, such as pollution dispersion, coastal risks, climate-change impacts, biodiversity responses and sustainable marine-resource management. EDITO-Model Lab delivers a suite of high-resolution global and coastal models, covering physical, biogeochemical and ecological processes, alongside toolkits that support both developers and end users. These resources will enable scientists, policymakers, businesses and other stakeholders to design their own local or thematic digital twins tailored to specific challenges. By providing accessible modelling tools and a unified computing and data framework, the project supports informed decision-making, environmental protection, innovation in the blue economy and broader public understanding of the marine environment.

title: A Digital Twin for the Port of Rotterdam
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Large ports depend on precise coordination between vessels, quay infrastructure, weather conditions, hydrological data, logistics flows and safety operations. The Port of Rotterdam digital twin translates this complex physical environment into a dynamic virtual representation of the harbour area, supporting more informed and timely operational decisions. The operational problem is that port managers need a continuously updated view of ship movements, infrastructure status, water levels, wind, visibility, currents and other variables that influence navigation and logistics. The implementation integrates real-time sensor data, infrastructure information, shipping movements and environmental readings through a cloud-based IoT platform developed with technology partners. At a conceptual level, the digital twin functions as an operational intelligence layer: it combines spatial, environmental and maritime data so that port authorities can monitor conditions, improve berth planning, support safer vessel movements and prepare for more automated port operations. The expected impact is greater efficiency, improved safety, better environmental monitoring and stronger readiness for autonomous shipping. The use case is significant because it applies digital-twin technology to one of Europe’s most complex logistics environments, where even small improvements in planning and situational awareness can have substantial operational value.

title: Digital Twin Munich
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Cities need integrated data environments to plan mobility, manage growth, adapt to climate risks and involve residents in decisions that affect the urban fabric. Digital Twin Munich provides a virtual representation of the city that supports analyses, simulations and “what-if” scenarios for municipal planning. The operational problem is that urban decisions often rely on separate datasets held by different departments, utilities and transport operators, making it difficult to assess combined impacts before action is taken. The implementation centres on Munich’s Urban Data Platform, which connects geodata, 2D and 3D city models, sensor data and specialised municipal information. At a conceptual level, the digital twin acts as a shared analytical infrastructure: planners can visualise change, test policy scenarios and integrate real-time information such as weather, traffic, air-quality, noise and environmental data. The expected impact is better traffic planning, stronger climate-adaptation capacity, improved urban-development analysis and more transparent citizen involvement. The case is particularly relevant because Munich presents the digital twin not as a single application, but as a permanent digital backbone for future smart-city services.

title: INCISIVE - Improving cancer diagnosis and prediction with AI and big data
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Cancer diagnosis increasingly depends on combining imaging, clinical information and specialist interpretation, but medical data are often fragmented across institutions and difficult to reuse securely for AI development. INCISIVE addressed this challenge by developing AI-based decision-support tools and a federated data repository for cancer imaging and associated clinical data. The operational problem was to improve the accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, interpretability and cost-effectiveness of cancer-imaging methods while respecting data-protection requirements. The implementation created an interoperable repository of anonymised medical images and clinical data, allowing AI models to be trained and validated across distributed European datasets without relying on a single centralised data pool. At a conceptual level, INCISIVE combines federated data governance, explainable AI services and clinical decision-support pipelines for breast, lung, prostate and colorectal cancer. The expected impact is better detection, staging, monitoring and risk assessment, as well as stronger European capacity to develop reliable AI tools for oncology. The use case is significant because it links AI performance to trustworthy data infrastructure, recognising that clinical AI depends as much on secure, representative and interoperable datasets as on model design.

title: Diella: AI - Driven Assistant for Citizen - Centric Digital Services
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Diella is an AI-powered virtual assistant designed to improve citizens’ interaction with digital public services. Integrated into the e-Albania ecosystem, Diella provides intelligent, real-time assistance by helping users navigate public services, access relevant information, and better understand administrative procedures. Beyond providing information and guidance, Diella enables a more proactive and interactive service experience by generating documents in real time based on citizens’ requests. Through natural language interaction, users can request specific documents or services, and Diella can support the immediate preparation and delivery of the relevant documentation, simplifying processes and reducing the time and effort required to access public services. Its main purpose is to simplify the user experience, reduce administrative complexity, and provide fast, consistent, and accessible support. By leveraging artificial intelligence and natural language processing, Diella enables more intuitive communication between citizens and digital government platforms, contributing to a more efficient, responsive, and citizen-centric public administration.

title: AI Model Combining Speech and Brain Activity for Depression Diagnosis
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Depression diagnosis often relies on interviews, questionnaires and clinical judgement, which can be affected by subjectivity, limited appointment time and differences in how symptoms are expressed. Researchers at Kaunas University of Technology developed a multimodal AI model that combines speech patterns and brain activity to support more objective recognition of major depressive disorder. The operational problem is that single-source diagnostic signals may be insufficient: speech can capture changes in pace, intonation and energy, while EEG data can reflect brainwave activity under controlled conditions. The implementation uses voice recordings and EEG signals converted into spectrograms, then analysed through a modified DenseNet-121 deep-learning architecture. At a conceptual level, the model treats audio and brain signals as complementary representations of mental-state information, using deep learning to classify whether a person is healthy or affected by depression. The expected impact is faster assessment, potential support for remote screening and reduced reliance on purely subjective interpretation. The case should be framed as research rather than clinical deployment, because further clinical trials, explainability improvements and validation are required before such a system could be used safely in healthcare settings.

title: AI4grids - AI - based planning and operational management of distribution grids
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Electricity distribution networks face increasing pressure from renewable generation, electric vehicles, heat pumps and changing consumption patterns. AI4Grids developed AI-based methods to support the planning and operational management of medium- and low-voltage distribution grids and microgrids. The operational problem is that solar and wind generation fluctuate, while new flexible loads can create local congestion or instability if not coordinated intelligently. The implementation develops algorithms for grid-state monitoring, load forecasting, renewable-generation prediction and operational recommendations. At a conceptual level, the system combines automated network-structure monitoring with weather and consumption data to build a more complete picture of grid conditions. In the event of a fault or abnormal operating state, AI-based control logic can generate recommendations for the control centre, helping operators restore stability more quickly. The expected impact is better integration of renewable energy, reduced need for costly grid over-dimensioning, improved reliability and more efficient use of existing infrastructure. The case is significant because it applies AI to a concrete energy-transition bottleneck: distribution grids must become more intelligent if decentralised generation and flexible demand are to be integrated at scale.

title: KIWA, an AI-based forest monitoring system
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Forest fires can spread rapidly and create simultaneous risks for people, infrastructure, biodiversity and local emergency services. KIWA addresses this challenge by combining drones, artificial intelligence and decision-support tools to support earlier detection of forest and wildfires and more effective coordination of response resources. The operational problem is that municipal fire brigades and disaster-control authorities often need real-time information on the location of a fire, the direction and speed of spread, and the resources required to contain it. Traditional observation methods may not provide sufficiently fast or detailed information, especially when fires spread across difficult terrain or visibility is limited. KIWA uses unmanned aerial vehicles equipped with cameras to collect images and videos of monitored forest areas. These data are transmitted through interfaces and analysed by AI models in real time to identify fire or smoke, while the decision-support system helps emergency services interpret the current situation and match available personnel and equipment to the threat. At a conceptual level, the system creates a continuous forest-monitoring and response-support loop: drones collect situational data, AI detects and forecasts fire-related risks, and municipal authorities receive actionable information through a dashboard or operational interface. The expected impact is faster detection, better deployment of firefighting resources, reduced ecological damage, improved safety for people and animals, and lower financial burden for municipalities affected by wildfire events. The case is significant because it connects environmental monitoring, civil protection and AI-enabled decision support in a scalable model for regions exposed to increasing climate-related fire risks.

title: MarghERita: Emilia-Romagna’s High-Performance Computing and Big Data Platform
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Regional administrations increasingly need high-performance computing capacity to process large datasets, run predictive models and support rapid decision-making in areas such as civil protection, environmental risk and public-service planning. MarghERita is the Emilia-Romagna Region’s HPC and Big Data platform, developed with Lepida to provide regional institutions with computing infrastructure that can support advanced modelling and data-intensive applications. The operational value of the platform is particularly clear in civil protection, where extreme weather events require rapid simulations and evidence-based prevention measures. After the severe floods that affected Emilia-Romagna in May 2023, the Civil Protection, the University of Parma, the University of Padua and the Region used MarghERita’s computing power to implement algorithms capable of simulating flood hydrographs in real time. These simulations applied predictive models of possible bank breaks along the Lamone River to assess and mitigate potential flooding consequences for surrounding territory. At a conceptual level, MarghERita acts as a shared computational backbone for public authorities: instead of each administration building separate high-capacity infrastructure, the regional platform provides the computing power needed for complex simulations, environmental modelling and decision support. The expected impact is improved prevention of hydrogeological risk, faster response during weather-hydrological alerts, stronger coordination between universities and public authorities, and more data-driven management of extreme climate events. The case is relevant because it shows how regional HPC infrastructure can move beyond research support and become part of operational civil-protection capacity.

title: SAVIA project: Artificial Intelligence for law quality
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Regional legislation can be difficult for both public officials and citizens to navigate because legal texts, implementing acts and territorial effects are often distributed across multiple documents and administrative layers. SAVIA addresses this challenge by using artificial intelligence to support consultation of Emilia-Romagna regional laws and their implementing measures. The operational problem is that legislative assemblies and local administrations need timely, accurate and comprehensible information about what regional laws require, how they are implemented by the Regional Council, municipalities and provinces, and what effects they produce on the territory. SAVIA is developed by the Legislative Assembly of Emilia-Romagna in collaboration with CINECA and is supported by the MarghERita Big Data platform. At a conceptual level, the system uses large language models and retrieval-augmented generation to answer natural-language questions on regional law.
