It will also establish AI campuses in Prague and Brno to complement the existing Ostrava ecosystem and support talent development. The expected impact is stronger Czech AI sovereignty, better industry uptake, improved public-sector capacity and closer integration into the European network of AI Factories

title: Shelfex AI - Predictive AI transforming shelf life management
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Food manufacturers need reliable methods to determine shelf life, prevent spoilage, ensure regulatory compliance and maintain consumer trust across complex supply chains. Traditional shelf-life management often relies on empirical estimates, laboratory testing at limited points in time and conservative date-marking assumptions that may not fully reflect real production and distribution conditions. Shelfex AI, developed by the Belgian food safety technology company Handary, addresses this problem by combining biotechnology, analytical science and artificial intelligence into a predictive framework for food integrity. The operational problem is that spoilage and microbial risk are dynamic: they depend on ingredient quality, processing parameters, packaging, storage conditions and distribution environments. Shelfex AI integrates laboratory data and production parameters to authenticate ingredients, predict spoilage before it occurs and support compliance with date-marking requirements. It is complemented by Microfier smart labels, which provide real-time microbial signals directly on packaging, and Hékôn intelligent micro-perforated membranes, which regulate gas balance and monitor storage conditions during distribution. At a conceptual level, the system turns shelf-life management from a retrospective or judgement-based process into a data-driven predictive control system. The expected impact is improved food safety, reduced waste, more accurate date marking, stronger supply-chain transparency and greater trust between manufacturers, regulators and consumers. The case is relevant because it shows how AI can support food safety and sustainability through predictive monitoring of product integrity, although it is primarily a private-sector technology rather than a public-administration deployment.

title: Blockchain for trade
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
task: Tracking of goods and assets along the supply chain
source_description: Illegal timber trade creates environmental, regulatory and geopolitical risks, particularly where sanctioned wood products may enter European supply chains through indirect routes or falsified documentation. The Lithuanian blockchain-for-trade case addresses this problem by proposing a blockchain-based traceability system for timber, with specific relevance to Russian and Belarusian wood entering EU markets. The operational problem is that conventional certification and paperwork can be manipulated, and authorities or buyers may struggle to verify whether timber was harvested legally, transported through legitimate channels and processed according to sustainability rules. Researchers from Kaunas University of Technology and Vytautas Magnus University developed a model that assigns each log a unique identifier and records its journey on a blockchain, from permits through transport and sale. Smart contracts are used to validate each action, including blocking attempts to harvest without permits or introduce fictitious suppliers. At a conceptual level, the system creates a tamper-resistant audit trail for timber, combining product-level identification, sustainability scoring and automated rule enforcement. The source reports that simulation tests processed up to 550 transactions per second and that participants with higher sustainability scores achieved up to 95% successful trades. The expected impact is stronger enforcement against illegal timber, better supply-chain transparency, improved buyer confidence and more effective implementation of sanctions and deforestation-related due diligence

title: Blockchain for Strategy Portfolio Rebalancing
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Institutional asset management often involves complex operational processes when portfolios must be rebalanced across multiple assets, trading venues and compliance requirements. In on-chain finance, these challenges become more pronounced because digital assets, tokenised securities and decentralised exchanges operate with different execution mechanisms and transparency expectations from traditional markets. 31Third’s strategy-based portfolio rebalancing use case addresses this operational complexity by providing blockchain-native infrastructure for institutional on-chain asset managers and index funds. The operational problem is that managers need to maintain portfolio allocations in line with predefined strategies, but manual trading across multiple assets can be costly, slow and operationally risky. The platform allows users to define target allocations and then automatically rebalance portfolios in a single transaction, supported by smart contracts, smart order routing and compliance features. At a conceptual level, the system uses blockchain to make portfolio adjustment more transparent, programmable and efficient: strategic allocation rules are translated into automated execution logic, while routing mechanisms seek efficient execution across decentralised exchanges, market makers and liquidity pools. The expected impact is lower operational cost, reduced manual intervention, more accurate alignment with investment strategies and improved transparency for institutional investors. The case is relevant for public-sector innovation catalogues mainly as a regulatory-sandbox example, because it demonstrates how blockchain infrastructure may reshape institutional finance under supervision and dialogue with regulators rather than as a direct government-service deployment.

title: Blockchain for Issuance- and Redemption-Triggered Rebalancing
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: On-chain exchange-traded funds and index products require the underlying asset basket to remain aligned with the fund’s intended composition when new shares are issued or existing shares are redeemed. In traditional fund operations, this process can involve intermediaries, manual reconciliation and delayed portfolio adjustment. 31Third’s issuance- and redemption-triggered rebalancing use case applies blockchain automation to this specific operational problem. The system is designed for on-chain ETFs and similar portfolio products where subscription and redemption events automatically trigger rebalancing of the underlying assets. At a conceptual level, the platform connects fund-share issuance, redemption logic and smart-contract-powered portfolio execution: when fund shares are created or redeemed, the system adjusts the underlying asset basket so that allocations continue to reflect the fund’s target composition without requiring separate manual intervention. This creates a more direct link between investor activity and asset management. Smart order routing can optimise execution across decentralised exchanges, market makers and liquidity pools, while compliance features are intended to support institutional-grade operation. The expected impact is more efficient fund administration, lower execution friction, better transparency for investors and stronger scalability for on-chain index products. The case is particularly relevant because it illustrates how blockchain can be used not merely to represent assets digitally, but to automate specific financial-market operations that are traditionally handled through administrative and intermediary-heavy workflows. As with the related 31Third portfolio-rebalancing use case, it should be treated as a sandboxed financial-innovation case rather than a public-service deployment.

title: Blocksquare – Notarised Real Estate Tokenisation Framework
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Real estate is traditionally illiquid, capital-intensive and difficult for smaller investors to access, while fractional ownership models often face legal, registry and enforceability challenges. Blocksquare’s notarised real-estate tokenisation framework addresses this problem by combining blockchain tokens with legally grounded property claims, notarised loan agreements and registered mortgages. The operational challenge is that real-estate tokenisation must provide more than a digital representation of value: investors need enforceable rights, transparency on the underlying asset and a legally recognised structure that can operate across European jurisdictions. Blocksquare’s framework enables property owners or marketplace operators to fractionalise economic exposure to real-estate assets while anchoring investor protection in notarised documentation and euro-denominated mortgage registration. At a conceptual level, the token becomes a digital instrument connected to a legally documented claim rather than merely a speculative blockchain asset. This structure can support decentralised trading, branded marketplaces and broader investor participation while attempting to preserve compliance with EU legal expectations. The expected impact is increased liquidity in real-estate markets, wider access to property-backed investment, more efficient marketplace creation and stronger transparency around tokenised assets. The case is relevant because it demonstrates a bridge between real-world assets and blockchain infrastructure. However, it is primarily a private-sector tokenisation framework, and the source should be used cautiously because it is industry media rather than a public regulator or government confirmation.

title: CHARONIUM GmbH - Legacy - Digital Inheritance Platform
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Digital assets such as cryptocurrencies, NFTs and tokenised real estate create practical and legal challenges for inheritance, because heirs, notaries, lawyers and financial institutions may not know what assets exist, how to verify ownership or how to transfer them securely after death. CHARONIUM Legacy addresses this problem by providing a blockchain-powered platform for digital estate discovery, verification and transfer. The operational problem is that traditional probate and inheritance procedures were designed for bank accounts, physical property and registered financial assets, while decentralised digital assets may be held across wallets, exchanges and tokenised platforms. CHARONIUM Legacy is designed for legal professionals, notaries and financial institutions, offering automated asset verification across blockchains such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, centralised exchanges and tokenised platforms. At a conceptual level, the platform converts digital inheritance into a structured workflow: assets can be discovered, tokenised into proofs of ownership, registered in tamper-proof records and transferred through smart-contract-based processes under legal conditions. The system also supports beneficiary and investor management, automated notifications, probate processing, cross-border compatibility, AML alignment and GDPR compliance. The expected impact is reduced legal uncertainty, lower administrative burden, fewer disputes, improved fraud resistance and clearer procedures for the inheritance of digital assets. The case is significant because digital estate management is becoming increasingly important as crypto-assets and tokenised property enter mainstream wealth portfolios. For public-sector cataloguing, it should be presented as a regulated blockchain innovation case involving legal-sector processes, not as a government-run inheritance platform.

title: Blockchain-Powered Digital Product Passport (DPP) for Battery Lifecycle Management
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Battery value chains involve manufacturers, users, collectors, recyclers, marketplaces and regulators, each of whom needs reliable information about product origin, chemistry, condition, ownership, usage and end-of-life handling. The blockchain-powered Digital Product Passport pilot involving Traced Systems, Instagrid, Batteriretur and Cling Systems addresses this information problem in the downstream phase of the battery lifecycle. The operational challenge is that batteries move through production, use, collection, recycling and secondary markets, but critical data may not follow the physical product in a secure, standardised and privacy-preserving way. The project developed and deployed a Digital Product Passport application over six months, with Instagrid providing manufacturing data, Batteriretur contributing collection and recycling logistics, Cling Systems supporting secondary battery transactions and Traced Systems deploying the Chromia blockchain for decentralised data management. At a conceptual level, the Digital Product Passport acts as a controlled data layer for the battery: different actors receive role-based access to relevant information, while blockchain supports traceability, provenance and integrity. Manufacturers can gain downstream insight into battery use, collectors can access chemistry and lifecycle information to improve sorting and recycling, and secondary-market participants can verify battery health and provenance. The expected impact is improved circularity, better recycling efficiency, stronger regulatory alignment, greater confidence in second-life markets and more transparent sustainability reporting. The case is relevant because it demonstrates how blockchain can support practical industrial data exchange under emerging European product-passport and circular-economy requirements.

title: Distributed ledger technology (DLT) to create a transparent, community-driven financial ecosystem
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Decentralised finance aims to reduce reliance on centralised institutions, but many systems still face governance, transparency, liquidity and manipulation risks. Multi, developed by Kunveno Teknologos, uses distributed ledger technology to create a community-driven financial ecosystem governed through on-chain proposal voting. The operational problem is that digital-asset reserves and basket tokens need credible mechanisms for asset selection, governance and liquidity provision if they are to operate transparently and sustainably. Multi’s design includes two core tokens: a governance token for the decentralised autonomous organisation, and a fully collateralised basket token backed by a dynamic reserve of crypto assets. Participants propose asset allocations, while the reserve structure is determined through a meritocratic, game-theoretic competition mechanism. At a conceptual level, the system transforms portfolio governance into a decentralised process: participants compete to improve reserve allocation, the DAO defines the rules of the competition, and rewards are distributed through staking mechanisms. The platform also functions as a decentralised exchange through an automated multi-party trade algorithm, issuing fully collateralised tokens according to liquidity needs and dynamically adjusting supply to maintain market balance. The expected impact is greater transparency, more resilient decentralised governance, reduced dependence on intermediaries and a new model for community-managed financial infrastructure. The case should be framed as a blockchain sandbox and decentralised-finance innovation case, because it concerns private-sector financial infrastructure rather than a public-service tool.

title: DOWSERS - blockchain for smart contracts
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Smart contracts can execute financial and operational logic automatically, but bugs or vulnerabilities in their code can lead to irreversible losses, exploitation or loss of trust in blockchain systems. DOWSERS addresses this problem by applying formal verification methods to smart contracts before or after deployment. The operational problem is that testing can identify known bugs, but it cannot prove the absence of entire classes of vulnerabilities across all possible execution states. This is particularly important in decentralised finance and token ecosystems, where a small error can expose developers, investors and institutions to major financial risk. DOWSERS provides a suite of software tools and algorithms that analyse source code from repositories and bytecode already deployed on blockchain networks. At a conceptual level, the platform applies mathematical reasoning to prove or disprove whether a smart contract satisfies specified properties, drawing on formal-verification techniques used in safety-critical sectors such as aerospace, nuclear systems, rail and automated transport. It can identify vulnerabilities including reentrancy attacks, race conditions, authorisation errors, buffer overflows and unsafe external calls, while also detecting ambiguities, inconsistencies and poor security practices. The expected impact is stronger trust in blockchain applications, better developer guidance, more informed investment decisions and reduced cybersecurity risk across decentralised systems. The case is relevant to public-sector and regulatory discussions because smart-contract assurance is a prerequisite for safe adoption of blockchain in finance, public registries, digital credentials and other high-trust domains.

title: Decentralised Coordination of Distributed Energy Resources
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Electricity systems are becoming harder to balance as renewable generation, heat pumps, electric vehicles and distributed energy resources create more variable patterns of supply and demand. Enoda ENSEMBLE™ addresses this challenge by using distributed ledger technology to coordinate decentralised energy assets so that they can provide frequency and ancillary services to the grid. The operational problem is that grid stability has historically depended on large centralised plants, including fossil-fuelled peaker plants, which can respond to frequency deviations but are expensive, carbon-intensive and poorly aligned with decarbonisation objectives. ENSEMBLE™ proposes a more decentralised model in which distributed assets can participate in balancing markets through secure, near-real-time coordination. The implementation uses a private-permissioned blockchain, smart contracts, cryptographic safeguards and compliance features covering issues such as AML, KYC, GDPR and data protection. At a conceptual level, the platform creates a trusted coordination layer between grid operators, aggregators and distributed assets, allowing performance data, transactions and balancing contributions to be recorded transparently. The expected impact is lower transaction costs, reduced barriers for renewable and distributed assets, greater grid flexibility and less reliance on conventional balancing generation. The case is relevant because it applies blockchain to a concrete energy-transition bottleneck: how to integrate decentralised clean-energy resources into operational grid services without losing trust, compliance or system stability. The source frames the case as part of the European Blockchain Sandbox third cohort rather than as evidence of routine market-wide deployment.

title: Fair Squares: Affordable Housinf Funding Protocol
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Affordable housing is a persistent challenge across the European Union, with many households facing high rents, limited supply and housing systems that can favour speculative returns over long-term social affordability. Fair Squares proposes a blockchain-enabled funding and governance protocol designed to make housing investment more transparent, community-driven and affordability-oriented. The operational problem is that traditional affordable-housing delivery often depends either on constrained public budgets or large private investors whose return expectations may not align with tenants’ needs. Fair Squares introduces a distributed digital funding model in which investors hold small, traceable shares of a diversified pool of real housing assets, while tenants, investors and housing organisations participate in a more collaborative governance framework. At a conceptual level, tokenisation is used to distribute ownership or economic participation across multiple investors, reduce concentration risk and make the financing layer more transparent. Community-powered rent control is central to the model: expected returns influence rent levels, and the system is designed to keep investor returns modest and stable rather than speculative. Digital identifiers support secure and verifiable records of ownership and tenancy. The expected impact is a more stable housing-finance ecosystem, better alignment between investor incentives and tenant affordability, increased transparency and broader participation in affordable-housing funding. The case is significant because it applies blockchain to a social-policy problem, not only to financial trading, but it should still be treated as a sandbox-stage financial and governance model rather than a confirmed operational public-housing programme.

title: Frictionless Markets Sarl (Frictionless Group Holdings Sarl)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Institutional finance still relies on settlement, custody, distribution and foreign-exchange processes that can be slow, intermediary-heavy and limited by market opening hours. Frictionless Markets’ OnFi platform proposes a blockchain-based infrastructure for institutional digital capital markets, aiming to combine regulated financial operations with on-chain execution. The operational problem is that cross-border, multi-currency institutional transactions may involve settlement delays, counterparty risk, reconciliation work and fragmented access to tokenised assets. OnFi addresses this by enabling instant, borderless, 24/7 settlement across multiple currencies and by converting ERC20 assets and regulated stablecoins into fully backed institutional deposit tokens. The platform also supports access to tokenised money-market funds, yieldcoins, on-chain foreign exchange, order-book management, digital capital raising and on-chain issuance. At a conceptual level, the system uses distributed ledger technology, multi-chain interoperability and decentralised oracle networks to connect traditional capital-market functions with blockchain-based settlement and transparency. Chainlink is used for features such as proof of reserves and atomic cross-chain transfer support. The expected impact is faster settlement, lower operational risk, more efficient distribution of private-market products, improved transparency and a scalable foundation for institutional tokenised finance. The case is relevant because it sits at the intersection of traditional finance, regulated digital assets and DeFi infrastructure. However, within the catalogue it should be presented as a regulatory-sandbox use case, not as proof that all described capabilities are already operating at full market scale.

title: EMERALD Blockchain-based trustworthiness system
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Cloud-service certification depends on evidence that must remain trustworthy over time, but evidence-management processes can be complex, manual and vulnerable to doubts about integrity. EMERALD addresses this problem through a blockchain-based trustworthiness system that supports cybersecurity certification and auditing of cloud services. The operational problem is that cloud service providers, certification bodies and auditors need to collect, store and verify evidence demonstrating security controls, while also preserving privacy and protecting sensitive technical information. EMERALD provides a framework in which evidence collectors can automatically generate proofs of integrity, while the wider system can automatically check whether stored evidence has been tampered with. Authorised users, including internal or external auditors, can also perform manual verification through a graphical interface. At a conceptual level, the blockchain layer does not need to expose all evidence publicly; rather, it records integrity proofs and supports long-term verifiability, traceability and resistance to modification. This allows certification evidence to remain auditable without compromising confidentiality. The expected impact is more efficient cybersecurity certification, stronger trust in cloud-service evidence, reduced administrative burden for auditors and providers, and improved capacity to demonstrate compliance over time. The case is relevant because it applies blockchain to assurance and certification, where trust depends on evidence integrity rather than on tokenisation or financial exchange. For catalogue purposes, it should be presented as a sandbox-stage cybersecurity assurance use case.

title: Blockchain-Based Age Estimation with Privado ID and Privately
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Online age verification creates a difficult policy trade-off: platforms need to restrict access to age-limited content or services, but conventional checks often require users to disclose sensitive personal information such as date of birth, identity documents or national identification numbers. The Billions Network, Privado ID and Privately use case addresses this challenge through a privacy-preserving age-verification model using self-sovereign identity, verifiable credentials, zero-knowledge proofs and on-device AI age estimation. The operational problem is especially relevant for online services operating across multiple EU Member States, where legal requirements differ and platforms must also comply with GDPR and the European Digital Identity Framework. The implementation combines Privado ID’s decentralised identity technology with Privately’s AI-based age-estimation approach. Trusted entities can issue digitally signed age credentials, which are stored in a user-controlled wallet. When accessing an age-restricted service, the user can generate a proof that they meet the required threshold without revealing their exact age, date of birth or broader identity data. At a conceptual level, the system separates eligibility verification from identity disclosure, reducing data exposure while maintaining regulatory accountability. The expected impact is stronger privacy protection, better cross-border interoperability, lower risk of data misuse and a more proportionate approach to online safety and age-restricted access. The case is significant because it uses blockchain and zero-knowledge cryptography to solve a concrete regulatory and rights-balancing problem, but it remains a sandbox-stage use case rather than a confirmed EU-wide operational standard.

title: Oneboard AG
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Financial institutions devote significant resources to Know Your Customer and Know Your Business processes, but these checks are often duplicated whenever a customer interacts with a new institution or when documents expire. Oneboard addresses this inefficiency through reusable, dynamically updated compliance profiles for financial institutions. The operational problem is that onboarding and monitoring processes are costly, repetitive and difficult to keep aligned with changing regulatory frameworks such as MiCA, DORA and anti-money-laundering rules. Oneboard proposes a model in which customers complete verification once, while their compliance data are stored securely, updated when documents expire and refreshed as regulatory requirements change. The platform integrates with existing banking and financial systems so that institutions can verify and monitor business customers without rebuilding compliance workflows from scratch. At a conceptual level, the system creates a portable compliance profile supported by decentralised storage, a compliance wallet and cryptographic security. This allows data integrity and privacy to be maintained while reducing repeated collection of the same documentation. The expected impact is faster onboarding, lower compliance costs, reduced manual workload, improved regulatory readiness and easier cross-jurisdictional operation for financial institutions. The case is relevant because it applies blockchain-inspired identity and data-management mechanisms to a highly regulated operational function. However, the available source describes the case within the European Blockchain Sandbox, so it should be treated as a regulatory-dialogue pilot rather than as evidence of full regular deployment across financial institutions.

title: Parfin – Institutional Blockchain Infrastructure for the European Blockchain Sandbox
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Regulated financial institutions are exploring tokenisation, digital currencies and blockchain-based settlement, but they require privacy, compliance, interoperability and scalability before digital-asset infrastructure can be used in institutional environments. Parfin’s Rayls platform addresses this challenge by providing an institutional-grade blockchain designed for banks, asset managers, financial market infrastructures and central banks. The operational problem is that public blockchains offer transparency and programmability, but they may not provide the confidentiality, governance and regulatory controls required by regulated finance. Rayls uses a hub-and-spoke architecture with private subnets, allowing institutions to operate in controlled environments while maintaining interoperability with broader blockchain ecosystems. The platform uses zero-knowledge proofs to protect transaction confidentiality while enabling regulatory oversight, and it is designed to support GDPR, KYC/AML and MiCA alignment. At a conceptual level, Rayls provides a regulated blockchain layer for issuing digital currencies and tokenised assets, conducting cross-border transactions, enabling wholesale CBDCs, supporting on-chain trading of tokenised securities and facilitating bank-issued stablecoins. The expected impact is faster settlement, improved liquidity, reduced costs, more efficient cross-border payments and a stronger bridge between traditional finance and digital-asset markets. The case is significant because it addresses institutional adoption barriers rather than consumer crypto use. For catalogue purposes, it should be framed as a sandbox-stage financial infrastructure case selected for regulatory dialogue, not as a fully deployed public-sector blockchain system.

title: PIXELPAI APS - financial compliance infrastructure platform
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Home care is a labour-intensive sector facing recruitment, retention and workforce-sustainability challenges, while care providers often operate under tight financial margins. CareCredits.io proposes a blockchain-enabled model that links verified care work to tokenised finance, creating incentives for care workers and new financing routes for compliant care SMEs. The operational problem is that home-care workers may receive limited additional reward for verified hours of care, while small and medium-sized care providers may struggle to attract investment or demonstrate compliance in a trusted way. The CareCredits smart contract, built on the KXCO.io platform, integrates with care scheduling software through an API and rewards workers with wrapped utility tokens for every verified hour of care. These tokens are designed to supplement wages and can be redeemed through existing supermarket loyalty schemes, without increasing employer costs. At a conceptual level, the model connects real-world verified labour, utility tokens, security-token-backed investment and digital identity. LEI-based KYC/AML, ISO-standard vLEI digital identities and cryptographic verification are used to establish trust in participating companies, officers and care workers. The expected impact is improved worker retention, stronger recruitment incentives, additional financing options for care SMEs and greater transparency in the care ecosystem. The case is significant because it applies tokenisation to a social-care workforce problem rather than only to financial assets. However, given its source, it should be treated as a sandbox-stage use case selected for regulatory dialogue.

title: Revolutionising home care system by linking verified care work to tokenised finance
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.

title: Blockchain to transform decentralised energy management and distribution
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Renewable Energy Communities need governance, financing and operational tools that allow households, businesses and public bodies to co-own, manage and benefit from local energy assets. The Stichting 2Tokens use case explores how blockchain technology, tokenisation, smart contracts and decentralised autonomous organisations can support transparent and participatory management of decentralised energy systems. The operational problem is that local energy communities must coordinate ownership, energy offtake, voting rights, financing, membership and investment returns among multiple participants, while also respecting energy regulation, data protection, tax rules and financial-market requirements. The proposed model uses tokenisation to represent different rights and instruments, including energy tokens, governance tokens, membership shares, ownership participations, loans and bonds. Participants use digital wallets to store and manage these assets, track energy value and participate in community governance. A DAO structure supports democratic decision-making, allowing members to develop and vote on proposals, allocate resources and shape the community’s strategy. At a conceptual level, the blockchain system becomes a governance and accounting layer for the energy community, making rights, obligations and transactions more transparent and auditable. The expected impact is stronger local resilience, broader access to investment, improved operational transparency and more inclusive participation in decentralised energy management. The Amelander Energie Coöperatie is highlighted as the practical community context, demonstrating how DLT could support community ownership and financing of shared energy systems. The case remains best classified as a sandbox pilot rather than a mature recurring implementation.

title: Blockchain to power intelligent, scalable Digital Product Passport (DPP) infrastructure
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Product value chains increasingly require structured, trustworthy and interoperable data on origin, materials, lifecycle impacts, repairability, resale potential and recycling pathways. This need is becoming more urgent as the EU moves towards Digital Product Passport requirements under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation. Tree Protocol addresses this challenge by providing a decentralised and tokenised knowledge-graph infrastructure for creating and managing Digital Product Passport data. The operational problem is that product information is often fragmented across brands, suppliers, logistics providers, repair services, resale platforms and recycling companies, making it difficult to share high-quality data across the full lifecycle. Tree uses blockchain-based smart contracts, API interfaces and developer SDKs to allow DPP applications to be built and connected across platforms. At a conceptual level, the protocol turns product data into a structured and shareable knowledge layer: brands can provide verified product information, while circular-economy platforms can use it to improve repair, resale, recycling and consumer-facing services. The use case is particularly relevant for textiles, where product composition, traceability and lifecycle information are essential for compliance and circular business models. Tree’s Shopify plugin and collaboration with Vaayu further support automated traceability-data collection through API integration. The expected impact is smoother DPP implementation, better compliance readiness, stronger circular-economy services and the conversion of compliance data into operational and commercial value. The case should be framed as a blockchain sandbox use case rather than a fully mature public infrastructure deployment.

title: Platform to deliver a blockchain-agnostic framework for tokenising real-world ESG assets
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Financing sustainable infrastructure often requires matching long-term environmental projects with investors who need transparency, liquidity, regulatory assurance and credible valuation. Bridge10X, operating through the Tokenforge framework, addresses this challenge by tokenising real-world ESG assets such as solar farms, geothermal plants and reforestation projects into compliant tradable digital securities. The operational problem is that many sustainability projects require substantial upfront investment, but access to such investments can be fragmented, illiquid and limited to specialised investors. The proposed model converts physical ESG assets into digital securities backed by the underlying asset, while also linking them to carbon-allowance-backed digital units to strengthen liquidity and environmental value. At a conceptual level, the platform combines blockchain-agnostic tokenisation, AI-driven asset valuation, smart-contract automation and regulated investment infrastructure. AI is used to assess fair market value by analysing market data and ESG metrics, while smart contracts automate investment flows and help verify environmental impact against recognised standards. The model is designed to support retail and institutional participation through a cooperative structure, while preserving compliance through AML/KYC, custody, liability coverage and registrar services. The expected impact is broader access to green investment, improved transparency of ESG asset performance, more liquid markets for sustainability-linked assets and more scalable financing for climate-positive infrastructure. The case is relevant because it shows how tokenisation can be applied to environmental finance, but it remains a sandbox-stage use case and should not be presented as a fully operational public investment platform.

title: Phase IV AI - Advanced AI Models for Health Data Privacy
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Healthcare AI depends on large, high-quality and representative datasets, but health data are often distributed across institutions and subject to strict legal, ethical and privacy constraints. PHASE IV AI addresses this structural barrier by developing privacy-compliant methods for using health data in AI development without requiring direct access to identifiable real-world patient data. The operational problem is that trustworthy AI systems for preventive healthcare, clinical decision support, education and health-technology assessment need extensive training and validation data, while hospitals and research organisations cannot simply pool sensitive health records in conventional centralised datasets. The project advances synthetic-data generation, testing and validation metrics, and multi-party computation protocols that allow AI development in privacy-preserving conditions. At a conceptual level, PHASE IV AI aims to create a “Health Data as a Service” model, where AI developers can access useful anonymous or synthetic data resources generated from decentralised de-identified sources, without exposing underlying patient information. The project also seeks to integrate data-market and data-service components into a cross-European health-data hub aligned with the European Health Data Space. The expected impact is improved access to usable health data for AI developers, stronger privacy protection, better validation of AI tools and greater adoption of health AI in high-impact disease areas, including cancer. The case is significant because it addresses one of the central bottlenecks of medical AI: how to make data useful while keeping it protected.

title: Florence's First AI-powered chatbot
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Municipal administrative procedures can be difficult for citizens to navigate, especially when they involve documentary requirements, eligibility conditions, deadlines and procedural steps that are spread across several web pages or offices. Florence’s FestinaLente chatbot addresses this problem by providing first-level AI assistance for citizens who need to change their official residence. The operational problem is that residence-change procedures generate many repetitive questions for demographic-services staff, while citizens may otherwise rely on phone calls, emails or in-person visits to understand what documents are required and how the process works. FestinaLente is designed to answer natural-language questions using official municipal documentation validated by the relevant staff. It supports 14 languages, making it useful not only for Italian residents but also for international users living in or moving to Florence. At a conceptual level, the chatbot acts as a structured conversational layer between the user and the municipal knowledge base: it does not replace administrative officials, but translates validated information into accessible guidance available at any time. The system is built on a modular AI platform that allows the city to choose among different large language models, with ChatGPT used as the main engine. The expected impact is reduced routine workload for municipal employees, clearer access to demographic-service information, fewer procedural errors by citizens and a better user experience for residents interacting with the municipality. The case is relevant because it shows how generative AI can be applied to a narrow, high-demand municipal procedure in a controlled and document-based way.

title: Chatbot to revolutionise tax return analysis
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Finance Department's Economic-Fiscal Studies and Research Directorate
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Tax administrations process millions of declarations containing income, expenses, VAT data and other fiscal indicators, and manual review cannot efficiently identify all relevant patterns or inconsistencies. Italy’s Finance Department chatbot is intended as an internal AI assistant for analysing tax-return data and supporting more timely fiscal analysis. The operational problem is that traditional tax-control workflows depend on automatic checks, formal checks and deeper substantive review, but the increasing volume and complexity of tax data make it difficult for officials to identify discrepancies, risk indicators or broader fiscal patterns quickly. The reported system was developed with Sogei and the Department of Finance’s Economic-Fiscal Studies and Research Directorate, and is described as capable of analysing documents, aggregated data, expenses, income and VAT information. At a conceptual level, the chatbot functions less as a public-facing assistant and more as an analytical interface for officials: users can query large fiscal datasets, carry out calculations, compare information and surface anomalies that may require further human assessment. The expected impact is faster analysis of declarations, better targeting of potential irregularities, improved understanding of fiscal trends and more efficient allocation of official attention to complex cases. The case should be handled carefully because secondary sources describe the system’s capabilities, but I did not find a directly accessible official MEF technical page confirming all operational details. It should therefore be presented as an internal fiscal-analysis AI tool supported by media reporting, not as an autonomous enforcement decision-maker.

title: German government hotline 115: AI-based chatbot for 24/7 support
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Citizens often need simple, reliable answers about administrative procedures, but public-service information in Germany is distributed across federal, state and municipal responsibilities. The 115 service is intended to make access to administrative information easier, and its chatbot upgrade responds to the limitations of earlier rule-based digital assistance. The operational problem was that the previous chatbot relied heavily on predefined questions and decision-tree logic, which limited its ability to understand varied wording or respond flexibly to citizens’ needs. The new AI-based version is designed to interpret natural-language queries more effectively and provide more relevant guidance on public services, administrative procedures and contact points. At a conceptual level, the chatbot acts as a conversational access layer to the knowledge base behind the 115 public-service information system. Instead of requiring citizens to formulate their question in exactly the expected way, the system can process broader phrasing and guide users towards the appropriate service information. The expected impact is easier access to administrative guidance outside office hours, reduced frustration for users, better handling of routine questions and lower pressure on human support channels. The case is relevant because it illustrates a typical public-sector AI upgrade path: a rule-based assistant is introduced first, its limitations become visible in practice, and it is then replaced or enhanced by a more flexible AI-powered version. The main value lies in improving accessibility and usability, not in automating administrative decisions.

title: Sovereign AI for Public Administration in France
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: France’s sovereign AI partnership with Germany, Mistral AI and SAP SE is designed to address a strategic public-administration challenge: how to adopt AI at scale while preserving European control over data, infrastructure, governance and critical digital dependencies. The operational problem is that public administrations need AI tools for productivity, decision support, financial management, service guidance and compliance, but reliance on non-European technology stacks can create concerns around sovereignty, interoperability, security and long-term control. The planned partnership focuses on four pillars: an intelligent sovereign ERP platform tailored to French and German administrative requirements; AI-augmented financial management, including invoice classification and audit checks; digital agents for civil servants and citizens; and joint training and innovation capacity through AI-ERP labs. For France, the initiative is framed as a strategic shift towards more efficient, resilient and sovereign public administration, enabling civil servants to use generative agents for drafting, scenario simulation, budget justification, compliance support and eligibility guidance. At a conceptual level, the partnership aims to create a European-controlled AI stack that combines Mistral AI’s models with SAP’s enterprise systems and sovereign infrastructure principles. The expected impact is improved public-sector efficiency, stronger auditability and traceability of AI systems, better service responsiveness and reduced dependence on external technology providers

title: Sovereign AI for Public Administration in Germany
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Germany’s sovereign AI initiative with France, Mistral AI and SAP SE is intended to create a trusted European framework for applying AI in public administration while preserving digital sovereignty and institutional control. The operational problem is that German administrations, like their French counterparts, increasingly require AI-enabled enterprise systems and digital agents for financial workflows, compliance support, drafting, service guidance and internal productivity. However, deploying such systems in government requires interoperability with existing administrative architecture, secure handling of public data, explainability, auditability and long-term resilience. The announced partnership focuses on a sovereign ERP platform with embedded AI, AI-supported financial management, digital agents for public services and shared training and innovation capacity. In the German context, SAP’s role is particularly relevant because of its long-standing presence in enterprise software used by public and private organisations, while Mistral AI contributes European model capabilities. At a conceptual level, the initiative aims to place AI inside the administrative operating system rather than deploying isolated chatbots. It is designed to create tools that help civil servants classify invoices, check audits, draft documents, simulate scenarios, justify budgets and guide citizens through forms or eligibility checks. The expected impact is more efficient administration, stronger interoperability, lower dependence on non-European providers and better alignment with European sovereignty objectives

title: OpenAI For Greece - ChatGPT Edu in Secondary Education
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Education systems need to prepare teachers and students for AI while ensuring that adoption is structured, responsible and aligned with pedagogical goals. OpenAI for Greece addresses this challenge through a partnership between OpenAI, the Government of the Hellenic Republic, the Onassis Foundation and Endeavor Greece, with an education component centred on ChatGPT Edu in upper-secondary schools. The operational problem is that generative AI is already entering learning environments informally, but teachers need training, secure tools and clear guidance if they are to integrate AI constructively into classroom practice. Greece’s pilot will start with teachers from upper-secondary schools selected to reflect regional and socio-economic diversity. The first phase focuses on AI literacy, teacher productivity and responsible integration of AI into education. ChatGPT Edu is described by OpenAI as a version of ChatGPT built for academic institutions, offering access to OpenAI’s latest models with enterprise-grade security and controls that support GDPR compliance. The Onassis Foundation will lead implementation with local partners, including The Tipping Point, while OpenAI will co-design teacher training, provide technical support and share best practices for safe classroom use. At a conceptual level, the initiative treats AI not merely as a student tool, but as a system-level capacity for teacher training, lesson support, responsible use and national skills development. The expected impact is improved AI literacy, more confident teacher adoption, support for classroom innovation and a pathway to wider national rollout if the pilot demonstrates successful outcomes
vendor_reported: Open AI; Onassis Foundation; Endeavor Greece; The Tipping Point

title: OpenAI For Greece - Greek AI Accelerator to support local AI‑focused start‑ups
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.

source_description: Greece’s AI Accelerator is designed to strengthen the country’s start-up ecosystem by helping local founders build, test and scale AI-driven products in sectors aligned with national priorities. The programme responds to a structural innovation challenge: Greece has a strong base of STEM graduates and technical talent, but many highly skilled professionals pursue opportunities abroad, weakening the domestic pipeline for advanced digital entrepreneurship. The accelerator creates a pathway for AI-focused start-ups to access technical resources, international expertise and investor networks while remaining connected to the Greek innovation ecosystem. Selected companies receive access to OpenAI technology and credits, technical mentorship from OpenAI engineers and global experts, tailored workshops on scaling, compliance and safety-by-design, and international exposure, including links to leading investors and innovators. The programme gives particular attention to education, public services, healthcare and climate, where AI can generate both economic and public-interest value. At an operational level, the accelerator helps start-ups move from prototype development to scalable products by combining model access, technical advice, policy alignment and market visibility. At ecosystem level, it supports talent retention, creates stronger links between Greek founders and global AI networks, and contributes to the government’s wider objective of positioning Greece as a competitive hub for applied artificial intelligence.
