title: Digital Doctor Assistant
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Greece’s Digital Doctor Assistant introduces artificial intelligence into the national electronic health-record environment to help doctors access, interpret and use patient information more efficiently. Public health systems generate large volumes of clinical data, including histories, medications, laboratory results, diagnostic information and previous treatments, but this information is not always easy to retrieve quickly during a consultation. The Digital Doctor Assistant addresses this challenge by allowing healthcare professionals to interact with the patient record through natural-language queries, including spoken interaction. Through the MyHealthDoc system, doctors can request summaries of a patient’s medical history, ask which medicines were administered over a given period, retrieve personalised results and navigate clinical information without manually searching across the full record. The tool is intended to reduce bureaucracy, shorten the time needed to access relevant information and support medical decision-making inside the National Health System. Its value lies in improving the clinical information workflow: doctors remain responsible for diagnosis and treatment, while the assistant helps surface relevant data faster and in a more usable form. The initiative also supports broader digital-health transformation by embedding AI directly into a national public-health platform rather than treating it as a separate experimental application.

title: Greek Government and Sword Health team up for AI-driven initiative
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Greece’s partnership with Sword Health uses AI to strengthen the national healthcare access pathway, starting from the National Health Information Line 1566. The initiative addresses a common public-health challenge: citizens often need guidance on where to seek care, which service to contact, or how to navigate the health system, while frontline teams face high volumes of routine and urgent enquiries. By integrating AI into triage and coordination processes, the programme aims to increase the capacity of the health information line, improve response times and provide more consistent support across the country. The AI layer is designed to work alongside healthcare professionals rather than replace them, absorbing repetitive and high-volume tasks, helping direct citizens towards appropriate services and giving health-system leaders better visibility over emerging needs. This is particularly relevant for a national system that must serve urban, rural and remote populations with different levels of access to healthcare resources. At operational level, the initiative creates an AI-enabled “front door” to healthcare: citizens can be guided more efficiently, hospitals can face lower avoidable pressure, and frontline staff can focus on cases requiring human judgement or clinical escalation. The wider ambition is to build a more responsive and resilient public-health access model that combines AI-based coordination with human care.

title: City of Częstochowa will become the first in Poland to begin using the Polish Large Language Model (PLLuM)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Local administrations process large volumes of routine text, including residents’ enquiries, official letters, reports, summaries and internal procedural materials. Częstochowa’s pilot use of PLLuM, the Polish Large Language Model, addresses the practical question of how a national language model can support municipal administration while preserving linguistic quality and public-sector control. The operational problem is that generic commercial AI models may not be optimised for Polish administrative language, legal terminology or public-sector workflows, while staff need safe tools that can help with repetitive drafting and analysis without replacing human judgement. Under a pilot with Poland’s Ministry of Digital Affairs, Częstochowa became the first city to use PLLuM in local administration. The model is intended to support officials in tasks such as drafting official correspondence, summarising long or complex documents, analysing residents’ requests and providing quick internal guidance. At a conceptual level, the system acts as a Polish-language productivity assistant adapted to public administration: it helps transform incoming or internal information into structured drafts and summaries, which staff can then review and approve. The expected impact is reduced processing time, improved consistency in written communication, faster analysis of citizen enquiries and better evidence on the practical value and limitations of national LLMs in government. The case is relevant because it tests generative AI in a real municipal setting while supporting a broader national objective: developing sovereign Polish-language AI capacity rather than relying only on foreign-language general-purpose tools.

title: Bilingual AI Chatbot and Mobile Robot
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Malta’s Life Events Robot provides AI-supported assistance for citizens dealing with major civil life events, including marriage, birth, divorce and other registration-related procedures. These services generate high volumes of recurring questions, and citizens often need clear guidance in both Maltese and English. The Life Events Robot addresses this challenge through a bilingual conversational assistant that combines retrieval-augmented generation, curated public-service information and natural-language interaction. The system retrieves relevant administrative and legal content from authoritative life-event datasets and presents it in a conversational format that is easier for users to understand than navigating multiple web pages or contacting a helpdesk. It also supports speech-to-text and text-to-speech functions, enabling voice-based interaction and improving accessibility for users who may find written digital services difficult to use. The mobile-robot component extends the same assistance into physical service environments, allowing citizens to receive on-site guidance through a Temi V3 robot in government service centres. At operational level, the solution reduces repetitive demand on staff, improves consistency of answers, supports 24/7 availability and creates a reusable platform that can later be extended to other public-service domains. Its bilingual design is particularly important in Malta’s administrative context, where digital public services must remain accessible in both national service languages.

title: Introduction of Microsoft 365 Copilot within the public sector
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Malta’s public-sector rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot introduces generative-AI productivity support across the administration to reduce routine workload and modernise daily work practices. The initiative responds to a common administrative challenge: public officers spend significant time drafting documents, summarising information, preparing communications, managing email and performing repetitive knowledge-work tasks that can be accelerated with AI support. Through a EUR 4 million investment, Microsoft 365 Copilot is being made available to more than 8,000 public officers over a two-year period, with direct deployment on employees’ laptops and structured training to support effective use. The initiative also includes a Centre of Excellence operated through collaboration between Microsoft, the Government and MITA, providing a hub for guidance, best practice, governance and innovation. A distinctive feature is the integration of Maltese-language support, enabling public officers to use Copilot across core Microsoft applications in Maltese as well as English. This improves accessibility, reinforces the use of Maltese in digital administration and supports language inclusion within the public-sector workforce. At operational level, Copilot assists with drafting, summarisation, document preparation and routine administrative work, while employees remain responsible for reviewing and validating outputs. The initiative is part of Malta’s broader digital-transformation agenda and is positioned as a workforce-empowerment measure rather than a replacement for public officials.

title: Mon parquet assistant - My assistant prosecutor
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Ministry of Justice, Paris Public Prosecutor's Office
source_description: Mon parquet assistant supports criminal-case processing in the courts under the Paris Court of Appeal by helping magistrates review, search and analyse procedural files more efficiently. Criminal files can be lengthy, heterogeneous and administratively demanding, particularly in high-volume proceedings where magistrates need to identify the nature of offences, locate relevant information and understand the structure of a case quickly. The tool is designed to allow users to upload one or more procedures, whether natively digital or scanned, into a dedicated interface. It then supports the detection of the offence types under investigation, offers a rapid view of the case by answering predefined questions linked to the relevant offence category, and enables deeper review by displaying source passages in a PDF reader and highlighting relevant sections. Users can also interrogate the procedure directly, making it easier to search through large files without manually reading every page in sequence. At operational level, the tool reduces repetitive, low-value document-handling tasks and gives magistrates faster access to the information needed for procedural analysis. It supports both overview and detailed review, while preserving the magistrate’s responsibility for legal assessment and prosecutorial decision-making. The initiative forms part of the Justice incubator approach to building practical digital tools around real professional workflows in the justice system.

title: SNCF’s AI Maintenance Scheduler Reduces Train Downtime by 45%
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Rail operators need to reduce unexpected failures, improve punctuality and use maintenance resources efficiently across large fleets and infrastructure assets. SNCF’s predictive-maintenance work addresses this challenge by using data and AI to detect technical problems before they become operational disruptions. The operational problem is that time-based maintenance can lead to two opposite inefficiencies: some components may be serviced too early, wasting parts and labour, while emerging faults may still be missed if they develop between scheduled inspections. SNCF’s official predictive-maintenance material describes the use of sensors and 4G/5G connectivity to collect train data and assess equipment in real time. The organisation reports being able to analyse thousands of train variables, including variables collected in real time, across more than 1,100 trains simultaneously. At a conceptual level, predictive maintenance converts rolling stock from a passive asset into a data-generating system: sensor streams, historical failure patterns and operating conditions are analysed to identify risks, prioritise interventions and plan maintenance before faults affect passengers or freight. The expected impact is improved reliability, fewer delays, better use of maintenance staff and parts, and reduced service disruption. The specific claim in the user-provided source that downtime was reduced by 45% should be treated cautiously because I found stronger official evidence for SNCF’s predictive-maintenance capability, but not an official confirmation of that precise figure in the available sources. The catalogue entry should therefore emphasise SNCF’s implemented predictive-maintenance programme without over-relying on unverified performance metrics.

title: Microsoft Copilot in Cyprus' Public Administration
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Ministry of Research, Innovation and Digital Policy
source_description: Cyprus is introducing Microsoft 365 Copilot across public administration to accelerate routine work, improve productivity and support the wider digital modernisation of government services. Public officials manage large volumes of written material, administrative data, reports and internal processes, much of which requires drafting, summarisation, analysis and coordination. Copilot provides an AI assistant integrated into the Microsoft 365 environment, enabling civil servants to draft reports, manage routine tasks, analyse large information sets and automate simple actions while remaining within the productivity tools already used by the administration. The first phase provides 350 user licences and dedicated training, ensuring that public servants can use the tool safely and effectively. The initiative also includes data-security considerations and is connected to a wider EUR 5 million “AI in Government” programme, which seeks to encourage AI-driven solutions for state challenges such as labour-market matching and climate response. At operational level, the rollout helps public officials complete repetitive knowledge-work tasks more quickly, freeing staff capacity for higher-value work and direct service improvement. At strategic level, it creates an initial public-sector user base for generative AI and helps the administration develop the skills, governance practices and organisational experience needed for broader AI integration across government.

title: MyMDT - My Medical Digital Twin
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Norwegian University of Science and Technology
source_description: MyMDT develops a personalised medical digital twin for hypertension, combining physiological modelling, machine learning, statistical methods, biosensor data and population-based research to support patient-specific prevention and treatment. Hypertension is a major public-health challenge because it contributes to heart failure, kidney disease, stroke, dementia and substantial healthcare costs, while ageing populations increase the demand for personalised and preventive care. MyMDT addresses this challenge by creating a “living” digital model of the patient that can evolve over time as new data become available. The platform integrates physiological simulations of cardiovascular function with machine-learning methods and data streams from sensors or wearable devices. It also draws on exercise physiology, cardiovascular modelling, biobanks and population studies, including NTNU’s research expertise in physical activity, arterial compliance and hypertension risk. At operational level, MyMDT is designed to support diagnostic, prognostic and treatment decisions by modelling how individual physiology and lifestyle factors interact. This can help identify prevention schemes, guide targeted data collection and support more personalised management of primary and secondary hypertension. At research level, the initiative brings together multiple disciplines—medicine, biomechanics, machine learning, statistics, biosensors and population health—to create a clinically meaningful digital-twin platform. The expected impact is better prevention, more personalised intervention, improved health outcomes and reduced healthcare costs for a common chronic condition.

title: HARMONIE project (Health Assessment Refinement for Mitigating Noise and Air Quality Effects)
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: HARMONIE uses digital twin technologies to help cities understand and reduce the health impacts of air and noise pollution. Urban pollution affects exposure, respiratory health, quality of life and environmental justice, but policymakers often lack tools that connect environmental monitoring, mobility behaviour, health indicators and long-term policy impacts. HARMONIE addresses this by combining real-world pilot studies with advanced digital simulations across five pilot cities: Barcelona, Lausanne, Sarajevo, Gävle and Barakaldo. The project collects data on air and noise pollution, including emerging indicators such as oxidative potential, and links them with citizen mobility patterns, exposure levels and health indicators, with attention to vulnerable groups. These data feed two complementary digital twins: a Lung Digital Twin, which models the interaction between pollutants and the human respiratory system, and a Citizen-Centric Digital Twin, which models exposure patterns and policy impacts at urban scale. The initiative gives policymakers a safer analytical environment for testing interventions before implementing them in the real city. Measures such as traffic restrictions, green infrastructure, behavioural interventions and urban redesign can be assessed for their environmental and health effects. HARMONIE’s added value lies in connecting environmental science, public health and digital modelling into a practical decision-support framework for cleaner, healthier and more equitable cities.

title: HARMONIE project: Lung Digital Twin
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Lung Digital Twin within HARMONIE focuses on the physiological effects of air pollution by modelling how inhaled pollutants move through and affect the human respiratory system. Air-quality policy often relies on ambient pollution measurements, but individual health risk depends on how pollutants enter the airways, where particles are deposited, how susceptible a person is and how exposure contributes to respiratory disease over time. The Lung Digital Twin addresses this gap by creating high-resolution simulations based on patient-specific geometries and detailed models of inhaled pollutants. It simulates airflow, particle transport and deposition inside the airways, helping researchers assess inhaled dose, susceptibility and health-impact pathways linked to oxidative stress. At operational level, the model connects environmental exposure data with physiological mechanisms, allowing health authorities and researchers to move beyond general pollution maps towards more precise understanding of respiratory risk. The Lung Digital Twin can support the assessment of how different pollutants affect vulnerable populations and how exposure-reduction policies may translate into health benefits. It also complements the urban-scale Citizen-Centric Digital Twin by adding a direct human-health layer to city-level environmental modelling. The expected impact is improved evidence on pollution-related respiratory risks, stronger prevention strategies, better-informed urban policy and more targeted protection for citizens most exposed or most biologically vulnerable to air pollution.

title: HARMONIE project: Citizen-centric Digital Twin
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The Citizen-Centric Digital Twin within HARMONIE models how people experience air and noise pollution across urban environments, linking environmental conditions with mobility patterns, social behaviour and health exposure. Cities need to understand not only where pollution is generated, but also where and how citizens encounter it during daily life. A street with high emissions may affect residents, commuters, pedestrians, schoolchildren or vulnerable groups differently depending on mobility routines, time of day, housing conditions and access to green or quieter spaces. The Citizen-Centric Digital Twin integrates pollution mapping, mobility information, social dynamics and exposure modelling to show how environmental burdens are distributed across urban populations. It enables “what-if” simulations in which policymakers can test measures such as traffic restrictions, green infrastructure, zoning changes or behavioural interventions before implementing them. At operational level, this allows local authorities to compare policy alternatives according to both environmental effectiveness and equity of health benefits. The twin also supports citizen engagement by making individual and collective contributions to pollution reduction more visible and understandable, including through personalised information and behavioural feedback mechanisms. The expected impact is more adaptive, community-driven and evidence-based urban policy, helping cities reduce exposure to harmful pollutants while improving liveability and fairness. The Citizen-Centric Digital Twin gives urban planners a practical way to connect environmental data with real human experience.

title: Compar:IA - the chatbot arena
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Generative AI models are increasingly used by citizens, professionals and public administrations, but many users rely on single systems without understanding differences in quality, bias, environmental footprint, language performance or cultural alignment. Compar:IA addresses this challenge by creating a public chatbot arena where users can compare two anonymised AI models, judge their answers and contribute to open preference datasets. The operational problem is that high-quality human preference data are scarce for French and other European languages, while AI literacy among citizens also needs to improve as generative AI becomes more common. The platform allows users to ask questions, interact with two anonymous models, vote on the preferred answer and later learn more about the models’ characteristics. These interactions generate anonymised preference data that can be published as open datasets and used to improve future models, especially for French and other European languages. At a conceptual level, Compar:IA combines public education, model evaluation and data collection in one interface: citizens learn not to trust one AI answer uncritically, while their feedback contributes to a shared resource for language-model improvement. The platform also highlights the environmental footprint of AI queries, adding an awareness dimension that goes beyond output quality. The expected impact is stronger AI literacy, better understanding of model differences, more open language-specific preference datasets and support for European digital sovereignty. The case is significant because it treats the public not only as AI users but also as contributors to model evaluation and linguistic diversity.

title: Daisy - an AI "granny"" that will waste scammers' time"
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Daisy is an AI-powered anti-fraud tool developed by Virgin Media O2 to disrupt phone scammers by keeping them engaged in long, unproductive conversations. Phone fraud often targets vulnerable people, particularly older citizens, by using social engineering, urgency and deception to extract money or personal information. Daisy reverses this dynamic by acting as a convincing potential victim who can absorb scammers’ time without exposing a real person to harm. The system combines several AI models that listen to callers and respond in real time, imitating the voice and conversational style of an elderly person. Daisy tells rambling stories, discusses family, knitting and everyday topics, and provides false or confusing information to keep fraudsters on the line. During testing, the AI was able to keep scammers engaged for up to 40 minutes, reducing the time they could spend contacting genuine victims. At operational level, Daisy functions as a scam-baiting and awareness tool rather than a conventional customer-service chatbot. Its role is not to investigate or prosecute fraud directly, but to waste criminal resources, expose scammer tactics and demonstrate how AI can be used defensively in consumer protection. The initiative also raises public awareness of fraud techniques, especially the manipulation methods used against older or vulnerable people. Its broader value lies in showing how conversational AI can be deployed creatively to protect citizens from social-engineering threats.

title: mAIGreece - the digital AI assistant for visitors
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Tourists often need fast and reliable information during travel, particularly on health services, emergency support, consular offices, police stations, museums, beaches and official visitor guidance. mAiGreece addresses this need by providing an AI-powered digital assistant for visitors to Greece, created by the Ministry of Tourism and the Ministry of Digital Governance. The operational problem is that travellers may not know which official source to consult, may face language barriers, or may need urgent information while moving through unfamiliar locations. The platform brings together information on hospitals, health centres, embassies and consulates, police stations, Blue Flag beaches, museums, content from Visit Greece and frequently asked questions. It also includes an important safety function: users can send an SMS with their geographical location to the Ministry of Civil Protection’s operations centre through the 112 emergency number, supporting rapid assistance where necessary. At a conceptual level, mAiGreece acts as a multilingual travel companion and official public-service gateway, combining AI-driven question handling with location-aware safety support. The system supports written or spoken natural-language questions and offers information in 31 languages, improving accessibility for a diverse international visitor base. The expected impact is a better visitor experience, easier access to official information, stronger tourist safety and improved coordination between tourism promotion and public-service guidance. The case is relevant because it shows AI being used not only for marketing, but also for practical visitor support and emergency-related information in a national tourism context.

title: AmigaAI - Chatbot for the legal sector
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: AmigaAI is an Austrian legal-AI initiative designed to improve access to legal information and increase the efficiency of legal workflows through a domain-specific large language model. Legal language is highly specialised, context-dependent and difficult for non-experts to understand, while legal professionals also spend considerable time searching, interpreting and structuring complex information. General-purpose AI models are not always suitable for this environment because they may fail to capture the nuances, terminology and legal context of Austrian law. AmigaAI addresses this by developing a legal-specific language model capable of understanding and interpreting Austrian legal language more accurately. The initiative is led by the Vienna-based legal-tech company GesetzeFinden.at and brings together an interdisciplinary consortium including the Psychological Faculty of Sigmund Freud Private University, CERHA HEMPEL and Fraunhofer Austria. The project combines legal expertise, psychological research on human-machine interaction and technology acceptance, and applied technical development. A distinctive feature is the “Society of Minds” approach, in which several AI chatbots communicate internally and collaborate on the answer before presenting a result to the user. This design aims to improve output quality while allowing the use of smaller and more resource-efficient models. At operational level, AmigaAI is intended to support both professionals and the wider public by making legal information easier to retrieve, understand and apply, while maintaining reliability, usability and alignment with European AI governance expectations.

title: JUANO - app to anonymise court decisions for publication on the justice internet portal
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Publishing court decisions improves transparency, legal certainty and access to justice, but it also requires careful protection of personal data. JUANO addresses this challenge by supporting the anonymisation of court decisions before they are made available on Luxembourg’s justice internet portal. The operational problem is that court judgments often contain names, addresses, personal identifiers and other sensitive details that must be removed or generalised consistently before publication. Manual anonymisation can be slow, repetitive and vulnerable to inconsistency, particularly when large volumes of decisions need to be processed. JUANO uses an artificial-intelligence engine to recognise entities that should be anonymised and to suggest categories based on the content of the text. At a conceptual level, the application functions as decision support for legal publishing: it identifies potentially sensitive elements, proposes how they should be treated and facilitates a more standardised anonymisation workflow. The expected impact is faster preparation of judgments for publication, more consistent data-protection practice, better access to case law for lawyers and interested parties, and stronger compliance with privacy requirements. The system should not be framed as replacing legal or judicial responsibility, because anonymisation in legal texts still requires careful validation and contextual judgement. Its value lies in reducing the burden of repetitive entity recognition and improving consistency across decisions. The case is relevant to digital justice because anonymisation tools are a practical prerequisite for expanding access to case law while respecting fundamental rights and data-protection obligations.

title: AI in Rectruitment Procedures

title: Assitance in drafting judgments JUAIDE
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Judicial drafting requires rapid access to legal texts, previous court decisions and accurate references while the judge is developing the reasoning of a decision. JUAIDE supports this work by integrating an artificial intelligence component into the drafting process for legal documents. The system analyses the context of the text being written in real time and identifies legal sources that may be relevant to the point under development. Instead of requiring the judge to interrupt drafting in order to conduct separate legal research, JUAIDE brings potentially applicable legal texts and case law directly into the workflow. This reduces the time spent searching for references, strengthens the accuracy of citations and helps ensure that judicial reasoning is supported by relevant legal material. At operational level, the tool acts as a drafting and research assistant: it does not replace judicial reasoning, but helps the judge identify and verify sources more efficiently while preparing legal documents. Its value lies in combining contextual analysis with immediate access to authoritative legal information, allowing drafting to become more fluid and better supported. The expected impact is faster preparation of judgments, improved quality of legal references, reduced repetitive research work and greater efficiency in the judicial process. The initiative is relevant for digital justice because it applies AI to a core professional task in a controlled way, preserving the judge’s responsibility while improving access to the legal materials needed for high-quality decision-writing.

title: UrbIA - AI for cadastral data
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Luxembourg’s cadastral data contain a long historical record of property information, including graphic materials such as cadastral plans and sketch maps and tabular records documenting changes in property rights. UrbIA supports the Land Registry and Topography Administration in making this historical information more usable by applying AI and data-interpretation methods to old handwritten cadastral registers. The operational challenge is that property-rights information from 1824 to 1972 was recorded manually in structured tables, creating a large archive that is valuable but difficult to exploit efficiently in modern digital workflows. Manual interpretation of these registers is time-consuming, specialist-dependent and not easily scalable across municipalities. UrbIA compares different technical approaches for interpreting selected registers in a given municipality, identifies the most effective method and then prepares implementation within the Administration. At operational level, the tool strengthens the digital transformation of cadastral management by converting historical handwritten information into data that can be searched, structured and reused more easily. The initiative helps preserve the continuity between historical land records and modern cadastral systems, improving access to information on property rights and supporting more efficient administrative processing. The expected impact is faster interpretation of historical registers, better integration of legacy cadastral data into contemporary systems, reduced manual workload and improved reliability of property-related public records. UrbIA is particularly relevant because it applies AI to a long-term institutional archive that remains essential for land administration, legal certainty and territorial information management.

title: "Iwwersetzungskorpus fir d'Lëtzebuergescht"" - multilingual parallel corpus "
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Zenter fir d'Lëtzebuerger Sprooch (ZLS – Centre for Luxembourgish Language)
source_description: High-quality machine translation and language AI depend on structured parallel datasets that show how the same content is expressed across different languages. Luxembourgish remains under-represented in such resources, creating barriers for translation technologies, language-model training and computational linguistics research. “Iwwersetzungskorpus fir d’Lëtzebuergescht” addresses this need by establishing a multilingual parallel corpus centred on Luxembourgish as the source language, with translations into German, French and English. The operational problem is that AI systems cannot provide reliable translation or language support for Luxembourgish unless they are trained on high-quality aligned texts that reflect real usage, terminology and linguistic variation. The corpus creates a reusable linguistic dataset that connects Luxembourgish with three major languages used in Luxembourg’s administrative, legal, educational and social environment. At operational level, the corpus provides the foundation for advanced machine translation, language-model training and multilingual public-service applications. It can also support researchers working on computational linguistics, language preservation and multilingual communication. The expected impact is improved digital treatment of Luxembourgish, better translation quality, stronger support for multilingual administration and greater inclusion of the national language in future AI systems. The initiative is particularly important because language technologies shape how citizens interact with public services, access information and participate in digital life. By building structured Luxembourgish-centred data, the project strengthens linguistic sovereignty and reduces dependence on datasets designed primarily for larger language markets.

title: AI Reader - enhancing the efficiency of data entry processes
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Commissariat aux affaires maritimes (CAM – Commission for Maritime Affairs)
source_description: Maritime administrations handle official documents that contain structured data needed for service delivery, verification and case management. AI Reader supports the Commissariat aux affaires maritimes by automating the extraction of predefined information from documents such as visas, whether they are submitted as text-based PDFs, image PDFs or JPEG files. The operational challenge is that customers and agents otherwise need to enter and verify data manually, creating delays, avoidable errors and repetitive administrative work. In the Seafarers’ service, this can affect the efficiency of document handling and the quality of information injected into administrative systems. AI Reader reads incoming documents, identifies the relevant fields and extracts the required information without manual intervention. At operational level, the tool reduces the amount of data that customers must provide directly, limits errors at the point of entry and reduces the need for later verification and correction by CAM agents. The extracted information can then be automatically integrated into the relevant internal systems, improving workflow continuity between document submission and case processing. The expected impact is faster handling of seafarer-related services, fewer data-entry mistakes, reduced administrative burden and a more streamlined user experience for applicants. The initiative is relevant because it applies AI to a common but important public-administration bottleneck: transforming unstructured or semi-structured documents into reliable data that can be reused in business processes. This type of document automation creates practical efficiency gains while preserving administrative control over final validation and service delivery.

title: AI4DI - AI-Powered Automation of Information Requests
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Data-protection authorities receive a wide range of information requests from citizens, organisations and professionals, often through multiple channels such as email, post and telephone. AI4DI supports the National Commission for Data Protection by automating the retrieval of relevant information and the preparation of draft responses for its Information Requests service. The operational challenge is that, as the number of questions and answers grows, staff need to search through existing databases and previous responses manually, which can be time-consuming and may slow down the delivery of consistent guidance. AI4DI uses a large language model-based tool to identify relevant information in the existing knowledge base and produce an initial draft response that staff can review. At operational level, the system acts as a knowledge-retrieval and drafting assistant: it accelerates the first stage of response preparation while leaving final validation and responsibility with CNPD staff. This is particularly useful in a field such as data protection, where many questions recur but must still be answered accurately and in line with current rules and institutional positions. The expected impact is shorter response preparation time, greater consistency across replies, better reuse of accumulated institutional knowledge and improved service capacity for citizens and organisations seeking guidance. The initiative is relevant because it applies AI to a regulatory authority’s public-information function, helping manage growing demand while maintaining human oversight in a legally sensitive domain.

title: Legal and normative text analyser
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Luxembourg Office of Accreditation and Surveillance (OLAS)
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Accreditation bodies must work with complex and frequently updated legal, technical and normative materials, including national laws, EU law, international standards and accreditation requirements. The Legal and Normative Text Analyser supports the Luxembourg Office of Accreditation and Surveillance by automating parts of this documentation analysis. The operational challenge is that OLAS needs to identify, collect and interpret relevant documents from recognised sources such as Legilux, EUR-Lex, ISO, CEN, EA, ILAC and IAF, as well as locally stored files, in order to determine applicable requirements for the accreditation of specific activities. Manual review can be time-consuming and requires specialist knowledge across multiple sources and standards. The tool analyses reliable databases and local files, identifies relevant documents or information demonstrating compliance, extracts applicable requirements and generates detailed reports based on the results. At operational level, it functions as a regulatory and normative intelligence assistant for accreditation workflows. It helps staff move more quickly from a broad documentation search to a structured understanding of which requirements apply to a conformity assessment body or activity. The expected impact is faster accreditation preparation, more consistent identification of applicable requirements, reduced manual effort and improved traceability in the analysis of legal and normative sources. The initiative is relevant because it applies AI to a highly specialised compliance function where reliability, source quality and structured reporting are essential for institutional credibility and for the proper supervision of accredited activities.

title: ScreenreaderLB - AI-Powered Luxembourgish Accessibility for the Visually Impaired
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: The ScreenreaderLB solution, developed by the Government Information and Press Service, addresses the increasing need for accessible content in Luxembourgish for visually impaired users. Currently, the absence of speech synthesis technology for this language requires blind or visually impaired individuals to rely on screen readers in German or other languages. ScreenreaderLB aims to create a screen reader specifically for Luxembourgish, providing smooth and accurate speech synthesis to allow visually impaired users to interact more effectively with digital content, enhancing both their browsing experience and access to information.

title: Digitalising key administrative processes using blockchain technology in the Municipality of Chieti
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Municipal social-service procedures often involve sensitive information, repeated documentation and several administrative steps, making transparency, data integrity and processing times particularly important for citizens. The Municipality of Chieti use case applies blockchain technology to selected administrative processes in order to strengthen traceability, automate parts of the workflow and improve trust in the handling of citizens’ information. The operational problem is that many social-service files require the municipality to verify eligibility, manage documentation and preserve the chronology of procedural steps, while also respecting privacy rules and avoiding unnecessary repeated requests for the same data. The project, supported by Mangrovia Blockchain Solutions and A Software Factory, integrates a distributed ledger into the management of specific municipal practices. Initial experimental processes included maternity allowances, elderly home-care access, transport services for persons with disabilities, socio-health contribution requests for residential care, educational home-care support for sensory disabilities and home-care services for disabled persons. At a conceptual level, blockchain is used as an administrative integrity layer: it certifies data ownership, chronology and process steps, while smart contracts can support secure automation and the “once only” principle. The expected impact is greater transparency, reduced manipulation risk, faster handling of socially relevant files and a stronger basis for extending similar traceability to procurement and accounts-payable workflows. The case is significant because it applies blockchain to ordinary municipal administration, not only to financial or experimental digital-asset use cases.

title: Blockchain Pilot for Transparent Food Redistribution in Cosenza
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Food redistribution programmes need to connect supermarkets, charities, municipal welfare services and vulnerable households in a way that is efficient, transparent and credible for all participants. The Cosenza pilot applies blockchain technology to the reuse of near-expiry food stocks from large-scale retail distribution, with the aim of reducing waste and increasing the resources available to families in need. The operational problem is that surplus food redistribution involves several actors and incentives: retailers need confidence that donations are properly certified, charities need reliable information on available goods, and public authorities need visibility over social needs and the actual destination of donated products. The project was launched by the Municipality of Cosenza with NTT DATA, the University of Calabria and Banco Alimentare. The University of Calabria contributed a mathematical model to support the platform, including the calculation of rewards for donating businesses according to the characteristics of the products and the social benefit generated. Blockchain is used to certify donations, preserve traceability and ensure data immutability across the redistribution chain. At a conceptual level, the system transforms food donation into a verifiable welfare process: goods approaching expiry can be recorded, assigned, rewarded and distributed with greater transparency. The expected impact is lower food waste, greater availability of goods for non-profit organisations, clearer evidence on local social needs and stronger incentives for businesses to participate in solidarity-based redistribution. The case is relevant because it connects blockchain with welfare policy and circular economy objectives.

title: Italy’s First Green Blockchain Municipality
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Small municipalities with renewable-energy assets often face the challenge of making local infrastructure financially sustainable while complying with rules that limit direct self-consumption of municipally generated energy. Borgo d’Anaunia, a municipality of around 2,500 residents in northern Italy, addressed this challenge by converting part of the output of its municipal hydroelectric plant into computational power for blockchain operations. The operational problem was economic as well as technological: the century-old hydroelectric plant depended on variable water flow, electricity prices were relatively low, and fixed maintenance costs reduced the plant’s value for the municipality. By partnering with Alps Blockchain, the municipality installed mining equipment powered by renewable hydroelectric energy, allowing part of the plant’s output to be monetised as computational power rather than only as electricity sold to the grid. At a conceptual level, the project treats blockchain mining as a local revenue-generating service connected to renewable energy production. The system is designed to remain adaptable to hydrological conditions: when water flow is insufficient, the mining equipment can be switched off, while the remaining energy continues to be sold through conventional channels. The expected impact is higher revenue from an existing public asset, experimentation with more sustainable blockchain operations and a new model for small municipalities seeking to valorise renewable-energy infrastructure. The case is significant because it links blockchain with local public finance and renewable energy, although its primary purpose is municipal revenue generation rather than direct citizen-service delivery.

title: Blockchain for waste management
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Waste-management systems require accurate data on how much waste households produce and how correctly they separate recyclable fractions, especially where municipalities want to apply “polluter pays” principles or reward responsible behaviour. Miglianico, a municipality in the province of Chieti, introduced a blockchain-enhanced waste-management system built around RFID-tagged bins and certified tracking of individual waste contributions. The operational problem was to make waste collection more transparent, measurable and fair, while also reducing costs and encouraging citizens to separate waste properly. The municipality had already adopted an RFID-based system that allowed collection operators to identify bins and measure contributions. Blockchain was then added to certify the resulting data, making records more secure, immutable and auditable. At a conceptual level, the system creates a trusted data layer for timely waste charging and behavioural incentives: each household’s waste contributions can be associated with certified records, supporting more accurate tax calculation, management control and feedback on abnormal waste patterns. The reported results were substantial: separate collection reached nearly 85%, waste-collection expenditure fell from around €900,000 to around €660,000, and virtuous citizens reportedly benefited from savings and rewards. The expected impact is lower municipal expenditure, higher recycling performance, more transparent waste taxation and greater citizen engagement in circular-economy practices. The case is relevant because it demonstrates blockchain as an integrity mechanism for local public-service data, integrated with RFID and incentive-based waste policy rather than used as a stand-alone technology.

title: Blockchain-based platform for sustainable tourism and local commerce in mountain communities
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: BLOCCHI is a blockchain-based platform developed by the University of Turin to promote sustainable tourism and local commerce in mountain communities. Integrating blockchain with an interactive map (FirstLife), it enables tokenisation to create incentives, loyalty programs, and rewards for visiting lesser-known locations and purchasing local products. Using the CommonsHood wallet app, tourists can collect tokens, redeem coupons via QR codes, and earn badges for completing circuits of local businesses. Local businesses and municipalities can create promotional coupons and track engagement. The project is part of NODES, funded by Italy’s PNRR and the EU, aiming to strengthen innovation ecosystems and local leadership in research and development.

title: Blockchain for smart working
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Public administrations that introduce smart working need to manage flexible work arrangements while ensuring accountability, data protection, traceability and continuity of service delivery. The Municipality of Bari smart-working pilot, developed with Fincons Group under the EU-funded H2020 CITADEL initiative, applied blockchain technology to support secure and transparent management of agile work by municipal employees. The operational problem was that smart working requires new forms of performance monitoring and organisational control: employees may work partly from offices and partly remotely, with flexible time arrangements, but the administration still needs reliable evidence of work processes, security of information and compliance with GDPR. The project envisaged a prototype using Ethereum distributed-ledger technology combined with advanced encryption techniques. At a conceptual level, blockchain is used as a trust and traceability layer for work-related data, certifying information flows and preserving integrity without compromising privacy. The pilot also reflects a wider shift in public administration towards more citizen-centred, inclusive and efficient digital services, because internal working models influence the quality and continuity of services offered to users. The expected impact is improved organisational flexibility, better employee work-life balance, secure data handling, more efficient administrative processes and a practical demonstration of innovative ICT adoption in local government. The case is relevant because it applies blockchain to internal public-administration work organisation, rather than to external registries or citizen-facing payments.

title: PROMPT - Narrative Intelligence for Information Integrity
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Disinformation campaigns increasingly rely on recurring narratives, rhetorical patterns and coordinated circulation across media outlets, social platforms and online knowledge spaces. PROMPT, or Predictive Research On Misinformation & Propagation Trajectories, addresses this problem by developing AI-supported narrative intelligence for information integrity. The operational challenge is that fact-checking individual claims is necessary but insufficient when manipulative campaigns spread through broader stories, frames and emotional patterns that can reappear across languages and platforms. PROMPT analyses large volumes of textual data to identify malicious or manipulative narratives, focusing on case studies such as the war in Ukraine, LGBTQI+ rights and the 2024 European elections. The project combines large language models with dynamic network analysis to detect formal patterns across media outlets, social networks and Wikipedia in eight languages. At a conceptual level, the system moves from isolated content detection to narrative mapping: it seeks to understand how misleading stories are structured, how they travel, which actors amplify them and why they resonate with audiences. Outputs include a refined language model, a narrative-monitoring dashboard and training material for civil-society actors. The expected impact is stronger disinformation analysis, better support for journalists and fact-checkers, earlier recognition of manipulation strategies and improved public understanding of information threats. The case is significant because it applies AI to democratic resilience while preserving the analytical role of journalists, researchers and civil-society organisations.

title: Provinc.IA: a provincial AI governance and pilot framework for trustworthy, reusable and interoperable AI adoption in local governments
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Diputación Provincial de Castellón / Provincial Council of Castellón
source_description: Provinc.IA is the Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Provincial Council of Castellón, Spain. It provides a provincial governance and pilot framework to help small and medium-sized municipalities adopt AI in a trustworthy, legally sound, useful and reusable way. The case addresses a structural public sector challenge: many local governments lack the technical, organisational and legal capacity to deploy AI safely. Provinc.IA combines strategic planning, multi-level governance, stakeholder mapping, ethical and legal safeguards, pilot projects, monitoring mechanisms and capacity-building. Its aim is to make AI adoption feasible for local administrations with limited resources, while supporting better services, administrative innovation and evidence-informed policy-making across the province.

title: AI-powered virtual assistant for payments
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Turin and the Piedmont Region are positioning the city as a European laboratory for autonomous urban mobility, combining the region’s automotive heritage, research capacity and urban infrastructure with AI-enabled transport experimentation. The initiative responds to the challenge of moving autonomous-driving technologies from controlled environments into real public-service mobility settings. Turin’s candidacy aims to secure a formal role within the European network of pilot cities for autonomous driving, with the ambition of testing driverless public mobility services such as taxis or shuttles on public roads. The city’s ecosystem provides strong enabling conditions, including the Politecnico di Torino, an established automotive supply chain, existing innovation infrastructure and previous experimentation around the university campus area. AI models are expected to support real-world testing by monitoring vehicle flows and helping analyse traffic conditions during trials. At operational level, the initiative would allow public authorities, researchers and industry actors to test autonomous vehicles in an urban environment where safety, service quality and interaction with ordinary traffic can be assessed under realistic conditions. The expected impact is stronger European leadership in autonomous mobility, attraction of investment, development of local expertise and creation of a model for AI-supported public transport innovation. The initiative also connects transport innovation with broader regional industrial policy, using Turin’s automotive strengths to support the transition towards software-defined, AI-enabled and service-oriented mobility.

title: Sof-IA: management of online medical appointments
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
source_description: Patients looking for healthcare appointments often know their symptoms, preferences and constraints, but not the exact specialist, service or search criteria they should select on a booking platform. Sof-IA, developed by iDoctors, addresses this problem by using artificial intelligence to make the search for a suitable medical specialist faster and more personalised. The operational problem is that conventional search filters require users to know how to translate their need into a speciality, procedure, location, cost range or availability window. Sof-IA allows users to describe their request in natural language, including symptoms, location, preferred time, budget and other practical needs, and then returns specialists matching those criteria. For example, a user can ask for a dermatologist in a specific area, a gynaecologist available at a certain time, or a doctor within a maximum price range. At a conceptual level, the system acts as a natural-language interpretation layer above the iDoctors search engine: it analyses the patient’s request, extracts relevant constraints and maps them to structured search results. Importantly, iDoctors states that Sof-IA is not designed to provide diagnoses or recommend treatments, but only to help users identify the specialist they need. The expected impact is easier appointment search, better matching between patient needs and available professionals, reduced friction for users unfamiliar with medical terminology and a more accessible digital healthcare booking experience. The case is relevant because it applies AI to navigation and matching in healthcare, while explicitly limiting the system’s role to search support rather than clinical decision-making.

title: Saro: AI-powered educational digital assistant
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
organization: Romanian Ministry of Education and Research
source_description: Saro is an AI-powered educational assistant designed to support pupils, students and teachers in Romania by improving learning engagement, motivation and administrative efficiency. The initiative addresses a major challenge in education systems: learners often need personalised feedback and encouragement, while teachers and institutions face growing demands for monitoring progress, supporting different learning needs and reducing bureaucratic workload. Saro uses artificial intelligence to provide personalised support, motivational analysis and guidance on learning tasks. Its role is to help students remain engaged, complete assignments and receive assistance that is adapted to their learning path, while also supporting teachers in understanding where additional intervention may be needed. At operational level, the assistant can help structure learning objectives, provide feedback, identify patterns of reduced engagement and support more continuous interaction between students and educational institutions. It is introduced through a partnership between Digital Nation and the Romanian Ministry of Education and Research, building on Digital Nation’s broader experience in digital skills programmes for students, teachers, SMEs and adult learners. The expected impact is stronger student motivation, improved assignment completion, reduced risk of dropout, more personalised educational support and less administrative pressure on teachers. The initiative is relevant because it embeds AI into the national education system as a practical support layer for both learning and institutional management. It also reflects a wider move towards AI-assisted education in Romania, where digital tools are used not only for content delivery but also for engagement, retention and learner success.

title: Similis: for the identification of similar and identical amendments
source_attribution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (2026), PSTW: Public Sector Tech Watch latest dataset of selected cases, doi:10.2905/JRC.J1MWC9R; September 2026 snapshot. Fields selected and normalized; no endorsement implied.
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Parliamentary amendment procedures can generate very large numbers of texts, many of which are identical or highly similar. This creates a practical burden for legislative offices, committees and parliamentary staff who must organise, compare and process amendments efficiently. Similis was developed by the IT Department of the Italian Senate in collaboration with the Institute of Legal Informatics and Judicial Systems of the National Research Council to calculate similarity between Senate amendments. The operational problem is that duplicate or near-duplicate amendments can slow legislative analysis, make debates harder to organise and reduce the transparency of the amendment-review process. Similis addresses this by automatically comparing amendment texts and grouping those with similar wording. The system is oriented towards syntactic similarity rather than full semantic interpretation, meaning that it is particularly useful for identifying amendments with similar structure, vocabulary and phrasing. At a conceptual level, each amendment is represented computationally and compared against others so that clusters of similar texts can be identified. The GitHub repository indicates that the tool can be invoked either through a REST interface or from the command line using a JSON file containing amendments. The expected impact is more efficient parliamentary document management, faster identification of duplicated proposals, better organisation of legislative work and support for transparency in amendment handling. The case is relevant because it demonstrates a focused, explainable and open-source digital tool for legislative support, rather than a broad autonomous AI system.
